text:
The founder of America's most famous Black town gave away a hundred and twenty-three thousand Black votes to keep it. His name was Isaiah Montgomery, he was the only Black delegate in that Jackson hall in 1890, and Frederick Douglass called it treason four months later.

Every viral post about Mound Bayou leaves this part out, which means the whole thing has been handed to you backward. Go find out what the man actually said that day, because it is not what you think.

One man wanted his town left alone. To get it he stood up in a hall in Jackson in the summer of 1890 and offered Mississippi the ballots of a hundred and twenty-three thousand Black men.

He was the only Black delegate in the room. He was also the founder of Mound Bayou.

Three years before that, in the fall of 1887, Isaiah Montgomery had walked a small group of men off a train into a stand of hardwood in Bolivar County. Booker T. Washington wrote down what happened next and published it in 1907.

Montgomery waved a hand toward the trees. This is a pretty wild place, he told them.

The men looked where he was pointing and said nothing.

But this whole country was like this once, he went on. You have seen it change, and you and your fathers performed most of the work that made it what it is.

Then the line that ends the scene in Washington's telling. You and your fathers did this for some one else, he said, so can't you do as much now for yourselves?

The men picked up their axes and went at the wilderness.

That is where the retellings stop. The next five years cost more than anybody puts in a caption.

Fewer than seventy-five acres of the tract could be planted. The rest was cane and hardwood so thick a man went through it with a hatchet.

Swamp fever got some of them. There were bears and panthers in the timber, so men stood watch while other men cut.

Simon Gaiter arrived with a hundred and seventy-five dollars. That was every cent he had in the world, and after he paid for his land and his provisions he had ten dollars left.

For years the settlement lived off what it chopped down. They sold the timber as cross ties and staves to the same railroad that held their notes.

Some sharecropped on the side to stay afloat. Some sent their wives and children out to pick cotton for white planters and clean white people's houses, which is how they kept the wolf from the door.

At the end of five years a good many of them still owed the railroad money. Montgomery was one of them.

On the twelfth of August, 1890, one hundred and thirty-four men sat down in a Jackson hall in the deep of a Mississippi summer to write the state a new constitution.

The convention president, S. S. Calhoon, had already said out loud what the body was for. They had come to exclude the Negro, he said, and nothing short of that would answer.

A white delegate from Jasper County named Marsh Cook had run on Black voting rights. He was killed on a country road, riding alone, before he could take his seat.

Judge J. J. Chrisman sat in that hall and said out loud that there had not been a full vote and a fair count in Mississippi since 1875. He is also on record crying out whether there was to be no higher ambition for the young white men of the South than keeping the Negro down.

His name went on the finished document.

Montgomery was forty-three. He weighed maybe a hundred and thirty-five pounds, and they had seated him on the franchise committee, the one holding the pen.

He spoke for about an hour. The phrase he used was that he was laying the suffrage of his fellow men at the feet of this convention.

Give the vote only to men who can read, he argued, and call them the stable and prudent element among the citizens. He knew better than any man in that room whose fathers had been forbidden by law to learn their letters.

His reasoning was not stupid and it was not sudden. The ballot in Mississippi had already been taken by fraud and by gunfire, and he believed trading a right nobody was permitted to use might buy his people a generation of quiet.

Two weeks later he told a northern newspaper it did not wholly suit him. It was the best that could be done, he said, and they had to take the best they could get.

The New York World printed the address that September.

In October, Frederick Douglass stood up at Metropolitan African Methodist Episcopal Church in Washington and called it treason to the cause of the colored people. He also said he had heard inside it a groan of bitter anguish, and the voice of a soul from which all hope had gone.

Both of those things were true at the same time. Douglass was old enough to hold them together.

Mound Bayou got what it was bought for.

The town incorporated in 1898 with about a hundred and eighty registered voters, in a state where walking up to a registrar could get a Black man killed. It got a bank in 1904, three cotton gins, a sawmill, a train station and its own schools.

Its Carnegie library was the one institution in town that white people ran. That part never makes the posts.

Theodore Roosevelt had his train stopped there. From the platform he called it an object lesson full of hope for the colored people and therefore full of hope for the white people, too.

Booker T. Washington came in November 1912 to open the cottonseed oil mill. Delta families had bought into it at a dollar a share.

Outside the town line the arithmetic ran the other way. By the 1892 elections the new registration lists in Mississippi carried about seventy thousand white voters and about nine thousand Black ones.

Something like fifty-two thousand white men lost the vote as well. Black registration fell from better than nine in ten voting-age men during Reconstruction to fewer than six in a hundred.

Then cotton prices dropped and the shelter started leaking. State examiners closed the Bank of Mound Bayou in 1914.

To rescue the oil mill the town brought in Benjamin B. Harvey, a white cotton man out of Memphis who was to lease the plant and keep up the bond payments. He took the money, and the mill stood empty for years.

The dollar shares went with it.

Montgomery lived another thirty-four years and never took back a word of the speech in public. In a private letter to Booker T. Washington he admitted what he had worked out.

The men talking about pure government wanted Black Mississippians pushed back toward serfdom. Nothing short of federal force was going to stop them.

He died in March 1924. A white planter and politician named Walter Sillers gave the eulogy.

The tomb they laid him in was paid for by a subscription taken up among white men.

A missionary passing through wrote that no Black Mississippian was hated by Black people more than he was. The men who collected for that tomb were the only ones who ever got what they came for.

The town did not go into the ground with him.

A fire tore through the business district in the early 1940s and took most of what was left of the storefronts. The next thing built on that ground was a hospital.

In 1942 the Knights and Daughters of Tabor opened a forty-two bed hospital on the highway. Twenty-five thousand members, most of them sharecroppers, had paid for it out of their own assessments.

Perry M. Smith had gone plantation to plantation collecting it a little at a time.

By 1944, dues of eight dollars and forty cents a year bought a member thirty-one days of care, surgery included. Every doctor and every nurse in that building was Black, and a Black patient walked in the front door and was seen.

Between 1942 and 1964 that hospital treated more than a hundred and thirty-five thousand people.

In 1951 its chief surgeon, T. R. M. Howard, started the Regional Council of Negro Leadership in Mound Bayou. The next year a young insurance salesman named Medgar Evers moved to town to work for him.

The council's rallies pulled ten thousand people into a town of a couple thousand. Myrlie Evers described them as an all-day camp meeting, part pep rally, part revival, part Sunday church picnic.

Fannie Lou Hamer sat in those crowds, and so did Amzie Moore and Aaron Henry. They ran voter registration drives out of the one town in Mississippi whose founder had helped write the rules against them.

The town was carrying a higher NAACP membership, measured against its Black population, than anywhere else in Mississippi, and the bargain had been meant to keep it quiet.

In September 1955 Howard's house on the edge of town filled with people who could not safely close their eyes anywhere else in Mississippi. Emmett Till's mother slept there, and so did Congressman Charles Diggs, the Black reporters covering the trial, and the witnesses.

Armed guards worked the property around the clock and the house was full of weapons. Mississippi would not issue a Black man a permit to carry, so Howard drove with a pistol in a compartment built into his car.

More than once that year he was carried out of a meeting inside a casket, because a hearse was the one vehicle nobody stopped and searched.

At night Howard and Medgar Evers and the Black press went out on the county roads looking for people who had seen something. In the courthouse at Sumner the sheriff greeted those same reporters every morning with a slur.

After the first day of the trial they gathered in Howard's front room. Medgar Evers was there, and Ruby Hurley of the NAACP, and three newspapermen named James Hicks, L. Alex Wilson and Simeon Booker.

The reporters wanted to run what they had that night. Howard made them sit on it until the witnesses were somewhere safe.

One of those witnesses was an eighteen-year-old named Willie Reed.

He was a sharecropper's grandson out of Drew. He had watched two white men drive a boy into a barn on the Milam place, and he had heard what went on inside it.

One of those men had already come and stood in front of him and asked whether he had seen anything. No, sir, he said.

Did you hear anything, boy. No, sir.

On the morning of the twenty-second he walked out of Howard's house, rode the forty-two miles to Sumner, went through the crowd at the courthouse door and named J. W. Milam and Roy Bryant out loud in a Mississippi courtroom.

The jury took sixty-seven minutes. He was moved out of the state within days.

Ten years after that, the money came from a direction nobody in 1890 could have imagined.

In 1965 a doctor named Jack Geiger got federal War on Poverty funding to build two community health centers, one in Boston and one in the Delta. He put the Delta one in Mound Bayou, and it opened its doors to patients in 1967.

It was the first rural community health center in the United States. The federally funded community health center system this country runs on traces back to that clinic and its sister project in Boston.

The staff dug wells. They set pumps, built privies, cut drainage ditches and screened people's windows, because in the Delta the water and the flies were the disease.

Then Geiger started writing prescriptions for meat, milk, vegetables and fruit. People filled them at the grocery store, and the grocers sent the bills to the health center.

He paid them out of the pharmacy budget.

Washington sent a man down to tell him he could not buy groceries with health center money. Geiger told him that the last time he looked in his textbooks, the specific therapy for malnutrition was food.

Two Black farmers in Mound Bayou donated land, and the center turned it into a four hundred and twenty-seven acre cooperative farm.

John Hatch, who helped build it, put it plainly. These were people sitting on top of the richest soil in the nation, going hungry, who already knew how to grow food.

The woman they put in charge of those acres was named L. C. Dorsey. She had grown up on a Delta plantation picking other people's cotton, and she would end up running the whole health center from 1988 to 1995.

She said later that it was not a plantation named Tufts you were working for. This was your land.

Isaiah Montgomery had stood in a forest in 1887 and asked a handful of men whether they could do for themselves what their fathers had done for somebody else. Eighty years later he got his answer.

A hundred and twenty-three thousand ballots laid at the feet of a convention in 1890. A hundred and thirty-five thousand Delta patients through the doors of the Taborian between 1942 and 1964.

The record kept Isaiah Montgomery. It lost nearly every man who swung an axe at that forest.

What few names it did hold onto, like Simon Gaiter and his ten dollars, sit in books almost nobody opens.

So when Mound Bayou comes across your feed as a miracle in the swamp, put those men in the sentence with him. The founder made the deal, and they paid the bill for it in blisters and swamp fever and other people's cotton.

The Taborian is shuttered. Montgomery's house stands empty with the foundation cracked, and the town is down around fifteen hundred people.

On the far south side of Chicago, sometime in the early seventies, an orderly and a nurse's aide lifted a patient onto a gurney.

The orderly asked her for a kiss. She walked around to the other side of the bed and kissed him on the jaw.

His name was Willie Louis, which was not the name he was born with. He had been eighteen the last night he slept in Mound Bayou, and he had not said the other name out loud since.

**1. The NBA just made Kalshi and Polymarket its official prediction market partners**
The league named both exchanges its preferred partners on Oct. 26, signed an MOU with the CFTC, and won the right to approve which NBA markets they can offer, with official Sportradar data settling the trades. The leagues spent years fighting these markets in court. Now they are charging rent and calling it integrity, and every other league is watching the price they got.

https://t.co/dduQPmk8xA

**2. Jefferies says the casino stock trade is now about efficiency, not size**
Wynn is projected at $180,000 in EBITDA per Las Vegas room this year, against $83,000 for Caesars and $77,000 for MGM. The Strip is a hospitality business with a casino attached now, not the other way around, and the operator with fewer rooms and richer guests is winning the math.

https://t.co/I0M7XQYUsi

**3. The Venetian is the first major Strip poker room to switch to slide dealing**
Cards stay on the felt instead of being pitched, cutting the angles for peeking and hidden cameras, and MGM says it is exploring the same move across its poker rooms. Game protection used to be a surveillance job. Now it is a dealing procedure, and the rooms that move first get to set the new standard.

https://t.co/YFPFXY7v07

**4. Ted Cruz is planning a state-oversight bill for prediction markets**
The Texas senator plans to introduce legislation after the November midterms giving states authority over event contracts, a direct challenge to the CFTC's federal oversight that the White House backs. The NBA deal today and a Senate bill next month are the same fight from opposite ends: who gets to regulate the new sportsbook, Washington or the states.

https://t.co/If13V1dTmW

Regulus puts an 80% chance on a long limbo where the provisional ban lapses but expired operator licences are never restored, leaving the black market to fill the gap. Licensed sites went dark Oct. 6. When regulators kill a legal market without a replacement, the players do not quit. They just stop paying taxes.

Alcohol sales stopped Oct. 23 at the off-Strip property, with no official explanation and staff theories ranging from an insurance lapse to tax or licensing trouble. A casino without a bar next to a future ballpark site is a strange look. The last dry spell lasted about 10 days, and the clock is running again.

text:
State regulatory and legislative groups urge Treasury to expand stablecoin safe harbors to issuers under state regimes
GENIUS Act’s limits on payment stablecoin issuance and on the offer and sale of payment stablecoins by digital asset service providers (previously covered by InfoBytes here). The groups urged Treasury to create safe harbors that let issuers operate under qualifying state regimes as of the act’s effective date. They said this would carry out “the GENIUS Act’s clear intent to preserve an important role for state regulation of payment stablecoin issuers.” They noted that the proposal already includes a safe harbor for issuers seeking federal approval as of the effective date.

Under the GENIUS Act, a state regulator certifies that its regime is “substantially similar” to the federal framework, and the Stablecoin Certification Review Committee then reviews that certification under a different standard, namely whether the state regime meets or exceeds the act’s federal requirements. The groups said the time between a state’s certification and the committee’s approval creates uncertainty and, because federal applicants already have a safe harbor, the gap could also push issuers toward OCC approval even if they would prefer a state regulator. They asked for a safe harbor covering issuers under certified but not yet approved state regimes, including the 180-day period a state has to fix its certification after a denial. They also said most of the relevant implementing rules remain unfinished, even though the statute required them by July 18.

The groups asked for a second safe harbor, with conditions, for issuers waiting on states that have filed a conditional certification with the committee. It would apply where the state expects to submit a final certification by January 18, 2028, and the issuer meets GENIUS Act requirements and the state’s existing stablecoin rules. The state would also have to let the issuer keep issuing while it finalizes its regime. The protection would end if the state indicates it will not submit a certification by that date. The letter also requested another safe harbor for issuers in states whose annual recertification the committee denies after a material change to the state’s framework. Without that protection, the groups warned, states could be locked into their originally certified regimes, which could hold back new business models. Finally, the groups asked Treasury to state in the final rule that the GENIUS Act does not set up a comprehensive regulatory framework for digital asset service providers, and that state laws still apply to them. https://t.co/nJQ3xnNQQv

It houses ambassador gray wolves (currently including ones like Nikai, Silas, and Kinari) that help teach the public, plus critically endangered Mexican gray wolves and red wolves involved in captive breeding and reintroduction efforts. text:
One day after the Constitutional Convention ended, Thomas Jefferson wrote a letter from Paris. Now it’s being offered for sale with three inscribed books at an asking price of $285,000.

The nearly 700-word letter is dated Sept. 18, 1787. The young United States was struggling under the Articles of Confederation, and leaders from 12 of the 13 states had just met in Philadelphia to consider the nation’s future.

Writing to his close friend, scientist David Rittenhouse, Jefferson said America should focus on peace, paying its debts, improving its constitutions, and expanding agriculture.

He also addressed unrest in Europe, the Middle East, and Russia.

The timing mattered. The Russo-Turkish War had begun about a month earlier, and Jefferson feared a wider war could follow. He hoped the United States could stay out of it.

The letter comes with a three-volume set of Antoine-François de Fourcroy’s Elements of Natural History and Chemistry, also inscribed by Jefferson.

The books were sent to James Madison, who was to deliver them to Rittenhouse, later director of the U.S. Mint.

The collection was displayed at Texas A&M International University from 2008 to 2026 on loan from a private collector in Texas. The owner decided to sell everything together rather than divide it, and the Raab Collection calls it the most unique piece of Jeffersonian history it has acquired in nearly 40 years.

In the 250th anniversary year of the Declaration of Independence, the collection offers a rare look at Jefferson’s priorities for the young nation and at the dangers he hoped America could avoid.

The Constitutional Convention had ended just a day earlier, but Jefferson was already thinking about how the young nation could avoid being drawn into war.

text:
Southwest prices $1.25 billion in senior notes

Southwest Airlines Co. announced on October 26, 2026, that it had set the terms for an underwritten public offering of senior notes totaling $1,250,000,000 in aggregate principal. (The company’s announcement establishes the offering’s stated size, not that it has already closed.) The total is split into $600,000,000 of 5.750% notes maturing in 2029 and $650,000,000 of 6.000% notes maturing in 2031. (The 2031 tranche has more principal and a higher stated coupon than the 2029 tranche.) Together, those two principal amounts make up the full $1,250,000,000 offering, with the 2031 notes accounting for the larger share and the 2029 notes for the smaller share. (This compares the principal assigned to each tranche, not the amount of interest the company will ultimately pay.) Southwest says it expects to direct the net proceeds toward general corporate purposes, while identifying repayment of debt and other obligations as possible applications. (The announcement does not commit the company to one specific use of the proceeds.)

The use Southwest specifically describes as a possibility is paying off all of its $300 million of 3.000% notes when those notes reach maturity on November 15, 2026. (That stated amount is less than either new tranche and less than the total principal of the new offering.) The existing notes’ maturity date falls after the offering announcement dated October 26, 2026, and before the expected closing around November 2, 2026. (The closing date is an estimate, not a confirmation that the transaction will be completed on that day.) Southwest also allows that funds could be used to repay or redeem other debt or corporate obligations, without naming a particular additional obligation in the announcement. (The possible maturity repayment and the broader debt-related options are stated as possible uses, alongside general corporate purposes.) The announcement therefore sets out both a general purpose and examples of potential applications, but it does not say how much, if any, will go to the November notes or to other obligations. (This distinction follows from the company describing the applications as possible rather than as a final allocation.)

The two new tranches differ in principal, coupon and maturity: the 2029 notes have $600,000,000 principal at 5.750%, while the 2031 notes have $650,000,000 at 6.000%. (The stated terms make the later-maturing tranche the larger one and give it the higher coupon.) Those coupon figures describe the rates attached to the notes, whereas the principal figures describe the amounts being offered in each tranche. (They are distinct measures, and the announcement gives both for each group of notes.) The release does not provide a final allocation of proceeds between the two maturities or specify how the proceeds will be divided among corporate purposes. (It states the total offering amount and possible uses, but not a use-by-use breakdown.) The possibility of repaying the $300 million notes is consequently narrower than a claim that the new offering will refinance that debt: Southwest identifies the payment as one possible use, not a definite plan. (Its wording also leaves open repayment or redemption of other obligations.)

Southwest expects the offering to close on or about November 2, 2026, provided customary closing conditions are met. (The announcement presents this timing as expected, so the date does not establish that closing has taken place.) The transaction is described as an underwritten public offering, and five institutions are identified as joint book-running managers: Barclays Capital Inc., BNP Paribas Securities Corp., Standard Chartered Bank, U.S. Bancorp Investments, Inc., and Wells Fargo Securities, LLC. (The release assigns those firms that role in the offering.) Southwest says a shelf registration statement for the securities has been filed with the SEC and is effective. (The filing status is separate from the expected closing and does not replace the conditions attached to that closing.) The company says the offering can be made only through a prospectus supplement together with a base prospectus; it reports that preliminary versions of both have been filed and that a final supplement will also be filed with the SEC. (The release describes the documents through which the securities may be offered.)

Southwest classifies statements about the offering’s terms, completion, timing, size and use of proceeds as forward-looking statements. (Those subjects include the expected closing and intended or possible applications of the money.) The company warns that risks and uncertainties could make actual outcomes materially different from what those statements indicate. (The caution applies to the forward-looking statements described in the release.) It also says readers should not regard such statements as predictions of actual results. (That warning is relevant to the expected timing and the uses Southwest says it may make of the proceeds.) The release thus distinguishes the terms it has announced from outcomes that remain subject to uncertainty, including whether the offering closes as expected and how the net proceeds are ultimately applied. (Both completion and use of funds are among the matters the company treats as forward-looking.)

The offering announcement concerns Southwest’s financing, while the release also gives company background: it says service began on June 18, 1971, with three Boeing 737 aircraft serving Dallas, Houston and San Antonio. (Those details describe the airline’s starting operation as presented by Southwest.) As of September 30, 2026, Southwest reported a fleet of 803 Boeing 737 aircraft and service to 120 destinations in the United States and near-international countries. (The date attaches to the fleet and destination figures, rather than to the note offering’s expected closing.) The figures place the company’s stated current scale alongside its reported beginnings with three aircraft and service in three named Texas cities, although the measures describe different things. (One account gives aircraft and destinations at a specified later date; the other describes the initial service.) These operating details provide context about the airline named in the financing announcement, but the release does not connect the fleet or destination counts to the size or allocation of the note proceeds. (The stated use remains general corporate purposes, with potential debt payments among the examples.)

A separate Simple Flying report described Southwest’s Las Vegas network as including 11 new routes, comprising eight domestic routes and three international routes. (The domestic and international counts together equal the reported total.) That report said its route comparison relied on Cirium Diio data and represented a snapshot dated October 26. (This is a separate account and measurement from Southwest’s note-offering announcement.) The route figures concern a Las Vegas network comparison, while Southwest’s company-wide figure reports 120 destinations in the United States and near-international countries as of September 30, 2026. (The different descriptions and dates mean the two counts should not be treated as the same measure.) The route report supplies operating context but does not state that the routes are funded by the offering or that they change the stated purpose of its proceeds. (Southwest identifies general corporate purposes and possible debt repayments as uses.)

Simple Flying also reported that Southwest announced its Icon Lounges project in September 2026 and assigned the project that name on October 15. (Those reported project milestones precede the October 26 note announcement.) A separate Simple Flying report said a Southwest flight attendant sued the airline on October 20, alleging discrimination related to the company’s response to her severe allergy to pets. (The report describes an allegation in a lawsuit, not an established finding about the company.) The lounge report and lawsuit report concern other developments involving Southwest; neither gives a stated connection to the note offering or to how its proceeds will be used. (The offering announcement instead names general corporate purposes and possible repayments.) Read alongside the financing announcement, these separate reports show that the company was also the subject of coverage about a lounge project and a legal allegation, but they do not alter the announced principal amounts, note terms or expected closing conditions. (Those financing details are specified in the company’s release.)

The offering’s central change is the pricing of two proposed senior-note tranches with combined principal of $1,250,000,000, rather than the completion of a transaction already confirmed as closed. (Southwest announced the pricing on October 26, 2026, and described closing as expected on or about November 2, subject to conditions.) The principal split, coupon rates and maturity years are specified, while the final application of net proceeds is not fixed in the announcement. (The company gives examples of possible debt payments but describes general corporate purposes as the expected use.) The company’s filing statements and risk language add procedural context: it reports an effective shelf registration, identifies required prospectus documents and cautions that forward-looking statements may differ from actual results. (These statements do not remove the customary closing conditions.) For now, the announced figures define the proposed financing’s scale and structure, while the company’s own qualifications leave completion, timing and allocation subject to the stated conditions and uncertainty. (Southwest says these matters should not be read as predictions of actual results.)

text:
●● "Title: Holograms and Memory: The Imaginary and Practical Sides of Modi’s Conversation with Swami Chinmayananda" ●●
<*><*><*><*><*>
On 23 October 2026, at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi during the Chinmaya Amrit Mahotsav marking 75 years of the Chinmaya Mission, Prime Minister Narendra Modi interacted with a holographic avatar of Swami Chinmayananda. The spiritual leader, who founded the Mission in 1951, had passed away in 1993. For roughly five minutes, Modi spoke with the digital figure, recalled their 1993 meeting in Vadodara, and sought blessings. He later described the experience as emotionally transporting him back 33 years.

From an imaginative standpoint, the event felt like science fiction brought to life. A person who left the world decades ago appeared seated and conversational, creating a powerful sense of presence and reunion. For many observers, and for Modi himself, it offered an emotionally charged encounter that blended devotion with modern technology, making the past feel momentarily alive.

Practically, however, the interaction relied on established projection techniques (often based on variants of Pepper’s Ghost), archival audio and video, digital modeling, and AI-generated or scripted responses. It was not a free, spontaneous dialogue with the actual person but a carefully prepared digital recreation drawn from existing records. This raises familiar questions of authenticity, consent, and the risk of the avatar being shaped to deliver particular messages.

Similar experiments have been carried out with other notable figures. A photorealistic hologram of former U.S. President Ronald Reagan has been a permanent exhibit at his presidential library since 2018, using his real speeches. In entertainment, posthumous holograms of Tupac Shakur (Coachella 2012), Michael Jackson, Elvis Presley, and Whitney Houston have performed on stage. Plans and prototypes have also explored interactive AI holograms of scientists such as Stephen Hawking and religious figures such as Fulton Sheen. Private families have likewise used the technology to recreate loved ones for memorials.

The technology can preserve and share memory in striking ways, yet it remains an approximation rather than a true return. Balancing emotional impact with clear awareness of its constructed nature remains essential.
- Pandit Mustafa Arif

text:
WHAT HAPPENS TO THE RETURN FREIGHT?

A Driver’s Perspective | 
News That Matters
Monday, October 26, 2026 

A small manufacturer needs a truck to haul its product 600 miles to a customer. The carrier can offer a competitive rate partly because it expects to find another load for the trip back.

Now imagine more of that return freight moving through autonomous networks operated by large carriers. The small manufacturer still needs its product delivered, but the truck serving it may have fewer opportunities to earn money on the way home.

WHO PAYS FOR THOSE EMPTY MILES?

That is a question I believe deserves more attention as autonomous trucking expands.

On October 8, Kodiak AI and Charger USA announced they were hauling dry and refrigerated freight between Dallas and Laredo, Texas. Kodiak says it plans to begin long-haul operations without a driver in the cab by the end of 2026. That driverless launch is a plan, and the Dallas–Laredo announcement does not establish what is happening to other carriers’ return loads. 

But the direction is clear: companies are building networks around major freight corridors and working to keep their trucks productive. That means finding freight in both directions whenever possible.

For an owner-operator or small carrier, a return load can make the difference between a profitable trip and a truck traveling hundreds of miles without revenue. If those loads become harder to find, the carrier may have to charge the outbound customer more, accept less profit, or stop serving that lane altogether.

The effect could reach a small furniture maker, cabinet shop, or other manufacturer that depends on a human-operated truck to reach its customers. A higher transportation bill can squeeze margins, raise the delivered price of a product, and make it harder for that business to compete.

That outcome is a POSSIBILITY, not something the available evidence proves is already happening. Freight rates move for many reasons, including fuel costs, demand, available trucks, and seasonal changes. Autonomous networks may also create new opportunities for drivers handling local pickups, deliveries, and freight outside their routes.

Still, I believe we need to look beyond the price of one automated trip and examine the economics of the whole lane. If the most dependable return freight moves into larger networks, what happens to the businesses that rely on carriers outside those networks?

The question for shippers, carriers, and policymakers is straightforward: AS AUTONOMOUS NETWORKS GROW, WHO GETS THE RETURN LOADS, AND WHO ABSORBS THE COST WHEN THEY ARE NO LONGER AVAILABLE?

That is a question worth answering before we assume every gain in efficiency is shared across the industry.

Will Cook
A Driver’s Perspective

text:
Kentucky football head coach Will Stein made it clear just how much the job means to him and his family.

“I love everything about this job. Number one, I love our fans. I love the Bluegrass. I love being homegrown guy from Kentucky. I just love UK.”

Stein also revealed that Kentucky was the one job he had circled while serving as Oregon's offensive coordinator.

“This is a spot when you talk about places that I circled. This is really the one job when I was at Oregon that I felt like if I ever got offered, it was a no question take it because I would have always been sick to my stomach looking at this job with somebody else in the seat, given the opportunity that I had.”

The first-year Kentucky head coach emphasized that he and his family are happy to be home in the Bluegrass and want to continue building their future there.

“So, yes, I love it here. My family loves it here. I'm obviously close to home, being from Louisville, and want to continue to to to grow here and and grow my family.” 🏡😼 #BBN

In case you didn't follow the Tide today:

>🏈Alabama at LSU on Nov. 7 kicks off at 3:30 PM ET on ABC

     - First daytime Bama game in Tiger Stadium since 2010

>🏈DB Dre Kirkpatrick Jr. was arrested Friday on two misdemeanor charges, harassing communications and doxing, per court records. He was suspended Saturday, and Kalen DeBoer said Monday, "He's not with us."

>🏈DeBoer is hopeful WR Ryan Coleman-Williams (knee) will be ready for LSU

>🏈LG William Sanders had TightRope surgery on his right ankle Sunday. DeBoer says he's "probably two to three weeks" out

>🏈DL Fatutoa Henry is the SEC's Co-Defensive Lineman of the Week after two fourth-quarter sacks vs. A&M

>🏈18-year first-round streak watch: Devan Thompkins (15) is the only Tide player in CBS's updated top 32

     - Next up: Yhonzae Pierre (47), Bray Hubbard (87), Ryan Coleman-Williams (106), Zabien Brown (112). The 10-year run of multiple first-rounders could get tested

>🏈On my poll, you voted C Racin Delgatty as the guy Bama needs back most (46%), ahead of Ryan Coleman-Williams (34%)

     - Plenty of you wrote in DT Terrance Green too

>🏈Fans on the afternoon kick: some are thrilled to skip a night game in Death Valley, others think the SEC didn't want to go head to head with Notre Dame-Miami in primetime

>🏀G Aden Holloway made the Bob Cousy Award watch list

>📝2027 IOL Xavier Endicott (Oxford, Ala.) committed two days after Bama offered: "Alabama showed me love before anyone else did."

text:
Kalshi just became the NBA's official prediction market partner.

We went through the court records, regulator filings and Kalshi's own statements. 

Here's what this announcement left out. 🧵

1/
The deal makes Kalshi a "Preferred Prediction Market Exchange of the NBA."
Kalshi gets NBA logos, marketing rights and official league data to settle its NBA markets. Polymarket got the same deal.
2/
Here's what makes it strange.
In May 2025, after Kalshi started offering spreads and moneylines on NBA games, an NBA lawyer wrote to federal regulators asking for protections against the integrity risks of prediction markets.
17 months later, Kalshi is a partner.
3/
The NBA has reason to worry.
Former Raptor Jontay Porter admitted he left games early to help bettors who bet the "under" on his stats. He pleaded guilty to federal wire fraud conspiracy and was banned for life.
4/
In October 2025, the FBI arrested Terry Rozier in a case centered on a March 2023 game he left after less than 10 minutes. Sportsbooks had flagged suspicious betting on his stats.
The NBA reviewed that game in 2023 and found no rule violation.
Rozier has pleaded not guilty. His trial is set for February 2027.
5/
To be clear, those bets ran through sportsbooks, not Kalshi.
But they show where the risk is: inside information about who plays and who's hurt.
6/
Kalshi listed markets on exactly that.
It offered contracts on athlete injuries, including how long players would be sidelined and whether specific NFL players would suit up for Week 1.
Kalshi has since pulled them.
7/
Then there's Giannis Antetokounmpo.
He became a Kalshi shareholder in a deal signed on NBA trade deadline day. Earlier that week, Kalshi listed markets on where he'd be traded.
Kalshi says the deal wasn't in place while those markets ran, his stake is under 1%, and he's barred from trading NBA markets.
8/
Kalshi says it isn't a sportsbook.
But its ads promoted sports betting as legal in all 50 states. And according to a federal appeals court, sports made up 95% of its 2025 revenue.
In August, that court ruled 3-0 that Kalshi's sports contracts are, in substance, sports gambling.
9/
In most states you must be 21 to bet on the NBA at a sportsbook. On Kalshi, it's 18.
CNN estimates 18-to-21-year-olds traded $5.4 billion on Kalshi so far this year. Kalshi has also recruited "ambassadors" on college campuses.
10/
Sportsbooks let problem gamblers ban themselves through state self-exclusion programs.
A Massachusetts man who had self-excluded says in a lawsuit that Kalshi offered no such option, and that he lost tens of thousands of dollars there in one month.
11/
Kalshi's ads said "We aren't the house."
But Kalshi owns a trading company, Kalshi Trading, that takes the other side of some customer bets.
And Bloomberg reported that Jump Trading agreed to take an equity stake in Kalshi in exchange for trading on the platform.
12/
So who wins?
Kalshi's own data: over 70% of traders lost money over six months.
Over the long run, traders and analysts surveyed by How Gambling Works estimate only 2–5% of users come out ahead.
13/
Then there's the fine print.
Traders put more than $54 million on whether Iran's Supreme Leader would be "out." When he died, Kalshi paid at the last price before his death, about 40¢ instead of $1, citing a rule about death.
It refunded fees and net losses. Traders sued anyway.
14/
In January, Kalshi didn't pay winners on some NFL season markets.
It paid them after users complained publicly.
15/
New York sued Kalshi in July, seeking at least $36 billion.
Kalshi told its federal regulator a "market emergency" would follow, and the CFTC used emergency powers to order Kalshi to keep operating.
When a Michigan judge ordered refunds on completed trades, the CFTC told Kalshi not to follow that part.

1SG, WOGBTC DAILY ORDER — October 26, 2026
HEARD BY GOD. READY TO BLESS.
Evening training • Builds on AWP Promise #299

1 — THE ORDER

Return blessing. Let Christ govern your next response.

“not returning evil for evil or reviling for reviling, but on the contrary blessing”

— 1 Peter 3:9, NKJV, excerpt

Battle Line: God hears my prayer. I will guard my tongue, speak truth, and pursue peace.

2 — THE TRAINING

Warrior Doctrine — Being heard by God frees you to listen to others.

Today’s AWP established that God sees and hears you. Tonight, practice what that assurance makes possible: bringing your hurt to Him without passing it to the next person.

Read 1 Peter 3:8–12 together. Peter joins prayer with compassion, humility, restrained speech, and the pursuit of peace. The person who irritated you remains someone to treat with dignity. Their conduct does not determine your obedience.

Blessing means seeking another person’s good before God and in your actions. You can refuse a cruel remark, offer practical help, or correct a false statement calmly. You can also say:

“I want to resolve this, but we need to speak respectfully.”

Prayer is not a technique for controlling another person’s response. Place the outcome with God while taking responsibility for your words and conduct. Romans 12:18 recognizes the limits of your control; pursue peace as far as your part reaches.

Spiritual Battle — Identify the real target.

Ephesians 6:12 teaches that our struggle reaches beyond flesh and blood. Resist the temptation to treat a person as the enemy. Stand against bitterness, deception, and the urge to repay hurt; meet the person with truth and love.

Armor Fit

Belt of Truth: Separate what happened from what you assumed.
Breastplate of Righteousness: Choose conduct that honors Christ even while you feel hurt.
Shield of Faith: Entrust your need to be understood to the God who hears.
Boots of Peace: Take a deliberate step toward a truthful, peaceful resolution.

Training Drill — PAUSE • PRAY • BLESS

PAUSE: Name the feeling and identify the facts before speaking.
PRAY: “Lord Jesus, guard my tongue. Help me see this person clearly.”
BLESS: Choose one truthful sentence or useful action that seeks their good.

Practice scenario: A coworker dismisses your effort. Before defending yourself sharply, ask, “What specifically needs to change?” Listen, clarify the facts, and respond without a personal attack.

Trainer’s Check: Ask, “What would blessing look like here, and what boundary might be needed?” Have the learner practice one sentence. Assess truthfulness, tone, and purpose—not whether the other person immediately agrees.

3 — THE EXECUTION

Commander’s Orders

Review one difficult moment from today. Name your response honestly before God.
Where your words caused harm, make a direct apology without attaching an excuse.
Check on one person. Give them enough attention to hear the answer.
Prepare one peaceful sentence for a situation you expect tomorrow.

Mission Purpose:
I belong to Christ, and I will care for the people He places in my path.

Prayer of Deployment

Father, You see what happened and hear what I struggle to express. Through Jesus, forgive my sinful responses and train me to return blessing. Guard my tongue, strengthen my discernment, and help me speak truth with gentleness. Show me when to listen, when to help, and when to set a clear boundary. I entrust the outcome to You. In Jesus’ name, amen.

Cross-References — NKJV: Psalm 34:12–16; James 1:19–20; Romans 12:14–21; Ephesians 6:10–18.

Evening Review: Did I pray before responding? Did my words serve truth and peace? What will I practice tomorrow?

Thought for 12s

Detailed timeline, official FBI materials, stills, and investigation/charges status for the September 10, 2025, Utah Valley University shooting of Charlie Kirk and the related FBI rooftop-escape footage.⁠Fbi

Timeline (key points)
September 10, 2025, ~12:20–12:23 p.m. MT: Charlie Kirk (31), co-founder of Turning Point USA, is shot once in the neck while speaking at an outdoor event on the UVU Orem campus. The shot came from a rooftop roughly 140–200+ yards away (reports vary on exact distance; one later testimony cited ~415 feet). He is transported to a hospital and later dies. Thousands of people were present.⁠Newsweek
Immediately after: Suspect (later identified as Tyler James Robinson, then 22) runs across the rooftop of a campus building (Losee Center area), lowers/jumps from the edge (leaving palm impressions, forearm imprint, and shoe impressions consistent with Converse-style shoes with white soles), crosses grass/parking area, and flees toward a wooded area. A high-powered bolt-action rifle and ammunition are later recovered from the woods.⁠Fbi
September 11: FBI/Utah DPS release photos of the person of interest (dark clothing, black long-sleeve shirt with American flag/eagle design, cap with triangle/logo, sunglasses, backpack) and later the rooftop-jump CCTV footage during a press conference. $100,000 reward offered. FBI Director Kash Patel and others participate. Tips exceed 7,000+ (later higher).⁠Archive
Evening of September 11 / early September 12: Family member/family friend tip leads to Robinson turning himself in peacefully (with parents) at the Washington County Sheriff’s Office in southern Utah. He is taken into custody ~10 p.m. local on the 11th (about 33–36 hours after the shooting). Booked into Utah County Jail on suspicion of aggravated murder and related offenses. No bail.⁠AP News

September 16, 2025: Formal seven-count charging document filed by Utah County Attorney Jeff Gray. Prosecutors announce intent to seek the death penalty. Aggravating factors include targeting based on political expression and presence of children/bystanders.⁠NYTimes

Later 2025–2026: Held without bail. First in-person court appearance December 2025. Multi-day preliminary hearing (evidence including video, DNA, texts, roommate interview, confessions/admissions) in July 2026. Judge Tony Graf finds probable cause on all counts on September 1, 2026, and binds the case over for trial. Not-guilty pleas entered. Prosecutors continue pursuing death penalty.⁠Thecourier
October 2026 status: No trial date yet set. Defense seeks start in Q3 2029 (citing capital-case complexity, evidence volume, jury selection, motions); prosecution prefers ~January 31, 2028 (estimating ~17-week trial). Erika Kirk’s counsel has pushed for a faster timeline. Next scheduling hearing set for November 9, 2026. Robinson (now 23) has pleaded not guilty to the seven counts.⁠Fox News

Official FBI public releases (video and updates)
Primary video page (rooftop jump and flight footage): FBI Video Repository – Video Footage of Shooter in Utah Valley University Shooting. Description matches the shotlist: subject climbs to rooftop around noon Sept. 10, shoots Kirk, jumps off, flees; weapon/ammo recovered in woods; shoe impressions, forearm imprint, palm print collected.⁠Fbi

Main updates page: FBI Utah Valley Shooting Updates. Notes suspect in custody; links to video, photos, tips (1-800-CALL-FBI or https://t.co/OwkiCn4oOp), and related statements (including Patel’s Sept. 12 remarks).⁠Fbi
Related: FBI Salt Lake City social posts and YouTube version of the footage; original press-conference narrations by Utah DPS Commissioner Beau Mason.
The footage is restricted for editorial use (standard for such handouts). Public stills from it and related campus CCTV circulated widely in September 2025 coverage.
Stills / visual examples from the footage
These are publicly circulated frames from the FBI-released CCTV and related coverage:
📷📷
(Additional stills appear in contemporary CNN, KSL, AP, and other reports of the press conference.)
Charges and investigation specifics
Robinson faces seven counts (Utah County, Fourth District Court):
Aggravated murder (capital felony) — intentionally/knowingly causing Kirk’s death while knowingly creating a great risk of death to others.
Felony discharge of a firearm causing serious bodily injury (first-degree felony). 3–4. Two counts of obstruction of justice (second-degree felonies) — concealing/removing the rifle and disposing of/concealing clothing. 5–6. Two counts of tampering with a witness (third-degree felonies) — directing roommate to delete incriminating texts and to stay silent if questioned.
Violent offense committed in the presence of a child (class A misdemeanor).
Victim-targeting enhancements apply to some counts (alleging selection based on political expression). Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty. Evidence cited includes campus surveillance (arrival, rooftop movement, flight), DNA/trace evidence, recovered weapon, texts/Discord messages, a note, and admissions to family/roommate.⁠Thewrap

Investigation was a joint FBI–Utah DPS/local effort with heavy public-tip volume. Motive discussion in filings and hearings has centered on political disagreement (Kirk’s views on certain social issues).
Sources for the above include https://t.co/ALzsifOo6J pages, contemporary and later reporting from AP, Reuters, CNN, Deseret News/KSL, court-related coverage, and charging documents. Qatari mediators are working on an agreement in which the United States and Iran would trade concessions over five days, two diplomats briefed on the talks told The New York Times on Monday. Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping, and the United States would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports. 

The main obstacle, the diplomats said, is sequencing: who moves first. They added that the mediators are pressing Iran to offer a concession on its nuclear program in the first phase. Tehran has resisted that. Last week Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, vowed that "not a single particle of enriched nuclear material" would leave the country, the Times noted.

Iran has its own version on the table. According to Iranian state outlets cited by Iran International, Tehran resubmitted a plan to restore Hormuz shipping in stages over seven days, but says the clock starts only once $24 billion in frozen reserves becomes fully accessible. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Iranian technical negotiators are studying US counterproposals on lifting the blockade. 

Monday's meeting in Tehran with Saudi Arabia's defense minister, Pakistan's army chief and Turkey's intelligence chief ended with a joint statement that the four countries "agreed to continue consultations," with no date set. A Gulf official told the Times the visit was meant in part to urge Iranian flexibility. Riyadh's foreign ministry called for negotiations to "prevent the return of military escalation," Reuters reported. Rezaei drew a different lesson: "security in West Asia must come from within the region."

Washington's message ran on the economic track. In an interview with Iran International, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent predicted Iran's economy would shrink by more than 25 percent in the year to March 2027 and said "the next eight weeks is going to get even more intense." He told Iranians to stock up on heating fuel and said "everyone should fill up their tanks now." Iran, he said, has "no oil on the water" and no loadings at Kharg Island. Asked whether Tehran could wait out the Nov. 3 midterms, he said: "Nothing will change in terms of President Trump's calculus."

This is the off-ramp to watch while the military option stays loaded: CNN reported Monday that US forces could launch major strikes within 96 hours of an order. A five-day swap would reopen the waterway that has kept Brent above $115 and gasoline near $4.29. Qatar wants a nuclear step up front, and Tehran says no. Neither Washington nor Doha has confirmed the Times account.

text:
🇺🇦🇪🇺🇺🇸🇷🇺

Putin sells Trump diesel he doesn’t have. Americans pay even more at the pump while US money flows to russia as it bombs Ukraine. Now Putin wants Trump to deliver Ukraine on a platter & carve up Europe. The diesel was just the appetizer 👇

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗹 𝗶𝘀 𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝘄𝗻-𝗽𝗮𝘆𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁.

Trump waived sanctions so Putin can sell diesel he does not have. The cash funds missiles on Ukrainian cities and the hybrid campaign already running across Europe. Americans still pay near-record prices. In Putin’s hometown the pumps are dry. The leaders get the photograph and the money. Everything else is already being built around that single, trivial transaction.

𝗧𝗿𝘂𝗺𝗽 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗶𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗽𝗲𝗿 𝗱𝗶𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗹 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗥𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗮𝗻 𝗱𝗲𝗮𝗹. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗿𝗸𝗲𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗻'𝘁 𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗸. 𝗣𝗿𝗶𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝘄𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝘂𝗽 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗱.

9 October: 300,000 tons “immediately,” then 500,000, then a million, plus three million more “depending on the refineries.” Waiver until April 2027. The market shrugged. U.S. diesel still sits at roughly $6.28–6.32 a gallon. The United States is a major exporter. The first 40,000-ton tanker left Primorsk for a mid-November arrival — after the midterms. Three ships, Novak says. Tiny barrels. Maximum optics. No relief for the trucker or the farmer.

𝗣𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗹 𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘂𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿.

Rosbalt reports diesel at just 62% of stations in St. Petersburg and the Leningrad region. Dry pumps, rationing, queues whenever fuel arrives. Independent stations are suffering most. Ukrainian strikes have cut Russian diesel production by roughly 30%, yet Moscow keeps exporting it.

𝗧𝗿𝘂𝗺𝗽'𝘀 𝗥𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗮𝗻 𝗱𝗶𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗹 𝗵𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘆𝗺𝗼𝗼𝗻 𝗺𝗮𝘆 𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝗮 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗴𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗶𝗻𝘃𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.

On 26 October, senior Democrats and Republican Thom Tillis demanded that major U.S. banks and ports preserve all records of Russian diesel deals. Their warning: possible sanctions violations, criminal liability and money financing Putin's war.

An investigation is being prepared for after the midterms if control of the chamber flips. The first tanker hasn't even docked.

𝗘𝘂𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝘁𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲𝘁.

Putin intends to use the Ukraine talks to force NATO back to its 1997 borders — withdrawal of troops and weapons from Poland, the Baltic states, Finland and Estonia. That is why Ushakov insists Europe must sit at the table. Western diplomats see the demand clearly and reject it. Peskov stated yesterday that Russia will not stop military operations during the “peace” talks; the armed forces continue massive strikes. Local humanitarian pauses (Oleshky, Melania Trump’s initiative) are offered as theatre. Kaja Kallas, same day in Paris: little hope for imminent peace. Russia continues attacks on Kyiv and is sinking civilian ships in the Black Sea. The EU’s task, she said, is to help Ukraine withstand and raise the cost for Moscow. New sanctions this month; more coming. The diesel opening, the fertilizer talk, the Novatek channel in Alaska — all of it is designed to drag Moscow out of isolation while Europe absorbs the hybrid pressure and the political bill.

After nationalising over 800 European companies worth 7.6 trillion rubles, Putin now promises “favourable conditions” for those who stay. He even claims Europe has plenty of friends of Russia who were “forced to leave.”

𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗸𝗼𝗳𝗳 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗱 𝗣𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗻 𝗮 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗶𝘀𝘁. 𝗛𝗼𝘂𝗿𝘀 𝗹𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗿, 𝗯𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗺𝗶𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝗵𝗶𝘁 𝗞𝘆𝗶𝘃.

“You are a humanist also, sir, and I salute that.” Putin then expressed regret about the losses. Hours later Russian forces launched a massive ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Why stop killing when Washington applauds your humanity? A few words of sorrow cost nothing. The bombing continues.

𝗧𝗿𝘂𝗺𝗽 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝗼𝗿 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗱𝗶𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗹. 𝗣𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗻 𝘄𝗮𝗹𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝗶𝗻 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗮 𝗺𝗮𝗽 𝗼𝗳 𝗘𝘂𝗿𝗼𝗽𝗲.

The diesel is the appetizer. The real meal is a New Yalta in which three men decide Ukraine’s fate in a room where Ukraine is not invited, and NATO is invited only to be dismantled. Trump gets the photograph and the illusion of mastery. Putin gets cash, sanctions relief, time, and a chance to rewrite the European security order. Ukraine pays in blood. Europe is expected to pretend the price is acceptable.

𝗨𝗸𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼 𝗳𝗼𝗼𝗹. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗮𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘁𝗲𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝗮𝗿𝘆 — 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗞𝘆𝗶𝘃 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝘀𝗮𝗶𝗱 𝘀𝗼.

Sources close to Zelensky dropped it today: the suspension of strikes on Russian refineries is only a pause. The United States and others asked for it. Kyiv is waiting for answers. It will not last.

While Moscow sells scraps of diesel it does not have, Ukrainian strikes continue on the real targets. In the last days: the Energiya plant in Yelets — Russia’s sole producer of power batteries for glide bombs, Iskander-M missiles and cruise missiles — was hit and burned. The main microchip workshop at Proton-Electrotex in Oryol, which feeds components for ballistic and cruise missiles, was destroyed. Radars, command posts and other air-defence nodes in Belgorod Oblast were struck. Russia is already dry on diesel. Its air defence, stretched thin and failing to intercept, is dropping its own munitions across Belgorod. The city is being hammered by both Ukrainian drones and the debris of Moscow’s own systems.

Putin keeps losing allies and still demands that Europe surrender Kyiv so he can roll NATO back to the 1997 borders. Peskov has already confirmed that the “peace” process will not pause the killing. Every serious assessment of the war, from historians to Western intelligence agencies, says the same thing: a settlement that leaves Russia intact is only a pause that lets it rebuild for the larger war it is already preparing in Europe. Trump is arranging the division of spheres of influence with Putin and Xi. The diesel is only the down-payment. The rest — the New Yalta, the pressure on NATO’s 1997 borders, the continued killing — is already under way.

Trump’s America has now crossed a line that earlier administrations, for all their other failures, treated as non-negotiable. Calling the organizer of the largest land war in Europe since 1945 a humanitarian is not a slip. It is a public announcement that the American side has decided the moral accounting no longer applies. The release of one elderly American teacher is treated as sufficient counterweight to the systematic targeting of Ukrainian civilians, the abduction of children, and the deliberate destruction of energy infrastructure ahead of winter. The comparison is not between two acts of mercy. It is between a hostage release and an ongoing campaign of extermination. Treating them as equivalent is the definition of the stain.
For Putin the genocide of Ukraine stopped being a policy years ago. It became the fixed idea that holds the entire construction together.
Half Trump’s term was spent exposing him. The rest may be spent trying to stop him. Washington will debate the depth of his stupidity while Putin continues slaughtering Ukrainians.

text:
8 PM Top-of-the-Hour News

Former FBI Director James Comey is being charged by federal prosecutors for leaking national defense information. In a new case, the Justice Department alleges Comey knowingly communicated information related to national defense to a person not entitled to receive it, with reports indicating "the person" was a reporter.: “The next couple of years are going to be hard for all of us. It's really important that we stand straight. And keep the faith in America. ”
This marks the third time the DOJ has charged Comey.  He still faces charges for allegedly threatening President Trump by posting on Instagram a photo of seashells on a beach arranged to form the numbers "86 47."

Russia is intensifying its attacks on Ukraine -- as the country struggles with disruptions to Starlink internet service. A week after Starlink service was disrupted -- Ukrainian President Zelenskyy says the network has yet to return to full capacity. The Wall Street Journal reports President Trump personally urged Elon Musk to restore service -- but the president is not saying who was responsible for restricting access: “Now who ordered the Starlix access in Ukraine to be restricted? Who was it? Well, I wouldn't tell you if I did know. I have. ”
Musk has acknowledged limiting Ukraine's access -- defending the move by arguing the service should not be used to carry out offensive drone attacks against Russia.

The Pentagon is pushing Congress to officially change its name from the Department of Defense to the Department of War.: “President Trump authorized the new title last year. I think Department of War and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has already begun using it across the department. Yes, we love everything that the Department of Defense represented, but this is a new era of the Department of War. That is focused on winning wars, not just perpetually defending. But only Congress can make the name change official under federal law. The Pentagon estimates the rebranding will cost about $52 million so far. Supporters say the name better reflects the military's mission to fight and win wars. Critics question the cost and argue the change is unnecessary. Stacy Linn, Worldwide News Network, Washington. ”

The Archdiocese of New York has reached an 800-million-dollar settlement with 13-hundred people who say they were sexually abused by Roman Catholic lay leaders and clergy members.: “Having all the survivors agree to what has been a negotiated proposed resolution with the archdiocese is really a monumental step, a real important step in closing this chapter of their journey. ”
That lawyer for the victims says each plaintiff will get a lump-sum payment of at least 250-thousand dollars, or a potentially larger amount after a review of how much abuse they endured.

Microsoft says that it is offering buyouts to a wide swath of employees.
The software maker announced a new voluntary exit offer for certain workers in the U.S., Canada, India and the United Kingdom.
Around 60-thousand people are eligible, according to internal sources who spoke to the Associated Press.

A new prostate cancer drug is showing promise.: “Johnson and Johnson says phase one clinical trials of its oral prostate cancer pill JNJ 6143 caused tumors to shrink or disappear completely. The trial involved patients with advanced prostate cancer who had received at least 4 treatments. Side effects for some patients included nausea and elevated cholesterol levels. Michael Woblish, Worldwide News Network. ”

Pope Leo's trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru next month will go ahead
The Vatican says that the pontiff's recovery from lung cancer surgery is on track and that he's fit enough to make the trip.
The 71-year-old had surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung after a diagnosis of lung adeno-carcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.

Three blind Army veterans ran the Army Ten-Miler in Washington, D.C. this month, in pouring rain.

AI glasses described the course out loud: the water stops, the bridges, the Capitol, the finish line. Human guides ran beside them every step, because the tech isn't perfect yet.

"I've never been able to see a finish line," said Thomas Panek, the blind runner who leads the nonprofit Lighthouse Guild. This time it was described to him as he crossed it.

Free AI glasses and training are now offered to every legally blind U.S. veteran, more than 130,000 people. Know one? Send them to https://t.co/ffg2DgwYLI.

text:
WORLD NEWS REPORT — OCTOBER 26, 2026
Global Conflicts, Politics, Economy, Science, Health and the Environment
MONDAY | INTERNATIONAL NEWS BRIEFING
1. MIDDLE EAST — FEARS OF A WIDER WAR
Tensions are intensifying across the Middle East as Washington weighs renewed military action against Iran. President Donald Trump has suggested further strikes remain possible, although the White House says no American attack will occur before the November 3 midterm elections.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, facing elections October 27, has received Trump's endorsement and argues that confronting Iran requires continued strong leadership.

Yemen's Houthi movement claims to have attacked Saudi oil infrastructure and Riyadh's international airport. Saudi authorities have not confirmed every claimed strike. The disruption threatens energy exports and international shipping.

In Lebanon, security sources tell Reuters that Hezbollah is rebuilding military capabilities with Iranian financial assistance. Another major confrontation with Israel remains possible, although renewed full-scale war is not confirmed.

reuters.com+2📷
2. GAZA — UNITED NATIONS ISSUES SERIOUS FINDINGS

A United Nations investigative commission released a report accusing Israel of continuing genocidal acts against Palestinians in Gaza following the October 2025 ceasefire.
Israel strongly rejects the findings, describing them as politically motivated misinformation.

Palestinian authorities report more than 74,000 deaths since Israel launched its military response to the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks, which killed approximately 1,200 people in Israel.

The commission also describes worsening violence and displacement in the occupied West Bank.

Its conclusions represent the commission's findings, not a new final judgment by an international court. Civilian protection, accountability and reconstruction remain unresolved.

https://t.co/5eOSzZwwVD📷
3. UKRAINE — DEADLY STRIKES AND NEW PEACE EFFORTS

Russian missiles struck Kyiv on October 26, killing at least one person and injuring 10, according to Ukrainian officials. Residential buildings, educational facilities and transportation infrastructure suffered damage.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy renewed demands for faster delivery of Western air-defense ammunition.

Diplomatic developments offer cautious hope. Russia and Ukraine agreed to humanitarian arrangements in Oleshky beginning October 27 and anticipate renewed technical-level negotiations in November.

The countries recently exchanged 270 prisoners each. Major disagreements remain over occupied territory, security guarantees and Ukraine's future relationship with Western powers.

A comprehensive peace settlement is not yet assured.

reuters.com+1📷
4. UNITED STATES — MIDTERM ELECTIONS APPROACH

America's November 3 congressional elections are approaching amid intense debate over inflation, energy costs, foreign military involvement and presidential authority.
Trump is campaigning for Republican candidates as Democrats seek greater influence in Congress.

Competitive Senate contests have attracted substantial political spending. The administration also faces controversy over election-related litigation and its handling of relations with Russia.

The election could significantly affect domestic legislation, government oversight and American foreign policy during the remainder of Trump's presidency.

https://t.co/qqrtlpgTmW📷
5. EUROPE — SERBIA EXPERIENCES HISTORIC CHANGE

Serbia's student-backed opposition movement defeated longtime leader Aleksandar Vučić in Sunday's election.
With nearly 99% of ballots counted, student-supported candidates received approximately 52.7% of the vote against 39.2% for Vučić's governing alliance.

The victory follows two years of demonstrations that began after a deadly railway station canopy collapse in Novi Sad.

Supporters hope for stronger democratic institutions and reduced corruption. Analysts caution that the inexperienced movement faces difficult decisions involving Russia, China, Kosovo and European integration.

The next challenge is forming an effective government.

https://t.co/5eOSzZwwVD📷
6. WORLD ECONOMY — ENERGY PRICES AND INFLATION

Oil prices remain a major economic concern following months of Middle Eastern conflict.
Brent crude approached $117 per barrel last week before easing, reflecting uncertainty about future supply disruptions.

The Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan face important monetary-policy decisions this week.

Higher energy costs threaten household purchasing power and business profitability.

Investors are also examining whether enormous corporate spending on artificial intelligence will produce sustainable returns.

reuters.com+2📷
7. BRAZIL — LULA WINS FOURTH PRESIDENTIAL TERM

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured reelection after defeating Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in Sunday's runoff.
The result surprised investors who had anticipated a Bolsonaro victory and potentially more business-friendly economic policies.

Brazil now faces continuing disagreements over government spending, economic inequality, environmental protection and relations with Washington.

The election also demonstrates the persistence of sharp political divisions across Latin America's largest economy.

https://t.co/5eOSzZwwVD📷
8. ASIA — CHINA AND REGIONAL SECURITY

China's currency reached a four-year high against the dollar as investors awaited important Communist Party meetings in Beijing.
Chinese leaders face challenges involving domestic demand, international trade and technological competition.

Meanwhile, tensions persist between China and the Philippines over disputed waters in the South China Sea.

Manila recently protested remarks by China's ambassador that Philippine officials interpreted as threatening.

Both governments maintain competing territorial positions, making diplomatic restraint increasingly important.

reuters.com+1📷
9. AFRICA — SUDAN'S HUMANITARIAN CRISIS

Sudan's electricity operator reports that drone attacks damaged power facilities and disrupted electricity across four southeastern states.
The company blamed the Rapid Support Forces, although Reuters could not independently verify responsibility.

Sudan's civil war began in April 2023 following a power struggle between the military and paramilitary forces.

Continuing attacks on infrastructure threaten hospitals, drinking-water systems and essential civilian services.

Ending the conflict remains an urgent international humanitarian priority.

https://t.co/5eOSzZwwVD📷
10. CLIMATE — POWERFUL EL NIÑO WARNING

The World Meteorological Organization warns that an exceptionally strong El Niño could develop during the coming months.
Forecasts indicate unusually high Pacific Ocean temperatures, potentially contributing to severe droughts, flooding and agricultural disruption.

United Nations officials estimate that approximately 50 million people could face increased hunger risks.

These are projections, not confirmed future outcomes. Governments are being urged to strengthen disaster preparedness and food-security measures.

https://t.co/5eOSzZwwVD📷
11. SCIENCE, MEDICINE AND TECHNOLOGY

Medical innovation continues despite global instability.
Recent developments include experimental personalized cancer treatments, artificial intelligence systems designed to assist medical diagnosis, and research into preventing serious disease.

Merck and Moderna have reported encouraging results involving an experimental melanoma vaccine combined with immunotherapy.

These advances require careful evaluation of clinical evidence, safety and regulatory approval before broad medical adoption.

Meanwhile, AI companies face growing scrutiny over development costs, profitability and their potential effects on employment.

Medical & Healthcare News+1📷
GLOBAL OUTLOOK — WHAT MATTERS MOST

The world's immediate priorities are preventing another Middle Eastern escalation, protecting civilians in Ukraine and Gaza, resolving Sudan's humanitarian emergency and managing economic instability.
Upcoming elections in Israel and the United States could influence international diplomacy.

At the same time, scientific innovation and emerging political movements offer opportunities for progress.

The central challenge facing world leaders is balancing national security, economic stability, human dignity and lasting peace.
