text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

In the late autumn of 1964, with the presidential contest between Lyndon Johnson and Barry Goldwater already all but decided, a former Hollywood actor named Ronald Reagan stepped before the cameras in a Los Angeles television studio and spoke for half an hour on behalf of the Arizona senator. The address, later known as “A Time for Choosing,” was not delivered before a roaring convention hall. It was a carefully prepared, nationally televised appeal, filmed in advance and aired on the evening of October 27. Reagan was fifty-three years old. He had spent most of his adult life in front of audiences—first as a radio sportscaster, then as a movie and television star—and he understood the power of a clear, unhurried voice and a well-chosen story. What he had not yet done was ask an entire nation to consider the future of its own government.

The country that heard him was prosperous and restless. The economy was strong, but taxes were rising, federal programs were multiplying, and the Cold War remained the central fact of American life. Johnson’s Great Society was just beginning to take legislative form. Goldwater’s campaign had been painted, by friend and foe alike, as a dangerous experiment in ideology. Into that atmosphere Reagan offered a different argument. He set aside the familiar language of left and right and insisted that the real choice lay between “up” and “down”—up toward the maximum of individual freedom consistent with ordered liberty, or down into what he called the ant heap of totalitarianism. The Founding Fathers, he said, had understood that a government powerful enough to control the economy would inevitably control the people who lived under it, and that such control could be achieved only by force. Public officials, however well intentioned, would always ask for a little more money and a little more authority. Once a program began, it almost never ended. “A government bureau,” he observed, “is the nearest thing to eternal life we’ll ever see on this earth.”

He spoke of debt, of inflation that quietly eroded savings, and of the growing habit of looking to Washington for solutions that once had been left to communities and families. He told the story of a Cuban businessman who had escaped Castro’s regime. When an American remarked how lucky they were to live in the United States, the refugee answered that at least the Americans still had someplace to escape to. Reagan’s conclusion was plain: if freedom were lost in America, there would be nowhere left to go. This, he said, was the last stand on earth. On the subject of communism he was equally direct. He called it the most dangerous enemy mankind had ever faced and argued that peace would come not from accommodation but from the demonstrated willingness to pay a price and draw a line. He closed by borrowing the cadence of earlier American leaders, telling his listeners that they and he had a rendezvous with destiny: they would preserve for their children the last best hope of man on earth, or they would sentence those children to take the first step into a thousand years of darkness.

The speech did not save Goldwater. Johnson won in a landslide. But the half-hour address raised substantial sums for the Republican cause and, more lastingly, introduced Reagan to millions of Americans who had never heard him speak as a political figure. Two years later he was elected governor of California. Sixteen years after that October evening he entered the White House. What lingered was not merely the eloquence of a single night, but the conviction that the habits of self-government, once surrendered, are difficult to recover, and that the choice between freedom and its alternatives remains open in every generation.

text:
The First Official SSN
Once the SSN records were received in Baltimore they were grouped in blocks of 1,000 and the master records were created. On December 1, 1936 the first block of 1,000 records were assembled and were ready to start their way through the nine-step process that would result in the creation of a permanent master record and the establishment of an earnings record for the individual. When this first stack was ready, Joe Fay, head of the Division of Accounting Operations in the Candler Building, walked over to the stack, pulled off the top record, and declared it to be the official first Social Security record. (This was the first point in the process where there was enough control to designate an official first card--it would have been impossible to try and identify the first card typed in one of the 1,074 typing centers around the country.) This particular record, (055-09-0001) belonged to John D. Sweeney, Jr., age 23, of New Rochelle, New York. The next day, newspapers around the country announced that Sweeney had been issued the first SSN. It would be more accurate to say that the first Social Security record was established for John David Sweeney, but since master records were invisible to the public and the Social Security card was a very visible token of the program, the newspapers overlooked the nuance.

And so John David Sweeney, Jr. is the closest thing we have to the first person to have received a Social Security card--although his status is more symbolic than actual.

Mr. Sweeney was the son of a wealthy factory owner, and had grown up in a 15-room Westchester County home staffed with servants. In an effort to learn the family business, Mr. Sweeney was working as a shipping clerk for his father at the time he filled out his application for a social security card. The Sweeneys were Republicans and the whole family voted for Landon in 1936, although John Jr. allowed that he liked the new Social Security program even though he didn't think much of the New Deal. John Sweeney died of a heart attack in 1974 at the age of 61 without ever receiving any benefits from the social security program; however, his widow was able to receive benefits based on his work until her death in 1982.

What are the new heaven and the new earth?
Answer
In Revelation 21:1, John sees something spectacular: “Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth,’ for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” This new earth and new heaven are sometimes referred to as the “eternal state.” As seen in Revelation chapters 21—22, the new earth will be the eternal dwelling place of believers in Jesus Christ. Scripture gives us a few details of the new heaven and new earth.

The current heaven and earth have long been subject to God’s curse because of mankind’s sin. All creation “has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth” (Romans 8:22) as it awaits the fulfillment of God’s plan and “the children of God to be revealed” (verse 19). Heaven and earth will pass away (Mark 13:31), and they will be replaced by the new heaven and the new earth. At that time, the Lord, seated on His throne, says, “I am making everything new!” (Revelation 21:5). In the new creation, sin will be totally eradicated, and “there shall be no more curse” (Revelation 22:3, NKJV).

The new heaven and new earth are also mentioned in Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; and 2 Peter 3:13. Peter says that the new heaven and new earth will be “where righteousness dwells.” Isaiah says that “the former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind.” Things will be completely new, and the old order of things, with the accompanying sorrow and tragedy, will be gone.

The new earth will be free from sin, evil, sickness, suffering, and death. It will be earth as God originally intended it to be, prior to the curse of sin. It will be Eden restored.

A major feature of the new earth will be the New Jerusalem. John calls it “the Holy City . . . coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). This glorious city, with its streets of gold and pearly gates, is situated on a new, glorious earth. The tree of life will be there (Revelation 22:2). This city represents the final state of redeemed mankind, forever in fellowship with God: “God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. . . . His servants will serve him. They will see his face” (Revelation 21:3; 22:3–4).

In the new heaven and new earth, Scripture says, there are seven things notable for their absence—seven things that are “no more”:
• no more sea (Revelation 21:1)
• no more death (Revelation 21:4)
• no more mourning (Revelation 21:4)
• no more weeping (Revelation 21:4)
• no more pain (Revelation 21:4)
• no more curse (Revelation 22:3)
• no more night (Revelation 22:5)

The creation of the new heaven and new earth brings the promise that God “will wipe every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). This event comes after the tribulation, after the Lord’s second coming, after the millennial kingdom, after the final rebellion, after the final judgment of Satan, and after the great white throne judgment. The brief description of the new heaven and new earth is the last glimpse into eternity that the Bible gives.

I am a member of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, and I would like to report that the President of the United States finally has a Nobel Peace Prize medal.

Not the prize. The medal. There is a difference, and the difference is the entire story. Allow me to tell it properly. 

It is October again. The rain is hanging in the air over Henrik Ibsens gate the way it does, not quite falling, just waiting for you to commit to an umbrella. My shoes are wet. Someone has brought kanelboller. Kissinger is still on the wall.

You will remember that last year we gave the prize to María Corina Machado, the Venezuelan opposition leader, a woman who spent months in hiding and escaped her own country in disguise to collect it. You will also remember that the gentleman in Washington had wanted it very badly, and had told the world so, and had other heads of state tell the world so on his behalf. We gave it to her anyway. She dedicated it to him. That was her right. Laureates may dedicate their prizes to whomever they like, including their mothers, their movements and, as it turned out, the man who wanted it more than anyone alive.

Then, in January, she offered to give it to him.

We issued a statement. I would like you to read it slowly, because it is the most Norwegian paragraph this committee has ever published. “Once a Nobel Prize is announced, it cannot be revoked, shared or transferred to others. The decision is final and stands for all time.” We added that we do not comment on what laureates do afterwards. Kristin read the draft aloud at the table, and when she reached “stands for all time,” she paused, and said “well,” and we all knew exactly what “well” meant, and we sent it.

The day before our statement, the President told an American television host that accepting the prize “would be a great honor,” and that it was “a major embarrassment to Norway” that he hadn’t won it. A week later Ms Machado went to the White House and handed him the medal, “as a recognition for his unique commitment with our freedom.” He posted that she had presented him with her Nobel Peace Prize “for the work I have done.” He told reporters she had said nobody “in history” deserved it more.

The press asked us what we thought. We said nothing, because we had already said it: “stands for all time.” The medal is a disc of gold. The prize is a sentence in our records, and the sentence still has her name in it, and will when every person at this table is a portrait.

So here is what he has. He has a gold medal with Alfred Nobel’s face on one side and three naked men embracing on the other, which is the design of the Peace medal, and which I would give a great deal to see on the Resolute Desk. He does not have the prize. He has, if you will forgive the Norwegian bluntness, the packaging.

I said in an earlier season that the medal finds those people, and flees the ones who chase it. I would like to issue a correction. The medal can be carried. Someone can pick it up and walk it across a room. What it cannot carry is the reason it was given.

You might think that holding a peace medal would make a man think about peace, even a little, even out of politeness. Within days of receiving it, he sent our Prime Minister a message. “Dear Jonas,” it began, and I would like it engraved somewhere. “Considering your Country decided not to give me the Nobel Peace Prize for having stopped 8 Wars PLUS, I no longer feel an obligation to think purely of Peace.” He went on to explain why the United States must have “Complete and Total Control of Greenland,” noting that Denmark’s claim rested on a boat that had landed there hundreds of years ago, but that America had boats too.

Most laureates take years to disappoint us. This one did it in a long weekend, with someone else’s medal.

Our Prime Minister replied, not for the first time, that the prize is awarded by an independent Nobel Committee, and not by the Norwegian government. He has explained this so often that I believe it is now his most-repeated sentence in English. It is also, I am told, the one sentence in this entire affair that nobody in Washington has read.

This October we gave the prize to Navi Pillay, a South African judge who has spent half a century deciding what the law requires when nations do terrible things. The President described her at a campaign rally as “a mystery person.” “I never heard of the person,” he said. “Nobody did.” I find this lovely. It may be the most accurate thing anyone has said about our laureates. Most of them were mysteries to the powerful. That is usually why they qualified.

He called our decision “an indelible stain on the country of Norway.” He said, “We will not forget, Norway.” He said he should have received eight Nobel Peace Prizes, one for each war. I did the arithmetic on the tram. At one medal a year, he would have to live to roughly 2034 to collect them all, and we would have to agree, eight times, which we have never once done about anything, including the buns.

Then came this week.

Ms Machado has gone home to Venezuela, where the government that replaced the dictator she fought is one Washington has decided to work with. Asked about her return on Sunday, the President told reporters: “I don’t know anything about it, but I think she’s a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else? And I hope she’s safe.”

I have read that sentence perhaps thirty times. “She gave me her Nobel Prize, so how can I say anything else?” In one breath it tells you what the medal bought. Not her country’s election. Not her safety. A sentence of politeness, and the admission that politeness was purchased.

I keep a note on my desk about another medal. In 2022 the Russian journalist Dmitry Muratov auctioned his Nobel Peace Prize medal. It sold for $103.5 million, the highest price ever paid for one, and every dollar went to UNICEF for Ukrainian refugee children. That is what a peace medal can buy, if you sell it to the right people for the right reasons. Ms Machado’s medal bought one sentence. I don’t blame her. She paid full price, with the only currency a dissident has, which is hope. The man who accepted it was the one who set the exchange rate.

Medals have had strange lives before. In 1940, when the Nazis occupied Copenhagen, the chemist George de Hevesy dissolved two Nobel medals in a jar of acid so the soldiers would not find them. The jar sat on a shelf through the war, a brown liquid nobody looked at twice, and afterwards he recovered the gold and the Nobel Foundation recast them. When we gave the prize to Carl von Ossietzky in 1935, while he sat in a concentration camp, Hitler responded by forbidding Germans to accept any Nobel Prize at all. In 1973 Le Duc Tho refused the prize we gave him jointly with Kissinger, because there was no peace yet in Vietnam.

So the record includes a man who refused a prize he had won, a dictator who banned his citizens from accepting one, and a chemist who dissolved two to keep them from tyrants. It did not, until this year, include a man who accepted a prize he had not won, and then used it as a receipt.

And this week, according to the headlines, the President added Norway to a list of countries he does not think highly of, citing the Nobel. I will not repeat the word. We are a small country of five million people who mostly want to be left alone with our coffee. To be put on a list by the most powerful man on earth because a committee of five pensioners declined to give him a medal he already owns is, I confess, the greatest honor this country has received since the Winter Olympics.

People ask me whether we will ever give it to him. I answer as we always do. We do not discuss candidates, and anyone can be nominated, and the will of a dead Swedish arms dealer says the prize goes to whoever did the most for fraternity between nations. I will only add that fraternity between nations is a difficult case to make for a man who has just put a nation on a list.

It is dark now. Four o’clock dark. Kristin said “well” an hour ago, about something else entirely, and we went home. Somewhere in Washington there is a gold medal in a drawer or a frame, with Nobel’s profile and the three men embracing, catching the light in a room where a man is explaining to a camera that he no longer feels obliged to think purely of peace.

In Caracas, a woman who gave him that medal is back in her own country, hoping, and her name is still in our records, exactly where we wrote it. It stands for all time. We said so in January, in our most Norwegian paragraph, and we meant it.

The medal can travel. The prize cannot. He has the gold. She has the honor. Norway has the list.

Takk for i dag. My tram is late. It is the only thing in Norway that ever is.

text:
The Cuban Missile Crisis didn’t end because one side blinked.

On this day in 1962, the crisis hit its most dangerous point. That evening, Robert Kennedy met the Soviet ambassador privately in Washington.

The offer: the US would remove its nuclear missiles from Turkey, as long as no one ever said so publicly.

Khrushchev announced the Cuban withdrawal the next morning. The missiles in Turkey were quietly removed in April 1963. Washington didn’t acknowledge the trade until 1989.

The crisis ended in a compromise. The legend needed a winner.

Monday, November 2nd at 7pm CET, we will have Jeremy Pitt sharing a framework that he and collaborators have been developing for some time now, on 

* The Architecture of Re-Empowerment and Self-Governing Systems. 

https://t.co/1sWJSCIxIL

"This talk is divided into two sides: the dark side and the less dark side. On the dark side, we consider the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the Digital Transformation, and observe that despite the plethora [sic] of ethical guidelines, design methodologies, international standards, and even international regulation, AI is still being used, and is going to be used, as a tool for abstracted power and abnegated responsibility. It will consider a range of threats in the form of "Untrustworthy AI", which can potentially bring about democratic backsliding, or a kind of "digital feudalism", and even diminish the very essence of "being human". Then, on the less dark side, we discuss our attempts to offer an alternative approach, based on the idea of self-governing systems. This idea aims to integrate ideas from psychology economics and political science with architectures and algorithms from computer science, as a way of operationalising socio-technical systems in the public interest and common good; however, barriers to progress and adoption are also considered."

text:
This dog is running the exact test Stanford used to predict human futures. He is winning it. And you have never once passed it.

Not the way he does.

I'm going to tell you what is happening inside that skull in the three seconds before anything moves. By the end, you will not look at an animal, a snack, or your own willpower the same way.

Read slowly. The good part is at the bottom, and it is not what you think.

1/ THE TEST WITH NO NAME

In 1972, a psychologist named Walter Mischel sat a four-year-old at a table in a Stanford nursery school. One marshmallow in front of the child. One simple deal: wait about fifteen minutes and get a second one. Eat it now and the deal is dead.

Mischel did not care about marshmallows. He cared about something nobody could measure directly: the gap between wanting and doing. The tiny, invisible gap where a brain decides whether a feeling gets to drive the body.

Neuroscientists call that gap inhibitory control. It is the ability to not do the thing you are about to do.

Everything you respect in a person lives inside that gap. Patience. Discipline. Courage under fear. Not sending the text. Not taking the bet. Not taking the bait.

Everything you hate in a person lives there too.

For decades the headline was dramatic: kids who waited longer supposedly went on to better grades, better health, better lives. Then in 2018, researchers re-ran the numbers with larger and more diverse samples, and the effect shrank hard once family background was controlled for. The honest version is messier: waiting is partly a skill, partly a symptom of how safe and predictable your world has been.

That second part matters. Hold onto it. It comes back.

Because the animal you are about to watch is running Mischel's test with no instructions in his language, no promise of a second reward, and a lot more on the line than a marshmallow.

2/ THE THREE-SECOND WAR

Here is what happens in a brain when food is placed within reach and the order is: do not.

Layer one is ancient. Deep structures, including the striatum, treat the reward as a countdown to action. They do not ask permission. They fire.

Layer two is the newcomer. The prefrontal cortex is the part of the brain that says "not yet." It is slower, more expensive, and the first thing to fail when you are tired, stressed, or hungry.

These two layers do not cooperate. They fight. And the fight is not metaphorical: it shows up as measurable activity pulling in opposite directions.

Now add the chemical that makes it worse.

In the 1990s, Wolfram Schultz recorded dopamine neurons in monkeys and found something that rewired how the field thinks about desire. Dopamine does not spike when the reward arrives. It spikes when the reward is predicted. The signal for "something good is coming" is stronger than the good thing itself.

Read that again.

The wanting is the drug. The prize is almost an afterthought.

So the hardest moment for any brain is not the moment of eating. It is the stretch right before it, when prediction is at maximum and permission has not been granted. That is the window where self-control lives or dies.

And that window is where a dog can outperform most adults.

3/ THE MACHINE ON THE FRONT OF HIS FACE

Before we talk about his mind, we have to talk about the equipment he is fighting against.

A human nose carries roughly 6 million olfactory receptors. A dog's can carry up to 300 million, depending on the breed. The part of the dog brain that processes smell is, proportionally, dozens of times larger than ours.

Put differently: where you get a sentence, he gets the full book, with footnotes.

And here is the engineering detail almost nobody knows. When a dog exhales, the air does not leave through the same path it came in. Researchers who filmed airflow in dog noses found that exhaled air exits through slits at the sides, which sweeps new scent toward the nostrils instead of blowing it away. Humans breathe in and out through the same opening, which scatters the odor. Dogs run a continuous sampling loop.

Each nostril can work on its own, giving a kind of stereo smell: not just what, but which direction.

Some studies of trained detection dogs put their sensitivity in the range of parts per trillion. That is a teaspoon of something dissolved in an Olympic-size pool, and the dog still says "yes, it's in there."

So when a treat sits close to that nose, he is not "looking at" a snack.

He is being flooded by a data stream so rich that a human brain could not parse it. Every molecule says: eat me now.

And he waits.

Hold that thought. We are not done making this harder.

4/ HE WAS BUILT FOR THIS. LITERALLY.

Labradors did not become the world's favorite dog by accident.

Their ancestors worked the cold coasts of Newfoundland, hauling fishing lines and retrieving fish that slipped off the hooks. In the 1800s, British aristocrats imported them to retrieve waterfowl, and they bred for one trait above all: the "soft mouth."

A soft mouth means a dog can carry a bird in its jaws, over water, over distance, without leaving a mark. Think about what that demands. Powerful jaws, wired to a brain that has learned to hold back the very thing the jaws are built for.

Restraint was not a side effect of the breed. It was the job description.

For 31 consecutive years, from 1991 to 2021, the Labrador was the most popular dog in America by American Kennel Club registrations. Three decades at number one is not about cute. It is about a dog that can be trained by almost anyone, in almost any home, to do almost anything.

Which brings us to the part that surprised even the scientists.

5/ THE GENE THAT SHOULD MAKE THIS IMPOSSIBLE

In 2016, a team at the University of Cambridge led by Eleanor Raffan published a paper in Cell Metabolism about a single genetic change in Labradors.

A 14-letter deletion in a gene called POMC.

POMC is part of the machinery that tells a body "you have eaten, stop." The deletion disrupts two of the signals involved in switching hunger off. Dogs carrying it were measurably more food-motivated and heavier. The study found the deletion in about 23 percent of pet Labradors.

Now the twist, and I want you to sit with it.

Among Labradors selected as assistance dogs, the dogs trusted to guide people, work in public, and ignore food lying around in a world full of it, about 76 percent carried the deletion.

Read the numbers one more time.

The dogs most hungry by genetics were over-represented among the dogs that graduate as the most disciplined professionals in the breed. The researchers' leading idea: because training runs on food rewards, a dog that wants food badly learns faster, so those dogs are disproportionately chosen.

Translation: the strongest self-control in that group may not come from not wanting.

It may come from wanting a lot, and learning that waiting is how you get it.

Every productivity book you have read says to remove temptation. This says something stranger: the people, and animals, who can hold the line hardest are often the ones who feel the pull hardest. They just learned what the pull is for.

Hold that. We will use it.

6/ WHAT TRAINING ACTUALLY IS

Most people think training a dog means teaching it to obey.

It does not. It means building a conversation with a creature that cannot speak.

The foundations were laid more than a century ago. Edward Thorndike showed that behaviors followed by good outcomes get repeated. B. F. Skinner formalized it as operant conditioning. Then trainers like Karen Pryor brought a precise tool from marine mammal work into dog training: the marker. A sound that means "that exact thing you just did is what earns the reward."

The timing is brutal. Reinforcement works best when it lands within a couple of seconds of the behavior. Miss the window, and the dog learns something else entirely, like the wrong thing you were doing when the treat arrived.

So a well-trained "wait" is not a single command. It is thousands of repetitions of a tiny, repeated contract:

You hold. I release. You are rewarded for the hold itself.

Notice what is actually being taught. Not "don't eat." That is a punishment, and punishment teaches fear.

What is taught is "not yet." Which is a completely different mental object. A "not yet" has a future inside it. It is a promise that a decision is only postponed.

That is the first time most dogs in history have been asked to trust a future.

And humans take that exact trick for granted.

7/ THE DEAL WITH A 15,000-YEAR-OLD CLAUSE

Why does any of this work on a dog and not on, say, a wolf of the same weight?

Because of something that happened tens of thousands of years ago that scientists still argue about the exact date of. Somewhere between roughly 15,000 and 40,000 years back, a population of wolves started hanging around human camps. The bold, less fearful ones got more scraps. Over generations, a new animal emerged.

One of the strangest proofs came from a Soviet experiment that began in 1959. Geneticist Dmitry Belyaev and his team in Siberia bred silver foxes, selecting only for one thing: tameness. Not looks. Not size. Just who could tolerate a human hand.

Within a handful of generations, the foxes started changing in ways nobody had selected. Floppy ears. Curly tails. Patchy coats. Wagging, whining, seeking eye contact.

Select for friendliness and a whole body plan comes with it.

Then came the finding that should give you chills: in 2002, Brian Hare and colleagues showed in Science that dogs read human pointing gestures better than chimpanzees, our own close relatives. Even puppies do it. The ability is not learned from us. It is built into them.

This animal did not just learn to live with us. Its brain was reshaped to read us.

Which is why a human face looking at a dog is not a trivial thing. It is a signal that a dog's entire evolutionary history says is worth betting on.

8/ THE PART OF THE LOOP NOBODY SEES

In 2015, a Japanese team led by Miho Nagasawa published a study in Science that sounds like a joke until you read it.

When dogs and their owners gazed at each other, both sides showed a rise in oxytocin, the bonding hormone that normally links mothers and infants. It formed a loop: more gazing, more oxytocin, more gazing.

When oxytocin was given to dogs, they looked at their owners longer, and their owners' oxytocin rose too.

This is not a pet and a human. It is two nervous systems wired into one feedback circuit.

So when a dog sits, locked on a person's face, frozen in the most tense posture an animal can hold, it is not just resisting a snack.

It is looking for the signal. A look. A word. A shift in the face that means release.

The wait is not a wall. It is a listening posture.

Almost all of that dog's attention, the part of his brain we usually imagine is busy with the food, is turned toward you.

9/ THE EYE THAT SEES TIME DIFFERENTLY

Here is a fact that makes a still dog feel stranger.

Humans perceive a flickering light as steady once it flashes faster than about 60 times per second. For dogs, the threshold is often cited as roughly 70 to 80. They see motion in finer slices than we do.

Dog eyes are also tuned for dim light and movement rather than sharp detail, and their color vision is reduced compared to ours. At close range, much of the world is handled by whiskers, which sense small air currents, and by nose.

What that means is uncomfortable. When something drops, bounces, or moves, a dog may be processing that motion in a richer temporal resolution than you can.

Imagine your reaction time and then imagine someone who sees the world in more frames.

Then imagine that person choosing to do nothing.

That is not slowness. That is a fast machine deliberately set to idle.

10/ THE DOG WHO KNEW 1,022 WORDS

If you think this is only about reflex and food, meet Chaser.

Chaser was a border collie trained by retired psychology professor John Pilley. In a 2011 paper, Pilley reported that Chaser had learned the individual names of 1,022 toys. Not commands. Names. Say a name, and she would fetch that specific object out of a pile.

Even more interesting, when shown a brand-new object and asked for something with a name she did not know, she could pick the new one by exclusion. Children do exactly this around age two or three, and it is considered a sign of a real language-learning mechanism.

So this is the baseline we are working with. An animal that can map sounds onto objects, infer by elimination, read pointing, track a human gaze, and run a long-term contract about what happens next.

Now put that animal in a room with a reward he wants more than almost anything, and ask him to do something that requires no movement at all.

The most advanced thing in the room is not the camera.

11/ WHY YOUR BRAIN CANNOT LEAVE

Let us talk about you for a second.

Why do some clips make you stay for ten seconds like someone nailed your feet to the floor?

Because tension is the oldest storytelling engine there is. Open a loop. Delay the closure. Let the audience feel the pressure build. The brain hates unfinished business. Psychologists have argued for decades about the details of the so-called Zeigarnik effect, the idea that interrupted tasks stick in memory, and the lab results are mixed. But the practical truth every editor, comedian and magician knows is simple: when you promise a payoff and make people wait, they stay.

Dopamine does the rest. Remember Schultz: the spike comes from anticipation, not arrival. Every second of delay is a second of rising prediction. The wait is not the cost of the reward. The wait is the product.

That is why the strongest clips on the internet are rarely about the thing happening. They are about the almost.

The nearly. The held breath. The half-second where two outcomes are both still possible.

A pitch before it crosses the plate. A drop before the beat. A hand hovering over a button.

You are not watching an event. You are watching a decision be made in public, in real time, by a creature that cannot explain itself.

And you will watch it again. Most people do. The second time is not for the ending.

It is for the three seconds before.

12/ WHAT THE DOG KNOWS THAT YOU DO NOT

Back to Mischel, because the story did not end in 1972.

Later researchers found that the children who waited longest did not just grit their teeth. They used tricks. They covered their eyes. They sang. They turned their chairs around. They imagined the marshmallow as a cloud, a picture, something not edible. In other words, they did not out-muscle the temptation. They changed what the temptation was.

That is the real skill. Not suppression. Reframing.

And the second finding, the one I told you to hold on to: children waited longer when the environment gave them reasons to trust the adult. In follow-up experiments, kids who had first experienced an unreliable researcher, who broke small promises, gave up on waiting quickly. Kids who had met a reliable one waited far longer.

Waiting is not only willpower. Waiting is trust in a future that someone else controls.

Now look at the animal again.

He is not holding on because he is strong. He is holding on because, across thousands of repetitions, every single "not yet" ended in "now." The person across from him has never once broken the deal.

His self-control is built out of a reliable relationship.

That is a much more human sentence than any about willpower.

13/ THREE RULES YOU CAN STEAL

You do not need a dog. You need his architecture. Here is how it translates.

Rule one: decide before the moment arrives.

In 1999, psychologist Peter Gollwitzer described implementation intentions, plans in the form "if X happens, I will do Y." A later meta-analysis of nearly a hundred studies found that making these specific if-then plans had a medium-to-large effect on goal achievement, bigger than most motivational techniques people pay for. The dog's wait command is exactly this. If food appears, then I hold. The decision was made in advance, when the brain was calm.

You will not out-argue a craving in real time. You pre-commit.

Rule two: give your attention an anchor.

The dog does not stare at the snack. He stares at a face. Attention is the one resource you can aim, and what you aim it at decides what wins. Looking away from the thing you want is not weakness. It is engineering. Cover the screen. Leave the phone in the other room. Change the object of your focus, not the strength of your fist.

Rule three: build a release signal.

Restraint without a release is just suffering. A dog can hold because he knows precisely what ends it. A word. A look. A tiny, clear "go."

Most people fail at discipline because they have no end condition. They try to resist forever. No brain can. Write the finish line, the reward, the time you are allowed. Then enjoy it without guilt, because a reward you feel guilty about teaches your brain nothing.

Hold. Wait. Release.

Three verbs. One complete system.

14/ THE UNCOMFORTABLE QUESTION

Now flip the lens.

Where in your life are you the one at the table, with something you want sitting inches from your face, and no deal on offer?

Be specific. Not "I should be more disciplined." That is a vibe.

Name the exact situation. The exact time of day. The exact first move your hand makes before you decide anything.

Then ask: who is across from me? Is there anyone whose "wait" I trust enough to actually wait?

Because that is the quiet lesson underneath the cute animal. Self-control is rarely a solo sport. It is a relationship between you, a goal, and someone or something that keeps its promises.

If you are failing at patience, check your environment before you check your character. The marshmallow kids who gave up fast were not weak. They had learned, rationally, that waiting does not pay.

Fix the contract and the behavior follows.

15/ THE MYTH OF THE SIMPLE ANIMAL

Here is a belief worth killing: that a trained dog is a dog that has been broken.

The best working dogs in the world are the opposite. Guide dogs are taught something called intelligent disobedience. If a handler commands "forward" into traffic, the dog is trained to refuse. A creature that has spent months learning to follow instructions is also taught precisely when to override them, because it understands the goal behind the order.

Detection dogs, the ones that work airports and disaster zones, are trained to find a target and then do nothing dramatic. No grabbing. No digging at a source that might be unsafe. A calm, fixed signal: here. They hold their position near something their nose is screaming about, and wait for a human to take over.

Search and rescue animals work through rubble where every instinct says dig, and they learn to mark and stay.

None of this is blind obedience. It is selective inhibition at professional level: knowing which impulse to follow and which to park.

Most humans never reach that standard in their own working lives.

16/ THE SCIENTISTS WHO PUT DOGS IN BRAIN SCANNERS

If you want to know what is going on inside, you could just ask. A dog cannot answer.

So at Emory University, neuroscientist Gregory Berns did something that sounded impossible. Starting around 2011, his team trained pet dogs to walk into an MRI machine and lie still, awake, with no sedation and no restraints. The scanner is loud, the space is tight, and moving blurs the image. The dogs volunteered, because the training turned stillness into a game they understood.

The images showed a dog's reward system lighting up in response to cues. In one experiment, the caudate, a region tied to anticipation of something good, responded strongly to the scent of a familiar person.

Read that sentence one more time. A part of the brain that evolved to predict food and safety lit up for the smell of someone the dog loves.

For a dog, the lines between "food", "safety" and "you" are not as separate as ours.

This matters for the thing you came here for. Because it changes the question. It is not "how does the dog resist?" It is "what is the dog choosing to want more?"

And the answer, again and again in the data, is the relationship.

17/ THE PRICE OF STILLNESS

Let us be honest about the cost, because it is easy to romanticize.

Holding still against a strong impulse is metabolically and psychologically expensive. In humans, studies on ego depletion suggested that willpower works like a muscle that tires. That theory has taken heavy criticism in replication attempts, and large efforts failed to reproduce the original effect. Honest science says: we do not fully know the mechanism.

But anyone who has watched an animal hold a posture for a few seconds longer than seems possible can see something in the body. A quiver. A tightening around the eyes. A tail that cannot decide. The impulse does not vanish. It has to be carried.

That is why the release matters so much. That is why a good trainer pays so generously for the hold. Not because it is easy.

Because it is not.

The loudest lesson on the internet is the one about being "disciplined." The most useful one is quieter: discipline is expensive, so spend it where it counts, build systems that reduce how often you need it, and pay yourself back every time you do.

One more thing about the stillness. It is contagious. A calm animal calms the person across from it, and a calm person steadies the animal back. Researchers who study working dogs keep finding that handler mood leaks down the leash. So when you try to hold a line, do not only manage yourself. Manage the room, the people in it, and the signals you are broadcasting. Nobody waits alone for long. Build a circle that keeps its promise, and the waiting stops feeling like a sacrifice and starts feeling like a real plan.

18/ WHAT THIS REALLY IS

Step back.

Strip away the cute. Strip away the music, the edit, the algorithm that put this in front of you.

What remains is a very old negotiation between two species. One brings a gift that cannot be eaten yet. One brings a decision that cannot be rushed. Both are betting that the other will keep the deal.

Humans have written entire religions about that bargain. We call it faith, or patience, or trust.

An animal that cannot read a word does it before breakfast.

And maybe the reason a short clip of a dog doing nothing at all can feel so oddly powerful is that it is one of the last places on a screen where you can watch someone choose the slow reward in a world designed to sell you the fast one.

Every app on your phone is built to collapse the gap between wanting and getting.

This is a creature that widens it. On purpose. For love.

19/ NOW GO BACK

Here is what I am asking you to do.

Watch it again. But this time, do not wait for the moment the tension breaks. Watch the stillness before it. Watch what the eyes are doing. Watch what the body refuses to do.

You are looking at the same gap Mischel stared at in 1972. The same fight between the old brain and the new. The same chemistry Schultz found in monkeys. The same engineered nose, the same ancient deal, the same oxytocin loop, the same 15,000 years of two species learning to read each other.

All of it compressed into a few seconds you would normally scroll past.

If it made you smile, good. That is the surface.

If it made you ask where in your own life you rush the reward, even better.

And if you only take one thing from this entire thread, take this: self-control is not about having less desire. The dog wants it more than you ever will.

It is about having a reason to wait that is bigger than the want.

Find that reason. Build the contract. Trust someone to keep their half.

Then hold.

If this made you think, repost the first post so another person can find it. Follow for more of the science hiding inside the clips you thought you understood.

And tell me in the replies: what is the one thing you could never wait for?

text:
Connecting the Thread

Our recent entries have taken us beyond Europe to examine Christian persecution in Africa and Asia.

Charles Lwanga was executed in Uganda after refusing to abandon his faith under royal pressure. Paul Miki was crucified in Japan when Christianity became associated with foreign political influence.

Andrew Kim Taegon encountered a comparable conflict in Korea.

All three lived in societies where rulers feared that Christianity could undermine established political and social authority.

But their experiences also demonstrate that Christianity had become a genuinely international religion, embraced by people whose cultures and political circumstances differed considerably from those of Europe.

The broader historical connection reaches back to the earliest Christian martyrs.

Under the Roman Empire, Christians sometimes faced punishment because their religious commitments appeared incompatible with public obligations.

Centuries later, medieval Europeans debated the competing claims of religious and royal authority. The Reformation intensified these disputes, while the English constitutional tradition and American founding gradually produced stronger protections for religious conscience.

Those developments did not directly create religious liberty in Korea, nor should Korea's history be reduced to an extension of Western political history.

But the underlying moral question was familiar:

Does political authority include the right to compel religious belief or punish peaceful religious allegiance?

Andrew Kim's life demonstrates the consequences of answering that question without meaningful limits on government power.

His story also offers a reminder that Christianity's history cannot be understood exclusively through the achievements of European civilization.

Korean believers developed their own religious communities, preserved their faith under persecution, and eventually established institutions that became deeply rooted in Korean society.

Their experience belongs to the wider history of Christianity while retaining its distinct Korean character.

Early Christian Martyrs → Medieval Church and Crown → English Reformation → Religious Conscience and Constitutional Liberty → Christianity's Expansion in Asia → Korea's Lay Christian Communities → Andrew Kim Taegon → Modern Religious Freedom

There is one final detail worth remembering.

Andrew Kim had spent years preparing for the priesthood.

He traveled enormous distances, endured dangerous conditions, learned foreign languages, and accepted separation from his family.

After all that preparation, he was permitted barely thirteen months of priestly ministry before his execution.

Measured only by the length of his career, his achievements might appear insignificant.

But his influence cannot be measured simply by the number of years he served.

He became a lasting example to Korean Christians because he returned to a persecuted community, remained faithful when imprisoned, and used his final words to encourage believers to care for one another.

Andrew Kim Taegon did not live long enough to witness the survival and growth of Korean Christianity. He died trusting that the faith he served would endure beyond him.

text:
Have you sat with 2nd Peter 2 lately? 

It feels like it was written for today.

Peter says false teachers will show up among us, just like false prophets did long ago. 

They tiptoe in with destructive ideas and even deny the Lord who bought them. 

They do not announce themselves. 

They use smooth words and Bible language, but they twist things until the real Jesus gets concealed.

Many people follow their sinful ways, and because of that, the way of truth gets talked about poorly. 

That sounds familiar? 

Teachers and influencers claim to follow Jesus, then treat sin like it is no big deal. 

Sexual behavior the Bible calls wrong gets celebrated.
Greed gets dressed up as blessing.
People chase whatever feels good and call it freedom. 

When real Christians push back, the world points at the mess and says that is what Christianity is. 

Jesus' name gets dragged through the mud.

These teachers are greedy. 

They use made-up stories to take advantage of people. 

You see versions of the gospel that are mostly about getting rich or living your best life, while they collect the money and the attention. 

They promise liberty, but Peter says they are slaves to their own corruption. 

They offer a way out of God's rules so people can do whatever they want, but it only locks them tighter into sin.

God has never been soft on this. 

He did not spare the angels who sinned. 
He flooded the world in Noah's day. 
He burned Sodom and Gomorrah as a warning. 

At the same time, He knows how to rescue those who stay faithful, just like He rescued Noah and Lot. 

Judgment is very real, but so is the rescue.

The chapter ends with a dog going back to its vomit and a washed pig rolling in the mud again. 

Some people hear the truth, step away from the mess for a while, then turn right back around.

So what do we do? 
We stay awake. 

We measure what we hear against Scripture, not against what is popular or what feels better. 

We stay close to the real Jesus. 

Even when false teaching spreads, God still knows how to keep His people. 

This chapter is a warning, but it is also a reminder that truth still matters and God still saves. 🙌

text:
The full speech from the Dock:

MY LORDS — I am asked what have I to say why sentence of death should not be pronounced on me, according to law. I have nothing to say that can alter your predetermination, nor that it will become me to say, with any view to the mitigation of that sentence which you are to pronounce, and I must abide by. But I have that to say which interests me more than life, and which you have laboured to destroy. I have much to say why my reputation should be rescued from the load of false accusation and calumny which has been cast upon it, I do not imagine that, seated where you are, your mind can be so free from prejudice as to receive the least impression from what I am going to utter. I have no hopes that I can anchor my character in the breast of a court constituted and trammelled as this is. I only wish, and that is the utmost that I expect, that your lordships may suffer it to float down your memories untainted by the foul breath of prejudice, until it finds some more hospitable harbour to shelter it from the storms by which it is buffetted. Was I only to suffer death, after being adjudged guilty by your tribunal, I should bow in silence, and meet the fate that awaits me without a murmur; but the sentence of the law which delivers my body to the executioner will, through the ministry of the law, labour in its own vindication, to consign my character to obloquy; for there must be guilt somewhere, whether in the sentence of the court, or in the catastrophe, time must determine. A man in my situation has not only to encounter the difficulties of fortune, and the force of power over minds which it has corrupted or subjugated, but the difficulties of established prejudice. The man dies, but his memory lives. That mine may not perish, that it may live in the respect of my countrymen, I seize upon this opportunity to vindicate myself from some of the charges alleged against me. When my spirit shall be wafted to a more friendly port — when my shade shall have joined the bands of those martyred heroes who have shed their blood on the scaffold and in the field in the defence of their country and of virtue, this is my hope — I wish that my memory and name may animate those who survive me, while I look down with complacency on the destruction of that perfidious government which upholds its domination by blasphemy of the Most High — which displays its power over man, as over the beasts of the forest — which sets man upon his brother, and lifts his hand, in the name of God, against the throat of his fellow who believes or doubts a little more or a little less than the government standard — a government which is steeled to barbarity by the cries of the orphans, and the tears of the widows it has made.

[Here Lord Norbury interrupted Mr. Emmet, saying — "that the mean and wicked enthusiasts who felt as he did, were not equal to the accomplishment of their wild designs."]

I appeal to the immaculate God — I swear by the Throne of Heaven, before which I must shortly appear — by the blood of the murdered patriots who have gone before me — that my conduct has been, through all this peril, and through all my purposes, governed only by the conviction which I have uttered, and by no other view than that of the emancipation of my country from the superinhuman oppression under which she has so long and too patiently travailed; and I confidently hope that, wild and chimerical as it may appear, there is still union and strength in Ireland to accomplish this noblest of enterprises. Of this I speak with confidence, of intimate knowledge, and with the consolation that appertains to that confidence. Think not, my lords, I say this for the petty gratification of giving you a transitory uneasiness. A man who never yet raised his voice to assert a lie, will not hazard his character with posterity, by asserting a falsehood on a subject so important to his country, and on an occasion like this. Yes, my lords, a man who does not wish to have his epitaph written until his country is liberated, will not leave a weapon in the power of envy, or a pretence to impeach the probity which he means to preserve, even in the grave, to which tyranny consigns him.

[Here he was again interrupted by the court.]

Again I say, that what I have spoken was not intended for your lordship, whose situation I commisserate rather than envy — my expressions were for my countrymen. If there is a true Irishman present, let my last words cheer him in the hour of his affliction.

[Here he was again interrupted. Lord Norbury said he did not sit there to hear treason.]

I have always understood it to be the duty of a judge, when a prisoner has been convicted, to pronounce the sentence of the law. I have also understood that judges sometimes think it their duty to hear with patience, and to speak with humanity; to exhort the victim of the laws, and to offer, with tender benignity, their opinions of the motives by which he was actuated in the crime of which he was adjudged guilty. That a judge has thought it his duty so to have done, I have no doubt; but where is the boasted freedom of your institutions — where is the vaunted impartiality, clemency, and mildness of your courts of justice if an unfortunate prisoner, whom your policy, and not justice, is about to deliver into the hands of the executioner, is not suffered to explain his motives sincerely and truly, and to vindicate the principles by which he was actuated? My lords, it may be a part of the system of angry justice to bow a man's mind by humiliation to the purposed ignominy of the scaffold; but worse to me than the purposed shame, or the scaffold's terrors, would be the shame of such foul and unfounded imputations as have been laid against me in this court. You, my lord, are a judge; I am the supposed culprit. I am a man; you are a man also. By a revolution of power we might change places, though we never could change characters. If I stand at the bar of this court, and dare not vindicate my character, what a farce is your justice! If I stand at this bar and dare not vindicate my character, how dare you calumniate it. Does the sentence of death, which your unhallowed policy inflicts on my body, condemn my tongue to silence and my reputation to reproach? Your executioner may abridge the period of my existence; but while I exist I shall not forbear to vindicate my character and motives from your aspersions; and, as a man, to whom fame is dearer than life, I will make the last use of that life in doing justice to that reputation which is to live after me, and which is the only legacy I can leave to those I honor and love, and for whom I am proud to perish. As men, my lords, we must appear on the great day at one common tribunal; and it will then remain for the Searcher of all hearts to show a collective universe, who was engaged in the most virtuous actions, or swayed by the purest motives — my country's oppressor, or —

[Here he was interrupted, and told to listen to the sentence of the law.]

My lords, will a dying man be denied the legal privilege of exculpating himself in the eyes of the community from an undeserved reproach, thrown upon him during his trial, by charging him with ambition, and attempting to cast away for a paltry consideration the liberties of his country? Why did your lordships insult me? Or rather, why insult justice, in demanding of me why sentence of death should not be pronounced against me? I know, my lords, that form prescribes that you should ask the question. The form also presents the right of answering. This, no doubt, may be dispensed with, and so might the whole ceremony of the trial, since sentence was already pronounced at the Castle before the jury were empanelled. Your lordships are but the priests of the oracle, and I insist on the whole of the forms.

[Here Mr. Emmet paused, and the court desired him to proceed.]

I am charged with being an emissary of France. An emissary of France! and for what end? It is alleged that I wished to sell the independence of my country; and for what end? Was this the object of my ambition? And is this the mode by which a tribunal of justice reconciles contradiction? No; I am no emissary; and my ambition was to hold a place among the deliverers of my country, not in power nor in profit, but in the glory of the achievement. Sell my country's independence to France! and for what? Was it a change of masters? No, but for my ambition. Oh, my country, was it personal ambition that could influence me? Had it been the soul of my actions, could I not, by my education and fortune, by the rank and consideration of my family, have placed myself amongst the proudest of your oppressor. My Country was my Idol. To it I sacrificed every selfish, every endearing sentiment; and for it I now offer up myself, O God! No, my lords; I acted as an Irishman, determined on delivering my country from the yoke of a foreign and unrelenting tyranny, and the more galling yoke of a domestic faction, which is its joint partner and perpetrator in the patricide, from the ignominy existing with an exterior of splendour and a conscious depravity. It was the wish of my heart to extricate my country from this doubly rivetted despotism — I wished to place her independence beyond the reach of any power on earth. I wished to exalt her to that proud station in the world. Connection with France was, indeed, intended, but only as far as mutual interest would sanction or require. Were the French to assume any authority inconsistent with the purest independence, it would be signal for their destruction. We sought their aid — and we sought it as we had assurance we should obtain it — as auxiliaries in war, and allies in peace. Were the French to come as invaders or enemies, uninvited by the wishes of the people, I should oppose them to the utmost of my strength. Yes! my countrymen, I should advise you to meet them upon the beach with a sword in one hand, and a torch in the other. I would meet them with all the destructive fury of war. I would animate my countrymen to immolate them in their boats, before they had contaminated the soil of my country. If they succeeded in landing, and if forced to retire before superior discipline, I would dispute every inch of ground, burn every blade of grass, and the last entrenchment of liberty should be my grave. What I could not do myself, if I should fall, I should leave as a last charge to my countrymen to accomplish; because I should feel conscious that life, any more than death, is unprofitable when a foreign nation holds my country in subjection. But it was not as an enemy that the succours of France were to land. I looked, indeed, for the assistance of France; but I wished to prove to France and to the world that Irishmen deserved to be assisted — that they were indignant at slavery, and ready to assert the independence and liberty of their country; I wished to procure for my country the guarantee which Washington procured for America — to procure an aid which, by its example, would be as important as its valour; disciplined, gallant, pregnant with science and experience; that of a people who would perceive the good, and polish the rough points of our character. They would come to us as strangers, and leave us as friends, after sharing in our perils and elevating our destiny. These were my objects; not to receive new taskmasters, but to expel old tyrants. It was for these ends I sought aid from France; because France, even as an enemy, could not be more implacable than the enemy already in the bosom of my country.

[Here he was interrupted by the court.]

I have been charged with that importance in the emancipation of my country, as to be considered the key-stone of the combination of Irishmen; or, as your lordship expressed it, 'the life and blood of the conspiracy.' You do me honour overmuch; you have given to the subaltern all the credit of a superior. There are men engaged in this conspiracy who are not only superior to me, but even to your own conceptions of yourself, my lord — men before the splendour of whose genius and virtues I should bow with respectful deference, and who would think themselves disgraced by shaking your blood-stained hand.

[Here he was interrupted.]

What, my lord, shall you tell me, on the passage to the scaffold, which that tyranny (of which you are only the intermediary executioner) has erected for my murder, that I am accountable for all the blood that has and will be shed in this struggle of the oppressed against the oppressor — shall you tell me this, and must I be so very a slave as not to repel it? I do not fear to approach the Omnipotent Judge to answer for the conduct of my whole life; and am I to be appalled and falsified by a mere remnant of mortality here? By you, too, although if it were possible to collect all the innocent blood that you have shed in your unhallowed ministry in one great reservoir your lordship might swim in it.

[Here the judge interfered.]

Let no man dare, when I am dead, to charge me with dishonor; let no man attaint my memory, by believing that I could have engaged in any cause but that of my country's liberty and independence; or that I could have become the pliant minion of power, in the oppression and misery of my country. The proclamation of the Provisional Government speaks for our views; no inference can be tortured from it to countenance barbarity or debasement at home, or subjection, humiliation, or treachery from abroad. I would not have submitted to a foreign oppressor, for the same reason that I would resist the foreign and domestic oppressor. In the dignity of freedom, I would have fought upon the threshold of my country, and its enemy should enter only by passing over my lifeless corpse. And am I, who lived but for my country, and who have subjected myself to the dangers of the jealous and watchful oppressor, and the bondage of the grave, only to give my countrymen their rights, and my country her independence, am I to be loaded with calumny, and not suffered to resent it? No; God forbid!

[Here Lord Norbury told Mr. Emmet that his sentiments and language disgraced his family and his education, but more particularly his father, Dr. Emmet, who was a man, if alive, that would not countenance such opinions. To which Mr. Emmet replied: ]

If the spirits of the illustrious dead participate in the concerns and cares of those who were dear to them in this transitory life, oh! ever dear and venerated shade of my departed father, look down with scrutiny upon the conduct of your suffering son, and see if I have, even for a moment, deviated from those principles of morality and patriotism which it was your care to instill into my youthful mind, and for which I am now about to offer up my life. My lords, you are impatient for the sacrifice. The blood which you seek is not congealed by the artificial terrors which surround your victim — it circulates warmly and unruffled through the channels which God created for noble purposes, but which you are now bent to destroy, for purposes so grievous that they cry to heaven. Be yet patient! I have but a few more words to say — I am going to my cold and silent grave — my lamp of life is nearly extinguished — my race is run — the grave opens to receive me, and I sink into its bosom. I have but one request to ask at my departure from this world, it is — THE CHARITY OF ITS SILENCE.

Let no man write my epitaph; for as no man who knows my motives dare now vindicate them, let not prejudice or ignorance asperse them. Let them and me rest in obscurity and peace; and my tomb remain uninscribed, and my memory in oblivion, until other times and other men can do justice to my character. When my country takes her place among the nations of the earth, then and not till then, let my epitaph be written.

- Robert Emmet

text:
I've been seeing quite a few people talking about $PONS again lately, so I wanted to share some thoughts on it, especially with Robinhood's Q3 earnings report coming up

Looking at the daily chart, $PONS is currently trading around a $200M market cap, down roughly 78% from its ATH of approximately $900M back in September

After a prolonged correction, price seems to be stabilizing around the $200M area. Selling pressure appears to be easing, but volume remains relatively weak, and there hasn't been enough buying interest to confirm a reversal

So for now, I'd rather treat this as an interesting area to watch than call it the bottom

What keeps me interested in PONS isn't just the chart, but its position within Robinhood Chain

Based on the data I've been tracking, Pons currently accounts for roughly 93.7% of launchpad fees on Robinhood Chain over the past 30 days. There hasn't really been another launchpad on the chain capable of challenging its dominance

However, having a dominant market share doesn't necessarily mean revenue is still growing

Over the past 30 days, Pons generated approximately $21.36M in fees, while protocol revenue came in at around $3.22M. Daily revenue has also dropped to anywhere from tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand dollars, significantly below the levels we saw during September's peak

This is probably the biggest issue right now. Pons still dominates its market, but that market itself has been shrinking

And when compared with larger launchpads like https://t.co/MDT1D8rHCr and other competitors, Pons still has quite a gap to close in terms of revenue

As for tokenomics, I still really like the buyback & burn mechanism

Around 80% of protocol revenue is allocated toward buying back and burning PONS

According to Dune data from mid-October, approximately 322.76M PONS had been burned, representing 32.28% of the original total supply

That's a pretty impressive figure, especially for a launchpad that's only been around for a few months

However, a large cumulative burn doesn't mean the current burn rate is still strong. As revenue declines, the amount available for buybacks naturally decreases as well

The mechanism still has long-term value, but for it to generate meaningful buying pressure again, trading activity on Pons needs to recover

Another thing I don't think we should overlook is the quality of tokens launching on the platform

Recent data suggests the graduation rate is only around 0.9%. Most tokens never make it past the bonding curve, while some projects have also faced rug-related issues and questionable supply distributions

To be fair, this is a common problem across meme launchpads. But if Pons wants sustainable growth, improving the quality of projects matters just as much as increasing the number of launches

Another person worth mentioning here is Bonk Guy (@theunipcs)

He's been one of the strongest PONS bulls since the early days, building his position when the market cap was still around $4M–$6.5M

Based on the recent portfolio data I've seen, he's still holding approximately 10.9M PONS, despite his overall portfolio taking a significant hit from its September peak

I genuinely respect that level of conviction. Holding such a large position through a drawdown like this isn't easy

Of course, a major trader continuing to hold doesn't guarantee a recovery, but it does suggest that his long-term thesis on Pons hasn't really changed

On the development side, the team is still actively building

@MEADGod recently mentioned preparations for the Pons Mobile App, alongside backend upgrades aimed at improving trading performance and the overall user experience

The new web app has also been rolled out, introducing features such as limit orders, social features, and support for additional trading pairs involving tokenized stocks

I actually like this direction. If Pons wants to maintain its position over the long run, it needs to attract real users rather than relying entirely on occasional memecoin frenzies

The Mobile App is one of the catalysts I'm looking forward to most, although there's still no confirmed release date

And the nearest catalyst I'm watching is Robinhood's Q3 earnings report on October 27

This isn't an event specifically focused on Robinhood Chain, but I'm curious whether Vlad Tenev will share anything new regarding Robinhood's blockchain strategy, tokenized stocks, or plans to bring more Robinhood users into its on-chain ecosystem

If we get some meaningful positive updates, I think Robinhood Chain could see another wave of attention, and Pons would naturally be one of the projects worth watching

That said, I don't expect a single earnings call to suddenly reverse the market trend. What matters more is whether that attention actually translates into trading volume and revenue

Looking further ahead, I think Pons' biggest challenge remains its dependence on Robinhood Chain

Even with over 90% launchpad market share, sustained growth will be difficult unless the ecosystem attracts fresh capital and new users

More importantly, Robinhood bringing users from its main app into on-chain products is the catalyst I'm most interested in over the long term

So where do I stand on PONS at these levels?

Personally, I'm still leaning slightly bullish, but not simply because the token is down nearly 78% from its ATH

What I like is that Pons still holds a dominant position, has a buyback & burn mechanism tied to actual protocol revenue, continues to ship product updates, and has several potential catalysts ahead

On the other hand, revenue has declined significantly, the burn rate has slowed, graduation rates remain low, and the entire growth thesis still depends heavily on a recovery in Robinhood Chain activity

For me, the $200M area is worth watching closely. If price manages to hold this range, volume starts improving, and the chart begins forming a healthier bullish structure, I'll have more reasons to turn bullish

But if volume continues to fade and this support breaks down, there's still a real possibility that PONS moves toward lower levels

I don't think PONS offers the same massive asymmetric opportunity it did when Bonk Guy first entered at a market cap of just a few million dollars

Still, if Robinhood Chain genuinely enters another growth cycle, Pons would be one of the first tokens I'd want to keep an eye on

For now, I'd rather stay patient, watch how the market develops, and see what Vlad has to share instead of rushing in just because the price has fallen so much

text:
“It's your edges, I think. They're softer.”

Her fingertips lingered against your temple. You felt their warmth before they touched you, and when she withdrew her hand, the sensation remained.

“Dreams do that sometimes. They forget where one thing ends and another begins.”

She lowered herself onto the mattress beside you. It dipped beneath her weight with a perfectly ordinary creak, although her reflection, visible in the dark water beneath the bed, remained standing by the window.

Eliana noticed it.

“Oh, don't be difficult.”

The reflection turned its head.

“You've already had your turn.”

It dissolved into a scatter of silver fish.

She watched them swim away with mild satisfaction before settling her attention upon you again.

For a while, she said nothing.

Her fingers found the edge of the blanket and began smoothing a little wrinkle that kept reappearing whenever she looked away. Outside, the moon had settled against the horizon, where it appeared to be listening to the distant sound of bells.

A pale butterfly drifted into the room.

Its wings were made of folded paper, covered in handwriting that changed whenever you tried to read it. It settled upon your pillow, opened its wings, and released the faint sound of someone laughing.

Eliana's expression softened.

“Oh. That one's yours.”

She leaned closer to examine it.

“I found it caught in a dream about a staircase. It was very upset. Apparently, someone had forgotten the rest of the house.”

The butterfly fluttered onto her outstretched finger.

“It wouldn't tell me whose laughter it was.”

She studied the shifting letters upon its wings.

“Perhaps you'll remember.”

Rather than asking, she offered her hand, allowing the little creature to step onto your fingers if you wished. Its paper feet were warm, and the laughter it carried felt strangely familiar, like the memory of an afternoon whose details had long since faded.

Eliana watched your expression with quiet curiosity.

“It's peculiar, isn't it? How something can be forgotten and still feel like home.”

A small silence followed.

Then, very softly:

“I think that's why I like dreams.”

Her gaze wandered toward the open window, where the sky was beginning to change. Pale gold gathered along the edges of the clouds, but the stars refused to disappear. They simply grew translucent, drifting among the morning colors like little pieces of glass.

“Things don't always have to leave just because they've finished happening.”

She rested her hand beside yours upon the blanket, close enough for your fingers to touch.

“Sometimes they become something else.”

The butterfly unfolded into a tiny white flower.

Eliana seemed pleased.

“Oh, that's much prettier.”

She leaned forward to smell it.

“Although I rather liked the laughter.”

A second flower appeared in her hair, then a third upon the pillow. Somewhere beyond the walls, a garden began growing through the morning, its branches brushing softly against the unseen edges of the room.

The ceiling darkened.

For a moment, the stars overhead went out.

Something moved behind them.

Eliana looked up.

Her expression did not change, but the hand resting beside yours shifted, her fingers gently curling around your own.

“Mm. No.”

The darkness paused.

“You weren't invited.”

A low sound passed through the room, like a distant door being dragged across stone. The shadows beneath the furniture stretched toward the bed, gathering into shapes that seemed almost familiar.

Eliana watched them with mild disapproval.

“That's rather rude. They've only just arrived.”

The darkness pressed against the ceiling.

She sighed, so quietly it was almost lost beneath the rain.

“I know. You're lonely.”

For a moment, something immense seemed to lean closer from the other side of the stars.

“But you can't keep frightening everyone just because you don't like being forgotten.”

Eliana raised her free hand.

[Cont]

In India, we believe that every village is protected by a particular goddess, lovingly worshipped as the Grama Devatha (village deity).
We believe that our beloved Vizianagaram is protected by Sri Sri Sri Paidithalli Ammavaru. 🙏❤️
Yesterday and today, devotees have been observing this beautiful tradition. They decorate clay pots, fill them with rice and dal, cover them with a diya (lamp), and carry them to the temple as an offering to the Goddess. Some devotees offer neem water as well. According to our local belief, the Goddess resides in the neem tree, which is why neem trees hold a special place in many of our homes.
It is truly beautiful to witness devotees walking barefoot all the way to the temple, carrying their decorated pots filled with offerings and hearts filled with unwavering faith.
What I love most about this tradition is the pure devotion behind it. Every offering tells a story of faith, gratitude, hope, and surrender. The beauty lies not merely in the rituals themselves, but in the heartfelt belief with which people perform them.
I believe that God lives in our faith — in the sincerity of our prayers, the purity of our hearts, and the hope we carry within us. ❤️🙏
May Sri Paidithalli Ammavaru bless everyone, fulfil the sincere wishes of her devotees, and bring peace, prosperity, health, and happiness to every home.
Sarve Janah Sukhino Bhavantu 🙏
May all beings everywhere be happy and live in peace. 🌸🌏
