text:
America's first chartered Black-owned bank was founded because a white shopkeeper in Charlotte County got scared and ran his mouth. He was holding a Black lodge's insurance premiums because no bank in the county would take Black money, and after a man named Richard Walker was hanged from a tree near Drake's Branch in May 1886 he told his white neighbors about the money Black folks down there were pooling. The lodge was ordered to disband and it disbanded. That is the reason the bank exists, and almost nobody tells you the man's name.

Before the Civil War, in Petersburg, Virginia, a woman who was legally somebody's property ran three mutual aid societies for enslaved women.

The rules under which they were allowed to gather required a white man to be sitting in the room every time they met.

Thirty-some years later, her name was the only woman's name on the charter of the first Black-owned bank ever chartered in the United States.

She was a laundress.

Her name was Eliza Allen, and almost nobody alive has heard it.

She was born around 1840 in Westmoreland County on the estate of Major Richard Beale, and she was later moved to Petersburg with the man who owned her, a professor named W. T. Davis.

In Petersburg she organized. She called her three societies the Consolation Sisters, the Sisters of Usefulness, and Tobitha.

The Sisters of Usefulness got up to about thirty members.

Understand what those women were doing on those Sunday afternoons.

They were enslaved. They had no legal claim to their own wages, their own children, or their own bodies, and they were putting money together anyway, so that when one of them needed something there would be something to give her.

And a white man had to sit there and watch them do it.

That is the entire problem of Black money in America in one room, seventy years before anybody had a word for it.

The war ended those societies. When it ended, Eliza Allen married a Petersburg shoemaker named James Allen, had five children, and went to work as a laundress.

She kept organizing for the rest of her life.

The man she would eventually put her name on a bank charter with was born Ben, in October 1849, on Benjamin Pryor's place in Habersham County, Georgia.

His parents, Joseph and Mariah Browne, had both been sold out of Virginia and met each other in the state they were carried to.

Pryor died when the boy was eight. The widow remarried, sold the plantation with Joseph and Mariah standing on it, and took their son with her into town.

He was kept and they were sold.

He did not get a say and neither did they.

In Rome, Georgia, she hired him out. He was an office boy for a lawyer, and he kept a store.

A Black child stood behind a white man's counter six days a week, taking money in and counting it back out and writing the figures down, and not one cent of it would ever be his.

That is the first job the record gives him.

Somewhere in those years, working that counter, he asked for permission to change his name.

He wanted to be called William Washington, after the general. He was told he could have it.

Somewhere around those same years he was sent to the slave pens and sold to a horse trader outside Memphis.

The sources disagree about which came first, the name or the sale, and about whether one caused the other. What nobody disputes is that a child asked to be called something other than what he was given, and that he was sold.

They trained him to ride. Other men's animals, other men's races, other men's purses, which is the store again with different weather.

When Memphis fell to the Union Army in 1862, his owners hauled him down into Mississippi to keep him away from it.

He ran, with two other boys, fifty miles on foot, straight back toward the city he had just been carried away from, because the army was in it.

In Memphis he got work as a waiting boy for a captain of the Sixth Missouri Infantry.

Then slaveholders began walking into that camp to look for runaways, and a twelve-year-old stood there and watched men hunt through a United States Army camp for people exactly like him.

He left, took work with a Jewish family in town, and when that soured he went down to the river and stowed away on a boat bound for Cairo, Illinois.

He got himself onto a Mississippi gunboat called the National.

He went to school in Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin, enlisted at fifteen in the Eighteenth United States Colored Infantry at St. Louis, and came out a sergeant major.

After the war he wanted his mother, and nobody had ever told him where she was taken.

So he wrote a letter to a man who had once owned him and asked, and that is how he found her, ailing, and that is why he went back South to teach.

He preached. He spoke against the Klan in Georgia and Alabama when that was a thing that got men killed.

When he applied to join the white Good Templars, they refused him and offered him a charter under a separate name instead.

He took it, because a separate thing you run beats a shared thing you are permitted to attend.

He arrived in Richmond at the end of 1880, and on 11 January 1881 he took charge of the Grand Fountain of the United Order of True Reformers.

For years his pay from it was small and late and sometimes absent. His wife Molly sewed for other people, and what she earned held that house up while he built.

Eliza Allen was already there. She had joined the order in the 1870s, by some accounts in 1875 and by others a few years later, founded one of its first three chapters, and built the Shiloh Fountain in Petersburg herself.

In 1881 the order elected her national Grand Worthy Mistress, an office that served jointly with the Grand Worthy Master, and she held it six years.

The laundress and the former jockey ran it together.

In 1885 they did the thing that made everything else possible. The True Reformers became the first Black fraternal society in America to price its insurance against real actuarial tables of life expectancy, which meant that when it promised to pay, it could.

White insurers were refusing Black customers outright or charging them ruinously. So they built their own and did the arithmetic properly.

That same year they opened a children's department and called it the Rosebuds, and Eliza Allen was made the Governess over it.

Read what the Rosebud rules actually said it was for.

Discipline for the young, training in thrift and economy, early lessons in the business methods of life, a fund for sick children, and a burial fund out of which, on proof that a child had died, the parents would receive "a sum not exceeding thirty-seven dollars."

Thirty-seven dollars.

That is what all of this was originally for. Black parents putting in pennies a month against the chance that they would have to bury their own child, and thirty-seven dollars was the difference between a coffin and a county hole.

By 1907 more than thirty thousand children were enrolled.

Then the order sent organizers into Charlotte County, down in Southside Virginia, and the county taught Browne the lesson he already knew by heart.

The new branch there had no bank that would take Black money. So the members handed their premiums to a local white storekeeper to hold until there was enough to send up to Richmond.

There was a white man in the room again.

In May 1886 a mob took a young Black man named Richard Walker out of custody in that county and hanged him from a tree near Drake's Branch.

He had been accused of something. He was never tried.

The county was still holding its breath when the storekeeper looked at the money stacking up in his keeping and worked out what it added up to.

Black people, organized, saving.

He told his neighbors what he was minding, and his neighbors went to the branch and told it to break up, and it broke up.

On 2 March 1888 the Virginia General Assembly passed an act chartering the Savings Bank of the Grand Fountain of the United Order of True Reformers. A Richmond attorney named Giles B. Jackson wrote the articles of incorporation.

Eliza Allen was the only woman whose name was on it.

The bank opened on 3 April 1889, and not in a bank building. It opened in the front room of Browne's own house at 105 West Jackson Street.

He chose that date on purpose.

April the third was the anniversary of the day the Union Army marched into Richmond and the capital of the Confederacy fell.

For a man who had been freed the first time by an army walking into a Southern city, the symbolism would have been hard to miss, and it would have been hard to miss in Jackson Ward either.

The clerk who sat down and wrote the deposits into the book was a Richmond schoolteacher named Mary Cary Burrell, the first woman ever to work there.

By closing she had entered one thousand two hundred sixty-nine dollars and twenty-eight cents.

Now watch what these people built on top of that parlor.

In May 1891 they opened a hall on North Second Street containing the bank, business offices, three stores, four large meeting rooms and a concert hall. It was the largest building in Richmond owned by Black people, and it was put up entirely by Black hands.

They put a concert hall in it. One generation out of slavery, and they built a room for music inside their own bank.

They ran a newspaper, the Reformer, with ten thousand subscribers by 1906.

They opened a real estate department in 1892. By 1906 it held twenty-seven buildings and three farms worth four hundred thousand dollars, and leased twenty-three more properties on top of that.

They chartered a mercantile association in 1899 and ran retail stores in several cities, clearing over a hundred thousand dollars a year.

They built the Hotel Reformer, which took a hundred and fifty guests and was considered one of the finest Black hotels in the South.

They bought land at Westham in Henrico County and ran a home there for their old people, so that members who had paid in all their lives had somewhere to go.

And in Washington in 1903 they put up the True Reformer Building, designed by the Black architect John A. Lankford. It is widely described as the first building in America designed, financed, constructed and owned by Black people after Reconstruction.

By 1903 the order had roughly sixty thousand members and chapters in nearly every state east of the Mississippi River.

W. E. B. Du Bois looked at it and called it probably the most remarkable Negro organization in the country.

Then came the panic of 1893.

Banks across Richmond slowed, restricted withdrawals, or shut their doors.

The bank in Jackson Ward honored every check and paid every account out at full value, and it was the only bank in the city that could say so.

For one season, in the former capital of the Confederacy, the safest money in town was in Black hands.

Browne did not get long with any of it.

In 1897 doctors found a cancerous tumor on his arm and told him the arm would have to come off, and he refused them.

It spread, and he died in Washington that December at forty-eight, and his funeral was one of the largest Black Richmond had ever held.

Reverend William Lee Taylor took over the bank.

By 1907 deposits had passed a million dollars, and Taylor had built himself a mansion at 526 North Second Street.

Underneath that, the order had begun lending its own depositors' money to its own ventures without security, and the ventures kept failing. In the spring of 1910 the board closed the stores, hoping that would stop it.

That October the state noticed something and sent a bank examiner.

What the state had noticed was roughly fifty thousand dollars in death benefits going unpaid.

Sit with that number for a second, because it is not an accounting term.

It means people had died. It means families across twenty-four states had proved it, and filed for it, and the money had not come.

The whole thing had been built so that would never happen.

The examiner reported that the bank was insolvent. The directors did not believe it, sat down, read their own books, and reached the same conclusion.

It was over inside a week. The state moved on 20 October 1910, the doors closed, and the order was in receivership by the 26th.

The bank's cashier, R. T. Hill, went with more than fifty thousand dollars he had taken out of it, and he was never found.

The receiver found the order's real estate valued at far more than it was worth and mortgaged besides.

Most of those account holders never saw their savings again.

In August 1911 six directors were indicted on twenty counts, including letting a bank they knew was insolvent go on taking deposits. The first trial hung, the second acquitted, and the charges against the rest were dropped.

The Richmond Planet reported in June 1912 that people were not satisfied.

Nobody was ever charged over the storekeeper in Charlotte County either.

The order limped on as a burial society until 1934, when its name came off the state's books.

So here is what to carry out of this, and it costs nothing to carry.

When somebody posts about America's first chartered Black-owned bank, they will give you Browne, the charter date, and the panic of 1893, and they will stop there.

They will not give you Eliza Allen, who was pooling money for enslaved women in Petersburg with a white man posted in the room to watch, and who was the only woman on that charter, and who washed other people's clothes for a living the entire time.

They will not give you Richard Walker. The year was 1886 and that was his name, and four extra words puts him back in the sentence.

And they will not tell you what any of it was for in the first place.

It was for thirty-seven dollars.

It was for a mother in Virginia who had put in a few cents a month for years, so that on the worst day of her life somebody would hand her enough to bury her child properly.

Twenty-four years later the money did not come, and there is no ledger anywhere with her name in it.

text:
Trump offers $1 million reward for voter fraud tips
The latest cash pledge adds to the US president’s growing list of pre-election incentives as Republicans fight to keep Congress
Published 27 Oct, 2026 (FULL)
https://t.co/AuNoRQwHpD
US President Donald Trump has offered a $1 million reward for reporting voter fraud in past elections or the upcoming November 3 midterms, provided the tip leads to an arrest and conviction.
Trump announced the offer on Truth Social on Monday, repeating it to reporters ahead of a rally in Corinth, Mississippi.
“Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid $1,000,000 upon the arrest and conviction of those that created the Fraud!” he wrote.
Trump did not say where the money would come from, who would distribute it, or how to report suspected fraud. The White House did not immediately respond to media requests for clarification.
The promise sparked legal questions online, with critics pointing out that Trump cannot simply hand out taxpayer money without congressional approval. Some joked the scheme could end up costing more than the Pentagon’s budget.
“If I do voter fraud and then report myself am I eligible for the 1 million dollars?” one user quipped.
“I’m forcing my partner to vote twice so I can report the transgression and get the money. What an opportunity!” another wrote.
Trump has long alleged widespread election fraud, notably refusing to accept his 2020 defeat to Joe Biden and repeatedly calling the vote “rigged” and “stolen.”
He and his supporters filed more than 60 lawsuits challenging the results, virtually all dismissed or rejected for lack of evidence – including by Trump-appointed judges. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency found no evidence of fraud capable of changing the outcome, while Trump’s own attorney general at the time, William Barr, publicly rejected his claims.
The million-dollar bounty adds to Trump’s growing list of cash incentives ahead of the midterms, as Republicans fight to keep Congress. The biggest carrot so far was his proposed $5,000 ‘Trump Dividend’ for every American adult citizen if Republicans retain both chambers. Announced at a Republican gathering in Dallas last month, the giveaway would cost roughly $1.3 trillion for an estimated 260 million adults, drawing bipartisan criticism. Trump has suggested congressional approval might not be necessary, although lawmakers, including House Speaker Mike Johnson, and policy analysts say such a massive payout would require legislation and congressional funding.
Trump has also cheered a separate multibillion-dollar giveaway by ally Elon Musk, who promised every US child a share of SpaceX next year. The pledge followed Musk’s renewed backing of Trump and the Republicans after their public feud last year over the president’s spending legislation. According to the New York Times, Musk has donated more than $276 million to Republican groups since July, bringing his 2025-2026 election-cycle contributions to roughly $366 million.
The cash promises come as Trump’s ratings sink amid frustration over the prolonged Iran conflict, gasoline topping $6 a gallon, and persistent inflation despite his pledges to cut living costs, while Republicans face increasingly grim midterm prospects. A Reuters/Ipsos poll last week put his approval at 31% – the lowest of either presidential term – with Democrats leading Republicans 47% to 35% among registered voters on a hypothetical congressional ballot. A separate New York Times/Siena University poll put Trump’s approval at a record-low 36% among likely voters, with Democrats ahead by 11 points in congressional races, 52% to 41%.
Republicans currently hold a slim 218-214 House majority and a 53-47 Senate advantage. However, polls indicate they face unexpectedly tight Senate races in Kansas, Texas, Iowa, Alaska, and Ohio – all states Trump comfortably carried in 2024. Democrats need a net gain of four seats in both the House and Senate to take control.

text:
For years John Wayne Gacy's neighbors complained about the smell coming from under his house. He told them it was just moisture in the crawl space. It was 26 bodies.

The neighbors knew him as Pogo. The clown with the red nose and the big painted smile who performed at their kids' birthday parties.

He threw huge summer parties for the whole street. He ran a construction business. He organized for the local Democratic Party. Months before his arrest he was photographed shaking hands with the First Lady of the United States.

Almost nobody knew he had already done prison time in Iowa for sexually assaulting a teenage boy. He got 10 years. He was out in 18 months.

Between 1972 and 1978 he killed 33 young men and boys. Many of them came to him looking for work. He offered them jobs at his company.

In December 1978 a 15-year-old boy told his mother he was going to talk to a contractor about a summer job. He never came home. The contractor was Gacy.

Police searched the house. Under the floor there was no room left. The last bodies he had thrown into a river.

In the video below, Gacy sits in prison and tells the interviewer he is innocent. He smiles. He jokes. He blames other people who had keys to his house.

Thirty-three dead, and he never stops smiling.

In his cell he painted clowns and sold the paintings to collectors.

He was executed in 1994. He never confessed.

The man who made children laugh at birthday parties went home every night and slept above 26 graves.

Was John Wayne Gacy a master manipulator, or did a whole neighborhood ignore the smell because the nice man next door threw the best parties on the block?

text:
I found out my wife was cheating on me with one of her students, and I swear, I have never felt so humiliated in my entire life.

It wasn't just the cheating. It was WHO she cheated with.

I had defended this woman in rooms where people questioned her character. I had listened to her complain about difficult students, celebrated her promotions, and watched her prepare lessons at our dining table while I made jokes about her being married to her job.

Sometimes, she'd tell me about a particular student who was struggling academically. She'd talk about his grades, his family problems, and how she wanted to help him succeed.

I remember telling her she had a beautiful heart. That student was the same person she was sleeping with.

And the worst part? I had met him before. He had been to our house once to drop off some documents. I shook his hand, offered him something to drink, and asked about school. He called my wife ma'am while sitting across from me.

I didn't know that the boy I was welcoming into my home was the same person who would eventually make me question everything I knew about my marriage.

I found the messages by accident. She had fallen asleep with her phone beside her, and a notification appeared on the screen.

I wasn't looking for evidence of an affair. I wasn't even suspicious that night. But the message said something that made my stomach turn. He called her by a pet name I had never heard her use with anyone else.

I opened the conversation. I wish I hadn't.

There were messages, pictures, and conversations that made it painfully clear this wasn't some stupid mistake that happened once after a few drinks. This had been going on for months, right under my nose, while I was busy building a future with a woman who had apparently built a separate life behind my back.

I sat on the edge of our bed reading everything until my hands started shaking. Then I came across a message where she told him she wished she had met him before she got married.

I read that sentence so many times that the words eventually stopped looking real. Before she got married?

We had been together for six years. Married for three. I had held her while she cried over losing her father. I had stayed awake beside her when she was sick. I had sacrificed things I wanted because I thought we were building something that would eventually belong to both of us.

And she was telling another man she wished she had met him before me. I didn't wake her up.

I went to the sitting room and stayed there until morning, trying to understand how the woman sleeping peacefully in our bed could be the same woman whose messages had just destroyed my understanding of our marriage.

When she finally woke up, she found me sitting at the dining table with her phone in front of me. She looked at the phone. Then she looked at me. For a few seconds, neither of us spoke. I asked her one question. "How long?"

She started crying immediately. She said it wasn't what I thought, that things had become complicated, that she never intended to hurt me. I let her talk until she ran out of explanations.

Then I asked her whether she understood who she had been sleeping with. Her face changed.

I don't know how to explain what I felt at that moment. It wasn't even anger anymore. It was the realisation that the person I trusted most in this world had crossed a line I never imagined she would approach.

She was supposed to be his teacher. He was supposed to be able to trust her. His parents trusted her. And somehow, she had turned a position of responsibility into something neither of us could ever pretend was harmless.

She begged me not to tell anyone. She said one mistake shouldn't destroy her career, her reputation, and our marriage. Our marriage. That was the part that nearly made me laugh.

She wanted me to protect the same life she had been willing to gamble away for secret messages and stolen moments.

text:
Good morning, friends. As the first light of October 27, 2026, gently fills the sky, I invite you to pause with me for a few quiet moments of encouragement before the day unfolds.

"Fear not, Abram! I am your shield; your reward will be very great." These tender words from Genesis 15:1 were spoken to a man standing at the edge of the unknown, carrying questions about his future and his family. God met him right there with reassurance and promise.

We know that feeling today. Many wake with worries about rising costs, job security, or the health of someone they love. Others feel the weight of distant conflicts and rapid changes in our communities that leave us wondering what comes next. It is easy for fear to whisper in those spaces.

Yet the same voice that spoke to Abram speaks to us: God offers Himself as our shield. Not a distant guard, but a personal protector who stands between us and the things that would harm our peace. The shield does not remove every difficulty, but it ensures we never face them without help and strength.

The promise of a very great reward reminds us that our quiet trust and small acts of faithfulness are seen and cherished. A kind word offered in a stressful meeting, patience shown to a tired child, or simply choosing hope when headlines feel heavy—these matter deeply.

As you move through this morning, let the verse settle in your heart. When anxiety rises, remember you are shielded. When the path feels unclear, remember the reward is great. May this truth bring steady warmth and hope to every step you take today.

text:
Look at India, for example, where the gap is even more grotesque.

Standard entry-level salary at a service-level company like TCS or Infosys today remains stuck around 3 to 3.6 lakh a year. While there are specialized roles now, like Infosys’s SP track, which can go up to 21 lakh for good talent, for the vast majority, this base number has been stagnant for over a decade. Real wages for new graduates have barely grown, even as rents and the cost of living have exploded.

Now look at the men at the top. Infosys CEO Salil Parekh took home 82.6 crore in FY26. Tech Mahindra's CEO earned 67.5 crore. Wipro's CEO, 49.6 crore. And let's not even start on HCL's CEO, who took home a staggering 175 crore. There are other companies too; one says give eg of.

The ratio at Infosys is ~742 times the median employee. At Tech Mahindra, it's nearly 1,085 times. At Wipro, 524 times.

People say, "but employees get shares too"; look at how that CEO pay is structured. At Infosys, 50.75 crore of Parekh's package came purely from exercised stock options and restricted stock units. The equity is not "shared." It is concentrated at the very top. TCS, notably, doesn't even offer ESOPs to its staff at all.

This has to change. And it's not just about software services. Even in core engineering- mechanical, civil, electrical- entry-level salaries often sit at just ₹3–5 LPA, and professionals frequently have to chase jobs at foreign MNCs for good, stable work-life balance and just to get a livable wage, because domestic firms won't pay and exploit at low wages. The gap is way too much

text:
Tuesday we are doing a deep dig into some archaeological history here in Arkansas

Long before Arkansas had highways, towns, or even a name, a woman was laid to rest in what is now Washington County. And not far from her burial, someone had carefully buried a dog. This is one of the most fascinating archaeological discoveries in Arkansas.

In 1932, archaeologists excavating Brown Bluff, a prehistoric rock shelter in the Boston Mountains, discovered the partially mummified remains of a Native American woman believed to have been between 35 and 49 years old. But she wasn't buried without her belongings.

Among the objects associated with her burial were woven materials, pieces of basketry, cordage, a bone awl used for piercing materials, and what may have been a carrying strap or sling. There was even a brush that researchers initially thought might have been used for grooming hair, although it may have been used for working with plant fibers.

These weren't treasures of gold or silver. They were everyday objects that tell us something about how she lived.

And then there was the dog.

About three feet from her feet, archaeologists discovered a dog that had been deliberately buried in a pit lined with grass and leaves. Someone had taken the time to prepare that animal's final resting place.

We don't know whether the dog belonged to the woman or whether their burials were connected, but it's certainly something to think about.

Now, here's another part of this story that I think people should know.After her remains were discovered in 1932, they were removed from the rock shelter and taken to the University of Arkansas Museum in Fayetteville. For decades, her partially mummified body was displayed in a glass case for the public to see.

That display eventually ended. Today, laws and museum practices recognize the importance of treating Native American human remains with dignity and returning them to their communities when appropriate.

However, I haven't been able to establish whether this particular woman's remains were ever returned to a tribe, reburied, or are still in university custody.

The Brown Bluff site was excavated again in the 1990s when construction of what is now Interstate 49 threatened the area.

Think about everything this woman has been through. She was buried by her people, remained undisturbed for generations, was discovered by archaeologists, and eventually became a museum exhibit.

We don't know her name, who loved her, or what her life was like. But the belongings buried with her offer a small glimpse into her world. And I keep coming back to that carefully buried dog.

Do you think ancient people had the same emotional attachment to their dogs that we have today? And what do you think should happen to human remains discovered during archaeological excavations?

text:
The note on the back of the page says it is the Lord's Prayer, written out in Arabic by a devoted Christian called Uncle Moreau. It is not the Lord's Prayer. It is a chapter of the Qur'an about the day the faith wins, written from memory by a man whose real name was Omar ibn Said, and the general who owned him spent the summer of 1857 handing it around a Virginia resort as proof of a soul saved. Go and look at that page yourself, it is free and online, and see which one of them was telling the truth.

Forty-seven years earlier, the same man had reached down and picked something up off the floor of a cell. A piece of burnt wood, gone cold, small enough to hold between two fingers.

Omar ibn Said had been in America three years then, and he could not yet put a sentence together in English. He turned to the wall and began to write, right to left, in a small and practiced hand.

It was the last week of August 1810, in the county jail at Fayetteville, North Carolina.

He had been walking about a month by then, roughly two hundred and twenty miles, out of the South Carolina rice country and north through forest, swamp and river crossings. He had stopped at some buildings to pray, a boy on horseback had spotted him and ridden off to tell his father, and men had come back with a pack of dogs and walked him the last twelve miles into town.

When he wrote about that building years later, he did not call it a jail, because he did not have the word for it. He called it a great house he could not go out of.

He was in it sixteen days, and he covered the walls. Prayers, out of memory, in Arabic, the letters running the wrong direction across the plaster for every eye in Cumberland County.

When the wall filled up, people said he started on the floor.

And the town came to look. Word went up and down the Cape Fear that the runaway in the Fayetteville jail was making strange marks, and men and women walked down to see them the way you would walk down to see a two-headed calf.

Not one person who came could read a single word of it.

The people filing past that door lived in a state where formal schooling was scarce and writing was a skill a good many of them did not have. The man they were lining up to stare at had spent twenty-five years in formal study, under three teachers, one of whom was his own brother.

He was the most educated person in that building, and he was the one behind the door.

They did not know that, so they guessed. One account later reported that his walls were covered with pleas to be released, which was a guess wearing the clothes of a fact, because nobody asked him and nobody could read him.

That guessing is what saved his life, and it is also what buried him.

On a Friday the jailer opened the door onto a crowd of men, some of them calling questions at him, trying to work out whether his name was Omar or Seid. The local sheriff, Bob Mumford, took him out of the jail and home, and he stayed at Mumford's four days.

Mumford had mentioned this runaway to his new son-in-law, one of the wealthiest men in the district. James Owen was a state legislator and planter in his mid-twenties, with two plantations straddling the river, Milton and Owen Hill, and the older brother of a future governor of North Carolina.

In the census taken that same year, James Owen reported owning forty-three people.

Then the man from Charleston finally arrived to claim him, and it was not Johnson. His name was Mitchell, and he came holding a bill of sale, claiming he had bought Omar cheap from Johnson after the escape.

Omar's answer to that survives in his own handwriting, and it is the least composed sentence he ever wrote down. No, no, no, no, no, no, no.

Mitchell watched the distress in the room and started playing hard to get. According to an account handed down in the Owen family, Owen offered him two white carriage horses.

When Mitchell hesitated, the same family account says Owen added a thousand dollars on top, a sum that at the time bought a young and healthy man outright. A crowd of strangers had filed past a jail door to look at marks nobody could read, and the marks had just been given a price.

The man they had just paid for had been a scholar, a teacher and a trader in Futa Toro, in what is now northern Senegal, and he described where he came from in one short phrase: Fut Tur, between the two rivers.

His father was killed in fighting when he was about six years old, one of eleven children, and he was raised into a Qur'anic school where boys chanted the book aloud until the whole of it was inside them. That method exists precisely so that a man who loses everything he owns still has the text.

He kept going after the schools, travelling for the deeper training of Sufi Islam, until he was initiated into what is called the knowledge of secrets, which included how to construct amulets and talismans that ask God for protection.

At thirty-one he went home and lived six ordinary years, praying five times a day, giving alms in gold and silver and seeds and cattle and sheep and goats and rice and wheat and barley. Then three things happened almost on top of each other.

On the second of March 1807, Thomas Jefferson signed the law that would close the Atlantic slave trade at the end of that year. The following month, the ruler of Futa Toro was murdered.

And that year an army came into Omar's country, killed a great many people, and took him to the sea.

The timing was the worst timing available in the century. With the door about to shut, ships were racing to fill their holds off the West African coast, and the Senegal River was one of the busiest loading grounds on it.

Charleston counted 5,386 enslaved Africans sold in the city in 1804. In 1807 the number was 15,676.

He was thirty-seven years old, and he was freight on one of the last legal voyages America ever ran.

The ship came up the Cooper River to Gadsden's Wharf and joined a line of slave vessels already tied up there. On one day that January, nine ships advertised their cargo for sale at that wharf at the same time, and a British visitor said the noise of it was like the Old Testament story of Babel.

Somewhere in that noise he was sold to a man he later described in four words that have outlived Johnson entirely. Small, weak, and wicked.

Johnson put a middle-aged scholar into the South Carolina rice fields, where enslaved people died young as a matter of routine.

About two years of that, and Omar walked, which is how he came to be sitting on a jail floor in Fayetteville with a piece of coal in his hand.

Nine years after that door opened, in 1819, he tried to write his way out a second time. The Owens had begun leaning on him to convert, and they were part of a national circle of colonization men who wanted freed Black Americans shipped to Africa, to whom a converted African scholar was worth more than any argument they could make.

So Omar sat down and wrote two pages in Arabic and put them into the hands of John Owen, Jim Owen's brother, then a state senator.

He filled them the way a scholar fills pages. Passages from eight different chapters of the Qur'an, lines from the Arabic grammar textbooks he had learned as a boy, and, drawn large in the middle of the first page, a Sufi talisman with six interlocking arabesques.

Written inside the talisman was the name Jim Owen.

That figure is what the knowledge of secrets was for. Setting a name inside one can be done to bind two people together, and it can be done to pull them apart.

Halfway down the second page he drew a small five-pointed star, which in that tradition asks for protection. Then, in the middle of all the scripture, he wrote one sentence that is not scripture at all.

He wanted to be seen again in his own land, in Africa, at a place on the river.

He closed the page by quoting the chapter of the Qur'an about God's sovereignty, and he stopped on the line that says a person may whisper or shout, and God knows what is inside them either way. He had just written a request for his freedom in a language his owners could not read, and signed off with a verse about the only reader he had left.

John Owen could not read a word of it, so he passed it to John Louis Taylor, the first chief justice of the North Carolina Supreme Court. Taylor could not read it either.

On the tenth of October 1819, Taylor wrote to a lawyer in Georgetown, asking for help finding someone who could translate the enclosed manuscript. The lawyer was Francis Scott Key, who had written the words of The Star-Spangled Banner five years before.

Taylor's covering letter explains the enclosure to Key. It says the man is believed to have been powerfully connected in his own country and uncommonly educated, that he is grateful for the unbounded confidence and indulgence of the family that owns him, and that he is unwilling to return to his native country.

The letter Taylor was holding said the opposite, in the man's own hand, and Taylor had no idea.

Taylor also asked Key for a second favour. They needed an Arabic Bible, so that once the man could read the Christian scriptures for himself he would have no excuse left for holding on to his own faith.

The note filed with Taylor's letter describes the enclosure as an Arabic amulet. They were correct about the object and wrong about everything else in the room.

The Bible came. The translation never did.

The book arrived leather-bound, eleven inches tall, over four hundred pages, and when he opened it he was looking at the first Arabic words he had seen in thirteen years that were not his own.

He sewed a soft leather bag for it and hung it on a chair. Over the years he made six cloth covers for that Bible, wrapping each new one around the worn one underneath, the way a man protects a book he loves.

At the front of it and again at the back of it, he wrote a line in Arabic. Praise be to Allah.

A few weeks before Christmas in 1820, he went upriver with the Owens and was baptized at First Presbyterian in Fayetteville, in a sanctuary where the white members sat in the pews and the Black members sat in the balcony.

The membership roll entered him under People of Colour as Moroe, property of Geo. Owen. The man who owned him was named James.

He would not sit in the balcony, and he was not going to be seated in the pews. An Owen descendant wrote that he kept his own chair and set it in the aisle.

Out on the plantation he went on writing prayers in Arabic and tacking them to trees, which is a thing people did where he came from. White people who walked past them assumed they were thank-you notes about the Owens.

Every morning he tied one end of a length of cloth to a tree or a post, took the other end, and turned in place until his head was covered, and the Owen children were still describing it decades later. People outside the house were beginning to describe him too.

In the summer of 1825, an unnamed Fayetteville doctor published an article about him in a Philadelphia magazine titled Prince Moro, and the editors promised their readers a faithful statement of facts.

The article decided he was a prince from somewhere deep in the interior, perhaps Timbuktu, which is about seven hundred miles from Futa Toro and in a different country. It also reported that he now blessed the God who had brought good out of evil by making him a slave.

The Owen family ran with the royalty story so far that when they offered him his choice of a wife from among the enslaved women in the house and he declined, a descendant explained it by writing that a Fulah prince could not marry beneath himself.

He never wrote a word about being royalty. He never wrote about a wife or children either, only short prayers for his mother, whose name survives on this continent in exactly one place, in a line he wrote in Arabic asking God to comfort her resting place.

Uncle Moreau, Uncle Moro, Prince Moro, Omeroh, Umeroh, Moro, Morro, Meroh, Monroe. Every name on that list was handed to him by white people.

In its 1830 session, five years after the Prince Moro article ran, the North Carolina General Assembly made it a crime for any free person to teach an enslaved person to read or write, and set thirty-nine lashes for any enslaved person who taught another. The act stated its reasoning in its own opening lines, that teaching slaves to write tends to excite dissatisfaction in their minds and to produce insurrection and rebellion.

John Owen was governor of North Carolina at the time, and had personally circulated David Walker's abolitionist appeal to state lawmakers as a warning. That August, Nat Turner led a rebellion in Virginia, about a hundred and sixty-five miles from Bladen County.

In that atmosphere, the colonization men needed proof that some Africans were worth saving, and they began collecting life stories from enslaved people to make the case. So James Owen handed his sixty-one-year-old slave a blank tablet of cream-coloured quarto paper and asked him to write his life.

The statute could punish anyone who taught an enslaved person to read or write. It had no way at all to reach the twenty-five years of learning Omar had carried into North Carolina with him.

Omar dipped a pen in iron gall ink and started with an apology.

He wrote that he could not write his life, because he had forgotten too much of his own language and too much of his Arabic, and he asked the man who requested it not to be hard on him. He said he was a man of weak eyes and a weak body.

Then, before his birthplace, before his teachers, before anything, he wrote out the sixty-seventh chapter of the Qur'an from memory, complete, headed by a blessing on the Prophet.

It opens by saying that all sovereignty belongs to God, who holds it in his hand and has power over everything. He wrote that on paper handed to him by a general, in a house he was owned in, in a state that had just criminalised teaching an enslaved person to write, in the year his owner's brother was warning the legislature about rebellion.

Then he wrote three words that the next hundred and eighty years of captions never managed to cancel. I am Omar.

The rest of the fifteen pages does what it had to do. He praises Jim Owen and John Owen, asks the people of the Carolinas whether they have two such men among them, and reports that in twenty years he has not gone hungry or naked or been beaten or made to do hard work.

He also writes that he used to love reading the great Qur'an, and describes the life he had before, the mosque before daybreak, the five prayers, the alms, the pilgrimage.

Read it in 1831 and it is a conversion story. Read it now with the first page attached and it is a man standing exactly where he always stood, in a form his owners could hold in their hands and still not open.

The historian Sylviane Diouf later gave it the right name. A document of resistance.

Five years on, the pages were sent to the one man in America best placed to read them.

Lamine Kebe was a Qur'anic teacher from what is now Guinea who had run schools for years before he was kidnapped. He was taken while he was out buying paper for his students.

After about forty years enslaved in America he had been freed, and in 1836 he was in New York about to sail for Liberia, performing the same careful act Omar performed, agreeable to the colonization men, quiet about what he actually believed.

Omar's fifteen pages reached him with a ship waiting. He did not carry them home.

He handed them to Theodore Dwight, a white scholar in New York, and a rough translation was finally made seventeen years later, and Dwight did not publish it until the year after Omar died.

The pages went around the entire abolition and colonization circuit of the United States and never once landed in the hands of somebody who could read them and do something about it.

While the pages were doing that circuit, James Owen sold Milton and moved the household down to Wilmington, into a three-storey house on Front Street with chandeliers and gifts from around the world in the rooms.

The family entertained there constantly, and Omar was the centrepiece. A visiting doctor described a fine-looking man in a black coat that came below his knees, who was summoned into the room and announced that he would read the twenty-third Psalm.

The same guest asked him to write the psalm out in Arabic, and he did. The Owens' minister, Matthew Grier, said he would never forget the old man's face as he read the part about the dark valley.

Carl Ernst, one of the two scholars who finally worked through everything Omar left, put the performances in plain language. It is overwhelmingly probable that he learned those passages in order to recite them on request.

The Wilmington church roll listed him as Morrow, servant to James Owen, an Indian Prince.

One Owen daughter, writing to her little sister at boarding school, quoted something he used to say. It is not the leaning tree which always falls first.

That is the only line of his ordinary conversation anyone in that house wrote down in fifty years.

On the twenty-seventh of July 1857, General James Owen was at Rockbridge Alum Springs, a resort in Rockbridge County, Virginia, taking the waters. He had brought a souvenir.

He handed a sheet of Arabic to a minister's daughter named Mary Jones. Somebody wrote the explanation on the back of it in English.

It says that this is the Lord's Prayer, written in Arabic by Uncle Moreau, a native African, now owned by General Owen of Wilmington, North Carolina, that he is eighty-eight years of age and a devoted Christian.

It is not the Lord's Prayer. It is the hundred and tenth chapter of the Qur'an, al-Nasr, the last chapter revealed to Muhammad before his death.

The chapter says that when the help of God comes, and the victory, and you see the people entering God's religion in crowds, then give praise and ask forgiveness.

He signed it. My name is Omar.

That paper was carried to a Virginia resort by the man who owned him and passed around a room full of white guests as evidence of a soul saved, and what was actually on it was a promise that the faith wins in the end.

Another sheet from that same summer went to a different Virginia spring. It carries the fifty-first Psalm and the Lord's Prayer, and at the head of the psalm Omar wrote the invocation that opens a chapter of the Qur'an and asked God's blessing on the Prophet Muhammad.

The note attached to that one describes him as an aged servant man imported many years ago.

Three years later, the 1860 census recorded him as a ninety-one-year-old African prince called Monroe.

Two years after that, with the war on and his own health failing, James Owen moved back inland to Owen Hill and brought Omar with him, two old men going home to the same piece of ground.

Omar died there in the summer of 1863, at about ninety-three, before the end of the war would have freed him. He had been the legal property of the same family since the Friday the jail door opened, fifty-three years earlier.

They buried him in the Owen family graveyard. Owen died two years after him, and the plantation house burned down one Sunday morning in 1876.

The autobiography was printed once, in a historical journal in 1925, and then it went out of sight for about seventy years.

It turned up in 1995 in an old trunk in Virginia. On the twenty-eighth of March 1996 it was auctioned in New York, at that house's first sale devoted entirely to African American books and manuscripts, and almost nobody in the room wanted it.

It went for twenty-one thousand, eight hundred and fifty dollars to a Black collector named Derrick Beard, who spent the next twenty years driving it around the country so that people could stand in front of it. In 2002 he told the Library of Congress it should be theirs, because it belonged to everybody and not to him.

The Library bought it in the summer of 2017, Beard died a couple of months later at fifty-nine, and in January 2019 the whole collection went online, forty-two documents, free to anyone with a phone.

And people finally started reading. Mbaye Lo and Carl Ernst went through everything and found him quoting a twelfth-century Andalusian Sufi master and a sixteenth-century Egyptian religious poem, from memory, in a Carolina plantation house, an ocean and a lifetime away from the last library he ever sat in.

In 2021 two journalists carried copies of his letter and his autobiography into Futa Toro and put them in front of the imams there. In a village called Dimat Walo, one of the most learned men in the region read out the place name Omar had written in his plea.

Coppe, a village that has sat on the bank of the Senegal River for four hundred years.

The journalists drove out to Coppe with the pages. The elders read the letter aloud, decided the man was one of theirs, and prayed for him.

Then the village asked if they could keep the papers, and the journalists gave them up.

Back in North Carolina, the record has been busy. A Fayetteville mosque took his name in 1991, the state raised a highway marker to him in 2010 on Murchison Road, and in 2023 an opera built out of his fifteen pages won the Pulitzer Prize for Music.

In the 1980s, before any of that, the leading white historian of Omar in North Carolina co-wrote a state history textbook that told schoolchildren he had apparently been sold into slavery by his own people as punishment for a crime, an idea a missionary made up in 1856 and nobody checked for a hundred and thirty years.

And the catalogue entry at the Library of Congress still carries the title an old hand wrote on the cover in English, calling it the life of a Fullah slave in Fayetteville, owned by Governor Owen.

He was never owned by the governor. He was owned by the governor's brother, and even the caption on his own life story has the wrong man's name on it.

His pages are photographed and posted and free, in his own handwriting, with translations beside them. Before believing what anybody tells you about this man, including this, go and read the first page he wrote and see what he chose to put there.

The ground itself got no such care. Owen Hill today is at the end of a rural side street with houses and mobile homes on it.

In a field of thorny vines and trash there is a brick wall about three feet high, enclosing a rectangle roughly ten feet by twelve.

Inside it a thin tree is growing straight up through the grave of the man who founded the plantation, and an empty jelly jar is lying in the weeds. The family's headstones are in there somewhere, in broken pieces.

Nothing marks where Omar is. There was a stone once, and the stories about what happened to it do not agree.

A few years ago a handful of men from the mosque in Fayetteville that carries his name drove out to that field to pay their respects and found the state of it. They stood in the brambles and did the only thing they had.

They said the opening of the Qur'an over the ground.

Their imam realised, while they were saying it, that this was almost certainly the first time those words had been spoken on that spot since Omar said them himself. Nobody had brought him anything else.

A country that could not read him has given him a marker, a mosque, a Pulitzer Prize and a permanent shelf in its national library. It never gave him back the stone, and the only thing laid on him in a hundred and sixty years is a few lines in the language nobody around him could read.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter. If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/AeER0VXcAK
Every coffee helps me keep creating.

text:
In the Race to Be Called Modern, We Have Abandoned Things of Great Value

In our race to be called modern, we have given up so many precious things.

We searched for convenience and ended up creating difficulties for ourselves.

Today, we can no longer step outside wearing a dhoti, even though, after centuries of trial and error, it was the one garment perfectly suited to our climate. We imposed jeans upon ourselves and then installed air conditioners in our rooms to make wearing them bearable. We reserved our traditional shawls for fancy dress shows and adopted coats and jackets that restrict our shoulders. We found empowerment in cutting off our beards, moustaches, and long hair. And when fashion changed, we felt equally empowered growing them back!

Aren't we the luckiest people on earth?

We abandoned lassi and grabbed bottles of Coke.

We gave up sattu, a traditional roasted-grain drink, and started pouring ourselves glasses of slush.

We declared tamarind and dried plums unhygienic, yet we bought sealed cartons of juice containing their extracts and served them to our children. The packaging is made of cardboard, so we cannot even see what is inside.

We chose to trust what we could not see and declared what we could see with our own eyes unhealthy.

We abandoned homemade desi ghee, extracted from milk, and happily embraced oils extracted from seeds.

We gave up fresh, white butter and started licking yellow, fashionable margarine instead. When its potential harms became established, we were left stumbling around, unsure of what to believe.

We cannot tolerate a milkman adding water to milk, yet we gulp down milk adulterated with urea. Alhamdulillah!

We complain that real milk gives tea an unpleasant smell, yet we happily drink tea whitener—a product whose own packaging tells us it is not milk. We could have kept a buffalo right beneath our homes, but instead, we chose to buy powdered milk imported from foreign countries. What a wonderful decision we made!

We are the kind of people who drink mango juice from glass bottles even when mangoes are in season.

We once called jaggery a rustic, backward food and fell in love with refined white sugar. Then brown sugar returned to restaurants and slapped us in the face. Now we rub our cheeks while looking around in embarrassment. Yet even when we eat jaggery, we prefer the yellow variety, because the brown one still doesn't appeal to us simply because of its colour.

Come and meet us. We are the kind of people who might die of thirst in an emergency because we cannot drink tap water at home—not even after boiling or filtering it. We buy our drinking water, too.

We are the children of the land of the Sutlej, Ravi, Chenab, and Indus rivers, yet we pay foreign companies to sell us water.

We even buy mint chutney sealed in packets. We pay 150 rupees for a taste that our grandfathers could have prepared using a small amount of yogurt and freely available mint. Had they been served the packaged version we enjoy today, they might have walked away from the dining table in disgust.

We used to find sohanjna—the drumstick tree—bitter. But ever since it became moringa and arrived in capsule form, we happily spend 2,000 rupees on a fifteen-day supply. When a traditional healer offered us the same dried, ground leaves for fifty rupees, we refused to believe they were worth anything.

We will happily spend 500 rupees on cough syrup, but we won't even hold a five-rupee piece of liquorice root between our teeth.

"It has such a strange taste!"

We sleep on polyester pillows, wear clothes blended with nylon, and keep our feet enclosed in shoes through both summer and winter. We put on additional layers beneath our clothes and rush out onto the highway of life. And when night falls, we inevitably find ourselves reaching for antihistamines to deal with allergies.

We can no longer speak our mother tongue in the natural accent of our parents. We raise slogans in the name of our language, yet

text:
The Boston Martyrs were four Quakers executed by hanging in the Massachusetts Bay Colony between 1659 and 1661 for repeatedly entering the colony in defiance of laws that banished Quakers on pain of death. In Quaker tradition they are remembered as martyrs who died for conscience and the principle of the “Inner Light.”

William Robinson — A London merchant who had traveled with other Friends (including on the ship Woodhouse). He felt divinely led to enter Massachusetts in 1659 to witness against the anti-Quaker laws.

Marmaduke Stephenson (also spelled Stevenson) — A Yorkshire ploughman. In 1655, while working the fields, he experienced what he described as being filled with the love and presence of God. He left his family, went to Barbados, then Rhode Island, and joined Robinson in protesting the Massachusetts laws.

Mary Dyer — The best-known of the group. An English Puritan who had earlier supported Anne Hutchinson and been banished from Massachusetts in the 1630s Antinomian controversy. She later became a Quaker, lived in Rhode Island (where her husband William was a freeman), and returned to Boston specifically to challenge the laws. She was the mother of several children.

William Leddra — A Cornishman and clothier who had lived in Barbados. He was a zealous Quaker minister who continued to enter Massachusetts even after the earlier executions.

In October 1658 the Massachusetts General Court passed a law that any Quaker who was not an inhabitant, once convicted and banished, would face death if they returned. Local residents who adopted Quaker beliefs faced imprisonment and potential banishment on the same terms. The law was passed by a narrow majority amid growing alarm at Quaker missionary activity that had begun in 1656.

October 27, 1659 (Boston Neck / Boston Common area): Robinson, Stephenson, and Dyer were arrested after returning, tried, and sentenced to death by Governor John Endecott. They were marched to the gallows under heavy guard with drums beating so the crowd could not hear them speak.

Robinson said he suffered “for Christ, in whom I lived, and for whom I will die.”

Stephenson declared, “Be it known unto all this day that we suffer not as evil-doers, but for conscience sake,” and added that they would “be at rest with the Lord.”
 Both men were hanged. Mary Dyer had the noose placed around her neck and her face covered when she was suddenly reprieved (after her son’s petition and possibly other intercession). She was again banished.

June 1, 1660: Dyer returned to Boston in May 1660, again demanding repeal of the “unrighteous laws.” When brought before the court she affirmed she was the same Mary Dyer previously sentenced. Endecott ordered the sentence carried out. She was marched to the gallows with drums again used to drown out any speech. Offered a chance to leave and save her life, she replied that she came in obedience to the will of God and would remain faithful to death. She was hanged. Her final recorded words included an affirmation of the happiness into which she was entering.

March 14, 1661: William Leddra, who had been imprisoned, chained, and previously punished, was tried and hanged on Boston Common. He was the last Quaker executed in New England. He affirmed he suffered for bearing testimony against “deceivers and the deceived.”

(More)

Tuesday, October 27, 2026

Tonight's Conference USA doubleheader features four programs fighting to establish momentum in the second half of the season. Both matchups carry significant implications for bowl eligibility, quarterback execution, defensive personnel and conference positioning.

GAME 1: DELAWARE AT WESTERN KENTUCKY
Quarterback news: Minicucci's return changes Delaware's offense

The most important personnel development is the return of Delaware quarterback Nick Minicucci.

Minicucci missed two games before returning against Missouri State on October 20. His impact was immediate: 20 completions in 29 attempts, 225 passing yards, five touchdown passes, one interception and another touchdown rushing.

His season totals stand at 1,063 passing yards, 10 touchdowns and four interceptions in five appearances.

Delaware had relied on multiple quarterbacks during his absence. Trey Bell threw for 306 yards and two touchdowns in the 33-30 loss to Middle Tennessee on October 13, but Minicucci's return restores the Blue Hens' more established offensive leader.

The quarterback's mobility is particularly important against Western Kentucky. He can extend possessions when protection breaks down and creates additional responsibilities for linebackers defending the run-pass option.

Western Kentucky's quarterback situation

Western Kentucky has its own quarterback considerations.

Brock Glenn has handled most of the passing responsibilities over the last two games. His season numbers entering tonight are 67 completions in 128 attempts, 663 yards, five touchdowns and two interceptions.

Against Sam Houston, Glenn completed just 14 of 30 passes for 127 yards and one touchdown. However, he contributed 54 rushing yards on 22 attempts.

Rodney Tisdale Jr. provides a different passing profile, completing 79 of 118 attempts (66.9%) for 856 yards, four touchdowns and two interceptions.

That difference in completion percentage is substantial.

Glenn's running ability can help sustain possessions, but Delaware's defense must also prepare for the possibility of a quarterback change or situational deployment.

The biggest question is whether Western Kentucky can establish consistent downfield passing efficiency rather than relying on quarterback runs and short completions.

Injury intelligence: Western Kentucky's skill-position depth

Western Kentucky has several meaningful personnel concerns.

Wide receivers Nigel Johnson and K. Hutchinson have appeared on injury reports, while running backs Adrion Boyd and Sincere Baines have also been listed.

A recent game-day availability report identified Johnson, Boyd and Baines as out, with offensive lineman Karsten Upchurch and edge defender Nathan Gonzales also unavailable. Their status for tonight requires confirmation.

Defensively, tackle Mackavelli Malotumau, linebacker Jaylen Wester and tackle Rylen Su'a-Filo were questionable on that earlier report.

The potential implications are significant.

If Western Kentucky remains short-handed at running back, its ability to establish a conventional rushing attack becomes more dependent on the healthy backs and Glenn's mobility. That can increase the quarterback's exposure to contact and make the offense more predictable on obvious running downs.

The defensive front deserves equal attention. Delaware is coming off its best rushing performance of the season, and missing defensive linemen could make it harder for Western Kentucky to control interior gaps.

Delaware's injury concerns

Delaware receiver Brandon Rehmann is questionable with an undisclosed injury.

Receiver Ty Salazer is expected to miss an extended period, while running back Greg Spiller has been ruled out for the season.

The Blue Hens also previously listed defensive tackle Noah Frazier out for the season and linebacker Colin Gallagher unavailable.

Those defensive absences matter against a quarterback capable of creating rushing yardage.

A depleted interior defensive rotation increases the burden on linebackers to finish tackles and maintain gap discipline, especially when the opposing quarterback escapes the pocket.

On offense, Delaware has already demonstrated that it can operate without Spiller. Jo Silver rushed for 101 yards against Missouri State, helping the Blue Hens accumulate 232 yards on the ground.

Silver's emergence is important because it reduces the need for Minicucci to carry the offense through passing alone.

Deceptive box score: Delaware 61, Missouri State 38

Delaware's 23-point victory looks like a complete domination, but the final score does not tell the entire story.

Missouri State actually led 28-24 at halftime.

Delaware subsequently took control, producing 61 points, 232 rushing yards and three forced turnovers. The Blue Hens did not punt.

The offensive performance was impressive, particularly with Minicucci back in the lineup. Nevertheless, allowing 38 points demonstrates that Delaware's defensive issues have not disappeared.

The distinction matters: Delaware's offensive improvement is supported by its quarterback's return, but the final margin alone should not be interpreted as evidence of an equally dramatic defensive improvement.

Deceptive box score: Western Kentucky 16, Sam Houston 3

Western Kentucky's previous victory was considerably more impressive defensively than offensively.

The Hilltoppers generated only 276 yards, including 132 passing and 144 rushing.

They held Sam Houston to 177 total yards and prevented the Bearkats from scoring a touchdown.

Western Kentucky won the yardage battle by 99 yards, a meaningful advantage despite the relatively modest final score.

However, the offense's inability to generate more than 16 points against a struggling opponent raises questions about its explosiveness.

This creates an interesting contrast: Delaware enters following an explosive offensive performance, while Western Kentucky enters after a strong defensive showing.

The other important question is whether Western Kentucky's defense can reproduce its performance against Sam Houston when facing a substantially more productive quarterback.

GAME 2: SAM HOUSTON AT MISSOURI STATE

Major personnel story: Missouri State's injury list continues to grow

Missouri State coach Casey Woods delivered a concerning assessment before tonight's game, warning that the Bears' injury report would be deeper than at any previous point this season.

That is particularly important for a team already allowing 34.9 points and 438.1 yards per game.

The reported injury concerns include:

Running backs J. Joyner and J. Dubar — questionable.

Wide receiver M. Miller — questionable.

Tight end J. Rexroat — questionable.

All four have undisclosed injuries, and their final availability has not been established.

The running back situation warrants particular attention. Missouri State averages only 129 rushing yards per game, ranking near the bottom of the FBS.

If the Bears are missing multiple rotational backs, the burden shifts toward Connor Lair and the remaining healthy runners. That could affect pass protection, short-yardage execution and the ability to sustain drives without relying on explosive passing plays.

The tight end situation is another consideration. A missing rotational tight end can reduce flexibility in two-tight-end formations and force the offensive line to handle more blocking assignments without assistance.

Missouri State quarterback Henry Belin IV
Henry Belin IV is the listed starting quarterback for Missouri State.
The Bears average 240.7 passing yards per game, significantly more than their 129 rushing yards.

That offensive imbalance makes Belin's protection and receiver availability central to the matchup.

Sam Houston has been exceptionally effective at limiting opponents' passing production, allowing only 141 yards per game, third nationally.

Missouri State's challenge will be to prevent Sam Houston from dictating obvious passing situations.

If the Bears cannot run effectively, Sam Houston can concentrate on disrupting timing routes, forcing Belin to hold the ball longer and contesting intermediate passing windows.

Missouri State's biggest offensive weapon: Isaiah Myers

One of the most consequential individual matchups involves Missouri State receiver Isaiah Myers.

Myers is coming off a remarkable performance against Delaware:

11 receptions, 242 receiving yards and two touchdowns.

That was the highest single-game receiving total in the FBS this season entering the week.

His season production is equally impressive:

796 receiving yards

113.7 receiving yards per game

Seven receiving touchdowns

20.95 yards per reception

Four games with at least 100 receiving yards

Myers leads Conference USA in receiving yardage and has generated 11 receptions of at least 30 yards.

He is a legitimate explosive-play threat against any defense.

However, Sam Houston presents a substantially different defensive matchup than Delaware.
The Bearkats have allowed only 141 passing yards per game, compared with Delaware's 270.3.
Missouri State must find ways to manufacture favorable matchups for Myers through motion, formations and route combinations.
His ability to produce explosive plays could be especially important if Missouri State's running back depth is compromised.
Sam Houston quarterback Landyn Locke: better than the record suggests

Sam Houston's 1-6 record conceals some legitimate offensive talent.

Sophomore quarterback Landyn Locke leads Conference USA with 236.1 passing yards per game and is tied for the conference lead with 12 touchdown passes.

Seven of those touchdown passes have covered at least 30 yards, with his scoring completions averaging 38.4 yards.

That is particularly noteworthy because Sam Houston's offense has otherwise struggled to produce consistent scoring.

Locke was added to the Manning Award Watch List on October 23.

His supporting cast includes receivers Chris Reed, Grady O'Neill, Tim Burns Jr. and Kyan Berry-Johnson.

The important matchup is Locke's downfield passing ability against a Missouri State defense allowing 253.7 passing yards per game.

The Bears have surrendered 34.9 points per game, creating an opportunity for Sam Houston to generate explosive plays if its offensive line provides adequate protection.

Sam Houston's running game remains a serious weakness

The Bearkats average just 83 rushing yards per game, among the lowest figures nationally.

Their recent performance against New Mexico State was particularly concerning.

Sam Houston managed only 20 rushing yards on 11 attempts while allowing 203 yards on the ground.

Alton McCaskill is a key running back, with Landan Brown and Jerrian Parker Jr. providing additional options.

The concern is not simply the lack of rushing yardage. An ineffective ground attack creates longer third-down situations and forces Locke to carry more of the offensive burden.

Missouri State allows 184.4 rushing yards per game, so this represents an opportunity for Sam Houston to improve its offensive balance.

If the Bearkats cannot run effectively against this defense, their season-long rushing problems will be difficult to dismiss.

Sam Houston tight end injuries

Sam Houston tight end B. Kuhl is out for the season with an undisclosed injury.

M. Whisner has also appeared on the injury report with an uncertain status.

Those absences potentially limit the Bearkats' flexibility in heavier offensive formations.

For a team struggling to run the football, tight end blocking becomes especially important. Reduced depth at the position can make it harder to establish the edge and provide additional protection on passing downs.

The effect is potentially greater in short-yardage situations, where Sam Houston has less margin for error.

Deceptive team record: Sam Houston's defense is much better than 1-6 suggests

The most revealing statistic in this matchup may be Sam Houston's year-over-year defensive improvement.

The Bearkats allowed 483.5 yards per game in 2025.

Through seven games this season, that number has dropped to 341.7.

That's an improvement of 141.8 yards per game, the largest improvement in the country.

Sam Houston also holds opponents to a 30.5% third-down conversion rate, allowing just 29 conversions on 95 attempts.

Those are meaningful defensive achievements for a team with only one victory.

The problem has been the inability to translate defensive stops into enough offensive production.

Sam Houston allows 25.3 points per game while scoring only 20.1.

Its defensive performance suggests that the team's overall record understates the quality of one side of the football.

However, there is an important weakness: opponents average 200.7 rushing yards per game against the Bearkats.

The contrast between outstanding pass-defense numbers and poor run-defense numbers is substantial.

Missouri State's offensive game plan should be influenced heavily by that imbalance.

Deceptive box score: Missouri State 38, Delaware 61

Missouri State's previous game is a prime example of a final score that requires closer examination.

The Bears scored 38 points against Delaware and led 28-24 at halftime.

Isaiah Myers was virtually unstoppable, collecting 242 receiving yards and two touchdowns.

Yet Missouri State ultimately lost by 23 points.

The Bears surrendered 30 unanswered second-half points before finally responding with a field goal.

Delaware scored on nine consecutive meaningful possessions during one stretch and on 10 of 11 overall, excluding kneel-down possessions.

The result raises legitimate concerns about Missouri State's defensive conditioning, adjustments and ability to finish games.

It also demonstrates that the Bears possess enough offensive firepower to threaten opponents even when the defense is struggling.

The final margin was ugly, but Missouri State's first-half performance and Myers' production should not be overlooked.

Deceptive box score: Sam Houston's 24-point offensive rebound

Sam Houston scored 24 points against New Mexico State after producing just three points in each of its previous two games.

That appears to represent meaningful offensive improvement.

However, the rushing statistics reveal a more complicated picture.

The Bearkats managed only 20 rushing yards while allowing 203.

Special teams also contributed significantly.

Railyn Adams intercepted a pass, recovered a fumble and recovered a blocked punt for a touchdown.

That combination is extraordinarily unusual.

The blocked-punt touchdown helped the scoring output but does not represent sustainable offensive production.

Consequently, the 24-point total should not automatically be interpreted as evidence that Sam Houston's offense has solved its underlying problems.

The quarterback's explosive passing ability remains legitimate, but the rushing attack is still a major concern.

text:
Among 6,300+ known exoplanets, few rocky worlds have atmospheres. Now Webb has added one more: HD 3167 b, a lava-world super-Earth 154 light-years away in Pisces.

Published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters by University of Chicago's Brandon Park Coy and Edwin Kite, the study reports evidence of an atmosphere on this intensely hot planet, which orbits its star in just one Earth day.

Using Webb's mid-infrared secondary eclipse method — measuring light lost when the planet passes behind its star — researchers estimated its dayside temperature. A bare rock should be as hot as theoretically possible. HD 3167 b is noticeably cooler, indicating heat redistribution to the nightside or reflective clouds — strong evidence for an atmosphere.

"What's so surprising is that the closer a rocky planet orbits its star, the harder it should be to have an atmosphere," said Kite. Yet most lava worlds studied seem to have them.

This is the fifth lava world with atmospheric evidence, but the coldest so far. It's the first result from a 10-planet survey led by Megan Weiner Mansfield (U. Maryland) to find if there's a critical temperature where thick silicate atmospheres develop.

The atmosphere may be vaporized rock, or heavier gases like CO2, CO, or water. Composition remains uncertain.

Why study uninhabitable worlds? Early Earth likely looked like a lava world, with a magma-ocean stage from planetesimal collisions. These observations offer a window into Earth's first few million years — and help understand atmospheric survival on rocky planets generally, crucial for the search for life elsewhere.

Ann Baker Furrow and her daughter, Lee Ann Furrow Tolsma, were the Girl Scouts of Southern Appalachians Honorees this year.

Ann Baker Furrow represents determination, leadership, and a commitment to opening doors for women when few opportunities existed.

For those of you who aren’t aware of the trailblazer for Women’s Athletics for the University of Tennessee that Ann Baker Furrow was, here’s a simple

Ann Baker Furrow, a native of Maryville and longtime Knoxville community leader, made history in 1963 when she became the first woman to receive a full athletic scholarship at the University of Tennessee and the first woman to play on a men’s varsity athletic team.

At just 17 years old, Ann was the nation’s top-ranked junior female golfer. Because UT had no women’s golf program, Athletic Director Bowden Wyatt offered her a full scholarship to play on the men’s golf team. She competed in 1964 and 1965, breaking barriers nearly three decades before UT established its women’s golf program. 

UT’s Women’s Athletics Department Began when in 1972 Congress enacted Title IX, prohibiting sex discrimination in federally funded educational programs and creating new opportunities for female athletes.

In 1975, UT Chancellor Jack Reese appointed a task force to examine women’s athletics. Ann Baker Furrow served on the committee working toward establishing a women’s athletics department.

In July 1976, UT officially established its separate Department of Women’s Intercollegiate Athletics, with Gloria Ray appointed its first athletic director.

The department initially supported seven sports, approximately 75 female athletes, and a budget of roughly $120,000.

In 1991, Ann partnered with Women’s Athletic Director Joan Cronan to establish UT’s first women’s golf program, which began competing in 1992.

She helped raise more than $2 million to support and endow the program.

Her other historic achievements include:

First woman appointed to UT’s Board of Trustees, serving 18 years.
First woman to deliver a UT commencement address.
Five-time Tennessee Women’s Amateur Golf Champion.
Inducted into the Tennessee Sports Hall of Fame in 2006.
Inducted into the Tennessee Athletics Hall of Fame in 2024. 

The significance is Ann Baker Furrow didn’t just break barriers for women in collegiate athletics, she helped build the opportunities that generations of female athletes at the University of Tennessee enjoy today.
