text:
IRAN'S SUPREME LEADER PUT HIS TERMS FOR ENDING THE WAR IN WRITING, AND OIL $USO GAVE BACK ABOUT A DOLLAR. THEY ARE THE TERMS WASHINGTON REJECTED IN SEPTEMBER:

United States Oil Fund (USO) at $166.23, -$3.30 / -1.95% on Monday, and $165.34 premarket, -$0.89 / -0.54% from Monday's close.

Brent crude reversed an early gain and is under $115 a barrel this morning after Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran's supreme leader, said in writing that the war can end once Iran's conditions are met. It is only about a dollar lower because those conditions are the ones President Donald Trump rejected a month ago. The $43 the war has added to a barrel rests on a blockade and on tanker attacks that one statement does not touch. For an American investor the war arrives as a $4.27 gallon of gasoline and a Federal Reserve that raised rates on it in September. The two things that can move the barrel more than Tuesday's dollar are today's Israeli exit polls and the decision Trump says he will make after November 3.

Khamenei's office said Tuesday that he met Mohsen Rezaei, the former Revolutionary Guards commander who has run Iran's Supreme National Security Council since August, and told him the nation's rights and the interests of the "resistance front" must be safeguarded by fulfilling the conditions the leadership has set, "with the aim of ending the war" and the state of "neither war nor peace." That state is the one Iran has lived in since its ceasefire with Washington collapsed on July 8: US strikes that come and go rather than a campaign, no deal, a US naval blockade of its ports since July 14, and Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Khamenei has not appeared in public since succeeding his father, Ali Khamenei, whom US and Israeli strikes killed on February 28, and he speaks only in written messages.

The barrel reversed an early gain and is down less than a dollar on the day; stocks and Treasuries barely registered it.
- Brent crude for December delivery, about 8am ET: $114.88, -$0.93 / -0.80% from Monday's $115.81 settlement, after $116.38 in early trading.
- S&P 500 futures: 7,735.25, +20.75 pts / +0.27% since Monday's close.
- 10-year Treasury yield: 4.98%, down less than a hundredth of a point.
The conditions have been public for a month. Abbas Araghchi, Iran's foreign minister, laid them out at the United Nations on September 25: the United States lifts the blockade, waives sanctions on Iranian oil, releases about $12 billion of frozen Iranian funds and observes a ceasefire that covers Lebanon, and Iran reopens the strait within seven days. Trump's answer the next day: "I'm rejecting their deal." On Tuesday morning Ali Bagheri Kani, the security council's deputy for foreign policy, said Iran would take a new path if Washington met seven conditions, and that Rezaei could accept four or five days instead of seven. Our read: the market sold a dollar on a leader restating a month-old offer and kept the rest.

The rest is built on facts a statement does not change.
- Brent on February 27, the day before the war began: about $72. Friday's settlement: $116.72, the highest since April.
- Iranian crude the blockade has kept in port since July 14, per US Central Command: $25 billion.
- The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve: about 283 million barrels, the lowest since 1982.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on October 22 that they hit four tankers in the Gulf and that three more struck mines. Brent rose 3.2% that day, and Trump accused Iran of "making up fake hits" to lift oil before the midterms. The oil itself is moving: Bloomberg estimates Middle East crude shipments are back near pre-war levels. Francisco Blanch, Bank of America's head of global commodities and derivatives research, said Monday that $120 a barrel is likely for the next few months if Iran resumes attacks on regional infrastructure.

For an American investor the war arrives at the pump and at the Fed. AAA's national average for regular gasoline is $4.27 a gallon this morning, against $3.05 a year ago; diesel is $6.35 against $3.66. The war splits companies into the ones that sell fuel and the ones that burn it: oil producers and tanker owners on one side; airlines, truckers and chemical makers on the other. The Fed raised its rate to 3.75% to 4.00% in September, its first increase since 2023, because fuel is where the inflation is. It decides again Wednesday at 2pm ET with a hold expected, and Kevin Warsh, the Fed chair, takes questions at 2:30pm.

Two dates can move the barrel more than Tuesday's dollar, and neither belongs to Tehran. Israelis vote today, with polls closing at 4pm ET and exit polls right after, and Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's prime minister, said while thanking Trump for his endorsement that the two have "a job to finish" in Iran. Trump told Fox News on Sunday, "I have a decision to make: Do I finish it off, which would be very easy to do, or do I make a deal?" He has said strikes could resume after the November 3 midterms, and CNN reported Monday that US forces could strike within 96 hours of his order. No date is set for an answer to Iran's seven conditions.

Khamenei's terms have not changed since September. The barrel has: it was $104 the week Trump rejected the deal and $115 the morning Iran's leader wrote the terms down again.

🇮🇷|October 27, 2026. Tehran. Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, posted is the written version of the quadrilateral meeting

“The United States has not brought security to any nation in the region. It has become clear that Washington is incapable of providing security guarantees. Security in West Asia must originate from within the region itself, and any foreign interference must be prevented.”

💥 This statement appeared the day after the quadrilateral meeting concluded

Rezaei did not make this remark during the meeting; he shared it afterward.

At the meeting, he sat across from the Saudi Minister of Defense, the Chief of Army Staff of Pakistan, and the head of Turkish intelligence. Once the meeting ended, he took to X to address the entire world.

This sequence of events is no coincidence. What was said at the negotiating table was intended for those three individuals; what was posted on  here was intended for everyone else. Yet, the core message in both instances was the same: You are already sitting here in Tehran now, transform this reality into your new strategy.

🎯 The Saudi Ambassador writes an article in Riyadh; Rezaei posts a tweet from Tehran

On that same day, Iran’s Ambassador to Saudi Arabia, Enayati, published an article in Riyadh suggesting that the four nations could “jointly play a leading role.” Meanwhile, in Tehran, Rezaei tweeted that “the United States is incapable of providing security guarantees.”

One message, delivered from two directions; one in Riyadh using the language of diplomacy, the other in Tehran using the language of security.

This is not mere “coordination”; it is an act of “encirclement.” The Saudi Ambassador’s article was aimed at the Saudi elite, while Rezaei’s tweet was directed at the Saudi decision-makers. By arriving in Riyadh within the same time frame, these two messages serve to shrink the space for hesitation.

📜 Who is the intended audience for the claim that the U.S. is “incapable of providing security guarantees”?

It is not the Iranians, they do not need to be convinced.

Rather, it is for those nations that, over the past few decades, have outsourced their security to Washington.  These are the nations that allow the United States to build bases on their soil, host the Fifth Fleet, and station the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM). These are the nations that have operated under the assumption that the "American umbrella" is a permanent fixture.

Rezaei’s point is this: the very protector you rely on was, the day after the quadrilateral meeting, openly labeled as "powerless" by its adversary—and you offered no rebuttal.

The communiqué from the quadrilateral meeting did not name the United States. Rezaei’s tweet, however, did. The communiqué stated that "foreign interference must be prevented." Rezaei’s tweet clarified: "The United States has brought no security." It is the same message, translated from the language of diplomacy into the language of security.

⚔️ An Unspoken Fact

The word "United States" does not appear in the quadrilateral meeting’s communiqué.

But it does appear in Rezaei’s tweet.

This is not a "discrepancy"; it is a "division of labor." The communiqué allows the signatories to save face, while the tweet draws a clear line for their strategic adversary. Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey may have refrained from naming the U.S. in the communiqué, but Rezaei named it for them.

And they did not deny it.

🔻 A Mirror

The United States claims: "We are protecting our allies."

Rezaei responds: "You have not brought security to any nation in this region and your allies were just sitting in Tehran."

The United States claims: "Our security guarantees are reliable."

Rezaei responds: "You lack the capacity to provide security guarantees. This has become clear and what is clear requires no debate."

This is not "propaganda"; it is a "timestamp." It marks the moment the day after the quadrilateral meeting when Iran’s top security official publicly declared that American security guarantees have ceased to be effective. And not a single one of the three nations that participated in that meeting has come forward to refute it.

A statement made the day after such a meeting is not a "prediction." It is the documentation of a reality that has already taken hold: in the eyes of its own allies, the American umbrella is no longer reliable. And the venue for this declaration? X (formerly Twitter). Not the United Nations, not a formal press conference but X. Because X requires no authorization from the UN Security Council. 

 Long live Iran. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

text:
✍️📖: Israel Votes Today, but the Real Decision May Come After the Ballots Are Counted

Israel goes to the polls today, and the Middle East, along with much of the world, is watching closely. Two questions dominate the attention: will Benjamin Netanyahu return to power, and who will lead the war against Iran, and for how long?

Much of the media coverage has been overly dramatic. It places heavy emphasis on the changes that would supposedly follow a Netanyahu defeat, as if a new prime minister would pull Israel back from its campaign against Iran or open the door to a Palestinian state. This reading does not hold up. None of the leading candidates offers a real alternative. None of them believes in a two state solution, and none intends to back down against Iran. What separates them is method, not direction. Netanyahu seeks regime change in Tehran as a path to long term transformation. His rivals prefer to dismantle Iran’s military capabilities, economy and infrastructure while leaving the clerical regime in place. The outcome for the region would be much the same.

The United States is deeply invested in the result and in the shape of Israel’s next government, and so are the major European powers. After today’s vote, there are two possible roads. Both lead to the same man, and this is increasingly understood in Washington and in European capitals.

Road One: A Clear Likud Victory
Netanyahu’s Likud wins the most seats and forms a government without serious challenge. Israel continues on its current path against Iran, and Netanyahu may once again bring far right figures such as Itamar Ben Gvir into his cabinet.

Road Two: Second Place, and a Second Life
Likud falls to second place behind Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party. On the surface this looks like a defeat for Netanyahu. In reality, it may be the road that saves him.

In this scenario, Washington and its European partners would press Eisenkot to build a coalition with Likud and to accept Netanyahu as prime minister for another term. Eisenkot has publicly ruled out serving under him, but Israeli politics has a long history of red lines drawn before an election and quietly erased after it.

Such an arrangement would come with conditions. The far right, including Ben Gvir, would be kept out of government. Israel would be expected to finish off Iran’s capabilities quickly and bring the war to an end. It would also be asked to deepen its partnership with the European Union and to commit to the first phase of Gaza’s reconstruction. In return, Netanyahu would keep the premiership, secure his pardon, see the International Criminal Court case against him set aside, and complete his war on Iran alongside President Trump.

At this stage, both the United States and Europe appear to see Netanyahu as the leader best placed to finish the war. To them, he is the most predictable and reliable partner, with decades of experience working with Western governments.

Why Road Two Suits Everyone
This section reflects my own opinion, based on the current relationships and the wider global context: Road Two is the outcome in which every party gains something.

Washington gets its war finished, and Trump gets a diplomatic achievement to present.

Europe gets the first phase of the Gaza reconstruction plan, which it hopes will ease migration pressure and allow it to end emergency measures. European governments have little appetite to fund Gaza’s recovery themselves, and an agreed settlement would also help them contain the more radical wing of pro Palestinian protest movements at home.

Europe also has a quieter interest in Iran itself. European powers would prefer a weakened regime in Tehran that remains intact and can be contained, rather than a full collapse. A country of nearly 90 million people sliding into civil war would likely trigger a refugee wave far larger than the one Europe faced from Syria in 2015, and few European governments believe their societies or their politics could absorb that. For Brussels, a broken but standing regime is the safer outcome. This is where Europe’s position differs most from Netanyahu’s goal of regime change, and why European capitals would want a say in how and when the war ends.

Netanyahu gets his pardon, his final war and four more years in office. Eisenkot, meanwhile, would sit at the heart of government and would most likely emerge as Israel’s next prime minister in four years.

Insider says Wisconsin Democrat was offered $250,000 by rival to exit governor’s race, but reentered when his rival dropped out | Not The Bee

Why does this not surprise me?

Over in the great state of Wisconsin, the Democratic gubernatorial primary apparently featured a bit of bribery. That is, according to an insider report from Daily Wire.

Crowley struck a deal with Lieutenant Governor Sara Rodriguez as part of an effort to consolidate the vote against socialist candidate Francesca Hong, according to the political operative with first-hand knowledge of the events. The advisor, familiar with the Rodriguez campaign's internal discussions, said that the deal involved Crowley exiting the race and endorsing Rodriguez in exchange for the transfer of $250,000 to his political coffers and a guaranteed role for his wife in a future Rodriguez administration.

I mean, that sounds right up Mr. Crowley's alley.

Back in July, the drama of this primary race was reaching NBA on TNT levels. Crowley abruptly announced that he was exiting the race, and it seemed like the right thing to do, as the extremist socialist Francesca Hong was rising in the polls and the Democrats really didn't want her as the nominee.

It was decided that $250,000 would be transferred to David Crowley's campaign and that Ericka probably would receive a position," the advisor said, adding that the job was not specified but "it was clear that it would be a paid position." Crowley's wife currently works as director of the Milwaukee Rental Housing Resource Center, an organization that focuses on homelessness.

Crowley denied the allegations that he was asked to step out of the race.

Let me be very clear about something: Nobody called me or anything like that to ask me to step out of this race.

HOWEVER, just over a week later, Sara Rodriguez dropped out of the race too, due to an accounting mishap involving duplicate contributions and a seemingly inflated campaign chest.

Without enough money in the campaign fund, Rodriguez wouldn't be able to pay any bribe.

So Crowley jumped back into the race and eventually beat Hong.

More from Steve Cortes:

Very important question there:

If he's willing to do this for $250,000, what will he do for millions of dollars?

Mr. Crowley has long been Milwaukee County Executive in one of the worst-run cities in the nation.

The Crowley campaign's response to this report was, "We have no idea what you're talking about."

Man, I love a good October surprise!

text:
In 1878, after the long winter killed most of the men in Eau Claire County, Wisconsin, seven Ojibwe and German widows ran the spring maple sugaring together. The lumber companies had taken the husbands; ice on the Chippewa River took the rest. 

But the sugar maples didn’t care. Every March, the women — Anna, Nodin, Greta, Mindimooyenh, Liesel, Ziibi, and Hilda — tapped 400 trees with hand drills, hung buckets made from hollow logs, and boiled sap day and night in cast-iron kettles. They slept in shifts, sang hymns in two languages, and kept each other’s children alive on syrup and snowbread. 

Lumber barons offered to buy their grove for pennies. Nodin told them: “You sell trees. We keep family. Not the same.” They made 200 gallons that year and paid off every farm. The grove still stands.

Une arène unifiée pour les agents LLM à travers divers jeux de société européens : https://t.co/ODYZR9SjnG

"A Unified Arena for LLM Agents across Diverse Eurogames Fengrui Zhang1,2 , Xiang Li3 , Ruomeng Ding4 , Jiayi Yuan, Yuchen Huang5 Zhaoyang Han6 , Xiaoliang Wang2 , Daoyuan Chen1 , Yaliang Li1 1Alibaba Group 2Nanjing University 3National University of Singapore 4Department of Computer Science, University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill 5The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology 6Peking University Abstract Interactive environments offer a practical way to evaluate large language model (LLM) agents, and competitive games extend this evaluation to decisions shaped by competing goals and other agents’ choices. Yet existing evaluations confined to individual games or execution frameworks leave unclear which competitive advantages persist across settings. We introduce DECE (Diverse Eurogame Competitive Environments), a unified arena spanning ten Eurogames with shared interfaces and evaluation protocols. These games combine lasting strategic commitments, competition over shared resources, and multiple routes to victory. Our primary study evaluates 12 model–harness configurations, spanning nine models and four execution harnesses, in 480 three-player matches across ten games. The main and supplementary studies comprise 1,032 completed matches in total. These comparisons reveal broad cross-game ranking agreement alongside game-specific strengths. Matched studies show that the same model can perform differently across execution harnesses, adding another source of variation to these profiles. These performance advantages do not consistently translate into better token or cost efficiency, making resource use an additional consideration when comparing configurations. Together, the findings support evaluating complete agent configurations by both their competitive performance across games and the resources needed to achieve it. 1 Introduction Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly act through tools in external environments (Yao et al., 2023). Interactive benchmarks evaluate their decisions over extended trajectories (Liu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024). In competition, opponents pursue their own objectives and change an agent’s available opportunities. An action’s value depends on both its future consequences and opponents’ choices. We ask: How can competitive environments support reliable evaluation of complete agent systems across diverse strategic demands? Strategy board games make this question tractable. They combine explicit rules, programmatically executable states and actions, and independently verifiable outcomes (Gaina et al., 2020; Balla et al., 2024). Their interactions can be represented as partially observable stochastic games (POSGs) (Hansen et al., 1 arXiv:2610.35773v1 [https://t.co/gQRNwvACTl] 26 Oct 2026 2004). Agents act on their observation histories; their actions determine state transitions and outcomes. We focus on Eurogames (German-style strategy board games), which combine persistent investments, competition over shared opportunities, and multiple routes to victory. In Splendor, development cards reduce later purchase costs; Azul placements constrain future spatial scoring (Space Cowboys, n.d.; Next Move Games, n.d.). These commitments shape both a player’s future options and opponents’ opportunities. Existing multi-game benchmarks and harness studies provide foundations for competitive evaluation (Costarelli et al., 2024; Hua et al., 2026). Turning these games into a common benchmark presents three challenges. Agents need consistent observation–action interfaces across diverse rules and information structures, while retaining their tools and context management. Analysis must distinguish recurring competitive strength from game-specific advantages and account for execution settings and resource use. Reliable comparisons require consistent rule enforcement, a common participant roster, seat-balanced protocols, and verifiable outcomes. Matched scenarios and uncertainty estimates support comparisons of execution settings. Ten Eurogame environments Resource markets · spatial play · engine building Splendor Azul Century Carcassonne 7 Wonders Harmonies Wingspan Burgundy Brass Ark Nova Model × Harness participants Choose a model + compatible harness Models Harness OpenAI DeepSeek Qwen Claude Gemini Grok … Codex OpenCode Qwen Code DeepSeek Harness(DSH) Claude Code Grok Build … DECE Arena Orchestrator Schedule · Execute · Record Common game tools · MCP / native adapters Run Seat-balanced multiplayer tournaments P1 × Private view P2 × Private view P3 × Private view P4 × Private view Observation Shared board Action Full trajectories + telemetry Competitive ranking Elo + uncertainty Cross-game profiles Across games / seats Harness comparison Matched comparisons Performance–cost Per-game Pareto frontier Elo Cost Figure 1: DECE overview. Shared interfaces connect games and model–harness systems. Seat-balanced matches produce trajectories and telemetry for four analyses. Icons show adapter families; Table 3 lists evaluated configurations. The mascot, pairings, and plots are schematic. We introduce DECE (Diverse Eurogame Competitive Environments), a unified evaluation framework spanning ten executable Eurogames.1 The games vary in their demands for economic development, spatial commitment, and coordination across scoring routes while retaining a shared competitive structure. As illustrated in Figure 1, a common interface exposes seat-specific observations and legal actions to pluggable execution harnesses. Each participant is a complete model–harness configuration, including its tools and context management. A common roster and seat-balanced protocols support cross-game comparisons. Separate matched studies compare the same model across harnesses, fixing setup seeds, focal seats, and opponent configurations within each scenario. Game engines enforce rules and scoring; execution records 1The name also echoes dé cè, a Chinese shorthand for Euro-style strategy board games. 2 support auditing and outcome checks. We quantify uncertainty by resampling whole matches or matched scenarios. We report token use and API-equivalent cost under a fixed pricing schedule alongside competitive outcomes. Our evaluation comprises 1,032 completed matches across the main and supplementary studies. The primary study evaluates 12 model–harness configurations, spanning nine models and four harnesses, in 480 three-player matches across ten games. Rankings formed on nine games agree with the held-out game at mean Kendall τb = 0.664 and 83.9% pair-order accuracy. Game-level profiles reveal distinct strengths and local reversals that the aggregate ranking obscures. Separate matched studies show that the same model’s performance can differ across execution harnesses. Performance–resource trade-offs vary across games, and token-based and cost-based comparisons favor different configurations. These findings support evaluating complete agent systems across multiple competitive environments, with game-level profiles and resource use reported alongside aggregate rankings. Section 2 reviews related benchmarks. Section 3 presents DECE’s environments and evaluation protocol. Section 4 examines cross-game performance profiles (RQ1), matched harness comparisons (RQ2), and game-specific performance–resource trade-offs (RQ3). Section 5 discusses implications for competitive agent evaluation. 2 Related Work Games provide a natural setting for evaluating LLM agents because they combine explicit rules, sequential interaction, and verifiable outcomes. Recent benchmarks span both digital and tabletop environments: Orak, BALROG, and LMGame-Bench evaluate agents across video games (Park et al., 2026; Paglieri et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026a) , while GameBench and MindGames study competitive and social reasoning in board, card, and strategy games (Costarelli et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026). FinBoardBench studies financial decisions and PTCG-Bench examines card play, harness ablations, self-evolution, and cost (Hu et al., 2026b; Hua et al., 2026). Complementary work such as TAG and From Code to Play provides executable tabletop environments or evaluates components used by search-based players (Gaina et al., 2020; Eberhardinger et al., 2024), while LudoBench studies reasoning from fixed game states (Peper et al., 2026). Position of DECE. DECE compares complete agent configurations across ten Eurogames with persistent investments, spatial commitments, and multiple scoring routes. A common roster measures cross-game agreement and local strengths; matched studies assess harness contrasts, and game-specific frontiers relate performance to dollars and tokens. Table 1 compares the benchmark scope. 3 DECE: Benchmark Design and Evaluation Protocol 3.1 Game suite and strategic diversity DECE selects ten score-based Eurogames that share persistent strategic commitments and competition over limited opportunities, while differing in how current decisions shape future options. Table 2 groups them by three dominant, overlapping demands: building future capacity, making persistent spatial commitments, and coordinating multiple action, resource, and scoring systems. These differences allow the suite to test whether competitive advantages recur across related strategic settings or remain specific to individual games. The games also vary in interaction and information structure: players compete entirely through legal game 3 Table 1: Game scope, decision demands, and evaluation focus of related tabletop benchmarks. Entries summarize reported tasks and selected analyses. Appendix C gives sources and scope. Benchmark Game scope Interaction Main decision demands Evaluation focus GameBench (2024) 9 board, card and social games Players or teams Spatial tactics, deck building and social inference Competitive play; scaffold comparisons MindGames (2026) 4 strategic and social games 2–6 players; rivals or teams Opponent inference, signaling, trust and deception Social reasoning; arena validity FinBoardBench (2026b) Cashflow, Acquire, Monopoly 4-player competition Cash flow, investment, mergers and negotiation Financial decision analysis PTCG-Bench (2026) Pokémon TCG; 5 decks 2-player competition Card combinations, resource recovery and action order Self-evolution; harness and cost analysis From Code to Play (2024) 12 TAG tabletop games 2–4-player tournaments Deck building, drafting and tactical card play Generate evaluators for search agents LudoBench (2026) 5 strategy board games Fixed states Perception, rule integration and local optimization Fixed-state question answering DECE 10 score-based Eurogames 2–4 players* ; competition through game actions Long-term investment, persistent placements and multiple scoring routes Cross-game rank agreement; matched harness contrasts; resource frontiers *DECE evaluates three-player matches in all ten games, with supplementary two-/four-player matches in Splendor and Brass, and four-player matches in 7 Wonders. actions, without dialogue or negotiation, and decisions may involve public or private information as well as sequential or simultaneous choices. Figure 2 characterizes this diversity along six rule-based dimensions: engine construction, spatial planning, action sequencing, opponent coupling, hidden information, and scoring coordination. Values 0/1/2 denote absent, limited, or prominent mechanisms. These annotations organize descriptive cross-game comparisons (Appendix B). The suite also spans substantially different interaction lengths, with median whole-match decision counts ranging from 54 in 7 Wonders to 473 in Ark Nova. These counts summarize interaction length at each interface’s action granularity (Appendix C). 3.2 Unified game interface and participant abstraction All games share an interface for setup, seat-specific observations, legal actions, state transitions, and terminal rankings. The engine enforces rules and scoring. Simultaneous choices use a frozen state and advance only after all required seats submit actions. Public information, private state, and unrevealed randomness remain separate. MCP and native adapters expose this interface; persisted states and execution records support auditing, replay, and resume (Appendix A.3). Each participant specifies a model snapshot, execution harness, prompts, tools, memory scope, inference settings, and resource budget. The shared interface permits different internal histories and orchestration strategies. The primary panel contains 12 configurations spanning nine model identities and four harnesses (Appendix A.2). text:
THE MASTER’S DAUGHTER AND THE MAN SHE DARED TO LOVE

North Carolina, America , a story of forbidden love, courage, and the price of freedom.

Imagine living in a world where a man could be punished for loving a woman, a woman could be condemned for loving the “wrong” man, and the law could treat one human being as another person’s property.

That was the cruel contradiction of slavery.

Her name was Ellen Craft. 
The man she loved was William Craft. And their real story was clever enough to make slave catchers look foolish.

Ellen had a secret that slavery could not explain away: she was the daughter of a white slaveholder and an enslaved Black woman. Because she had light skin, she could sometimes pass as white.

William was also enslaved.
 They fell in love and married in 1846, but marriage offered them no protection. Under slavery, the law could treat them as property, and their future children could be taken away and sold.

So the couple devised a plan that was almost unbelievable.

Ellen would disguise herself as a sickly white male slave owner. William would pretend to be her enslaved servant.

Think about that for a moment.

They would travel openly, in daylight, through a society where the colour of your skin could determine whether you were free or owned by someone else.

Ellen dressed in men's clothes, wore a disguise and covered parts of her face. She even arranged things so she would not have to sign documents or speak much.

Their journey took them through several cities, including Wilmington, North Carolina. Every stop brought the danger of discovery.

Imagine the irony: people were so accustomed to seeing Black people treated as property that they could look directly at William and fail to imagine that he might be travelling with his own wife.

Sometimes, the most dangerous lie is the one society already believes.

On Christmas Day in 1848, the couple reached Philadelphia, a free state.
 But their freedom remained at risk after the US passed the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, which made it easier to capture and return people who had escaped slavery.

They eventually fled to England, where they lived for years, raised a family and spoke publicly against slavery.

There is one important historical distinction: Ellen was not simply a slave owner's daughter who fell in love with an enslaved man.
 She herself was enslaved, and William was her husband. 

But their story gives us something even more powerful than a romantic legend.

It shows two human beings using intelligence, courage and love to challenge a system that denied them the right to live as free people.

And North Carolina was part of the journey.

That is why we must tell these stories. Not only the stories of those who were captured, but also of those who resisted, outsmarted their captors and fought to build families on their own terms.

KUNTA KINTE exists to preserve these memories, tell Africa's stories and remind the world that every person taken by slavery had a name, a family, dreams and a future.

 Our history. Our identity. Our future.

text:
Your landing page gets judged in 50 milliseconds.

Before anyone reads your headline.
Before they see your offer.
Before they know how good you are at what you do.

This isn't an opinion. It comes from research.

In 2006, researchers at Carleton University flashed website screenshots for just 50 milliseconds and asked people to rate how appealing they looked.

The ratings matched what people said after looking much longer.

So visitors decide how your page feels almost instantly. And that first feeling sticks. It's called the halo effect.

If the page looks good, people go easier on everything else.
If it looks bad, they start looking for reasons to leave.

Later, a study with Google researchers (2012) tested what drives that snap judgment. Two things:

1. Visual complexity. Busy pages were rated worse.
2. Familiarity. Pages that look like what people expect were rated better.

Simple and familiar won. Even a clean page lost points when it looked unusual.

Then there's trust. In a Stanford study, people left over 2,400 comments on the credibility of 100 websites. Nearly half were about the design.

Looking professional is read as being credible.

And speed matters too. A Deloitte and Google study of 37 brands found that a 0.1 second faster mobile site raised conversions by 8.4% on retail sites and 10.1% on travel sites.

Those are retail and travel, not coaching. Don't copy the numbers. But the direction is clear: faster pages convert better.

So what should you do with this?

→ One clear offer and one button. Not five.
→ Use a layout people recognise: headline, short explanation, proof, one call to action.
→ Cut clutter. No pop-ups, no extra links, no walls of text.
→ Compress your images and keep heavy videos out of the top of the page.
→ Keep the page up to date. Stale pages hurt trust.

One more thing.

Be careful with posts that say "this button color gave +300% conversions."

Teams at the biggest tech companies say most of their experiments don't beat the original. Big wins are rare, and many are just noise.

The boring basics, a simple page, a familiar layout and fast loading, are the ones with real research behind them.

If you're a coach or consultant, your page has one job: turn visitors into booked calls.

Follow me for more breakdowns of what makes landing pages actually convert.

Sources: Lindgaard et al. (2006), Tuch et al. (2012), Stanford Web Credibility Project, Deloitte x Google "Milliseconds Make Millions"

text:
NYC’s sanctuary DAs ordered prosecutors to downgrade charges to keep illegal immigrants in US, House GOP report finds | Josh Christenson & Thomas English, New York Post

New York City’s elected Democratic district attorneys are bending over backwards to keep illegal immigrants in the US, instructing prosecutors to downgrade charges to those considered “a non-deportable offense,” according to a stunning House Judiciary Committee report shared with The Post.

The GOP-led panel found that Bronx DA Darcel Clark trains her subordinates “to conceal facts from the record of conviction” and “pursue alternative charges” that would keep non-citizens free to roam in America.

Not even cases involving child sex crimes are off-limits — with Clark’s office asking assistant DAs in a 2019 guide to “immigration-conscious plea bargaining” to “[o]ffer something that does not have the child’s age as an element of the crime.”

Meanwhile, in Queens, DA Melinda Katz has told her prosecutors to “exercise extreme caution” and “not get caught up in the label of [f]elonies, [m]isdemeanors” for illegal aliens, according to the report published five months after the committee sent requests for information on the Big Apple’s so-called “sanctuary” policies to prosecutor’s offices in all five boroughs, as well as the NYPD and Department of Correction.

Those policies have had deadly consequences, as in the case of a 92-year-old Queens woman who was murdered by a Guyanese migrant, Reeaz Khan, after a federal detainer was lodged against him in 2020.

Katz’s office later secured a 22 years to life sentence against Khan.

The report found versions of the practice in every borough. The Brooklyn DA’s office has explicitly sought an “immigration-neutral” disposition since 2017, having staff trained “to avoid disproportionate collateral consequence, such as deportation, while maintaining public safety.”

In some cases, prosecutors in Brooklyn DA Eric Gonzalez’s office are instructed to offer “a plea for a lesser offense in light of the disproportionate immigration consequences a higher level offense may result in.”

Staten Island DA Michael McMahon has a whole unit dedicated to asking ICE to delay deportations.

But Manhattan DA Alvin Bragg’s office told the committee his once-expansive immigration policy is “outdated,” while admitting prosecutors still consider citizenship status on a case-by-case basis.

In 2022, Bragg had issued a memo to prosecutors requesting that they “seek dispositions that avoid immigration consequences for all misdemeanors, and all felonies for which non-carceral outcomes are the presumptive outcome.”

“When did protecting a criminal’s immigration status become a part of a DA’s job description?” asked New York City Council Member Joann Ariola.

“Our DA’s are entrusted with upholding the law and protecting the public,” Ariola told The Post. “If that’s not their priority, then they’ve got it backwards.”

According to the report, the NYPD has received nearly 10,000 detainer requests from Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) for illegal aliens charged with crimes in the past 12 months — and honored none.

The Department of Homeland Security revealed earlier this month that 16,070 detainer requests had been ignored by authorities across the Empire State, which, like New York City, doesn’t cooperate with federal immigration officials as a sanctuary jurisdiction.

In a report authored by Katz’s office last year, the Queens DA was confirmed to employ an “immigration specialist,” whose sole purpose is helping assistant DAs “navigate through plea options and assist in framing dispositions that will prevent unwanted immigration consequences.”

In 2020 alone, the “immigration specialist” helped get 21 convictions reduced or thrown out entirely. In six cases, Katz urged then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo to grant a pardon to prevent deportation.

Bronx DA Clark has also bragged that since 2020, “[p]rosecutors in my office must thoughtfully consider employment, immigration, family unification, and the broad range of other potential collateral consequences when initiating a prosecution.”

The House Judiciary Committee obtained office training materials from March 2023 titled “Crimmigration,” in which Bronx prosecutors were explicitly told to, “[a]s appropriate,” “strive to ensure that a conviction for certain offenses does not lead to unintended and severe consequences such as deportation that can tear families apart and destabilize communities.”

Screenshots of the “Immigration-Conscious Plea Bargaining” training from 2019 reproduced in the report also revealed that prosecutors were urged to “Offer a Non-Deportable Offense” for defendants to consider copping to.

Those training materials further suggest that prosecutors should consider pursuing charges for so-called “legally impossible” offenses — when a defendant believes they are committing a crime, but actually are not — because “[l]egally impossible crimes cannot serve as the basis for [immigration] removal proceedings” when appealed in the US federal court system.

The legal impossibilities often have a defendant being accused of having “two contradictory mental states … at the same time,” per the report.

In cases involving weapons offenses, Bronx prosecutors are instructed in training materials to “[k]eep the firearm out of the record of conviction” and “[o]ffer something that does not specify a firearm” in plea bargaining.

Accused wife-beaters get the same treatment. Prosecutors are told to “[k]eep the domestic relationship out of the record of conviction.” In stalking cases, they’re encouraged to offer a charge without “repeated instances or an intent to instill fear.”

Republicans argue this practice carries consequences beyond immigration court, and the same omissions that keep a defendant off ICE’s radar can keep him out of sight of law enforcement as well.

In Queens, the approach shows up in practice, not just in training. In a May 26 email obtained by the committee, an assistant DA in Katz’s office told a NYPD detective the office had “basically made a [plea] deal which is ‘immigration safe,’” assuring them that the defendant still pleaded guilty to multiple crimes and spent time behind bars.

Ken Frydman, a Democratic operative and also a police union rep, said, “Immigration specialists typically help immigrants navigate the immigration process, not help get convictions reduced or thrown out in order to keep illegal immigrants in the US.”

According to the Judiciary Committee, Katz spurned the committee’s initial May request, arguing state prosecutions fall outside Congress’ oversight jurisdiction.

She relented only after Chairman Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) and Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement Subcommittee Chairman Tom McClintock (R-Calif.) sent a second letter in August warning they might issue a subpoena.

Reps for the Queens, Bronx, Brooklyn, Staten Island and Manhattan DA’s offices didn’t respond to requests for comment.

text:
My father refused to move into my house while he could still walk. He asked to move in when he could no longer stand. By then, I was running out of ways to help him.

When Dad was diagnosed with cancer, I offered him the guest suite in my home outside Columbus, Ohio.

It had a private bathroom, a balcony, and enough space for him to maintain his independence.

He refused.

“I’m not moving into my son’s house,” he said. “I can take care of myself.”

For months, I drove him to appointments, picked up prescriptions, and called his doctors. Every suggestion became an argument.

He hated hospitals. He hated asking for help even more.

Whenever I suggested that he move in with me, he accused me of treating him like a child.

So I gave him space.

Then his condition worsened.

The man who once insisted on carrying his own groceries could barely walk from his recliner to the kitchen.

Eventually, he needed a wheelchair.

One evening, he called me.

“Son, I think it’s time I came to stay with you.”

I’d wanted those words for months.

But now, I had a problem.

My father was six-foot-four. I couldn’t safely lift him, and his medical needs had become more than I could manage alone.

I had a wife, two children, and responsibilities I couldn’t simply abandon.

I told him we’d need professional support.

He took it as rejection.

A few weeks later, he developed an infection around his medical port.

His doctor told him to go to the hospital.

I called and begged him to go, too.

“I’ll come get you,” I said. “You don’t have to do this alone.”

He refused.

I called again.

He refused again.

And then, everything changed.

text:
Pure Text-to-Video Native One-Shot Unbroken Temporal Consistency Zero External VFX, Inpainting, or Post-Processing Cross-Model Architecture-Agnostic Design.
정지된 인화지 속에서 세 세대의 시간이 동시에 숨을 쉽니다.
이번 프로토타입은 "하나의 프레임 안에 공존하는 다층적 시간성"을 다룬 서사적 실험입니다. 테이블 위에 놓인 낡은 인화지라는 정적인 물리적 세계와, 그 안에서 호흡하고 시선을 미세하게 움직이는 3인(청년기, 중년기, 노년기)의 동적인 세계를 단일 씬 안에 대비시켰습니다.
서사적 의도 (Narrative Architecture)사건의 급격한 전개보다는 관조적 응시에 집중했습니다. 기억의 매개체인 ‘사진’이라는 고정된 오브제 속에 세대 간 시간 축을 교차 배치하여, 디지털 휴먼의 정서가 시각적 장치(메타 프레임)를 통해 관객에게 잔잔한 감정적 무게로 전달되도록 구조화했습니다.

기술적 표현 (Technical Coherence)외부 VFX, 인페인팅, I2V 다단 변환 없이 순수 프롬프트 설계(Native T2V)만으로 다음의 제어 한계를 테스트했습니다.

부분 공간 모션 제어 (Sub-regional Temporal Control): 테이블의 우드 텍스처와 사진 프레임 테두리의 기하학적 형태는 완벽히 정지 상태로 유지하면서, 사진 내부 영역에만 모션 벡터가 국소화되도록 유도했습니다.

다중 피사체 정밀 보존 (Multi-Identity Preservation): 밀착된 3인의 서로 다른 세대별 피부 결, 의복 직물, 이목구비가 시간 축 경과에도 녹아내리거나 융합되지 않는 무결성을 확보했습니다.

text:
$SOFI... notes from the call Q&A...

One thing I'd mention: Even if I'm not perfect, nearly every bear note was VERY wrong. Very, very, very wrong...

Prepared remarks:
1) Growth Strategy (Noto) D*mn on the growth strategy. That is even stronger than I was thinking. I mean, Noto is an optimist, but how he's seeing the biz line growth (I think he said 5) is interesting. I wonder if he's seeing Biz banking as different from what SOFI is currently doing or just an offshoot. If yes, Biz banking (as ya'll know is part of my thesis) grows a bank VERY fast given the size of the deposits/transactions.

2) Hedging (Lapointe): Yup, they hedge, like everyone else on the street. And it buffered losses... b/c rates up IS NOT bad for banks... rates up 550bps in 1 year... that's different. But up to 100bps most are hedged in a variety of ways.

3) Credit Quality, Net Charge-offs (NCO's):  I mentioned in my quick reaction NCO's. This is really interesting. (image 2) makes it very hard to game any decline in credit quality. 

You're going to securitize these off, so your blended overall AFS book is even cleaner but offering a higher rate. 

In other words: What it has to offer as a package of loans is cleaner with a higher interest rate (aka a better product than last year, not worse or even equivalent.

Q&A
1) On Assumptions: Their assumptions (2 rate hikes) still is comfy for the middle of the range. This is b/c what they did in 2026 for investment gives them solid visability. They do not think these estimates are a stretch. Some of this is the roll-off, anniversary of the FinTech overhang from last year, which is gone by 2027 as a comp.

2) Clarification on why the ROTCE increase: It really is the mix of biz. This is likely misunderstood, aka how an investment-based biz can increase ROTCE b/c you have growth on growth (aka you own the deposits and, with no other spend, you have asset growth and the fees and services that come with it). It is the flywheel, but there are many sub-flywheels within that wheel. 

Also an interesting strategy point: you will have lower-margin lending coming in (this is like mortgages, etc.; low margin is low risk in finance), but b/c the financial services biz is so high margin, it both nets out and ends up with a composite mix of higher margin. So this is a strategy call, and I think he does it/can do it given what we're seeing already this quarter with margin expansion. 

Also, realize that I think most banks are dependent on low-margin, high-frequency biz coming back as a part of their strategy, aka CRE and Mortgage biz (lower risk, lower margin).

3) ROC growth, Clarification of Image 2... this is a 2028 and beyond thing, with 2027 being a demonstration of how it comes to pass. I get it. I think if they just get into the low teens by next year, they are better than most banks b/c their issue IMO is overcapitalization... but you know what, if you deploy it to growth, we're cool. 

4) Questions about rates tell me that the folks asking questions don't realize how banks make money. Help clarify why the question implies this:  depending on what rates are, there are different strategies you can deploy. If one knew how banks make money, the question would have been asked differently (so this - in poker -  is a tell). For me, this is helpful, b/c it tells me where the street is not understanding the biz model or where $SOFI sits within the larger financial landscape. Also... Noto... patient of a saint for sure, and I better understand why he's communicating as he is.

5) Loan demand: They are thinking it comes in personal loans and closed-end seconds (2nd mortgages). I think the latter gets more fun with rates. 

6) SOFI Tech arm's length to SOFI Bank. This aligns with my thesis and is how certain other financial services companies monetize their Fintech. So, like Aladdin at $BLK for example is being customized to $BLK's needs, but b/c they are the market leader in asset raising, the implications are that others would like to have this product. With $SOFI, this is similar in the sense that b/c they are consumer-focused (currently), and in that newest part of the market stablecoin and other online platform-based ways of growing assets- their security needs and their lack of legacy make the systems superior to what most banks might do by themselves. Unlike other fintechs that can skimp on capex to get to market, it's strategically smart to have this in-house in this particular manner. text:
Is the Phenomenon God? Part 2: Who Is on the Line

Part 1 described a chain of command: a God who touches people directly, and a staff of Watchers who handle the follow-up by guiding, testing and tricking. Part 2 picks up John Keel's phone and asks whether the staff still takes orders.

"May I Use Your Phone?"

At three in the morning on a cold, wet night in late November 1967, in the hills of the Ohio Valley near Point Pleasant, West Virginia, a young woman was woken by someone hammering on the door of her farmhouse. She opened it a crack, pulling her bathrobe tight.

On the step stood a man over six feet tall, dressed entirely in black: black suit, black tie, black hat, black overcoat, and black dress shoes caked with mud. He had a neatly trimmed mustache and goatee. Lightning flashed behind him. "May I use your phone?" he asked, in a deep voice with no West Virginia accent.

She backed away and fetched her husband, who turned pale at the sight of the stranger, said "We ain't got a phone here," and slammed the door.

The couple told their friends about the apparition. In a place where beards were rare and men in formal suits rarer still, the conclusion seemed obvious: he had been an omen, perhaps the devil himself. Three weeks later, on December 15, the couple were driving across the Silver Bridge over the Ohio River when it collapsed. They were among the forty-six people who died. Their friends remembered the dark stranger. A legend was born.

The stranger was John Keel.

He tells the story on himself in the first chapter of The Mothman Prophecies (1975). He had grown the beard the year before, on a friend's farm. That night his car had run off the road on a muddy hill where he and the reporter Mary Hyre had been watching a strange light, and he was going door to door in his good clothes looking for a working telephone to call a tow truck. "I certainly had no intention of launching new legends," he wrote. He predicted that some future scholar would one day write "a whole chapter of a learned book on demonology" based on the sighting, and that "the presence of the devil in West Virginia in November 1967 will become a historical fact, backed by the testimony of several witnesses."

Part 1 ended with Keel answering a phone that lied to him. Part 2 starts with Keel mistaken for the devil because he wanted to use one. The first answer to "who is on the line?" is the most ordinary one. Sometimes it is just us.

But not always. And the old texts have a lot to say about the other times.

The Bible's first story about this problem is a boy answering the wrong caller. In 1 Samuel 3, young Samuel sleeps in the temple and hears his name. He runs to the old priest: "Here am I; for thou calledst me." Eli says: "I called not; lie down again." It happens twice more, because "Samuel did not yet know the LORD." On the third run, Eli works it out and gives the boy the first rule of answering an unknown caller: "Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth." The voice came back, and this time "the LORD came, and stood," and the boy answered: "Speak; for thy servant heareth." He had left one word out of Eli's script. He did not say LORD.

The open question from Part 1 is whether the whole staff works for the same boss. The Bible gives three different answers, and all three are stranger than the Sunday school version.

The Lying Spirit Who Volunteered

The first answer is that even the liars are on assignment.

In the First Book of Kings, chapter 22, King Ahab of Israel wants to attack the city of Ramoth-gilead and asks his prophets whether he should. Four hundred of them say yes, go, the Lord will deliver it into your hand. His ally, King Jehoshaphat of Judah, is uneasy and asks whether there is one more prophet to consult. There is, Ahab says, a man named Micaiah, "but I hate him; for he doth not prophesy good concerning me, but evil."

Micaiah is brought in. At first he mockingly agrees with the others. Then he tells the king what he saw. In the King James Version: "I saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him on his right hand and on his left. And the LORD said, Who shall persuade Ahab, that he may go up and fall at Ramothgilead? And one said on this manner, and another said on that manner."

It is a staff meeting. Proposals go around the table. Then: "there came forth a spirit, and stood before the LORD, and said, I will persuade him. And the LORD said unto him, Wherewith? And he said, I will go forth, and I will be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets. And he said, Thou shalt persuade him, and prevail also: go forth, and do so."

So, Micaiah concludes, "the LORD hath put a lying spirit in the mouth of all these thy prophets." One of the four hundred, Zedekiah, walks over and slaps him across the face. Ahab orders Micaiah thrown in prison on bread and water until the king returns in peace. "If thou return at all in peace," Micaiah answers, "the LORD hath not spoken by me."

Ahab disguises himself for the battle. It doesn't help. "A certain man drew a bow at a venture," the text says, at random, and the arrow found the gap between the plates of the king's armor. He died that evening, propped up in his chariot.

In this picture, the deceiver is not a rebel. He volunteers in open session, states his method, and gets approval. The four hundred prophets are not frauds. They are hearing a real spirit, and it is lying to them on purpose, by permission. Keel's entities, who fed him a false alarm about a national blackout on the very night the Silver Bridge fell, would fit this model without any trouble.

The Adversary on a Leash

The second answer is that the tester has a permission slip, and the permission has limits.

The Book of Job opens in the same throne room. "Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan came also among them." In Hebrew he is ha-satan, "the adversary," with the definite article, more a job title than a name. God asks where he has been. "From going to and fro in the earth," he answers, "and from walking up and down in it." He is, in other words, a field inspector.

God points out Job, "a perfect and an upright man." The adversary is not impressed. "Doth Job fear God for nought?" Of course he is loyal: God has put a hedge around him. "But put forth thine hand now, and touch all that he hath, and he will curse thee to thy face."

The answer sets the terms of the test exactly. "Behold, all that he hath is in thy power; only upon himself put not forth thine hand." Job loses his herds, his servants and his children in a single day. He does not curse God. So the adversary comes back for a second round, and again the terms are spelled out: "Behold, he is in thine hand; but save his life."

The adversary goes as far as he is allowed and not one step further. He smites Job "with sore boils from the sole of his foot unto his crown," and Job sits in the ashes scraping himself with a broken piece of pottery.

This is the framework's Watcher in its purest form: a tester who runs hard trials but needs authorization for each one, with the scope written into the order. It also says something uncomfortable. In this book, the worst of Job's suffering is not a breakdown in the chain of command. It is the chain of command working as designed.

The Two Hundred Who Swore an Oath

The third answer is that some of the staff walked off the job.

Part 1 quoted the Book of Enoch on the two hundred Watchers who came down on Mount Hermon. The passage before it, in R. H. Charles's translation, has a detail worth slowing down for. The angels see the daughters of men and want them. Their leader, Semjaza, hesitates, and not out of virtue. "I fear ye will not indeed agree to do this deed," he tells the others, "and I alone shall have to pay the penalty of a great sin." He is a middle manager worried about being left holding the bag.

So they make a pact. "Let us all swear an oath, and all bind ourselves by mutual imprecations not to abandon this plan." Then they descend on Hermon, and the mountain, Enoch says, got its name from the oath they swore on it. In chapter 8, one of them, Azazel, teaches humans to make "swords, and knives, and shields," to work metals, and to make bracelets, ornaments, and eye makeup. The others teach spells, roots, and the signs of the sky.

The rebellion is real. But it does not go unanswered. In chapter 10, God dispatches his loyal officers one by one. Uriel goes to warn Noah. Raphael receives a precise order: "Bind Azâzêl hand and foot, and cast him into the darkness: and make an opening in the desert, which is in Dûdâêl, and cast him therein." He is to be covered with "rough and jagged rocks" until the day of judgment. Gabriel is sent against the Watchers' children.

So Enoch's answer to Part 1's question is yes and no. Some Watchers went rogue. The top still issued orders, and the loyal staff carried them out.

An Angel of Light

If some of the staff are rebels and some are licensed deceivers, then appearance proves nothing. Paul said so bluntly. Writing to the Corinthians about rival preachers, he warned: "And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light."

The early church had a model test case. Sulpicius Severus, who knew Martin of Tours personally, wrote around 397 that the devil once came to Martin as he prayed in his cell, "surrounded by a purple light," in "a royal robe," with "a crown of precious stones and gold" and "his shoes too being inlaid with gold," wearing "a generally rejoicing aspect." After a long silence the visitor spoke first: "Acknowledge, Martin, who it is that you behold. I am Christ." Martin said nothing. The visitor tried again: "Martin, why do you hesitate to believe, when you see? I am Christ." Martin's answer was the test: "The Lord Jesus did not predict that he would come clothed in purple, and with a glittering crown upon his head. I will not believe that Christ has come, unless he appears with that appearance and form in which he suffered, and openly displaying the marks of his wounds upon the cross." The devil "vanished like smoke, and filled the cell with such a disgusting smell" that there was no doubt. Sulpicius adds that he heard it "from the lips of Martin himself; therefore let no one regard it as fabulous." The test isn't about brightness. It asks whether the visitor carries the wounds.

The church took the warning seriously, sometimes to absurd lengths. The most remarkable case is Teresa of Ávila's, the sixteenth-century Spanish nun now ranked among the greatest mystics in Christian history.

In chapter 29 of her Life, she describes how, as her visions of Christ became frequent, one of her confessors decided they were from Satan. He gave her an order. Whenever she had a vision, she was to make the sign of the cross and "point my finger at it by way of scorn," and to be firmly convinced it was demonic. The translator's note gives the Spanish: y diese higas. She was to give the vision "the fig," a rude gesture made by closing the fist with the thumb poking out between the index and middle fingers.

Teresa obeyed, and it nearly broke her. "When I saw Him before me," she wrote, "if I were to be cut in pieces, I could not believe it was Satan." So that she wouldn't have to keep crossing herself, she held a crucifix in her hand almost constantly. She could not always bring herself to make the gesture. It reminded her of the insults the crowd threw at Jesus.

What happened next, by her account, is the most interesting part. The figure in the vision told her not to be distressed. She "did well to obey." But "He would make them see the truth of the matter." And then: "He told me to say to them that this was tyranny."

Older monks had a simpler method. The medieval theologian Jean Gerson, in a passage later quoted by the Jesuit demonologist Martín Delrío, told of a desert father to whom a demon appeared disguised as Christ, saying, "I am Christ, visiting you personally, because you are worthy." The old man covered his eyes with his hand and cried, "I do not wish to see Christ here; it is enough if I shall see him in glory." The apparition vanished. It is the same logic as the First Letter of John: "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God." A genuine messenger can wait. A deceiver needs to be believed right now.

"Nothing Is Unjust Which Is Just to God"

The most notorious failure of that test happened in a castle town in Bohemia in the spring of 1587.

For years, John Dee, the Elizabethan mathematician, astrologer and adviser to Queen Elizabeth I, had been holding sessions with a scryer named Edward Kelley, who gazed into a crystal and reported what spirits appeared and what they said. Dee wrote everything down. The spirits dictated an entire angelic language. By 1587 the two men and their wives were living at Třeboň, in southern Bohemia, under the patronage of a great nobleman, William of Rosenberg.

Dee's records of those sessions can still be read because, half a century after his death, the scholar Meric Casaubon printed them in 1659 as A True & Faithful Relation of What Passed for Many Yeers Between Dr. John Dee... and Some Spirits. Casaubon's purpose was to show that Dee had been deceived by devils. He had no need to embellish. The transcript does it for him.

One of the spirits was Madimi, who had first appeared to them in 1583, by Dee's index, "in the shape of a Girle." Now, through Kelley, she had delivered an instruction that the two men were to hold everything in common, wives included. Kelley was appalled. On Saturday, April 18, 1587, as Dee recorded it, Madimi appeared in the stone again, and Kelley cried, "Fie on thee, Devil avoid hence with this filthiness."

"In the Name of God, why finde you fault with mee?" she asked.

Dee answered that her words were "provocations to sin, and unmeet for any godly creature to use."

"What is sin?" said Madimi.

"To break the Commandement of God."

Then she said something no ordinary heckler would say: "Set that down, so." She wanted it in the record.

Her next question was the trap. "If the self-same God give you a new Commandement taking away the former form of sin which he limited by the Law; What remaineth then?"

Dee did not simply surrender. His answer, in Casaubon's print, runs on for most of a paragraph: if it is the same God who gave the Law to Moses and the New Covenant through Christ, and if "sufficient proof and testimony may be had that it is the same God," then "must the same God be obeyed." Madimi supplied the proof she thought was needed. She told them that what seems sin to men can be righteousness before God, that "the Apostle Paul abounded in carnal lust," and: "Beleeve me, that we are from above." Then she added a threat: if they forsook "the way taught you from above," evil would enter their senses, and their wives and children would be carried away before their eyes.

Kelley reported a vision: a white pillar bearing four heads, like the two men's heads and their two wives', under a crown of crystal. Then a half moon came down, inscribed in Latin: Injustum nihil quod justum est Deo. Nothing is unjust that is just to God.

They gave in. Dee's own note in the record says that "on Sunday the third of May, Anno 1587," at Třeboň, "I John Dee, Edward Kelley, and our two wives, covenanted with God, and subscribed the same," promising unity, charity and friendship "and all things between us to be common, as God by sundry means willed us to do."

Whoever was speaking through Kelley's stone, the transcript shows exactly where the danger lies. The spirit did not ask Dee to stop believing in God. It claimed to speak for God, offered a new commandment overriding the old ones, and asked him to write it down. That is the angel of light in its classic form, and Dee had even given it the logical opening it needed, with his own "if."

The Thief on the Line

Madimi claimed to speak for God. The old texts also describe a stranger caller, one who claims no authority and is still right: an eavesdropper.

The Testament of Solomon, a Greek book of demon lore whose date scholars still argue over, opens with a petty crime. While the Temple in Jerusalem is going up, a demon named Ornias visits the master workman's little boy every evening after sunset, takes half his pay and half his food, and sucks the thumb of his right hand. The boy grows thinner by the day, though the king pays him double. Solomon prays, the archangel Michael brings him a ring with an engraved seal, and the boy throws it at the demon's chest. Ornias begs him to take it off and offers him "the gold of the earth." He ends up cutting stone for the Temple.

Later an old workman throws himself at Solomon's feet. His only son beats him and pulls out his hair, he says, and he wants revenge. The son denies it. The father refuses to forgive him and says he would rather let him die. Solomon is about to pass sentence when he sees Ornias laughing.

Hauled before the throne, the demon explains that he was laughing at "this ill-starred old man and the wretched youth, his son. For after three days his son will die untimely." Solomon reconciles the pair, sends them home with food, and asks how the demon knows. The answer, in F. C. Conybeare's 1898 translation: "We demons ascend into the firmament of heaven, and fly about among the stars. And we hear the sentences which go forth upon the souls of men, and forthwith we come, and whether by force of influence, or by fire, or by sword, or by some accident, we veil our act of destruction." Up there, with nothing to stand on, they tire and "fall off like leaves from trees. And men seeing us imagine that the stars are falling from heaven."

Solomon keeps the demon under guard for five days, then sends for the old man. He comes in mourning, "with black face." His son has been dead two days.

Ornias did not pass that sentence. He overheard it.

The Talmud says the same thing in one dry line. Demons, a teaching in tractate Chagigah (16a) says, "know what will be in the future like ministering angels." The rabbis object that not even the angels know the future: "Rather, they hear from behind the curtain when God reveals something of the future." The Qur'an tells it from the thieves' side. In Sura 72 the jinn recall: "we used to sit therein in positions for hearing, but whoever listens now will find a burning flame lying in wait for him." Sura 37 calls the stars a guard against "every rebellious devil," except "one who snatches [some words] by theft," chased by "a burning flame." Shooting stars again, this time as the security system. A saying in al-Bukhari's collection explains why fortune-tellers sometimes hit: a jinn snatches the true word and pours it into the teller's ear "with a sound similar to the cackle of a hen," and "then they add to it one-hundred lies."

These are not three independent witnesses. They come from one Near Eastern world, and Qur'an scholars trace the eavesdropping jinn partly to older Jewish lore. But a rule repeated in that world for a thousand years deserves to be stated plainly: accuracy is not authority. A voice can know your future because it read the order, not because it wrote it, and not because it is on your side. Part 1's Apol fits the profile: plane crashes called correctly, a knife attack on the Pope with the place and date wrong, and nonsense in between. One stolen word, and a hundred lies.

The Channels That Are Hard to Forge

If the line can carry lies, what kind of channel is hardest to fake? Other essays in this series have looked at two safeguards, and they fit together here.

One is a guide that can only say no. Socrates' sign, as Plato described it, "always forbids but never commands." A voice like that can stop a mistake, but it cannot steer anyone into a new one. Madimi's whole case was a positive command. A Socratic sign would simply have said no.

The second is the sealed letter. In the best-recorded Marian apparitions, the message that settles the case is often one the seer cannot understand: Bernadette carrying the words "Immaculate Conception" to her priest without knowing what they meant. A courier who cannot read the letter cannot rewrite it. Kelley, by contrast, interpreted everything himself and was the only one who could see the stone.

Neither is proof. But they are the kinds of structures a careful system would build if it knew that its own staff could not always be trusted, and they match the advice of the old texts: test the spirits, distrust a spirit in a hurry, and be most suspicious of any voice that brings a new commandment.

The strongest version of that advice comes from a man who spent his last decades in daily conversation with spirits. On March 20, 1748, the Swedish scientist-turned-seer Emanuel Swedenborg wrote in his private diary, under the heading "That Spirits Relate Things Exceedingly Fictitious, and Lie": "When spirits begin to speak with man, he must beware lest he believe them in anything; for they say almost anything." If they were allowed to describe heaven, he added, "they would tell so many lies, and indeed with solemn affirmation, that man would be astonished." The worst danger was the one in Madimi's case: "They induce so strong a persuasion that it is the Lord Himself who speaks and who commands, that man cannot but believe and obey."

The séance room kept its own list of credentials that did not check out. In 1889 and 1890 the physicist Oliver Lodge sat with the Boston medium Leonora Piper, whose trance voice introduced itself as "Dr. Phinuit," a French physician. Phinuit supplied a biography and asked to be checked: born in Marseilles, "a Southern French gentleman," studied medicine at Metz, died at 70 "of leprosy, very disagreeable." "Get someone to look all this up, and take pains about it." His medical guesses were often uncanny, but the doctor's papers were thin. Lodge, writing in the Society for Psychical Research's Proceedings, put the problem plainly: "why if he was a French doctor has he so entirely forgotten his French? For though he speaks in a Frenchified manner, I am told that he cannot sustain a conversation in that language." Accurate information, false label: exactly the combination a discerning listener is told to expect.

Keel's Last List

Keel's own conclusion was darker than any of this. Part 1 quoted his saddest line, the list of everyone who had lied to him: the Air Force, the telephone company, the UFO entities, and, on occasion, his own senses.

Notice who is missing from that list. Keel did not include himself, though by his own account he was, for one stormy night, the devil of the Ohio Valley. He also did not include anything above the entities. He spent years talking to the staff and never got through to whoever, if anyone, they worked for.

The texts suggest that this might be the point. Micaiah's lying spirit told four hundred prophets exactly what their king wanted to hear, and the one man who heard the true message heard it by seeing the throne room itself. Teresa's confessor ordered her to give the fig to her visions, and the figure in the vision told her to obey and to call it tyranny. The desert father covered his eyes and said he would wait. Dee did not wait, and signed. Ornias laughed in court because he had already heard the verdict the judge had not yet given.

So, who is on the line? On the evidence of the oldest records, the honest answer is: it depends on the call. Sometimes it is a frightened couple and a stranger who needs a tow truck. Sometimes it is a tester working inside the terms of a permit. Sometimes it is a spirit authorized to lie. Sometimes it is a rebel who swore an oath on a mountain. Sometimes it is a thief who overheard the sentence. And every source that describes the system insists there is a top floor where the permits are signed, where the rebels are eventually bound, and where the fire in Part 1 came from.

What none of them offers is a way to tell from the voice alone. For that, the old advice is still the only advice: try the spirits, be wary of the one that is in a hurry, and never mistake the voice that read your sentence for the one that wrote it.

I was also categorized as a GATE student in elementary school. I also read the textbook cover to cover, but most of my teachers were pretty cool about it and gave me more stuff to do based on my interests in science and history. 

I remember one time I was basically telling everyone in 4th grade science what we would be covering today and explaining it all while interrupting my teacher to the point she got frustrated (understandably so) and asked if I wanted to teach class today. I didn’t realize she was probably being facetious and took her up on the offer which she actually let me do for about 15 minutes until she pivoted us to an activity. 

It probably helped that I went to a very small rural elementary school in Virginia and we actually had a couple of gifted resources teachers so I was able to do a lot of extra things with them each week. 

That all kind of died when I went to middle school though and I felt like the GATE program was basically a glorified smart kids club where we randomly had meetings and pizza parties and field trips but I don’t remember much extra learning or anything challenging. 

By high school I just got burned out by the volume of homework/busywork and preferred to enjoy the golden era of Xbox 360 in my free time when I wasn’t playing lacrosse (I didn’t get home until 7 pm most nights and had a good 2 hours of homework that of course I didn’t want to do while I was physically tired). 

Despite half assing my homework, I never had a class in high school where the test and quiz portion of my grade was below a B+. I used to wonder how much better I would have done on tests if I wasn’t staying up until 2-3 am playing Xbox each night. 

Around 9th grade I kind of realized I probably wasn’t going to Caltech so I just started looking for state schools out west with decent business and stem schools and made sure I did enough to meet those pretty (back then) low standards. 

Ended up bumbling through my first few years of college, almost dropping out, then pivoting and getting degrees in applied math and physics.

Found out I had ADHD after having a son and doing the parents questionnaire for him and noticing I had most of the same symptoms and ones he didn’t have. Probably would have been nice to have help for that as a kid, but also glad I had to teach myself how to create my own conditions to succeed.
