FASTBEAK | Human Capital Over Nuclear Escalation
A 20-Year State-Level Framework for Iran, Lebanon, Palestinian Reconstruction, and Regional Security

I. Strategic Assessment — The Current Regional Reality

Fastbeak assesses that Israel has achieved substantial conventional military successes against Hamas in Gaza, Hezbollah in Lebanon, and Iranian military assets, with material support from the United States. These developments have significantly weakened Iran's regional deterrence architecture and altered the strategic balance underlying future U.S.–Iran negotiations. Hezbollah's decision to engage Israel following Hamas's October 7, 2023, attacks exposed the organization and Lebanon to considerable military consequences. Fastbeak further assesses that the post-October 7 environment has strengthened Israeli political factions favoring expanded West Bank settlements and potentially more permanent territorial control, further complicating prospects for a negotiated two-state solution. Although these outcomes do not establish the permanent defeat of Palestinian political aspirations or the complete elimination of Hamas and Hezbollah, they materially constrain the military and diplomatic options previously available to Iran and its regional partners.

II. A Practical Assessment of Palestinian Circumstances

While I recognize the extraordinary humanitarian suffering, displacement, loss of life, and destruction experienced by Palestinian communities, practical evaluations of the military and political situation can be beneficial, even when their conclusions are difficult to accept. Fastbeak assesses that Israel's campaign has substantially dismantled Hamas's organized military capabilities, significantly reducing the armed leverage that Hamas previously sought to exercise in connection with Palestinian political objectives. This does not eliminate Palestinian legal rights, diplomatic claims, or entitlement to self-determination, but it does weaken the proposition that armed confrontation can presently deliver a viable two-state settlement.

Fastbeak also considers continued West Bank settlement expansion, displacement pressures, and proposals for territorial annexation to be serious indicators of a deteriorating environment for Palestinian statehood. These developments create a substantial risk of further territorial fragmentation, property dispossession, and displacement, although eventual annexation or mass eviction should not be treated as inevitable. The implications of these changes may take considerable time to register across Palestinian political institutions and communities, particularly given the historical significance of the two-state objective and the multigenerational investment in that political aspiration.

Under these circumstances, Fastbeak considers civilian security, preservation of family and property records, protection of legal claims, communication with displaced relatives, and the reconstruction of essential infrastructure to be immediate priorities. Gaza's recovery will require sustained international financing, accountable governance, and substantial engagement by Turkey, GCC countries, international institutions, and Palestinian civilian authorities. Iran may preserve its historical diplomatic and personal relationships with Palestinians while recognizing that its current military and economic circumstances limit its capacity to serve as the principal sponsor of reconstruction.

III. Iran's Strategic Crossroads — The Limits of Conventional Defeat

Fastbeak distinguishes between Israel's demonstrated capacity to degrade Iranian military capabilities and the more ambitious objective of permanently neutralizing Iran's strategic influence. Iran retains substantial population resources, domestic scientific and industrial capabilities, established regional relationships, and the potential to rebuild conventional military infrastructure. These attributes complicate any strategy premised upon the assumption that eliminating selected military commanders, political officials, or affiliated organizations will necessarily produce a durable strategic defeat.

Fastbeak identifies three dimensions of Iran's long-term strategic position: its regional relationships with Palestine, Lebanon, and Iraq; the future of its nuclear program; and its domestic scientific, industrial, and defense-manufacturing capabilities. A durable settlement would need to account for these interests without assuming that Iranian national capacity can be reduced indefinitely to a narrow set of political figures or non-state military networks.

The central question is whether Iran can establish a more sustainable regional security position through lawful state-level relationships and institutional development rather than relying primarily on proxy-based deterrence or nuclear escalation.

IV. Iran's Nuclear Decision — Escalation Versus Verified Restraint

Iran's enriched uranium inventory has generated significant international proliferation concerns, including estimates of the potential weapons-equivalent quantity of material available under certain technical assumptions. Such estimates do not establish that Iran possesses completed nuclear weapons or an immediately deployable nuclear arsenal.

Fastbeak assesses that pursuing nuclear weaponization would expose Iran to substantial risks of military retaliation, economic isolation, additional sanctions, and prolonged confrontation. Even if Iran ultimately established a functioning nuclear deterrent, that capability would not automatically neutralize Israel's conventional military superiority, intelligence infrastructure, cybersecurity capabilities, or access to international financial and technological support. Nor would nuclear weapons independently resolve Palestinian territorial claims or restore Gaza's civilian infrastructure.

Fastbeak therefore favors a negotiated nuclear framework involving enrichment restrictions substantially below 60%, expanded International Atomic Energy Agency inspections, verified treatment of existing enriched uranium inventories, and long-term commitments to peaceful nuclear activity. The purpose would be to reduce proliferation risks while creating space for a broader regional security arrangement.

V. Fastbeak's Proposal — A 20-Year Iran–Lebanon State-Level Agreement

Fastbeak proposes evaluating a 20-year security and institutional development agreement between Iran and Lebanon, aligned with a corresponding period of verifiable Iranian nuclear restrictions. Under the proposed framework, Iran would consider contributing approximately $2 billion annually toward a Lebanese state-administered security and defense program, subject to Lebanese sovereign approval, applicable sanctions, export controls, and international legal obligations.

Lebanon would seek additional domestic and international financing sufficient to sustain an indicative annual security and defense budget averaging approximately $4 billion over the agreement's duration. These figures represent proposed commitments rather than existing government agreements.

The Lebanese Armed Forces would retain exclusive responsibility for national defense planning, operational command, and procurement decisions. Eligible investment priorities could include border security, defensive surveillance, military communications, personnel readiness, logistics, maintenance, training, and institutional modernization. Potential procurement of Iranian-origin drones or air-defense technologies would require separate legal authorization, sanctions compliance, and appropriate safeguards against diversion to non-state armed organizations.

The governing principle would be the development of accountable Lebanese state capacity rather than the continuation of security arrangements dependent upon individual political figures or proxy organizations.

VI. How a State-Level Framework Could Alter a Post-Agreement Israeli Campaign

Fastbeak's strategic hypothesis is that a formal Iran–Lebanon agreement could change the diplomatic and institutional context of future Israeli security operations. In Fastbeak's assessment, Israeli military strategy has frequently emphasized relationships among Iranian political and military officials, state institutions, and affiliated non-state armed organizations. This framing can facilitate narrowly defined military objectives against particular individuals, facilities, or networks.

A transparent, internationally monitored agreement with the Lebanese state would create a different institutional framework. Iranian engagement would be conducted through recognized sovereign authorities, formal financing arrangements, accountable procurement procedures, and Lebanese Armed Forces command structures rather than through informal relationships with non-state armed groups.

Such an arrangement could make it more difficult diplomatically to characterize every Iranian regional relationship solely through the lens of proxy activity. A more capable Lebanese state could also become a significant consideration in Israel's northern-border security planning, potentially influencing its long-term allocation of diplomatic, intelligence, and defense resources.

However, the agreement would not automatically prevent Israeli military operations, prohibit strikes against Iranian targets, or guarantee that Israel would redirect resources away from Iran. Its effectiveness would depend on the defensive character of Lebanese capabilities, international oversight, reciprocal security assurances, and whether the arrangement demonstrably reduces threats to neighboring states.

VII. Israel's Strategic and Economic Incentives

Fastbeak considers Israel's potential incentives for accepting a regional framework to extend beyond immediate military considerations. Verifiable Iranian nuclear restraint would reduce a significant proliferation concern, while a more accountable Lebanese security architecture could provide opportunities for improved border stability and reduced cross-border escalation.

Israel also maintains a sophisticated defense technology, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, and advanced engineering ecosystem. Continued investment in these industries reflects a combination of national security requirements, commercial innovation, export opportunities, and institutional capital allocation.

Fastbeak's hypothesis is that a long-term regional security arrangement could remain compatible with sustained Israeli investment in these sectors. However, it would be speculative to conclude that Israeli policymakers would support the agreement primarily to justify higher defense expenditure or direct capital toward technology startups.

The stronger argument is that an agreement offering verifiable nuclear restraint and improved regional stability could create security and economic benefits without requiring Israel to abandon legitimate technological or commercial development priorities.

VIII. Implications for Iran, Lebanon, Palestinians, and Israel

For Iran, the proposed framework could provide an alternative to the risks of nuclear weaponization while preserving lawful regional relationships and creating opportunities for economic recovery, sanctions relief, and reduced military confrontation. Iran would retain its domestic scientific and industrial capabilities while pursuing a more transparent regional diplomatic strategy.

For Lebanon, the framework could provide predictable multiyear financing, stronger national institutions, improved border security, and greater sovereign control over defense affairs. Its success would depend on preserving Lebanese decision-making authority and preventing the diversion of state resources to non-state armed groups.

For Palestinians, the principal priority would remain reconstruction, civilian protection, property preservation, and the restoration of economic activity. Turkey, GCC countries, and international financial institutions could support these objectives through sustained financing and accountable civilian institutions.

For Israel, the principal benefits would include verified Iranian nuclear restraint, reduced proliferation risks, and the prospect of a more stable Lebanese border. A stronger Lebanese state could influence regional security planning, but it would not necessarily produce higher Israeli defense expenditure or guarantee the cessation of military operations.

IX. The Central Strategic Assessment

Fastbeak's central argument is that the weakening of Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iranian conventional military capabilities has changed the regional balance, making previous assumptions about armed deterrence and the prospects for a two-state solution increasingly difficult to sustain.

For Palestinians, this suggests placing greater immediate emphasis on civilian survival, reconstruction, legal rights, and preservation of economic assets, without abandoning the underlying right to self-determination.

For Iran, it suggests that continued high-level uranium enrichment and reliance on weakened regional armed networks may offer diminishing strategic returns relative to the risks of military escalation.

A lawful, verifiable, state-level security framework involving Lebanon could provide an alternative basis for regional engagement, although it would require significant diplomatic negotiation and cannot guarantee changes in Israeli military behavior.

X. Fastbeak's Conclusion — Human Capital Over Nuclear Escalation

Fastbeak considers a 20-year framework combining verifiable Iranian nuclear restraint, Lebanese institutional development, and internationally supported Palestinian reconstruction to be a more constructive long-term approach than nuclear weaponization or indefinite military escalation.

The proposed arrangement would seek to replace dependence on non-state military networks with accountable sovereign institutions, strengthen Lebanese national capacity, and provide Iran with an alternative to the economic and security costs associated with continued nuclear confrontation.

The fundamental proposition is that human capital, sovereign institutions, economic resilience, and lawful state-level relationships can generate more durable strategic value than nuclear escalation or the indefinite continuation of proxy-based conflict.

I recognize that the humanitarian consequences of these conflicts are profound and that the political realities may take time for affected communities to process. Nevertheless, practical assessments remain necessary to distinguish achievable near-term objectives from aspirations that current military and diplomatic conditions may not support.

From my personal perspective, I offer this as an independent strategic assessment rather than a commitment to continued involvement in regional affairs. Time is finite, and I have other professional, commercial, and personal priorities to pursue. I would prefer that any further development of these proposals be undertaken by the governments, diplomatic institutions, and regional stakeholders directly responsible for their implementation.

Blakeman is a terrible candidate who ran a piss poor campaign. Saddling up with a president who has historically low job approval ratings was bad strategy - esp running for governor in a state who didnt vote for him 3 times. 

Then he ran his campaign as if he was in 6th grade running for class president. “If I’m elected, no more homework.” 

Blakeman promised $35B in annual incometax cuts, 50% lower utility bills & 10% lower property taxes.

Yet he hasn’t produced a specifics detailed financial plan identifying which programs he’d eliminate, how much each cut would save or how he’d replace $35B in recurring revenue without devastating essential state services.

Which programs get gutted? Education? Medicaid? Infrastructure? Aid to local governments? And how much would each cut actually save?

You can’t simply eliminate $35B in revenue & assume the budget magically balances because you dislike welfare spending.

And about those utility bills: The PSC regulates delivery rates, not the governor. Eliminating certain energy surcharges doesn’t magically reduce an entire utility bill by 50%. Again, no detail/specifics offered.

Blakeman also proposes expanding natural gas production by reversing NU’s fracking ban. However, the prohibition is codified in state law. A governor cannot simply snap his fingers and repeal legislation. That generally requires action by the Legislature. Again, no details.

Even if the law changed tomorrow, developing new gas production would take time, investment, infrastructure and regulatory approvals. Where are the calculations demonstrating that this would cut utility bills in half? No plan/details.

And property taxes? Those are primarily levied by school districts and local governments. Again, a governor cannot simply decree a statewide 10% reduction. No details.

Hochul is a very flawed candidate that was ripe to be beaten. But between awful strategic campaign decisions coupled with a bumper sticker/flyer/sign/slogan type campaign messaging promising dramatic fiscal change with zero substance under the hood was also a miss.

text:
Is it still ARMED FORCES OF THE PHILIPPINES OR ARREST FORCES OF THE PHILIPPINES?? KALOKA! 😂😂🤦‍♀️🇵🇭

Goodness gracious! What on earth is happening to the AFP under the Marcos Jr. administration?

Since when did arresting politicians become a priority mission of the AFP? Isn’t the AFP’s constitutional mandate primarily to defend the state, protect national sovereignty, and safeguard territorial integrity? Are we now turning our soldiers into arresting officers for politically controversial cases and at the whims and caprices of BBM?? 

And here’s another question: Where is the legal basis for all this? Has an ICC arrest warrant against Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa been officially verified and transmitted through the appropriate channels? Is there an INTERPOL Red Notice? More importantly, what Philippine legal authority would permit its enforcement? 

Let’s be clear: An ICC warrant is not automatically an executable Philippine arrest warrant. An INTERPOL Red Notice, even if issued, is not itself an arrest warrant.

And excuse me, ₱50 MILLION REWARD FOR BATO’S CAPTURE? Seriously? If that amount is indeed being offered, who authorized it, from which public funds, and under what legal justification?

WOW! MAY PERA PALA ANG GOBYERNO! 🤣

We have Filipinos struggling with food prices, inadequate healthcare, insufficient educational resources, and rising living costs. Yet apparently, when it comes to politically charged operations, money is suddenly available?

And is this how the AFP and PNP now extend professional courtesy to a former PNP Chief and incumbent senator? Whatever one’s political affiliations, shouldn’t the same standards of due process, legality, and institutional professionalism apply to everyone?

Now, let’s talk about the ICC.

The Philippines withdrew from the Rome Statute in 2019. Why, then, is the Marcos Jr. administration seemingly so enthusiastic about facilitating ICC-related arrests? What is the precise domestic legal basis for cooperation?

Of course, withdrawal does not automatically extinguish the ICC’s jurisdiction over alleged crimes committed while the Philippines was a state party. But jurisdiction, cooperation, and the domestic enforceability of an arrest warrant are distinct legal questions. A government that claims to uphold the rule of law should be able to explain all three.

And while our security establishment appears preoccupied with this political spectacle, the peso is hovering around ₱64 to the US dollar!

Hello, Malacañang? Anybody home? 🤦‍♀️

Where is the credible economic response? Where are the measures to cushion ordinary Filipinos against imported inflation, rising costs, and the erosion of purchasing power?

Apparently, this administration has plenty of energy for political drama but precious little urgency for the economic distress of ordinary Filipinos.

Mr. President, perhaps you should remind your officials that governing a country involves more than pursuing political adversaries and making dramatic announcements.

The AFP is not supposed to become a political arrest squad. The PNP must uphold due process. And the presidency is not a reality show where political spectacle substitutes for competent governance.

Defend the country. Respect the Constitution. Protect the economy. Serve the Filipino people.

Priorities naman, Mr. President! Hindi puro political theatrics habang naghihirap ang sambayanang Pilipino!

KALOKA! 😂🇵🇭

🇮🇷|The Tenth Testimony, and a Regional Map Being Redrawn

October 27, 2026. Tehran. https://t.co/wmOl5JzSz7 released the tenth installment in its "Men of Sincerity" series: Basel Bahramnejad.

He joined the "Vali-e Amr" Corps of the Revolutionary Guards in 2001. For the next twenty-four years, he served on the Supreme Leader’s personal protection detail. On March 6, 2026, he was martyred during yet another bombing targeting the Office of the Supreme Leader. His father followed him in death just weeks later.

That same day, a memorial service for Ali Larijani was held at the University of Tehran. Larijani, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council was martyred on March 18, 2026, at the dawn of Ramadan, alongside his son, a deputy, and several bodyguards, in a joint U.S.-Israeli airstrike. At the ceremony, the Minister of Science remarked that what Israel feared most was "Larijani’s rational mind and his capacity for strategic analysis."

A bodyguard who spent twenty-four years protecting the Supreme Leader; a Security Council Secretary assassinated at the dawn of Ramadan. Two names, the same manner of death. And their passing has been documented, commemorated, and transformed by the very same system into a justification for its continued operation.

💥 The Supreme Leader Defines "Strength" Through Science

October 26, 2026. Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei addressed a gathering of elites and medal-winning scholars.

"Iran’s strength is built upon scientific and technological authority."

He invoked the framework *al-‘ilmu sulṭān,* "knowledge is authority." He argued that national progress requires "a profound and accelerated scientific leap," and that the key to making "every inch of Iran stronger" lies in the ability of its elites to "push beyond the frontiers of science." He called on officials to provide the necessary infrastructure and to fully harness the "individual capabilities and collective wisdom" of these elites.

This was no mere "speech about education."  Eight months into the war, this represents a redefinition of the source of "strength" for a nation currently enduring bombardment, sanctions, and the assassination of its scientists. It is not a matter of missile stockpiles or naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz; rather, it lies in laboratories, universities, and the minds of the youth. Missiles can be intercepted and mines can be cleared, but a system capable of consistently generating scientific breakthroughs cannot be destroyed by bombardment.

🎯 A Term Brought Back from the Supreme Leader by Rezaei: "Four-Way Consultation"

October 27, 2026. Following a meeting with the Supreme Leader, Mohsen Rezaei, Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council (SNSC), disclosed details of the discussions to the media.

The Supreme Leader characterized the SNSC as a forum for "four-way consultation" on national affairs an intersection of four domains: culture, politics, economics, and security. He emphasized that any decision within these areas must be accompanied by "corresponding annexes." He called for the development of a "roadmap based on a comprehensive vision from inception to conclusion" to ensure that decisions are both "precise and robust."

Regarding the war, the Supreme Leader offered a pivotal observation: the "desperation" of the enemy is the "fruit of national resistance." He stated that the path to ending the war and moving beyond the current state of "neither war nor peace" lies in "fulfilling the conditions set forth by Iranian state officials."

"Neither war nor peace".this phrase is the core of the entire discussion. Iran does not consider itself to be at "peace," as the bombardment, blockades, and assassinations have never ceased. Yet, it does not consider itself to be in a state of "war," as there has been no formal declaration of war nor a full-scale ground invasion. This "neither war nor peace" is an imposed state. The Supreme Leader’s message is clear: the way to end this condition is by realizing the terms proposed by Iran itself not through compromise, but through the fulfillment of these conditions.

📜 The Four-Way Consultation: The First Step Toward an Endogenous Order

In his report, Rezaei confirmed that the strategy currently being advanced by the Supreme National Security Council is to "organize and establish an endogenous regional order."  On October 26, 2026, this "endogenous order" gathered at the same table for the first time. A four-party meeting involving Iran, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan was held in Tehran. A statement issued afterward noted that the four nations "agreed to continue dialogue to strengthen cooperation in the realms of peace and security." The actions of Israel, along with the situations in Palestine and Lebanon, served as the "core topics" of the meeting.

Senior military and intelligence representatives from three of the signatories to the "Mecca Agreement," a pact with an implicit "anti-Iran" objective found themselves sitting in Tehran, discussing Israeli expansion and the occupation of Palestine. The framework for this meeting was what Iran terms an "endogenous order" the principle that regional security must emerge from within the region itself, and that foreign interference must be prevented.

⚔️ International Law: Attacks on Nuclear Facilities Constitute War Crimes

On October 10, 2026, the Human Rights Committee of the Iranian Judiciary released a legal report titled "Attacks on Nuclear Centers from the Perspective of Humanitarian Law."

The report’s conclusion is precise: any U.S. attack on Iran’s peaceful nuclear facilities would constitute a violation of the territorial integrity and independence of a UN member state. It would qualify as an "act of aggression" as defined by UN General Assembly Resolution 3314, and as the "crime of aggression" recognized under Article 8 bis of the Rome Statute. Furthermore, the report points out that under Article 56 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, attacks on nuclear facilities or any sites containing dangerous substances are prohibited and constitute war crimes.

This is not merely a "protest"; it is a "legal characterization." It translates a military operation into language that could be cited in a court of law. The timing of this report released in the eighth month of the war suggests that Iran is preparing a legal ledger for the post-war period.

🎯 Technology: Two Years to Regional Preeminence

On the same day.  First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref stated at a cybersecurity conference:

“Within the next two years, we must attain the number one position in the region in the field of emerging technologies.”

He added: “The nation’s cybersecurity must be bolstered to counter the actions of our enemies.” The path to achieving this lies in “leaps in research” and “maximizing the potential of our young elite.”

“Two years.” This is a verifiable timeline. It forms part of a single logical chain alongside the Supreme Leader’s call for “breaking scientific frontiers,” the “rational mindset” of the assassinated Larijani, and the “loyalty” of Basel Bahramnejad, who protected the Supreme Leader for twenty-four years that binds science, technology, and security into a unified survival strategy under wartime conditions.

🔻 The Mirror

The enemy claims: Decapitate the leadership, and Iran will collapse.

Basel Bahramnejad is dead. Larijani is dead. The Supreme Leader’s office has been bombed. Yet, the Supreme Leader declares: Iran’s strength is built upon science. And the First Vice President asserts: Within two years, we shall be the regional leader.

The enemy claims: Assassinating scientists will destroy Iran’s technological capabilities.

At Larijani’s memorial, the Minister of Science remarked that it was his “rational mindset” that Israel feared. Meanwhile, the Supreme Leader emphasizes that the elite’s breakthroughs at the frontiers of science are the key to strengthening every inch of Iran.

The enemy claims: Iran will be isolated.

A quadrilateral meeting takes place in Tehran, with Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan seated at the table with Iran within a framework defined by Iran as an “endogenous order.”

This is not “propaganda.” It is a “record.” It documents a nation that, in the eighth month of a war while burying its bodyguards, secretaries, and scientists has, in the span of a single week, delivered a discourse on science, hosted a quadrilateral summit, established legal frameworks, and set a timeline for catching up in science and technology.

A system capable of doing all these things simultaneously is not collapsing; it is organizing organizing every dimension of the war: memory, science, diplomacy, law, and technology.

  Long live Iran. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

text:
The Israeli government formed at the end of 2022 was not merely a coalition of political convenience. It represented a convergence of interests, united by a common imperative: the removal of  judicial restraints on the exercise of power.

For Netanyahu, the destruction of judicial independence offered a path towards weakening the Court capable of holding him accountable, not least in relation to his own corruption trial. For his Likud colleagues and coalition partners Smotrich and Ben-Gvir, the same project offered an opportunity to entrench Jewish supremacy, consolidate permanent domination over Palestinians, and pursue territorial acquisition and dispossession without meaningful legal constraint.

For the ultra-Orthodox parties, the bargain was different but no less consequential: the preservation of generous public subsidies, secured in exchange for sustaining a government committed to dismantling the constitutional restraints that might otherwise stand in its way.

What began as an assault on judicial independence became something considerably more consequential. An increasingly permissive environment for the commission of atrocity crimes. In Gaza, this has been accompanied by a campaign of physical destruction on an unprecedented scale. In the West Bank, by entrenching annexation, dispossession, forced displacement and violence against Palestinians.

The relationship between these developments is not merely chronological, following from October 23'. The weakening of domestic legal restraints and the intensification of unlawful conduct towards Palestinians are, in my assessment, constituent parts of the same political transformation. A State progressively freed from meaningful internal accountability is a State increasingly willing to disregard its obligations under international law.

And yet, I believe we are still witnessing the beginning of this transformation, not its conclusion.

The coming months may prove decisive. The foundations for the enduring, irreversible, entrenchment of Israel as a colonial tyranny are set by the entire spectrum of would-be governing parties. 

It would be comforting to believe that this is a temporary aberration, that the restoration of judicial independence alone would restore the rule of law, or that a change of government would necessarily reverse the direction of travel. I see little basis for such confidence. The structures of domination over Palestinians long predate the present coalition. What this government has done is to accelerate their consolidation, remove remaining inhibitions and expose the intimate relationship between authoritarianism within Israel and colonial domination beyond its recognised borders.

None of this means that the future is predetermined. But change for the better will not simply follow from the passage of time, the holding of elections or the replacement of one political leadership with another.

Politics is as much about hope as it is about power. But hope must not be confused with reassurance, still less with wishful thinking. There is no virtue in false hope, and no prospect of meaningful change founded upon a refusal to confront reality.

Hope, if it is to have any political or moral significance, must begin with an unfiltered assessment of the facts and the interests at work.

This is mine.

text:
I have said it before, and I will say it again: William Ruto’s Kenya Kwanza government has turned the hopes of ordinary Kenyans into a painful lesson in political deception. The promises were grand, the rhetoric was intoxicating, and the campaign theatrics were relentless. We were promised a bottom-up economic revolution that would put the hustler at the centre of national development. Yet, years into this administration, millions of Kenyans are still struggling to afford the very basics of human existence.

What exactly has changed for the ordinary Kenyan?

Taxes consume an ever-greater share of household income. The cost of food, fuel, electricity, transport and housing continues to suffocate families. Young people are desperately searching for jobs in an economy that offers them more uncertainty than opportunity. Small businesses are battling high operating costs, expensive credit and dwindling consumer purchasing power. Workers earn salaries that disappear before the month ends, while parents are forced to make impossible choices between food, school fees, rent and healthcare.

What does the government offer in response? More promises. More slogans. More political rallies. More speeches celebrating economic recovery while millions of citizens struggle to feel that recovery in their own pockets.

You cannot tax people into prosperity, lecture hungry families about economic transformation, or manufacture national progress through presidential propaganda.

The fundamental failure of Kenya Kwanza is the widening gap between its political narrative and the lived reality of the people it governs. A government can manipulate headlines, commission projects and produce impressive statistics, but it cannot permanently conceal the economic distress experienced in millions of homes. The ultimate measure of economic policy is not how impressive it sounds in a State House briefing; it is whether a parent can feed a child, whether a graduate can find meaningful employment, whether a worker can save, and whether a small business can grow without being strangled by taxation and the cost of doing business.

The hustler narrative has become particularly painful because it was built on the aspirations of people who had the least room for disappointment. Those who were promised economic liberation are now being asked to shoulder the burden of a system that offers them little relief. The very people who were told that government would work for them are left wondering why sacrifice has become their permanent condition while political leaders continue to congratulate themselves.

Leadership is not the art of making people endure hardship indefinitely. It is the responsibility to create the conditions under which hard work produces dignity, opportunity and a better standard of living. When citizens work harder but remain poorer, when businesses struggle to survive, and when young people see their futures narrowing, the government must answer for its economic choices.

Kenya does not need another carefully choreographed speech explaining why everything is improving. It needs policies that restore purchasing power, ease the tax burden, create productive employment, support small businesses, make healthcare accessible and ensure that public borrowing delivers tangible benefits rather than transferring an ever-heavier burden to future generations.

The question is no longer whether William Ruto can sell another political promise. The question is whether his government can justify the cost of its leadership to the people paying the bills.

A government that asks citizens for endless sacrifice must demonstrate tangible results. Patriotism cannot mean applauding failure, and democracy cannot mean giving leaders a blank cheque to govern without accountability. Kenya deserves better than an economy in which survival is becoming a full-time occupation.

text:
The Biafra Self-Referendum: Organizing Independence from Exile Under International Law

In a detailed response to public questions, the Alliance of Biafran Americans explained the mechanics and legitimacy of a self-referendum for Biafran independence organized by PM Simon Ekpa and the Biafra Republic Government in Exile (BRGIE). 

It stated that the process was not an ad-hoc online exercise but one conducted both physically in the claimed Biafran homeland and electronically among the diaspora. It asserted that #Biafrans themselves authorized Ekpa to lead the effort after electing him Prime Minister at an assembly in Helsinki, Finland, in 2023.

The referendum is presented as a response to long-standing grievances. 

The accompanying quoted statement of Dr. Michael Rubin @mrubin1971 noted that

“Nigerian repression grew against ethnic Igbo in Biafra and Nigerian Christians more broadly,” framing the vote as an exercise of self-determination amid allegations of marginalization, insecurity, and ineffective governance. 

Organizers reported that tens of millions participated and overwhelmingly chose independence, with plans for a convention to declare the “Restoration of Independence of Biafra.” 

Dr. Rubin emphasized that holding aspects of the process in #Finland is not disqualifying, drawing a parallel to Czechoslovakia’s 1918 declaration of independence, which took place in Washington, D.C., rather than on Czech or Slovak soil.

On verification and international standards, the PAC stated that ORB International monitored the process on the ground and published a report. 

It further argued that United Nations involvement is not a legal prerequisite for a referendum on self-determination. While a state or entity may invite the UN, international law does not mandate it. 

ORB’s published commentary focused on public-opinion polling showing that residents of Biafra regions were among the most likely to view the national government as ineffective and to report feeling unsafe, providing contextual support for the organizers’ stated motivations even if it did not independently audit every ballot.

Under the 1933 Montevideo Convention on the Rights and Duties of States, an entity may claim the attributes of statehood by possessing a permanent population, a defined territory, a government, and the capacity to enter into relations with other states. 

Article 3 of the Convention codifies the declarative theory: “The political existence of the state is independent of recognition by the other states.” 

Proponents of Biafran independence argue that a credible expression of popular will—through a referendum—helps demonstrate the existence of a permanent population seeking self-government and can support claims of an effective government and capacity for external relations, even if full international recognition remains a separate political question. 

Recognition is ultimately a discretionary act by existing states; meeting the Montevideo criteria is widely treated as a necessary but not always sufficient condition.

#Somaliland offers a relevant comparative example. After declaring independence in 1991, Somaliland held a constitutional referendum on 31 May 2001. Approximately 97 percent of those who voted approved the constitution, which affirmed independence. An international observer team from the Initiative and Referendum Institute concluded that the process was conducted “openly, fairly, honestly, and largely in accordance with internationally recognized election procedures,” despite limited participation in some contested areas. 

Somaliland has since maintained a functioning government, defined borders roughly corresponding to the former British Somaliland, and a permanent population, meeting the core Montevideo criteria in practice.

Spent my first day on @RaidLords testing things out after launch, and a few things quickly stood out 👇

Start with the $3 goal

The $1 entry fee, starter quests, and X tasks got me to the first $3 without spending extra. Pretty straightforward if you follow the starter path.

The Royal Mint matters more than you think

Your daily conversion limit starts at $2 without it. Upgrade it, and you can push that limit up to $35 at Level 7. Village upgrades help too. I always check “Gold you can sell” before going all in on a raid.

Pay attention to where your gold comes from

Mines, Campaign, bot-village raids, daily rewards, League bonuses, War Chests, and clan wars all offer sellable gold. Raiding other lords works differently: mine gold is fully sellable, but storage gold is only partially sellable. Gold bought with tokens can't be sold.

Knowing this makes choosing raid targets a lot easier.

Keep your army busy

Troops train one by one, but you don't have to sit around waiting. I kept raids going while the next troops trained and focused on comps that could clear the Keep without too many losses. Just remember, dead troops are gone for good.

Don't keep switching Champions

Pick a Champion, invest in it, and build from there. Gear, Valor, and stance stay with your knight. Guardian is great for safer defense, Warlord helps nearby troops with Rally Cry, and Berserker brings more damage and healing.

Join a clan early

Seriously, don't wait until your village is fully built. Garrison troops can make a difference, and clan wars give you another source of sellable gold. Getting involved early pays off.

Claim those launch rewards

The first collective goal already gave everyone 2 Builder Potions through the launch menu. There are also rewards tied to Raid Stars, trophies, and top clans. Definitely worth keeping an eye on.

One more thing: 50% of every in-game spend gets burned, and the other 50% goes back into the prize pool.

Find your rhythm

Upgrade the Mint, increase your conversion limit, train efficiently, strengthen your Champion, and make use of your clan. Each part helps the next, so the daily grind gets more rewarding over time.

Everything runs on Robinhood Chain.

text:
One of the most poignant stories about Sam Houston's final years concerns a quiet visit he made to the San Jacinto battlefield, accompanied by Jeff Hamilton, the formerly enslaved man who had served as his personal attendant for years. The story comes from Hamilton himself, and it offers a glimpse of Houston looking back on the greatest triumph of his life.

Hamilton was born enslaved in Kentucky in 1840 and brought to Texas as a child. In October 1853, when he was just thirteen, he was separated from his mother and sold at an auction in Huntsville. Sam Houston purchased him, and Hamilton subsequently became his personal attendant, traveling companion, and eventually a trusted member of the household. Hamilton remained with Houston after the latter announced the emancipation of the people he enslaved in 1862.

The battlefield visit is recounted in Hamilton's memoir, "My Master: The Inside Story of Sam Houston and His Time," originally published in 1940, which I highly recommend. Hamilton recalled that Houston instructed him to drive to San Jacinto before they returned home.

As Hamilton remembered it:
"The General didn't speak a word on the way – he was wrapped up in his own thoughts."

They eventually reached the large oak tree where Mexican general Antonio López de Santa Anna had been brought before Houston as a prisoner following the Battle of San Jacinto in April 1836.

"The General sat on the ground under the tree for a long time, never speaking to me or looking at me."

He described Houston as having a distant expression and noticed that his eyes were wet with tears.

It's a remarkable image. The man who had commanded the Texian army to victory, secured Texas independence, served as president of the Republic twice, represented Texas in the United States Senate, and governed the state was now sitting silently beneath a tree, contemplating the place where his life and the history of Texas had changed forever.

Houston died in Huntsville on July 26, 1863, with Hamilton at his bedside. Hamilton lived until April 3, 1941, dying in Belton just thirteen days before his 101st birthday.

I read Hamilton's account of this and thought that it's a remarkable image, isn't it? The old warrior returning to the scene of his greatest triumph, perhaps knowing that time was running out and thinking that this would be his last visit, recalling all his friends and ruminating on all that had happened to him over the course of his remarkable life.

Shown here: Jeff Hamilton (left) and Samuel Walker Houston at the Texas Centennial Celebration in Dallas, 1936. Jeff was 96 years old when this was taken.  You can buy Jeff's book online at all the usual places.

AA Leads Thadingyut Full Moon Candlelight Offering Ceremony in Mong Yu (105-Mile)

AK-News English | October 27, 2026

The Arakan Army (AA) led a candlelight offering ceremony on the occasion of the Thadingyut Full Moon Day, also known as Abhidhamma Day, in Mong Yu (105-Mile), Muse Township, northern Shan State, within the Brotherhood Alliance-administered area, on October 26.

The ceremony was held at the Shwe Taung Pagoda on the outskirts of the town, where participants offered 4,000 candles and 1,000 flowers as acts of Buddhist devotion.

Nearly 800 people, including members of the Arakan Army (AA), the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA), and local residents, took part in the event. Participants marched from the 105-Mile truck terminal to the hilltop pagoda, creating a lively and festive atmosphere.

During the Thadingyut Full Moon Day, Buddhists traditionally offer candles and flowers at pagodas and monasteries, release illuminated lanterns, perform meritorious deeds, and participate in religious celebrations.

Thadingyut Full Moon Day is observed to commemorate the Buddha's return to the human world after preaching the Abhidhamma teachings in the Tavatimsa Heaven. It is one of the most sacred occasions in the Buddhist calendar.

The Arakan Army has also been participating in various activities across the Brotherhood Alliance-administered areas, including planting shade trees, providing humanitarian assistance, and organizing friendly football matches in cooperation with its allied groups.

text:
Zimbabwean delegation draws resilience lessons from China’s Great Wall

The Great Wall of China offered powerful lessons in resilience and nation building to media leaders from 13 countries attending the two week Seminar for Heads of Journalists Organizations and Gen Z Media Youth Leaders from Belt and Road Countries.

Among the delegates is Varakashi4ED National Vice Chairman Cde Mairosi Watungwa, who joined fellow participants on a visit to the historic landmark.

Stretching 21 196 kilometres and built over more than two millennia, the Great Wall stands as an enduring symbol of sacrifice, engineering ingenuity and perseverance. It is also a major tourism attraction, drawing tens of millions of visitors annually.

Cde Watungwa said the monument carried profound lessons for Zimbabwe, whose liberation struggle was similarly anchored in sacrifice and determination.

“The Great Wall tells you something profound about China. A nation that could summon the discipline and collective will to build such an extraordinary monument over generations was never going to surrender its destiny to adversity. As Zimbabweans, that story speaks directly to us because our freedom was also born out of sacrifice, endurance and an unbreakable determination to triumph against overwhelming odds,” said Cde Watungwa.

Zimbabwe’s liberation ties with China run deep. President Dr @edmnangagwa led the first group of five ZANU recruits to China on September 22, 1963, for six months of military science training at the Nanjing Army Command College in Jiangsu and remains the sole survivor of that group.

Other liberation figures associated with military training in China included Cde Herbert Chitepo, Cde Robert Gabriel Mugabe, General Josiah Magama Tongogara and General Solomon Mujuru.

The same spirit of resilience continues to underpin Zimbabwe’s development trajectory under the Second Republic led by President Mnangagwa. The economy has expanded from US$16 billion in 2017 to US$66 billion in 2026, with the country pursuing Upper Middle Income status by 2030.

AA Leads Thadingyut Full Moon Candlelight Ceremony in Mong Yu (105-Mile), Northern Shan State

AB News | October 27, 2026

The Arakan Army (AA) led a candlelight offering ceremony on October 26, marking the Thadingyut Full Moon Day, also known as Abhidhamma Day, in Mong Yu (105-Mile), Muse Township, northern Shan State, an area administered by the Brotherhood Alliance.

The ceremony was held at the Myo-U Yaung Chi Hill Pagoda, where 4,000 candles and 1,000 flowers were offered in devotion to the Buddha.

Nearly 800 participants, including AA personnel, Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) members, and local residents, joined a procession from the 105-Mile truck terminal to the hilltop pagoda to celebrate the occasion.

On Thadingyut Full Moon Day, Buddhists traditionally offer candles and flowers at pagodas and monasteries, release illuminated lanterns, perform meritorious deeds, and participate in religious ceremonies.

The festival commemorates the Buddha's descent from Tavatimsa Heaven to the human world after preaching the Abhidhamma to celestial beings. It is considered one of the most sacred occasions in the Buddhist calendar.

Beyond religious celebrations, the AA has also been cooperating with its Brotherhood Alliance partners in the alliance-administered area through tree-planting initiatives, humanitarian activities, and friendly football matches, strengthening relations among allied forces and local communities.

Saudi Arabia reportedly offers Houthis $1 billion in Iran-brokered deal to halt attacks

Diplomatic sources in the Gulf say Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman traveled to Tehran to negotiate a ceasefire with the Houthis that would see Riyadh transfer $1 billion to the group through Iran.

One source claims the minister even brought the money aboard a military aircraft, although a Saudi official did not confirm any transfer.

The talks come amid Houthi attacks on Saudi oil facilities and Iranian efforts to strengthen Tehran's regional influence.

by  Danny Zaken 

Diplomatic sources in the Gulf say Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman's surprise visit to Iran was aimed at securing a ceasefire with the Houthis under a deal that would see Saudi Arabia transfer $1 billion to the Iranian-backed proxy through Tehran.

According to one source, bin Salman even brought the money with him aboard the Hercules military transport aircraft on which he arrived.

The visit was arranged by Saudi Arabia's partners in the Mecca defense pact. Also taking part in the talks are Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin and Pakistan's army chief, Field Marshal Asim Munir.

Pakistan and Turkey have failed to provide Saudi Arabia with meaningful assistance despite the agreement, sending only military advisers and no additional support forces, even though the defense alliance explicitly requires its members to provide military assistance if one of them comes under attack.

Iran was represented by President Masoud Pezeshkian, Supreme National Security Council Secretary Gen. Mohsen Rezaei and senior officials from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Iran offered to mediate between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis over the crisis in Yemen.

The Houthis have been attacking airports and, in particular, oil facilities in Saudi Arabia, inflicting enormous economic damage on the kingdom.

At the same time, Iranian attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz have disrupted oil exports from the Gulf.

The money at the heart of the negotiations

The Saudi Foreign Ministry addressed the meeting in an official statement, saying: "The visit to Tehran by Prince Khalid bin Salman, the defense minister, and representatives of the member states of the Mecca Joint Defense Alliance comes as part of the alliance's ongoing efforts to de-escalate tensions between the parties to the current crisis, encourage dialogue and diplomatic solutions, and support the mediation efforts undertaken by the State of Qatar and the Islamic Republic of Pakistan."

A Saudi official did not confirm that any money had been transferred.

However, speaking to Israel Hayom, the official noted that part of the dispute with the Houthis concerns the implementation of understandings reached three years ago.

Under those understandings, Saudi Arabia was to provide direct financial assistance to the Houthis as part of efforts to reach a settlement.

The funding was intended, among other things, to pay public-sector salaries in areas under Houthi control and rebuild civilian infrastructure.

In return, the Houthis were expected to uphold the ceasefire and halt their attacks on the kingdom.

In recent months, the Houthis have justified their attacks by claiming that Saudi Arabia reneged on those understandings.

Nevertheless, Iran is clearly behind the current escalation as part of its war with the US, arming the Houthis and supporting them in other ways.

The meeting in Tehran is therefore also a public-relations setback for the Saudis, signaling a willingness to make concessions, at least in the short term, to fully restore oil exports.

A diplomatic victory for Iran

Riyadh's official position remains that the kingdom categorically rejects a new ceasefire and refuses to give in to "military blackmail" or transfer funds to the Houthis before they return territory seized from Yemen's internationally recognized government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.

For Iran, the developments represent significant gains.

This is the first official meeting between representatives of the Mecca alliance and the Iranian leadership.

The initiative for the meeting emerged during the Pakistani army chief's visit to Tehran last week.

Iran is seeking to use the summit to advance a new regional security framework led by regional powers.

In doing so, Tehran is emphasizing its desire to prevent US or Israeli military intervention in the region while positioning itself as a regional diplomatic mediator.

text:
Israel’s elections could influence events far beyond the Middle East. Voting is underway, and the latest polls put the new Yashar party, led by Gadi Eisenkot, in the lead. But finishing first does not guarantee taking power. Everything will depend on who can reach an agreement with whom and form a government.

Even a change of prime minister, however, offers little reason to expect a rapid shift towards peace in the Israeli–Palestinian conflict. Eisenkot and Netanyahu both support tough security policies and oppose an independent Palestinian state. They differ significantly on other issues: judicial independence, military conscription for the ultra-Orthodox, and settlements in Palestinian territories. Eisenkot may be more open to certain compromises, but he remains willing to use force.

The prospects for peace depend in part on what Israeli politicians are prepared to call a victory. For some, weakening their adversaries and securing reliable security guarantees might be enough. For religious nationalists, territorial expansion is a goal in itself. They may therefore see abandoning annexation as a defeat, even if attacks cease. Netanyahu has to accommodate such partners to remain in power. Reducing their influence could matter at least as much as replacing the prime minister.

Better relations with the West could help Eisenkot both negotiate and wage war. He has already supported US–Israeli strikes on Iran and proposed a US-led regional security alliance. His government might find it easier to secure Western support for a limited military operation if it also curbed settler violence and agreed to negotiations over Gaza. Diplomatic flexibility would therefore not necessarily mean a less forceful military policy.

The next 6–12 months are likely to bring renewed attempts to use force to extract concessions, followed by a return to negotiations. One possible scenario is another US–Israeli campaign against Iran. Trump may be hoping for a short operation after which he can declare victory, strike a deal, and bring down energy prices. Israeli leaders may seek to use American support while it remains available. CNN reports that military options have been drawn up, although no final decision has yet been made.

Iran will find it difficult to make concessions as long as its leaders fear being overthrown. If Tehran believes that meeting the demands would leave it more vulnerable to attack, continued resistance will seem safer.

A limited operation could escalate into a major war despite the participants’ initial intentions. The trigger could be heavy American casualties, the destruction of energy infrastructure, or strikes that Tehran interprets as the beginning of an attempt to eliminate its leadership. Iran could respond by attacking more countries and targets, seeking to make the war too costly for its adversaries. The parties would then become increasingly embroiled in an exchange of strikes.

The war could intensify the very threats it was launched to eliminate. If conventional weapons and diplomacy fail to protect Iran from attack, advocates of acquiring nuclear weapons will gain another argument in their favour. Overthrowing the current leadership would not guarantee democracy either: military leaders could take its place, and the struggle for power could drag on for years.

Even if a major war is avoided, without an agreement the region could remain trapped between strikes and fragile ceasefires for a long time. Under this scenario, the US would avoid large-scale intervention, Iran would reject its demands, and Israel would continue conducting individual military operations. A similar pattern is already evident in Gaza and Lebanon: the intensity of fighting has declined, but disputes over disarmament, territorial control, and troop withdrawal remain unresolved.

An agreement between the US and Iran could offer both sides an acceptable way out of the confrontation. Tehran would agree to verifiable restrictions on its nuclear programme, an end to attacks, safe passage for shipping, and reduced military aid to groups that threaten its neighbours. In return, it would receive relief from the blockade and sanctions, alongside a commitment not to overthrow its leadership by military force as long as it complies with the agreement. Trump could present this as a diplomatic victory, while Iran would gain economic relief. Such an agreement would not rule out domestic political change in the country.

Trump may put pressure on Netanyahu if continued warfare undermines American interests. Washington bears military and economic costs, while Israeli leaders may consider further strikes necessary. According to media reports, some of Trump’s advisers are already dissatisfied with Netanyahu’s policies. A Republican defeat in the congressional elections could strengthen the White House’s desire to end the confrontation, although it would not, on its own, determine its decisions.

Iran’s neighbours seek to contain its influence but fear the consequences of its collapse. Further attacks on infrastructure, refugee flows, and prolonged instability would threaten their own security. Talks involving Saudi, Turkish, and Pakistani delegations in Tehran show that these countries are trying to shape events. Their interests nevertheless differ: the UAE may deepen military cooperation with Israel while opposing its policies towards the Palestinians.

For a lasting peace, an agreement with Iran must be coupled with a settlement of the Israeli–Palestinian conflict. Reducing the threat of a major regional war will not, in itself, remove the causes of local conflicts. The shared goals should be a secure existence for Israel, a sovereign Palestine, and mutual commitments by states to refrain from aggression.

To achieve this, Israel needs a government able to negotiate without depending on supporters of annexation. It would need to halt settlement expansion and settler violence, accept Palestinian statehood, and establish the terms for withdrawing troops. Eisenkot’s current platform does not include such changes. His coming to power could facilitate some negotiations, but a comprehensive settlement would require a broader reassessment of Israeli policy.

A Palestinian state must have effective authority over its territory and take responsibility for security within it. The two-state model entails agreed borders, mutual recognition, and protection for both peoples from attack. This requires Palestinian authorities with public support, accountable institutions, and control over all armed forces. Hamas cannot retain a separate army, and Israel cannot maintain indefinite military control that reduces Palestinian sovereignty to a formality. Statehood, governance reforms, and the disarmament of Hamas are linked in the 2025 New York Declaration.

Confidence in the agreements will depend on the US being willing to demand compliance from all parties. Washington could guarantee Israel’s protection while making part of its support conditional on adherence to the agreements. For Iran, fulfilling its commitments must bring real economic relief. The guarantees themselves must be secured in a way that allows them to withstand a change of US president.

Lebanon, Syria, and Yemen will need political settlements of their own. In Lebanon, there is already a basis for strengthening the national army and withdrawing Israeli troops, although implementation remains difficult. Regional agreements involving Iran, Turkey, and Arab states are needed on non-aggression, safe passage for shipping, and the prevention of military clashes. The Gulf states could support these efforts by funding reconstruction and expanding trade.

Peace will have powerful opponents, so it will need public support. For supporters of annexation, compromise would mean giving up territorial claims; for Iran’s security establishment, it would mean losing some regional influence. Hamas and Hezbollah leaders may see disarmament as a threat to their power and personal safety. Even weakened, they will retain the capacity to derail agreements. It will be easier to resist such efforts if people experience the practical benefits of peace: security, political rights, jobs, and the opportunity to rebuild their lives.

COAS, TANZANIAN LAND FORCES CHIEF MOVE TO DEEPEN MILITARY TRAINING, KNOWLEDGE EXCHANGE

The Chief of Army Staff (COAS), Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, has called for expanded military training and professional exchanges between the Nigerian Army and the Tanzania People’s Defence Force to strengthen operational capacity and enhance cooperation in addressing Africa’s security challenges.

General Shaibu made the call on Monday, 26 October 2026, during bilateral talks with the Chief of Land Forces of the Tanzania People's Defence Force, Major General Fadhil Omary Nondo, on the sidelines of the African International Defence Exhibition (AFRIDEX) 2026 in Lagos.

The COAS emphasised the need to strengthen collaboration in professional military education, intelligence sharing, joint training and exchange programmes across various military institutions, including national defence colleges.

He highlighted the Nigerian Army's established training institutions, including the Nigerian Defence Academy, Armed Forces Command and Staff College, Jaji, Nigerian Army Training and Doctrine Command, and Nigerian Army Resource Centre. He noted that these institutions have continued to develop highly professional military personnel for Nigeria and allied countries.

General Shaibu also underscored the Nigerian Army's extensive operational experience in counter-terrorism and counter-insurgency operations in the North-East, anti-banditry operations in the North-West and North-Central, as well as peace support operations across Africa and beyond. He observed that these experiences offer valuable lessons that could strengthen both armies through joint training, staff exchanges and the sharing of operational knowledge and military doctrines.

The COAS encouraged the Tanzanian Land Forces to take advantage of available training opportunities in Nigerian Army institutions and called for an expanded exchange of instructors and students to deepen professional relationships and enhance institutional capacity.

In his response, Major General Nondo commended the Nigerian Army for its operational experience, resilience and sustained efforts towards promoting peace and security across the African continent. He expressed Tanzania's readiness to strengthen military relations with Nigeria, particularly in leadership development, professional military education and operational capacity building.

He further noted that existing exchange programmes between the command and national defence colleges of both countries had enhanced professional interaction and facilitated the sharing of experiences, expressing confidence that expanded collaboration would yield greater benefits for both armies.

The meeting underscores the Nigerian Army's commitment to strengthening military partnerships across Africa through professional military education, institutional cooperation and the exchange of operational expertise in support of regional peace and security.

Read online | October 27, 2026

How Censorship Works

By Jeffrey Tucker

Commentary

The Holodomor (meaning death by hunger) was a man-made famine in Soviet Ukraine in 1932–1933 that killed millions of people, primarily Ukrainian peasants. It was part of a wider Soviet famine (roughly 1930–1934) that also affected parts of Russia and Kazakhstan, but the Ukrainian famine was intensified by specific policies directed at Ukraine.⁠

Under Joseph Stalin, the Soviet leadership forcibly collectivized agriculture starting in the late 1920s. Peasants were compelled to join collective farms, “kulaks” (better-off farmers). Resisters were deported or repressed. Whole villages were blacklisted and their grain confiscated. An internal passport system and border controls were created that prevented peasants from leaving famine areas.

Mortality was hideous, peaking in the spring and summer of 1933. Today we have all the evidence of widespread starvation, mass deaths, and cases of cannibalism.⁠ All told, as many as 5 million died. It was a genocide.

What is especially remarkable about this historical fact is that no one in the West knew anything about it while it was happening. U.S. newspapers had reporters on the ground in Russia but they consistently wrote stories that either ignored or debunked the claims of famine.

New York Times journalist Walter Duranty, the Moscow bureau chief from 1922 to 1936, had won a Pulitzer Prize for his reporting. “There is no famine or actual starvation nor is there likely to be,” he wrote. “Any report of a famine in Russia is today an exaggeration or malignant propaganda.”

As it turns out, he had a good relationship with the Soviet state and clung tightly to his privileges and access, the price of which was to turn a blind eye to suffering. It was other stringers like Malcom Muggeridge of the Manchester Guardian, following the lead of Welsh journalist Gareth Jones, who dared reveal these truths to the world, and he was largely dismissed at the time as a conservative alarmist.

How was this censorship possible? The sources of information were few and they were captured. No one on the ground possessed any technology to get the word out. There were no cell phone cameras or social media accounts to document anything. So it all happened while the victims were silenced and those who might have revealed the truth stayed quiet.

My mind keeps returning to this horrifying case because we like to think that this would never be possible in our times, not with all our information sources, not with all our social media, not with all our cameras and our ability to monitor the world around us in real time. Surely censorship on this level is impossible now.

I’m not so sure.

In December 2020, the U.S. government and the companies it backed released a shot promising to protect people from a virus that was circulating. Millions rushed to take it out of fear, and also a desire for life to get back to normal. After all, the whole society had been locked down since the previous March. The promise was that taking this potion would make everything get back to normal.

Some people worried about safety. The agency CDC responded with a service called V-safe. Sign up for it, report your experience, and if anything should go wrong, the agency will call you back and explain what’s happening and try to help. The very existence of the program boosted confidence. More than 10 million people rushed to sign up for it.

A robot contacted them on the first day, the next day, the following week, and all the way up to a year. The CDC did not tell anyone but there was no one reading those messages and reports. Sure, they ran some quick data scans and offered rosy reports in publications coming out over the following months.

What no one knew at the time is that something horrifying was happening out of sight. A third of respondents reported side effects that interrupted their lives. Between 7 and 10 percent of people had to seek some medical care. That’s the people who could afford it. Many of them could not. There were cries for help, suicide ideation, and death.

The worst among these reports chronicle splitting headaches, missed or excessive menstrual bleeding, screaming rings in the ears, rashes and bleeding welts on the body, a racing heart that would reach 150 and higher even at night, loss of mobility, growing blindness, palpitations, memory loss, confusion and fatigue, all symptoms that cause people to stop working, leading to despair.

The CDC had an automatic message for these people sent by email or by an automated phone call: call your doctor. That’s it. Many did. The doctor would have no idea so he would refer those injured to a specialist who would order tests and they mostly came back negative unless a cancer had shown up, which often happened. Many of these people report spending 20–50K on medical care with no results.

How many are we talking about here? Such injuries were not “very, very rare,” as Fauci promised. They were pervasive and devastating, for a shot that did not stop infection in any case and was not even needed by healthy children and adults if it had worked. Tens of thousands at least, that we know of, were likely harmed even for life, but possibly hundreds of thousands or millions were hit with adverse events, once you extrapolate the data to those about whom we do not know.

The victims mostly believed that their cases were highly unusual. The news media never spoke about the subject. Some people tried to start Facebook groups. When the company found out about them, they faced pressure from the White House to take the groups down. They did, one after another, thousands of them. When someone on Twitter tried to report this, their accounts were deleted. It was the same on all social media. They were all censored. As incredible as it seems, this population-wide wave of pharmaceutical injury and death was actually silenced.

As a result, these people—our families, friends, neighbors, fellow citizens—suffered and often died alone with no acknowledgement that this was iatrogenic. Doctors who tried to sound the alarm were investigated by their medical boards.

Reporters who wanted to cover this were told no by their editors. The editors who wanted to cover it were told no by their publishers. The publishers who wanted to cover it were told no by their advertisers, most of whom were pharmaceutical companies making money from the problem.

Suspicious attorneys began to file freedom-of-information requests. The CDC and FDA refused them. They had to go to court. This took years of litigation. Finally, the agency coughed up the results. We now have more than 10 million pages of data that they tried to keep silent.

Censorship today requires far more than merely issuing edicts. It relies on people who are afraid to break censorship with the truth.
