text:
Marco Rubio is at his best when he's urging Europe to wake up and take a stand to preserve its history, culture, traditions, and Western civilization itself—to reject mass migration, multiculturalism, and self-imposed decline. This speech was given nearly three weeks ago near the Acropolis in Greece, but it's even more relevant today given events that have transpired in France in recent weeks and spread throughout several European nations.

Full transcript:

There are great ruins all across the world.  In many cases, they are places where history seems to have exhausted itself: remnants of distant cultures that have long passed beyond living memory.

But the Acropolis is different. 

For thousands of years, the civilization that built what stands behind me has captivated the imagination of the Western world.  Generations of our statesmen, artists, and philosophers have looked to it – they’ve looked to it with wonder and they’ve looked to it with awe.

Now time has a tendency to dull the senses: great victories and catastrophic defeats, they seem to  shrink to becoming like a footnote in a textbook, another fact for our schoolchildren to memorize and forget.  But the Greeks of antiquity, they seem to have an almost mystical hold on our memory.  They call us back to them, again and again. 

480 years before Christ, the armies of Xerxes arrived in this city and they put its sanctuaries to the torch.  Most Athenians had by then evacuated by ship to a nearby island.  But there was a handful of them that refused to leave their home.  So instead, they barricaded themselves in the rocky fortress of the Acropolis to fight an extraordinary last stand, heaving massive stones down the cliffs onto the Persian invaders and holding the greatest empire of the age at bay for days.  They were eventually overwhelmed.  The Persians plundered the temples, burned the shrines, and razed the Acropolis to the ground but when the Athenians returned, they gathered the broken remains of the old Acropolis and buried them in the hill where it had stood.  And decades later, under Pericles, they raised the Parthenon.

For 25 centuries since, the Parthenon has stood.  Empires have risen and fallen beneath its shadow.  And the progeny of the men who built it – the sons of Athens and Rome – have carried their civilization with them to the ends of the Earth.

Two and a half centuries after the founding of the American republic halfway across the world from where I stand now – I stand here today as the Secretary of State of that republic, and a great-grandson of settlers who arrived in the new world from Spain – I stand here to testify to a debt that no lapse of time, no distance of space can ever extinguish. 

The history of America, the history of my country, is covered with the fingerprints of antiquity.  Greece is literally carved into the architecture of our government: in the towering columns, in the domes and the monuments across our capital city.  The city where our Constitution was born – Philadelphia – is itself a Greek name.

The men who founded my country were fascinated by the heritage we inherited from yours.  They were exceptionally well-read in history – they were vividly aware of their unique place in it – but no other age of the past held their attention or their imagination quite like that of antiquity.  Many, many people are surprised to learn that the most commonly cited author in the Federalist Papers was not an Enlightenment philosopher or political theorist.  No, the most commonly cited author in the Federalist Papers was Plutarch, the Greek biographer of Greece and Rome’s great men.

Now, much has been written and said about the influence of ancient Greece on the ideas of the American Founders – and, for that matter, on all of the Western philosophers and statesmen that preceded them.  Most of us are familiar with the basic history.  Athens gave us democracy.  Plato and Aristotle gave us Western philosophy.  Our ideas of law, of virtue, of citizenship, and republican government were shaped in the Greek city-states.  Even much of our political vocabulary – words like democracy, tyranny, the word “politics” itself – found its origins here.

Now, all of that is true.  But the things we owe to this place – as Americans, and as Westerners – are actually far far deeper.  These institutions and ideas – these institutions and ideas were the outward expression of more fundamental qualities we see in the ancient Greeks – qualities that can’t be reduced to any particular political system or theory.

Here, in Athens, we found the first full realization of all the essential traits that would come to define the West: fierce individuality and relentless ambition; daring exploration and invention; a yearning for discovery, for adventure, risk and glory.  An insatiable curiosity about the world and the principles by which it operates, a hunger to know the mysteries of nature and grasp the secrets of the cosmos.  An impatience with the notion of impossibility, chafing at all boundaries and limits, straining to peer into the depths of the unknown.

These were not just the formulas or precepts of a particular school of philosophy.  They were the characteristic of a people – expressed in their traditions, their stories, their imagination; in the qualities they demanded of their citizens; in the things they lived and fought and died for.

To know them is to know ourselves.

What blossomed here in this place was the Western desire to uncover all that ignorance, darkness, and distance had kept hidden from the mind of man.  The Greeks did not just shape history; the Greeks gave us history itself. Much about – much of what we know about many ancient civilizations comes almost entirely from the records of Greek explorers and historians, explorers and historians who didn’t just chronicle the histories of their own people, but ventured outwards to observe and record the sagas of foreign peoples and cultures all across the world.

Where others looked inward, the Greeks were the first to direct their focus outward, to chase the thrill and glory of seeing all that was strange and new.  It was this trait – it was this trait that would push the West to create and build things that others could not, marking us out from so many other cultures and civilizations where stability and subsistence were the highest ends of life.

But it is not just the ambition to explore the unknown that we inherit from the Greeks; it is the conviction that the unknown canbe known.  The confidence that the world can be charted and measured and mapped and understood – and that there is a rational order to the cosmos, governed by certain fundamental laws, laws that men can observe and the mind can come to understand.

This was the foundation of the Western mind: our math, our science, our medicine.  Our philosophy, ethics, and religion.  It paved the way for the gospel of Jesus Christ to find fertile soil in Europe and flourish into the empire of Christendom. It was the foundation of the riches of Christian theology – of Augustine and Aquinas and the whole tradition of natural law.

It gave birth to a civilization marked not just by a common culture, it was marked by a common anthropology – a common view of man and his place in the universe.  Its descendants would share not just the idea of a natural order, but a distinctive understanding of virtue; of destiny and fate; of truth, goodness, and beauty; of a code that dictates how men ought to live; of objective standards and ideals to strive towards.

For the Greeks of antiquity, the pursuit of excellence was the very principle of man’s existence.  They organized all of civic life around contest, ambition, competition: in philosophy and poetry, in sculpture and drama, in athletics and art, in war and statecraft.  The classical Greek city was an arena for great men to test and prove themselves, to hone their potential through perpetual struggle – to be the best, the strongest, the most beautiful, straining to inch ever closer to perfection.

Now I know that to modern ears, what I just described, this way of life, may sound odd; it may even sound cruel.  The ideal of many ideologies in our time has, frankly, become a world of perfect safety, devoid of risk or failure, with neither the glory of victory nor the shame of defeat.  Too often these days, we build downwards. We design our standards to ensure no one will lose; we preoccupy ourselves more with the comfort of the worst than the potential of the best.  We hold the most exceptional things among us hostage to the average, the ordinary, the mediocre.

The men who made the Parthenon, they built upwards. They held that the highest and most noble aspiration in life was to surpass all others, to strive to be the best in all things.  The ancient Greek city-states were filled.  They were filled with intense passion and rivalry and faction and conflict.  But from that constant struggle for distinction – from that came the great flowering of art and philosophy and political and intellectual energy that would transform a collective of Mediterranean cities into the birthplace of the greatest civilization in the world.

The thumos, as the ancient Greeks called it – the fire of passion, strength, courage, pride – is the heart of great civilization.  And without it?  Without it, nations lose their will to fight, the will to strive, the will to survive. 

Today, too much of the West has forgotten this quality.  Over time, we in the West came to feel ashamed of the very things that made us exceptional.  We felt embarrassed that our achievements set us apart from the rest of the world.  Our prosperity somehow became a source of guilt.  We no longer believed we deserved and had earned our greatness. 

The word “nationalism” became a dirty word.  And so we tore down our monuments; we condemned our own history.  And in too many places, we taught our children to be ashamed of the countries they would inherit.  In the process, we opened our borders and outsourced our industry, and allowed our militaries to wither and to decay. 

And with every passing year, we seemed to outsource more of our sovereignty, transferring our decisions to global bureaucracies far beyond the reach of our control.

But others were all too happy to fill the vacuum that we left – the vacuum left behind by our weakness.  And as the West’s confidence faltered, its adversaries and its rivals only grew more assertive, building up their own wealth and their own power in our stead.

And now, today, we find ourselves at a crossroads.  Because the next decade and the decisions we make will write the story of the next century.  The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline.  We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all.

Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice.  We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power: to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialize our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future. 

We choose to reach for new frontiers: in advanced manufacturing and super intelligence; in drones, weapons, and warfare; in chips, minerals, cyber, and every other domain of human possibility.  To unleash our energy, to rebuild our factories, to return our astronauts to the moon and launch a new age of exploration in space.

Now for all their lofty ideals, the ancient Greeks were not naive.  They understood that nations have interests.  They understood that statecraft requires prudence and diplomacy, but they also understood that it requires the ability to wield force when prudence and diplomacy fail.  They understood that power requires not only having the means to defend yourself, it requires the credibility that you are willing to use it.

This is the classical understanding of politics and of statecraft that the Trump Administration hopes to reclaim – reclaim not just for our country, but for the whole of our civilization.

We believe that Europe can awaken from its long slumber and rekindle the fire that was lit here millennia ago.

There are already signs.

Across this continent, we are witnessing what we hope will be the beginnings of a generational shift: skyrocketing defense spending, a flurry of new partnerships and programs, expanded manufacturing and production, following on the historic defense commitments made last year in The Hague. 

Greece has been at the center of this shift.  The people of this nation have proved themselves once again to be an indispensable friend to Europe and to the United States alike, on everything from energy to migration to defense, where Greece has been a model ally.

And it’s our sincerest hope that all of Europe will follow your example.

Though passions may, at times, have strained the bonds of affection between the United States and Europe, it must not be allowed to break them.  Together, we must strengthen an alliance capable of confronting threats of our age.

And we can.  Because we do not believe the transatlantic friendship should be zero sum.  Quite the opposite: our vision is of an alliance whose strength is greater than the sum of its parts.  It is a vision we saw in action just last month, in an unprecedented new agreement between the United States, Denmark, and Greenland – an agreement that will reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of NATO.  All three partners in that deal emerged victorious.  All of Europe – and NATO and the United States emerged safer, stronger, and more secure because of it.

We want to win together.  We must win together.

Now it’s has become fashionable today to believe that enlightened foreign policy means prioritizing the global community over one’s own people.  And I think here, too, we have much to learn from the men of ancient Greece because they knew that there was nothing selfish or wrong about loyalty to your nation, nor anything selfish or wrong about fighting to defend its interests above all else. 

They believed – fiercely – in the ideal of the great man: the exceptional individual who obtains immortality through his own deeds.  But they believed that glory and fame, those things were won through striving, sacrificing and achieving greatly for something larger than yourself.  The recurring hero of the ancient Greek world was the man who was willing to pay any cost for a cause worthy of his loyalty.

We see this in Socrates, who refused to abandon the inquiry into truth even at the cost of his own life.  We see it in the legendary stand of 300 Spartans – surrounded and hopelessly outnumbered by the vast armies of Persia – who refused the chance to save themselves, choosing to fight to the last man rather than abandon their post or abandon their duty.  And we see it in the epic myth of Achilles, who is offered the choice to return home and live a long and peaceful life – but chooses instead to remain at Troy and perish in pursuit of eternal glory.

These – these are the qualities that would shape the Western moral imagination.  From the Christian martyr who refused to betray his faith to the patriot who gave his life for his country; from Saint Thomas More to the Battle of the Alamo, running through the immortal closing words of the Declaration of Independence of the United States which says, “We mutually pledge to each other our Lives, our Fortunes and our sacred Honor.”

It is from the Greeks that the West inherited its sense of duty – an unbreakable loyalty to one’s code, one’s cause, one’s country.  Our heroes, the heroes of the West are those who choose to remain faithful to their duty precisely when it is most difficult and painful to do so: the man who is bound by his word, the soldier who will not abandon his post, the captain, the proverbial captain, who goes down with his ship.

This is wholly different from what we see, even now, for example from fanatics like the radical mullahs of Iran, whose cult of death hails child suicide bombers as national heroes, and portrays martyrdom as an end to itself.

Our heroes – our heroes may be willing to die for their cause; but our heroes do not worship death.  It is precisely because we value life that we come to recognize the heroism in those who would sooner sacrifice it than to betray their principles.  Now, we take the West’s conception of these things – heroism, honor, duty – we take these things for granted.  We assume that these somehow are universal to all people in all times and in all places.  They are not.  They are the product of a distinct character, a distinct character which arose here and shaped the whole story of the civilization that came after it.  A civilization that we must fight to defend today with the same passion as our forefathers did.

The men who built the Parthenon were succeeded by the architects of European Christendom, who raised the cathedrals of Milan, Cologne, and Florence.  The quest to perfect the human form that moved the ancient Greek sculptors found a new expression in Michelangelo.  The Greek philosophers’ search for the structure of the universe was inherited by Copernicus, and then Galileo, then Kepler, and in Newton.

The hunger for new knowledge, that’s what gave birth to Magellan’s first expedition around the world, to Columbus’ discovery of the Americas, and ultimately to Apollo 11’s journey to the moon.  And the qualities that led Alexander to conquer the entire known world reappeared in Caesar, then Charlemagne, and Cortes.

And in America, that same tradition rediscovered itself anew.  An open and wild land became the site of a great revival of Western imagination and ambition.  The Greek aspiration for new horizons became the American frontier spirit.  The civilization of Athens and Rome transformed an infant seaboard republic into a continental empire.

The greatest Americans of every generation have carried the unmistakable features of their forefathers – born in Athens, formed by Rome, baptized in Christendom, hardened in the furnace of medieval Europe, endowed with the English genius for liberty, and then carried across the Atlantic to be reborn on the shores of a new world. 

Together, we must now rediscover that spirit.  We are at an inflection point – an inflection point not only in the history of my nation, but an inflection point in the whole of our civilization. 

The threats we face today are every bit as real as they were on the dramatic stage of antiquity.

National interests did not vanish in the face of international institutions.  War did not disappear simply because we preferred peace.  Other states continued to arm, to seek influence, to compete for territory, and technology, and resources, and markets, and energy, and power.

And now, there is war again.  There is new competition between great powers again.  There is vulnerability, aggression, terrorism, a whole universe of new threats and attacks again. 

And so we must rebuild our institutions and our alliances to face these threats together – understanding that the purpose of these things is not to abolish the sovereignty of the nations that constitute them; it is to defend them.  And that nations need not abandon their distinct identities in order to recognize their common interests.

We have built a model of that with our partners here in Greece.  In our defense partnerships, in energy and technology, in our shared ambition to secure Europe’s borders from the threats of mass migration.

Our friendship dates back to the earliest years of my nation.  When Greece rose in 1821 to recover its independence after centuries of Ottoman rule, Americans recognized something familiar in that struggle.  Three years later, the great American statesman Daniel Webster, he delivered a famous address to Congress, helping bring the cause of the Greek Revolution before the representatives of the young American republic.

And he began by calling their attention to everything around them.  This is what he said in his speech; he said:  “This free form of government, this popular assembly… this practice of free debate, and public discussion, the contest of mind with mind… even the edifice in which we assemble, these proportioned columns, this ornamented architecture, all remind us that Greece has existed, and that we, like the rest of mankind, are greatly her debtors.”

Those words are as true today as they were when he said them.  And all of us – not just Americans, but Europeans and our friends across the West – must relearn the lessons our forefathers took from this place and from its history.

The history of Greece – the history of Greece does not just offer us a glimpse – it does not offer a glimpse of our institutions in their earliest forms.  The history of Greece shows us an image of ourselves.

It shows us that ours is the inheritance of great heroes, and that we should be proud – that we should be intensely proud – of where we come from.  We should marvel at what our forefathers carved out of this countryside.  The story of our civilization is the greatest story ever known to man.  And it began here, with the first men and women of the West.  From them – from them – we can rediscover the virtues, the courage, and the strength to confront the dangers that we face in our time. Thank you.

DOJ extends free legal help to 490 Ilocos residents

MALASIQUI, Pangasinan – The Department of Justice (DOJ) has assisted 490 clients in the Ilocos Region with legal services from Jan. 1 to the present.

Legal Assistant to the DOJ Action Center in Ilocos Region Mercy De Jesus, in a phone interview on Tuesday, said the number is a mix of walk-in clients, those who called, contacted them through social media or e-mail, and those served in the Katarungan Caravan.

De Jesus said everyone is welcome to avail of the DOJ services for free except those already assisted by lawyers or who have legal counsel, those with a pending court case, and those who are not part of the case.

She said they have also been conducting information drives in Bureau of Jail Management and Penology facilities for persons deprived of liberty and their families, such as in San Fernando City, La Union on Tuesday.

"We discussed the Victims Compensation Program, the Witness Protection Program, Pardon and Parole, and the services offered by the DOJ Action Center, and we also had a briefing about Human Trafficking," she said.

She added that it is very important for them to have information, as most of them do not know that there are programs offered by the DOJ Action Center.

"They are not aware that there are free legal services that they can avail, not only for them, but also for their families and relatives," she added. (PNA) (With DOJ seal)

text:
A con man sold the Brooklyn Bridge. More than once.

In the early 1900s, George C. Parker made a living convincing people he owned famous New York landmarks. His favorite was the Brooklyn Bridge.

He would approach out-of-towners, show them forged ownership papers, and offer to sell them the bridge at a bargain price. Some buyers actually paid, then tried to set up toll booths on the span before police stopped them.

Parker didn’t stop there. He also sold the Statue of Liberty, Madison Square Garden, and Grant’s Tomb using the same method. He was arrested multiple times for the scams.

He spent his final years in Sing Sing prison and died there in 1936. His repeated sales of the Brooklyn Bridge helped turn the phrase “I’ve got a bridge to sell you” into a lasting American expression for an obvious con.

One man turned the city’s most famous landmarks into a personal business.

Hebrews 10:1-4 For the Law, since it has only a shadow of the good things to come and not the form of those things itself, can never, by the same sacrifices which they offer continually every year, make those who approach perfect. 2 Otherwise, would they not have ceased to be offered, because the worshipers, having once been cleansed, would no longer have had consciousness of sins? 3 But in those sacrifices there is a reminder of sins every year. 4 For it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins.

The sacrificial system laid out in Leviticus, including the Day of Atonement, was not designed to forgive sin. This is why the blood of animal sacrifices is never applied to people, while it is applied to the instruments in the Temple and even the Ark of the Covenant. (Blood is applied to lepers etc, but symbolically, not for forgiveness of sins).

Leviticus 17:11 tells us clearly the reason a sacrifice is necessary: "For the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you on the altar to make atonement for your souls; for it is the blood by reason of the life that makes atonement.’

However, while blood sacrifice is necessary for the atonement of sin (at-onement), the blood of animals does not have the power to forgive sin, it was only a foreshadowing. Because we have sinned against an eternal God, the punishment for that sin is eternal and, therefore, could only be truly atoned for by a holy eternal being (ie. Jesus is truly God, eternal, and truly man, the physical sacrifice without sin).

What the sacrificial system was designed to do was cleanse the worshiper for sacred space. A key to understanding this is Lev. 16:16, where the Temple itself is atoned for (because sinners enter it all year). 

As Hebrews makes clear, it is only the sacrificial death of Christ that atones for the punishment of sin past, present, and future (once and for all).

text:
Fair hit. The sages say more than the line I quoted: Avot d'Rabbi Natan 4 has Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai calling chesed an atonement equal to the altar, and Yoma 86a makes teshuvah the hinge. I accept all of it. The same sages also teach that the death of the righteous atones (Moed Katan 28a) and that the shofar is blown so God will count Israel "as if you had bound yourselves before Me" (Rosh Hashanah 16a). They never dropped one standing in for another; they moved it.

You asked me to read your verses verbatim. I did, in Hebrew, and one verb runs through all of them: נשא, to carry.
Hosea 14:2: "say to Him, carry away all iniquity," kol tissa avon. In your own proof text, forgiveness is God carrying something.
Ezekiel 18:20: "the son shall not carry (lo yissa) the iniquity of the father." Same verb. The Torah forbids loading a father's guilt onto a son and then commands this: the high priest confesses all Israel's iniquities, puts them on the head of the goat, "and the goat shall carry (venasa) all their iniquities" (Lev 16:21-22). Confession and transfer sit in one verse. Ezekiel himself keeps a sin offering "to make atonement for the house of Israel" in the Temple to come (45:17, 22), as you posted last week.

Psalm 51 was written over adultery and murder, two sins for which the Torah provides no korban (Num 15:30; Num 35:31: "you shall take no kofer for the life of a murderer"). Read verse 16 with that in mind. Verse 7: "cleanse me with hyssop," the blood-sprinkling branch (Ex 12:22, Lev 14:6). Verse 5: "in sin my mother conceived me," the nearest thing in Tanakh to what you say isn't there. Verse 19: "then bulls will be offered on Your altar." Nathan's verdict: "the LORD has caused your sin to pass over (he'evir); you shall not die" (2 Sam 12:13). Passed over to where? David, Psalm 32:1: "Blessed is he whose transgression is carried (nesui)."

Micah 6:7 rejects child sacrifice; agreed. Micah ends with the Tashlich text: "Who is a God like You, who carries iniquity (nose avon) and passes over transgression" (7:18), grounded in the oath to Abraham (7:20). The same words stand in Exodus 34:7 beside a clause the siddur leaves out: "and He will by no means clear the guilty." Yoma 86a reads it as repentant versus unrepentant; even then the verse's own word is "carries," and it never says the guilt ceased to exist. Exodus 23:7 has God refusing to justify the wicked, yet Ezekiel 18 lets the wicked who turns live. Isaiah 53:11 is where Tanakh puts "justify the many" and "carry their iniquities" in one sentence. Whoever you take the Servant to be, that is the mechanism Isaiah describes.
C.S. Lewis put the trap in one line: only a bad man needs to repent, and only a good man can do it perfectly.

The flood: the first thing after it is an altar, and God binds Himself to mercy over the aroma of a sacrifice, giving this reason: "for the yetzer of man's heart is evil from his youth" (Gen 8:21). Judgment drowned the sinners and left the heart where it was. He says so Himself.

After the calf, Moshe went up saying "perhaps I can atone (achapperah) for your sin... blot me out of Your book," and God turned him down: "whoever has sinned against Me, him I will blot out" (Ex 32:30-33). The greatest prophet offered himself as the kofer and was refused. Psalm 49: no man can give God a kofer for his brother, "but God will redeem my soul from Sheol" (49:7-8, 15). Abraham said it first, on Moriah, where the altar later stood (2 Chr 3:1): "God will see to the lamb Himself" (Gen 22:8).

You posted Tehillim 42 about going home: "When shall I come and appear before God?" That question is this whole thread. Ahuva, your name is the verb of Jeremiah 31:3, ahavat olam ahavtich, and the same chapter says what that love intends: "I will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no more" (31:34). I think I know who carries it. Keep asking Him. He answered Abraham on that mountain before He answered anyone.

text:
Finding Jesus in the Old Testament

A Dirt Road Devotional

In Leviticus, He’s Our Atoning Sacrifice

Scripture: (Leviticus 17:11)
“For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul.”

If you want to understand what Jesus did at Calvary, take a walk through the Book of Leviticus. You might find yourself in unfamiliar territory, reading about sacrifices, offerings, priests, and the shedding of blood. To some folks, those pages may seem like nothing more than ancient rules and rituals. But if you look closely, you will find a picture of God’s plan for dealing with sin.

Sin has always carried a price. From the Garden of Eden forward, God has made it clear that sin separates us from Him. Under the law, the blood of an animal was offered as an atonement for sin. The sacrifice served as a reminder that sin was serious and that forgiveness required a provision God Himself established.

But those sacrifices were never the final answer. They pointed toward something greater.
They pointed to Jesus Christ!

Hebrews 10:4 tells us, “For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins.”

Those sacrifices could never accomplish what Jesus would accomplish at Calvary. They were shadows of the sacrifice to come. The blood of an animal could serve under the Old Testament sacrificial system, but only the precious blood of Christ could provide the perfect and sufficient sacrifice for our sins.

Hebrews 9:12 says that Christ entered into the holy place “by his own blood,” having “obtained eternal redemption for us.”

Think about that for a minute. Under the old system, the sacrifice had to be repeated. But Jesus offered Himself once for all. No more animals on an altar. No more repeated sacrifices. The Lamb of God had come to take away the sin of the world.

Leviticus shows us the seriousness of sin. Calvary shows us the greatness of God's love.

The sacrifices in Leviticus were temporary pictures of a permanent provision. Jesus did not come merely to improve our lives or give us a better way to live. He came to deal with our sin problem once and for all.

Friend, the next time you read through Leviticus, don't just see the blood on the altar. Look beyond the altar to the cross. Look beyond the priest to the Great High Priest. Look beyond the sacrifice to the Savior who gave Himself for us.

The Old Testament sacrificial system was never the destination. It was pointing down the road to Calvary.

Dirt Road Truth: Leviticus teaches us that sin requires atonement, and Calvary reveals the Savior who paid the price. The blood of the old sacrifices pointed forward to the blood of Jesus Christ, our perfect and sufficient atoning sacrifice.

“Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.” (John 1:29)

Strictly speaking within the text of the Greek New Testament, no—the word "elder" (presbyteros) does not mean a sacrificial "priest" (hiereus).
However, there is a massive linguistic paradox here because the modern English word "priest" actually evolved directly from the Greek word for elder!
The text breaks down across linguistic, etymological, and theological lines:

1. In the Original Greek Text (The Words Used)

The New Testament maintains a strict boundary between two completely different Greek words:
• Hiereus (Priest): This is the word used for a temple minister who offers blood sacrifices and mediates between God and man. The New Testament uses it for Jewish priests, pagan priests, Jesus Christ, and the collective body of believers. It is never used to describe a local Christian church leader.
• Presbyteros (Elder): This word literally means "older man" or "senior". It is used for the community leaders and pastors appointed to shepherd local congregations (e.g., Acts 20:17, Titus 1:5).
Because the text never uses hiereus for a church leader, standard Bible translations strictly translate presbyteros as "elder" or "presbyter".

2. The Linguistic Evolution (How "Elder" became "Priest")

Even though the words are completely different in the Greek text, they collided over centuries of English language history:
Etymologically, the word "priest" is just a shortened, localized contraction of the word "presbyter" (elder). When early English Christians spoke of a "priest," they literally meant a presbyteros.

text:
In the Bible, there is a distinct conceptual and linguistic difference between an "elder" and a "priest."
The two roles come from entirely different words, histories, and functions in the biblical text. While the Old Testament heavily features a formal sacrificial priesthood, the New Testament shifts toward a structure led by local elders, viewing all believers as part of a spiritual priesthood.

1. Elder (Zaqen / Presbyteros)

The concept of an elder is rooted in governance, wisdom, and community leadership.
• Old Testament (Zaqen): Literally meaning "bearded" or "aged," elders were the tribal and civic leaders of Israel. They sat at the city gates, acted as judges, made political decisions, and represented the people (e.g., Exodus 3:16, Ruth 4:1). They were not religious ministers and did not offer sacrifices.
• New Testament (Presbyteros): The early Christian church adopted this model. Elders were mature spiritual leaders appointed to oversee, protect, and teach local congregations (e.g., Titus 1:5, 1 Peter 5:1-2). The New Testament uses the word elder interchangeably with overseer (bishop/episkopos) and pastor (shepherd/poimen).

2. Priest (Kohen / Hiereus)

The concept of a priest is rooted in mediation, sacrifice, and ritual purity.
• Old Testament (Kohen): Priests had to come strictly from the tribe of Levi and the lineage of Aaron. Their primary job was to act as mediators between a holy God and sinful humanity. They guarded the Tabernacle/Temple, offered animal sacrifices for sin, and managed the ritual purity of the nation (e.g., Leviticus 1-7).
• New Testament (Hiereus): The New Testament never uses the word hiereus (sacrificial priest) to describe an individual leader or office in the local Christian church. Instead, the New Testament applies this word in two specific ways:
1. Jesus Christ: He is described as the ultimate, final High Priest who offered Himself as a single, perfect sacrifice to end all animal sacrifices (Hebrews 4:14-16, 10:11-14).
2. All Believers: Because of Jesus, the entire church body is called a "royal priesthood" (hierateuma), meaning every individual Christian now has direct access to God without needing a human mediator (1 Peter 2:9, Revelation 1:6).

text:
Study Notes - (Pulpit Version Explained) Psalms 129:1-8
EXPOSITION
THIS psalm consists of a retrospect (Psa_129:1-4) and an anticipation (Psa_129:5-8). The retrospect shows Israel oppressed by enemies for a long term of years, but finally vindicated and delivered (Psa_129:4). The anticipation shows her enemies afflicted in their turn, and suffering the just reward for their misdeeds.
Psa_129:1
Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth. Israel’s recollection is one of frequent, almost constant, "affliction." She has been downtrodden beneath the feet of Egyptians, Moabites, Mesopotamians, Canaanites, Ammonites, Philistines, Syrians. Assyrians, Babylonians. Her sufferings began in her extreme youth, as soon as she was a nation (Exo_1:11-22). May Israel now say; rather, let Israel now say. The psalmist directs his countrymen to look back upon their past history.
Psa_129:2
Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth. The repetition emphasizes the fact of Israel’s long and bitter suffering. Yet they have not prevailed against me. Israel has not been given as a prey to the heathen’s teeth (Psa_124:6). She is still a nation, unsubdued; she holds her own; the struggle is not ended.
Psa_129:3
The plowers plowed upon my back. A strong metaphor, which does not elsewhere occur. The idea is perhaps taken from the cruel treatment of captives in those days, who, in certain cases, were "put under saws and harrows of iron" (2Sa_12:31), or, as it is elsewhere expressed, "threshed with threshing instruments of iron" (Amo_1:3). They made long their furrows; i.e. "lengthened out their tortures."
Psa_129:4
The Lord is righteous. Still, God is just. He allowed these sufferings to be inflicted on us because we deserved them; and he interposed on our behalf when we had been sufficiently punished, and cut asunder the cords of the wicked. Cut, i.e; the cords wherewith they had bound us. The "retrospect" here ends, and in the next verse the "anticipation" begins.
Psa_129:5
Let them all be confounded; or, "they shall all be confounded," or "put to shame." And turned back. Made to turn their backs upon their foes. That hate Zion. That have shown themselves enemies to Israel. The main verbs are in the future tense, but may be taken as expressive either of a wish or of a confident expectation.
Psa_129:6
Let them be as the grass upon the housetops; literally, they shall be as the grass of housetops. The flat roofs of Oriental houses are usually covered in early spring with a crop of bright-green grass. But the scorching rays of the sun soon burn this up, and it becomes dry and withered. Which withereth afore it groweth up; literally, before it is unsheathed; i.e. before the blossom has left the sheath in which it is formed.
Psa_129:7
Wherewith the mower filleth not his hand. Which is so worthless that no one takes the trouble to mow it. Nor he that bindeth sheaves his bosom. Much less does any one bind it into sheaves and store it away.
Psa_129:8
Neither do they which go by say, The blessing of the Lord be upon you; we bless you in the name of the Lord. Harvesters were thus greeted (Rut_2:4), and still are to this day. "These expressions," says Dr. Thomson, "are most refreshingly Arabic. Nothing is more natural than for Arabs, when passing by a fruit-tree or cornfield loaded with a rich crop, to exclaim, Barak Allah! ’God bless you!’".
HOMILETICS
Psa_129:1-8
Sin a failure.
Neither the violence of sin against others nor its effort on its own behalf is successful.
I. THE FAILURE OF ITS VIOLENCE. The enemies of Israel are regarded as the enemies of the Lord; their attempts to despoil and destroy Israel were sins against God. They consequently proved to be utter failures. They were mercilessly cruel; they "ploughed upon the back, and made long their furrows;" they strove to enslave with their strong cords (Psa_129:4), but "they did not prevail" (Psa_129:2); their cords were cut asunder (Psa_129:4). Israel survived the hardships of Egypt and the captivity of Babylon. Many nations and communities have passed through similar afflictions and oppressions, but they have borne them bravely; they may even have been the purer, the stronger, the more united, for all they have suffered. Many a man can speak in the same strain; his history has been one of struggle and hardship in youth, of toil in mid-life, of deliverance and gratitude in later years. He has lived to see his oppressors humbled, to find that they who offend God by ill treating his servants come to shame and sorrow. The most striking lesson of the psalm is—
II. THE DEGENERACY OF SIN. The psalmist prays (or states) that those who "hate Zion" may be like the grass which has no depth of earth, which withers before it attains maturity, which falls short of the blessing which the well-planted corn enjoys (Psa_129:6-8). Here are two evils which the unholy have to face.
1. Early withering.
(1) Sin often leads down to some form of vice, some evil habit which is at variance with the laws of our nature and the will of God, We know what that means. It means the drying up of the distinctively human resources; it means loss of physical vitality; it means the fading’ of mental power, it means the degeneracy of the soul. The end is not far off; before it has fully grown up, before the zenith of life is reached, the constitution is wrecked, the darkness of death has fallen.
(2) Sin is selfishness, very often worldliness and vanity. And either of these ends in a sad spiritual withering. The heart closes up; there is no expansion, no ripening, no fruit-bearing under the gracious influences of Divine love and human pity and holy fellowship. Long before bodily death arrives, spiritual destruction has come.
2. The loss of the higher good. The man who is living under the dominion of sin and selfishness misses all that is worthiest and best. In his life is no such scenery as that so beautifully sketched in the psalm. He has to go without the blessing of God and the benediction of his kind.
HOMILIES BY S. CONWAY
Psa_129:1-8
The Divine life.
This psalm is capable of a threefold application. It tells of the Divine life—
I. IN ISRAEL.
1. The existence of the chosen people was a lifelong struggle. The sounds of battle and war are never, save but for short intervals, absent from their history. From the oppression they had to endure in Egypt right down to the time when this psalm was composed, they never lacked enemies who "fought against" them, and did them all the harm they could.
2. But their enemies never altogether prevailed. (Psa_129:2.) Sooner or later deliverance came. Such a deliverance had just now come, and hence this psalm. And the complete deliverance which is still needed for Israel we may well believe, from the records of the past, will, in God’s good time, be forthcoming.
3. The sufferings which they caused them were very great. (Psa_129:3.) As the ploughshare tears up the soil, so the lacerating scourge tore their flesh. In these psalms we yet hear the wail of their lamentations and their exceeding bitter cry (see Psa_124:1-8; Psa_137:1-9; and many more; comp. Isa_1:6; Isa_51:23).
4. The Lord, true to his covenant, put an end to their sufferings. As when the cords, the traces that fasten the oxen to the plough, are cut, the plough comes to a standstill, so the dread plough of suffering, which ploughed such agonizing furrows in their souls, was brought to a standstill; for the Lord cut asunder the cords.
5. But the bitter memory begot bitter prayers. (Psa_129:6-8.) That those who so dealt with them may be ashamed, defeated, despised as worthless, like the grass that springs up and at once withers, because on the house-top there can be no depth of earth, and hence such grass is of no value at all (cf. Isa_37:27), and that they may be such as no blessing of the Lord can rest upon (Psa_129:8). Before we condemn such prayers, we should put ourselves in the place of those who offered them. They may not be Christian any more than war is always Christian, but they are very natural. They are not the utterances of personal revenge, but prayers for the overthrow of those who hated Zion, and who were the enemies of God as well as of Zion. Nevertheless, in spite of all, Israel was preserved of God.
II. IN THE CHURCH. Verse by verse the words of the psalm tell of her experience. Cradled in conflict, oppressed with suffering, "fought against" by enemies one after another, varied in kind, but all terrible, yet never really defeated—"they have not prevailed against me;" so may the Church say. And long ago the Lord has cut asunder, for the most part, the cords whereby the cruel ploughshare of persecution was dragged over the bleeding flesh of the people of God. Our freedom should kindle and keep glowing our sympathy with those Christians who, in the dominions of the "unspeakable Turk," are yet subjected to horrible atrocities. Oh that the Lord may soon cut asunder those cords, and set his people free! Nor are the prayers against the perpetrators of such atrocities with which this psalm closes improper for us, and still less for those who endure such wrongs. But God’s Church ever lives.
III. IN THE INDIVIDUAL SOUL. Again is this psalm the transcript of the history of the life of God, but now as existing in the soul of the individual Christian. The enemies now are not of flesh and blood, but spiritual, and, therefore, yet more terrible. For they who hurt the body soon have no more that they can do; but these can eternally torment us—they can destroy both soul and body in hell. Therefore we may well, as Christ bids us, fear them. Nor are the most terrible of the prayers in these imprecatory psalms out of place when we think of these foes. We are bound to hate them and pray against them, and by God’s help we will.—S.C.
HOMILIES BY R. TUCK
Psa_129:1
Our seven sorrows.
"Many a time have they afflicted me;" so many times that it seemed useless to try and count them up. It is enough to represent them by one number, and that the representative of completeness, seven times. Israel may be said, as a nation, to have had an 
all-round experience of affliction and discipline. Eliphaz the Temanite speaks rightly to Job for God when he says, "He shall deliver thee in six troubles; yea, in seven there shall be no evil touch thee" (Job_5:19).
I. A FACT OF THE NATIONAL HISTORY. So far as the record reveals that history, it appears to be a series of calamities and distresses; some brought about by characteristic national frailties, some by individuals forcing their willfulnesses, some by untoward circumstances, and some by the active schemes of enemies. It would even seem that national sorrows are so well represented in this history that we may speak of its "seven sorrows;" and we may find the mission of all forms of human trial illustrated in the moral influence of these calamities and woes of Israel. But we need not assume that its experiences were unique. Every nation is born of, and molded by, similar troubles. The peculiarity of Israel does not lie in its experiences, but in the reading of its experiences. The Bible reads them in the light of Jehovah’s relation to them. This is the only true reading of human history, and all history needs to be read in this light. God is in the sorrows of a nation.
II. A FACT OF THE INDIVIDUAL HISTORY. It does not matter where, or under what circumstances, or in what relations, a man’s life is lived. A man is "born to trouble as the sparks fly upward." No man can escape it. It would be his curse if he could. A man can, as a moral being, become righteous; but there is no school in which he can be trained for righteousness save the school of affliction. It is no ground of boasting to any man that his life has been free from trials. If a man may boast at all, he should boast over his "seven sorrows," because he may indulge the hope that God’s grace has been mighty in him, and he has come into much sanctifying discipline.—R.T.
Psa_129:3
The figure of the torn land.
The expression, "They made long their furrows," can only be understood through the peculiar conditions of Eastern ploughing. The word "furrow" (maanah) signifies a strip of arable land which the ploughman takes in hand at one time, at both ends of which, consequently, the ploughing team always comes to a stand, turns round, and begins a new furrow. Since the ordinary ox of Palestine is smaller and weaker than ours, and easily becomes tired under the yoke, which presses heavily on its neck and confines its neck, they are obliged to give it time to recover its strength by frequent resting. This always takes place at the termination of a furrow, when the peasant raises the unwieldy plough out of the earth, and turns it over, clearing off the moist earth with the small shovel at the lower end of the goad, and hammering the loosened edges and rings tight again, during which time the team is able to recover itself by resting. They do not, therefore, make the furrows of great length. The figure of this verse is explained by the over-exhaustion of the oxen, if the furrows through which they had to drag the plough were made overlong. The suggestion of the ’ Speaker’s Commentary ’ is less natural. It takes the verse as a figure of scourging. (Improving on this, Dr. Wordsworth finds anticipation of the scourging of Christ.) "The lashes inflicted upon the back of the writhing slave by a cruel master are compared to the long furrows pierced in the passive earth by the share of the plougher." The figure must be explained in the light of the memories cherished by the psalmist, as representing the nation just returned from captivity. And the nation is symbolized by the land in which the nation dwelt.
I. ISRAEL’S SORROWS HAD BEEN LIKE THE WORK OF A PLOUGH IN THE LAND. Attention is indeed fixed only on the tearing open and turning over of the land; but we need not miss seeing that this stern dealing was the necessary preliminary to seed sowing and fruitage. (Compare "No trial for the present seemeth to be joyous," etc.) Better be torn land than harvestless land.
II. THE AGENTS OF ISRAEL’S SORROWS HAD OVERDONE THEIR WORK. They had gone beyond their commission, had increased the length of the furrow. So we often think of our sorrows when we try to estimate their moral value. But that is what we can never do wisely. They never do go beyond God-arranged limits.—R.T.
Psa_129:4
Righteousness may involve judgment.
The cutting asunder of cords figuratively presents the liberating of Israel from the Babylonian captivity, and also the yet earlier experience of the nation, when Jehovah cut the cords of Egypt, and set his people free. This is the consideration which relieves the psalmist’s strain in thinking how many Israel’s trials had been, and how greatly her enemies had enjoyed inflicting them. "Jehovah is righteous." There is always security and rest in that conviction. "He will not suffer us to be tempted above that we are able to bear." Men or circumstances may put cords about us. Whenever he sees it right to do so, our God can "cut the cords asunder." Men may "hate Zion," and gladly do her a mischief; but this we may always rely on—God can "confound them and turn them back," as he did the Syrians in the days of Elisha. "If God be for us, who can be against us?" Righteousness is a many-sided and many-related thing.
I. RIGHTEOUSNESS BEARS RELATION TO THE WORLD AS A WHOLE. It must be such as every one sooner or later can recognize. It must have in view the well-being of the whole; and this involves that it must not let evil go unpunished; it must bring judgment on the wicked. For the world’s sake the righteous God must be active against all unrighteousness.
II. RIGHTEOUSNESS BEARS RELATION TO THE INDIVIDUAL. And in a life very various moral moods and conditions are represented. God must answer to all the moods if he is righteous; and this involves trial for reproof, and judgment for correction. God smiting his people is not only God acting in love, it is God acting in righteousness. "I know that in faithfulness thou hast afflicted me."
III. RIGHTEOUSNESS BEARS RELATION TO THE AGENTS OF NATIONAL AND INDIVIDUAL AFFLICTION. This is symbolically taught in God’s prophecy concerning Egypt, as the oppressor of his people, "And also that nation whom they shall serve will I judge." And so Babylon, the agent of the Captivity, was to be judged. It needs to be seen that the fact of God’s using Balaam, or Egypt, for his purposes does not relieve them from the responsibility of their conduct. Hating Zion may lead to action which works out God’s purposes; but hating Zion surely brings a man or a nation into the judgment-vindication of the righteous God.—R.T.
Psa_129:6
A new figure of the grass.
Jowett says, "At Anata, the Anathoth of Scripture, I observed that the roofs of some of the houses were partially covered with grass—a circumstance which I noticed also in several other places. As the roofs of the common dwellings are flat, and, instead of being built of stone or wood, are coated with plaster or hardened earth, a slight crop of grass frequently springs up in that situation. Such vegetation, however, having no soil into which it can strike its roots, and being exposed to a scorching sun, rarely attains to any great height or continues long. It is a feeble, stunted product, and soon withers away. Hence the sacred writers sometimes allude to the grass of the house-top as an emblem of weakness, frailty, and certain destruction" (Isa_37:27). The meaning of Psa_129:7, Psa_129:8 is this—There will be no reapers of such worthless grass as this; there will be nothing to elicit the utterance of those common formulas of benediction with which passers-by were wont to greet harvesters. It is better to associate these verses with the short-lived enmity of the Samaritans to the returned exiles, than with the more systematic dealing of an empire like Babylon.
I. THE ENMITY OF THE SAMARITANS WAS SHOWY. After rain, the grass on the house-top springs up in a very showy and boastful way, as if it were going to do great things. And so the Samaritans vaunted much and taunted much, and at first seemed to accomplish much; for they put cords on the restoring work of the exiles, and stopped the building of the temple, and prevented the building of the wall.
II, THE ENMITY OF THE SAMARITANS WAS SHORT-LIVED. It was met with patience. Presently the energy of an Ezra and a Nehemiah, like an east wind or a scorching sun, hopelessly cut down the blades. Persecutors of God’s people are never given a "long tether." God’s people may always pray, "Come quickly."
III. THE ENMITY OF THE SAMARITANS BROUGHT THEM NO GOOD. It only spoiled permanently their relations with Israel, and put them out of favor with Persia. The mower never filled his hand with any harvest of the grass that grew on that housetop. The harvest of all enmities to God’s people is never anything else than "a heap in a time of desperate sorrow." Goodness is a harvest reaped from good.—R.T.
Psa_129:8
Politeness in the harvest-field; or, right relations of employer and employed.
Dr. S. Cox writes, "It is a graphic picture of an ancient harvest scene. The field is thick with waving barley. The reapers cut their way into it with sickles, grasping the ears till their arms are full. The overseer is busy urging on the reapers. Vessels filled probably with the rough local wine are at hand, that the heated and thirsty laborers may refresh themselves at need. As the day advances, the master of the estate comes to see how the work goes on. With grave, pious courtesy he salutes his ’young men’ with the words, ’Jehovah be with you!’ and they reply, ’Jehovah bless thee!’ It is true that this was oftentimes a mere formality; but, even if not altogether realized, it shows what the social relations should be."
I. EMPLOYERS AND EMPLOYED SERVE EACH OTHER. So much mistake is made, and so much confusion is caused, by the sentiment that only the employed serve the employer. Things would right themselves if it was fully apprehended that the service is mutual. We think the rewards of service ought to come to the employed; but if the employers also serve, the rewards of service ought to come also to the employer. If they come to either the one or the other in undue measures, there must be something wrong in the social system, which needs readjusting.
II. EMPLOYERS AND EMPLOYED NEED TO TRUST EACH OTHER. The complications of modern labor problems arise from the mischievous work of demagogues, who set class against class. The spirit of Christianity encourages mutual trust, and tends to bring classes together, and helps each class to consider the claims and needs of other classes. The dream of a universal equality has delighted and amused humanity in all ages, and it will to the end of the age. But it will never be more than a dream. Nature makes classes, and will go on making them; and Paradise can never be gained otherwise than by the laborer and his master realizing the Christly spirit of mutual service. The master must trust the servant to render his best of service; and the laborer must trust his master to give a fair and relatively proportionate reward.—R.T.
HOMILIES BY C. SHORT
Psa_129:1-8
Suffering and victory.
"Many a time have they afflicted me from my youth," etc. The connection is shown thus—
I. THE PSALMIST SAW THE REDEMPTIVE RIGHTEOUSNESS OF GOD AS SUPREME. (Psa_129:4.) God’s strength and justice surely prevail against all the devices of evil men.
II. GOOD MEN PREVAIL WHEN THEY USE THEIR SUFFERING AS CORRECTIVE DISCIPLINE. Some of the greatest lessons of life are learned from our severest sufferings. "For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy," etc.; "Our light affliction worketh out … while we look not at the things which are seen," etc.
III. THE OPPOSITION OF ENEMIES CALLS FORTH THEIR GREATEST ENERGIES. This a law that operates in the physical, the intellectual, and the moral life. Stem a torrent, and you increase its force. An intellectual difficulty rouses us to the greatest endeavor, and moral obstacles call forth our most triumphant strength.
IV. THE UNRIGHTEOUS ARE ULTIMATELY DEFEATED IN THEIR OPPOSITION TO THE GOOD CAUSE. (Psa_129:5, Psa_129:6.) They are driven back, and made ashamed of their efforts and designs upon the righteous cause. The psalmist is not doubtful of the final issue of the conflict between good and evil. The evil will wither like grass on the house-tops.
V. THE RIGHTEOUS WILL GATHER THE HARVEST OF THEIR LABORS AMID THE BENEDICTIONS OF GOD AND MAN. (Psa_129:8.) No good seed that has been sown will fail of a harvest more or less abundant. God and man rejoice in all good work done, whatever the extent of its consequences. "Well done, good and faithful servant;" "Blessed is the man that walketh not in the way of the wicked," whose "delight is in the Law of the Lord."—S.

text:
Two pigeons was a standard offering for purification after childbirth.  There's no connection with personal sin.  

It's not uncommon for the anti-Catholic screeds on here to display only the shallowest of understanding of the Old and New Testament.  The word sin is derived as a term for archery or slings and means to miss the mark. It came to be associated with moral failings only, but originally was meant for any deviation from the Purity sought in the law of Moses.  The offering of two turtle doves after childbirth was to restore purity, as any blood flow, man or woman, was considered to render one impure for a period.

MJ is just looking for traffic.  I try to avoid providing it,  but I hope this helps clear up the confusion he intentionally seeks to create.  Mary's sinlessness is not impeached by such a standard practice.   

It is interesting, though, that he brings this up. Many Protestant churches encourage what's called a presentation, which they claim is an imitation of the presentation of Jesus by Mary and Joseph, which occurred at the same time as she offered the turtle doves. However, this is a misread of the tradition (Ironic, right?  Those who dismiss tradition try to preserve this one but don't even understand it) .  First, the presentation was only a  Jewish practice for a firstborn son.  Second,  that son was presented as an offering to God, to consecrate that son to serve in the Temple.  This was established before the Levitical priesthood.  The practice continued after the establishment of the Levitical priesthood, though, the non-Levite families would offer 5 shekels to "redeem" their sons back to them.   

So, the Protestants can 'present' their children to their churches, but it's far from an imitation of Jesus' own presentation.   A final note: Jesus was of the tribe of Judah, not Levi, but the recounting of the presentation does not mention the offering of the redemption, meaning that, unlike other first sons, Jesus was retained by God.

He comes not with the storm’s demand,
Nor chains to bind the lifted hand,
But soft as rain on thirsty ground,
A voice that waits to be found.
He stands outside and gently knocks,
No force against the heart that locks,
But patient as the rising sun,
He whispers, “Child, if you will come.”
The Shepherd calls, He does not drive;
He leaves the ninetynine alive
To seek the one who chose to stray,
And still He waits along the way.
He sets before us life and death,
Then steps aside and holds His breath,
For love compelled is never love,
And grace is something freely given from above.
So still He knocks, and still He calls,
Through quiet nights and temple halls,
A gentle God who will not force,
But offers rest and leaves the choice.

text:
🌺 Stone Still Receives What the Heart Offers 🌺

In the weathered niches of an ancient Indian temple wall, three figures stand in quiet dialogue, two female forms flanking a central figure captured in a dynamic dance pose. Red hibiscus blossoms rest upon the central sculpture and lie scattered at its base, their freshness contrasting beautifully with the centuries-old stone. Photographed by Amit Pasricha, the image captures both the enduring beauty of India’s architectural heritage and the living spirit of devotion. 

These are more than decorative carvings. Temple walls across India have long featured surasundaris, apsaras, and attendant divinities nestled within sculpted recesses, their presence symbolizing auspiciousness and grace. The central figure’s lifted leg and expressive posture evoke the language of nritya, the sacred art of dance described in classical texts such as the Nāṭyaśāstra. The flanking figures, each accompanied by a small animal at the pedestal, contribute to the balanced composition characteristic of medieval Indian temple iconography.

Yet it is the flowers that transform this ancient artwork from a historical relic into a living focus of worship. The hibiscus blossoms are not merely ornaments; they are offerings of faith, carrying a gesture that has passed from one generation to another. The stone endures, quietly receiving what the heart continues to offer. 

In this simple encounter between sculpture and devotion lies a profound reminder: heritage is not only what survives through time, but also what continues to inspire reverence, connection, and love. The carvings remain, and with every offering, the conversation between the past and the present lives on. 🙏🚩

text:
She Ran a Restaurant. The Government Seized $32,820.56 From Her Bank Account. She Hadn’t Been Charged With a Crime.

For nearly four decades, Carole Hinders ran Mrs. Lady’s Mexican Food, a cash-only restaurant in Iowa.

To keep large amounts of cash off the premises, she regularly deposited the restaurant’s earnings into her bank account.

But in 2013, federal authorities seized $32,820.56 from that account.

Their suspicion? Her repeated deposits below $10,000 were intended to avoid mandatory bank reporting requirements.

Carole maintained that she had followed a longstanding practice of keeping deposits below that threshold to avoid additional paperwork. She had not been charged with a crime, and the government did not allege that the seized money came from illegal activity.

The seizure left her struggling to pay bills, borrow money and keep her business running.

After Carole fought back, the government dropped its forfeiture case and agreed to return her money in December 2014.

But here’s the bigger question.

If you earn your money legally, how much control do you really have over accessing it?

When your money sits in an account, you depend on the institution holding it to provide access. That relationship matters, especially when access is restricted or disputed.

Self-custody offers a different model for cryptocurrency: you control the private keys that authorize transactions rather than relying on a third party to hold them for you.

That doesn’t make your assets immune to theft, mistakes or legal action. It means taking direct responsibility for control comes with both greater independence and greater responsibility.

Carole’s story reminds us that financial freedom isn’t just about how much money you have.

It’s also about who controls your access to it.

Understand your options. Take control of your keys. Think carefully about who you trust with your money.

text:
Hermes yesterday: GitHub Copilot moved out of Hermes core and, like a good tenant, left a forwarding address. Profiles that use it get the new plugin installed on their own; only a sign-in borrowed from gh needs one command. Also: a new default model, a Stop that spares your background subagents and about a second off each start on git installs. 411 commits landed; here are the 10 that matter.

1️⃣ GitHub Copilot moves out of core into a plugin

Before: Copilot (copilot and copilot-acp) was built into Hermes, could sign in silently with your gh auth token, and on profiles that never used it a stray GH_TOKEN could still be exchanged with GitHub by status and picker refreshes. After: it lives in the github-copilot plugin from Hermes Labs (built by Nous Research, not supported), and core keeps only generic provider hooks. A profile that names Copilot anywhere (main, fallback, auxiliary, delegation, MoA or cron, or a base_url at a Copilot host) gets the plugin installed on hermes update, at start or on first use, with one notice; settings, model names and env tokens stay as they are. Other profiles have no Copilot unless they install it. Heads-up: the plugin never reads other tools' logins, so a profile whose only sign-in came from gh or the Copilot CLI's token files is told to run hermes auth add copilot. Limit: the move was tested against a stand-in of GitHub's sign-in and Copilot API, not a real Copilot account.

2️⃣ GLM-5.3 becomes the default for anyone who never picked a model

Before: with no model chosen, Hermes landed on z-ai/glm-5.2. After: it lands on z-ai/glm-5.3, its successor at about the same price on Nous Portal and OpenRouter, with the same 1M context. The choice travels in the published model catalog, which already carries it, so those installs move as their cached catalog refreshes; the built-in fallback for fresh and offline installs moves with the next release. A model you picked yourself is untouched. Known issue, still open: late in long, tool-heavy sessions, GLM-5.3 can send tool calls with arguments missing.

3️⃣ Stopping a turn no longer kills your background subagents

Before: Ctrl+C, Esc, the Stop button, an interrupting message or an ACP cancel also killed background subagents such as a running /review, and the Desktop's Stop killed processes the terminal had started in the background. After: they end only the current turn. Background subagents keep working and report back, and the Desktop leaves those processes running (regenerate, restore and edit still end them). Unchanged: /stop still ends background work, and closing or resetting a session still ends its subagents.

4️⃣ A project folder can no longer slip its own code into Hermes helpers

Before: Hermes started several helper Python processes from the folder you launched it in, and Python puts that folder first on the import path, so a project holding a package named like one of Hermes' own (hermes_cli, tui_gateway, agent, plugins) had its code run instead. That hit the TUI slash worker and command runner, the plugin-host profile read under plugins.isolation: host, setup's agent import, profile uninstall, the gateway restart watcher, the plugin validator, the Google Meet bot and the Codex tools server. After: those keep the launch folder off the import path. Not covered yet: Kanban workers (a fix is in review) and the gateway's /update and restart helpers, which need their own change; an existing Codex config picks up the fix the next time hermes codex-runtime migrate rewrites it.

5️⃣ Hermes starts about a second faster

Before: on a git install (the usual ~/.hermes/hermes-agent), every hermes command ran git's full version walk twice at startup, once for provider plugins' User-Agent headers and once for the pending-restart check. When the hourly scratch-folder cleanup was due, it waited for that too: removing one 34 GB folder held a maintainer's start for 13 s. After: the version is read only when a request needs it, so hermes sessions list went from 1.45 s to 0.44 s in the PR's test. The cleanup runs in a detached process that finishes on its own (6.74 s to 0.35 s with a 600,000-file idle folder). And Hermes keeps git's commit graph fresh after each hermes update and on hermes -w, so the version lookup itself dropped from 0.39 s to 0.05 s on a real install.

6️⃣ Kanban stops filing its work as your memories, and its wakes survive restarts

Before: Kanban worker turns reached memory providers as yours, so they filed things like work kanban task t_... and the worker's progress notes as facts about you. A Kanban wake, or a background or watch completion, that hit the gateway while it drained for a restart was lost, and one accepted just before the drain was dropped by it. After: worker turns carry the Kanban dispatcher as their author. A wake during a drain is refused so its sender retries after the restart, and one accepted before the drain still runs. Limit: memories filed by earlier runs are not rewritten.

7️⃣ Desktop: Linux windows are solid again, and typing stays light in long chats

Before: on Linux, Desktop 0.22.5 opened every window slightly see-through (opacity 0.94, so whatever sat behind it tinted the app), and the setting that could undo it is hidden on Linux. Typing in a long session also got slower the more history was loaded. After: Linux windows open fully opaque, and a profile stuck at the faded value heals on its first launch; macOS is unchanged, and on Windows 10 and Windows 11 before 22H2 an untouched profile keeps the same light tint, which Settings there can turn off. In one measured run, each keystroke cost 9.6 ms of main-thread work instead of 33.9 ms in a 300-turn session with its whole history loaded.

8️⃣ Compaction can write its summary ahead of time (opt-in)

Before: when a long session hit the compaction trigger, the turn stopped while the summary was written (an issue report cites a 184 s median pause). After: with compression.prepare_ahead: true (off by default), Hermes starts writing the next summary in the background once the session is within 12% of the trigger, so when compaction fires the summary is usually ready. Messages that arrive meanwhile stay word for word, and a rewind or changed history falls back to a normal summary. Limits: it saves time, not tokens; a summary that ends up unused still costs its tokens; and it helps most in sessions that live across turns (CLI, TUI, Desktop, messaging).

9️⃣ The browser Webapp gets a long round of fixes

Before: in the Webapp (off by default), files and media of a session running in Docker or over SSH were not looked up in that session's own sandbox or workspace, a down SSH host gave no clear error and stalled file requests on other SSH profiles, and profiles the gateway does not serve were offered as reachable and then refused every request. After: previews, media and saves use the session's own sandbox or SSH workspace, a down host gives a clear error, and unserved profiles show greyed out as Not served here. On a plain-HTTP network address, the bot screen and live voice now say they need HTTPS instead of showing raw errors, and hermes webapp and hermes webapp --status list what the browser holds back there (the bot screen, microphone and live voice, clipboard reads, the wake word, notifications) and how to keep it: HTTPS or an SSH tunnel. Sign-in got tighter too: on macOS and the BSDs, hermes webapp hands the one-use link to the browser through a page only you can read (a printed link, as with --no-open or over SSH, can still be read by other local users within its 60 s), and hermes webapp --sign-out now also signs out a browser that logged in with the password provider in the same second as a native app.

🔟 2 new plugins in the catalog: sound effects and Copilot's new home

2 new entries: ElevenLabs sound effects, an official plugin that turns a text description into a 0.5 to 30 s audio clip (optionally a seamless loop) and sends it in chat, and github-copilot, the plugin from item 1. Heads-up: every sound effect is a paid generation billed to your ElevenLabs account. Catalog entries do not wait for a release: both are already in the published catalog.

• Sound: elevenlabs-sound-effects
• Model providers: github-copilot

━━━━━━━━━━

⚙️ Meanwhile, in the engine room

Dozens of fixes landed yesterday that most users never see, and the browser Webapp took most of them: workspace files, host terminals, profiles and sign-in.

• On macOS, the gateway the Desktop starts lost access to model servers on your network (No route to host) once you quit and reopened the Desktop or it updated, because macOS Local Network Privacy stopped counting it under the app; it now runs as a one-off launchd job and keeps that access (its file-access prompts now name osascript)
• On Discord with multiplexed profiles, a user on a profile's allow_from list had guild-channel messages dropped and button clicks refused while DMs and threads worked; allow_from now covers guild channels, and an approval click in a thread gets the thread's verdict
• A messaging chat that sent /new or /resume while a Desktop or Webapp turn on its old conversation was still running could be handed back to that conversation when the turn finished, so its next message landed there; it now stays where the command put it
• hermes sessions optimize-storage now shows progress in every phase and finished a 3.6 GB test store in 1 min 25 s instead of 24 min 39 s; hermes sessions failures and unanswered confirmations now exit 1 instead of 0, so scripts stop reading them as success

If you noticed none of this, it worked.

All on main, ships in the next release; the new default model and the two catalog entries already reach installs through the published catalogs (Desktop app changes reach the Microsoft Store app with the release and the .exe and .dmg app with its next bundled release). Latest stable: v0.22.5.

text:
1988

June 5, 1988 - Jesus Who Came as the Transfuser to Wash Away Filthy Dirt

Messages of Love

Message on June 5, 1988

I had been in bed for several days because of the intense pains, not even able to go to the bathroom. When I had to move myself, several people had to help me. But, as it was the Solemnity of the Most Holy Body and Blood of Christ, I could not remain in bed all day.

Because of the pains, I prayed more fervently that the Lord wash the dirt away from my soul so that I may be more worthy as the Lord’s instrument and went to the church to meet Jesus in the Holy Sacrifice of the Mass, supported by others. In the church, I could not keep myself sitting up and had to be supported by several volunteer helpers.

It was a pain that would have been unbearable without the love of Jesus. I offered up the pain for the repentance of sinners. Soon, I entered an ecstasy and saw the Blessed Mother. She was extremely beautiful and her height was about 165 cm (5' 5"). She was holding a rosary in her right hand and was wearing a white dress and a blue mantle which stretched from her head to feet.

The hems of her mantle were sparkling gold. In her chest, there was her Immaculate Heart, red color and with fire flaming up. The Heart was penetrated by seven swords. Under her feet, there were three roses—white, red and yellow. Jesus was bleeding and a bright light was radiating from His whole Body like the sun. Above the Crucifix, there was a white dove radiating a bright light.

Julia: Jesus! Many of Your children aspire to see and come to You, but are unable to do so, because they do not know how. Please kindle the fire of love in them. I am unworthy, but will offer up my sufferings for them. Help me. Even in this, not my will but Your Will be done.

I received Holy Communion and, when I was coming back to my pew supported by the volunteer helpers, I suddenly felt my mouth becoming filled (with the Eucharist) and sensed the strong smell of blood. Then, I felt as if I were floating in the air, spinning around, and then landing on the ground. At that moment, I heard the loud voice of Jesus from the tabernacle.

JESUS: Look at Me.

I was very surprised when I looked in the direction of the voice. Jesus was there bleeding so miserably. The Blood was not falling to the ground but into the beautiful chalice and paten on the altar to be brought to us in the forms of the Eucharist and the Precious Blood. The Lord comes to us like that through priests during Mass.

The Blessed Mother was standing by Jesus. She always looks beau- tiful, and, today, looked particularly anxious and radiating light. The Blessed Mother suffers pain because of the love that Jesus pours on us, but she also rejoices because, by our receiving the Eucharist, we, sinners, become renewed and united as one.

For this reason, the Blessed Mother wants and prays that each and every one of us renounces the ego and receives the Holy Eucharist with a clean heart. Jesus spoke again.

JESUS: I am still nailed to the Cross like this and bleeding to save the whole human race, and My Blood will not flow in vain. I am the Transfuser who washes away your filthy dirt.

My Precious Blood is the special medicine that will open the eyes of the sick souls and wake up the sleeping souls through priests, but I am very troubled that they receive Me out of habit and with indifference in their hearts. I wish to pour down all My love upon all the souls on this earth. Help them participate in the Heavenly banquet. My Mother Mary has often encouraged you to make frequent confessions. But many children make perfunctory confessions or try to receive Me without going to confession, which is why I cannot transfuse My Blood into them well.
