During the 1940s and 1950s, the German colony on Mars expanded rapidly using Haunebu II craft flying from Base 211 and Argentina. By 1975, it grew into a massive, mostly underground facility named Aries Prime, composed of three interconnected bases:

▶️ Base 1: Logistics, Trade & Medical

  Serves as the primary receiving hub for food and space technology parts from Earth, fostering heavy inter-planetary traffic. It features an underground harbor capable of docking massive interstellar ships, houses 20 dedicated craft, and hosts a mixed population (100 humans, 350 hybrids, 30 ETs).

 Due to heavy galactic trade and commercial activity, it also functions as a hospitality center designed to welcome visitors from across the galaxy and offer facility tours. It uses hydroponics and underground water for food, and features a hospital with a psychiatric ward that employs advanced psionic technology—including memory implantation and removal—to keep everyone in line, suppress revolts, and maintain strict control over workers and large slave populations. Standard High German is the official language.

▶️ Base 2: Intelligence & Command Center

 Acts as the high-tech intelligence "nerve center" (similar to a combined CIA/FBI) overseeing all German Martian operations and issuing orders to the Lunar Operations Command (LOC). As of the late 1990s, it employed 400 ETs, 3,000 hybrids, and 500 humans.

▶️ Base 3: Training & Education Center

 Coordinates training and distributes orders via the Martian internet. Staffed by 350 Greys, 300 hybrids, and 75 humans, its elite trainers utilize a dedicated fleet of ships operated by 60 top pilots (humans are strictly prohibited from flying to prevent escape).

The first German expedition to Mars launched in April 1945 directly from Germany—rather than Base 211 in Antarctica—due to limited technological resources at the base and the strategic convenience of accommodating Japanese crew members already stationed at remote German facilities.

The mission utilized the Haunebu IV (a 74-meter-wide variant of the Haunebu III), powered by Andromeda tachyon electro-magnetogravitic engines and equipped with modified gun turrets and Kohler life-support converters. Because electronic automation was primitive, a massive all-volunteer crew was required to manually operate the controls. Originally envisioned as a high-risk mission, the true objective was to establish a human colony on Mars with the help of a friendly native Reptoid population.

After an eight-month journey—largely spent coasting after escaping Earth's gravity—the craft crash-landed on Mars, damaging its engines and rendering a return flight impossible. Consequently, the German Martian colony officially began in mid-January 1946.

text:
ARE WE WATCHING BRITAIN’S PAEDOPHILE GROOMING-GANG SCANDAL UNFOLD IN IRELAND — WITH THE VICTIMS BEING CHILDREN IN TUSLA CARE?

In an opinion piece in today’s Irish Mail, Brenda Power warns of a shocking child-safety scandal involving vulnerable children in State care being targeted by sexual predators while the authorities responsible for protecting them struggle to keep them safe.

Under the headline “Grooming gangs are the real threat, not grannies”, Power focuses on three cases involving teenagers in State care which recently came before High Court judge Mr Justice John Jordan. So concerned was the judge that he directed details to Children Minister Norma Foley, Justice Minister Jim O’Callaghan and Public Expenditure Minister Jack Chambers.

One case concerns a 14-year-old girl who, Power writes, was being preyed upon by organised paedophile gangs. The teenager, from a deeply troubled background, reportedly believed the men exploiting her genuinely cared about her.

Despite suffering physical symptoms associated with sexual activity with numerous men, the child was unable to recognise herself as a victim. Power argues that this illustrates the sinister nature of grooming: vulnerable children can be manipulated into interpreting exploitation as love and affection.

A second teenage girl in Tusla care was also reported as being sexually exploited by a large number of men.

The third case concerned a 16-year-old boy involved with an older criminal gang whom he regarded as friends and supporters. Gardaí had seized thousands of euro worth of drugs from him.

Power links the cases to the shortage of special-care accommodation. Despite 26 designated beds, only 15 were available. But she argues that the debate must go much further than beds.

The fundamental question is: who is sexually exploiting these children and what is being done to identify, investigate and prosecute them?

Power draws a disturbing comparison with Britain’s grooming-gang scandals, where vulnerable girls, particularly children in care, were systematically targeted by groups of men. She argues Ireland should learn from what happened there rather than wait for a comparable scandal to become fully exposed here.

She cites Irish Mail on Sunday reporting that organised criminal groups are exploiting the State’s inability to keep vulnerable children safe. Perpetrators allegedly contact children online, obtain information about residential care facilities and arrange meetings away from their placements.

Power describes children initially being offered attention, affection, money, drugs or alcohol before being passed between perpetrators and subjected to increasingly serious sexual exploitation. What may appear to be children voluntarily meeting adults can instead involve grooming, manipulation and coercion.

She strongly rejects any suggestion that children can meaningfully consent to their own exploitation. They must be recognised as victims rather than having their behaviour treated as the problem.

Power also questions whether Ireland’s in-camera rule, while essential for protecting children’s privacy, can prevent proper public scrutiny of organised exploitation.

Her broader argument is that the State risks concentrating on containing vulnerable children through secure beds and residential placements while insufficient attention is directed towards the adults allegedly exploiting them.

Ireland, Power argues, must confront the possibility that organised grooming and sexual exploitation of children in State care is already occurring here.

Her central message is stark: the vulnerable children are not the threat from which society needs protection; the adults grooming and exploiting them are.

text:
FUCK COLONIZERS

🪶 THE LIES, THE THEFT, THE KILLING — WHAT SETTLERS DID TO THE OJIBWE 🪶
Relatives — to understand Red Lake in 1907, you have to understand 100 years of planned destruction before that photo.
#### 1. THE LIE OF TREATIES — Land Grab for Pennies
The Ojibwe controlled all of northern Minnesota, Wisconsin, and Michigan — millions of acres of pine, wild rice lakes, copper, and fish. America wanted it. So they used treaties as weapons:
- 1837 Pine Tree Treaty: Minnesota Ojibwe ceded central Minnesota — millions of acres — for logging. In exchange they were promised the right to hunt, fish, and gather forever. Within months, Minnesota tried to deny those rights. State game wardens arrested Ojibwe for spearfishing — the same spearfishing you see in the canoe photo. It took until 1999 — Supreme Court case Minnesota v. Mille Lacs — to affirm they never gave up that right.
- 1854 Treaty of La Pointe & 1855 Treaty of Washington: Ojibwe were told to come to Washington in mid-winter, without knowing why. Cold, far from home, small groups signed away 2 million acres for 4 cents per acre in some bands. In the case of Bois Forte in 1866 — 2 million acres from Lake Vermilion to Canada for 4 cents per acre. Mining companies moved to Lake Vermilion in December 1865 MONTHS BEFORE the treaty was signed, claiming 3,000 acres.
- 1867 Treaty — White Earth: Engineered to concentrate ALL Ojibwe into one place — White Earth Reservation — to open valuable pine forests to logging. Individual scrip for 160 acres. Mixed-blood could only get scrip if they lived on the reservation, not transferable. That was ignored later. Timber baron Joel B. Bassett, who was the U.S. Indian Agent AND a lumber manufacturer in Minneapolis since 1850, was at the signing. He expanded his business from this treaty. By the late 1880s he was convicted of fraudulently harvesting 17,000,000 feet of timber from White Earth.
#### 2. THE KILLING — Sandy Lake Tragedy — 1850
This is the one they erased from Minnesota textbooks.
In February 1850, President Zachary Taylor ordered removal of all Lake Superior Ojibwe living on ceded lands in Wisconsin to west of the Mississippi. Minnesota Territorial Governor Alexander Ramsey and Indian Sub-agent John Watrous had a scheme: They told the Ojibwe their annuity payment — food and money owed for land already ceded — would no longer be at La Pointe (Madeline Island, their home) but at Sandy Lake, Minnesota — 285 canoe miles west — by October 25, 1850.
More than 5,500 Ojibwe journeyed there that autumn from Michigan, Wisconsin, and Minnesota. They arrived hungry after an arduous journey to find NO ONE there. No supplies. Wild game was scarce, fishing poor, wild rice wiped out for a second year.
The agent, Watrous, did not arrive until November 24 — a month late. He found many suffering and dying from meager and spoiled rations. Payment had not been authorized by Congress. He gave a small amount of provisions at high prices from local traders.
By early December, winter set in. Waterways froze. They had to abandon canoes.
On December 10, Watrous reported measles and dysentery, 150 dead. Chief Bagone-giizhig (Hole-in-the-Day) testified 4-6 people died every 24 hours. Rations were rotten — "the portion for an adult not being sufficient to fill my two hands."
On December 23, the Minnesota Chronicle and Register reported 167 Ojibwe had died at Sandy Lake from starvation and disease. According to Ojibwe leaders, another 230 died during the long, cold march home on foot in a foot of snow.
Total: About 400 dead — 12% of the people who went — mostly men, but also women, children, and elders.
Ramsey and Watrous violated federal law. They received NO punishment. Next year, they tried the same plan again. This was deliberate — an illegal plot to trap Ojibwe over winter to coerce them to move.
Out of that death came resistance — Ojibwe sent a delegation to Washington D.C. in 1852 without approval, and won permanent reservations in 1854 and 1855. The Mikwendaagoziwag ceremony today at Big Sandy Lake remembers them — "We remember them."
#### 3. THE FINAL LAND GRAB — Nelson Act & Clapp Rider — Ethnic Cleansing by Law
Nelson Act of 1889: Congressman Knute Nelson pushed it — officially "An act for the relief and civilization of the Chippewa Indians in Minnesota." Real goals: ethnic cleansing and opening forests to timber exploitation.
It mandated allotting communal Ojibwe lands to individual households and selling the "surplus" to whites. It attempted to move all Ojibwe outside Red Lake to White Earth. Red Lake agreed to cede 3,000,000 acres and kept the southern portion adjacent to Red Lake.
Result: Reservations became checkerboards. By 1902, people from nine different reservations plus 500 mixed-bloods from the Red River Valley were forced to White Earth.
Then the real theft: Clapp Rider of 1906 & Clapp Amendment: Senator Moses Clapp — Chairman of the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs and former attorney for several Minnesota lumber companies — pushed an amendment allowing any Ojibwe who claimed "mixed-blood" to sell their allotment immediately, bypassing the 25-year trust period. The law had NO definition of mixed-blood. The Supreme Court in 1914 held any degree of white ancestry was enough.
Lumber companies hired mixed-descent men to buy deeds for timbered lands at low prices from impoverished Ojibwe. They offered mortgages on timber-rich land, then foreclosed and bought land for a fraction of its worth.
Wirt Cook, a Duluth speculator, organized expeditions to select the best white pine. He paid entry men $50-$100 for each Timber and Stone patent worth $400 — worth ten times that. Charles Maginnis bought soldiers' additional homesteads from Spanish American War veterans cheap and used over 450 to patent Bois Forte lands.
The White Earth Tragedy: By 1910, three-quarters of allotments were lost. The President sent Warren Moorehead to investigate. He found whole families blinded by trachoma, tuberculosis spreading like wildfire as people lived in refugee camps. "We were almost wiped out as a people." Moorehead received death threats.
Between 1915 and 1930 most tribal members were forced off the reservation. They became the poorest people in Minnesota.
By 1983, only 54,125 acres were in tribal hands and 1,953 under allotment — 7% of the reservation. The largest landowners: federal, state, and county governments — one third.
Red Lake was the ONLY band that resisted and kept its land closed. That's why Ponemah in 1907 had no roads — they refused.
#### 4. THE EVILS THEY DON'T TALK ABOUT — Exploitation of Women
The treaty and allotment system created perfect conditions for exploitation.
Indian Agents, traders, and guardians held power over food, annuities, and whether a woman was deemed "competent" to keep her children and land. Historical records from White Earth and Red Lake agencies show:
- Marriage fraud: White men married Ojibwe women to become guardians of their estate and timber — the same pattern later used in the Osage murders. Under the Nelson Act, a white husband could control his wife's allotment. - Coercion at ration distribution: When annuities were delayed — like at Sandy Lake — women who went to agents for food for starving children were subjected to coercion and abuse. Missionary and agent correspondence from the 1860s-1890s documents widespread assault at agencies, but agents were rarely prosecuted because Ojibwe testimony was not accepted in territorial courts. - Boarding schools: Starting in the 1880s, children from Ponemah and Red Lake were taken to Morris, Pipestone, and later St. Mary's. Girls were specifically targeted for domestic labor training and suffered high rates of abuse — documented in the TRUTH Report on Minnesota boarding schools.
This was not isolated — it was systemic. When land was the goal, breaking families was the method.
He came in 1907 to photograph a vanishing race. What he found was a people who had survived government-planned starvation at Sandy Lake, who had survived having their pine stolen under the Nelson Act, who had survived having their women exploited and children taken — and were still spearfishing, still beading, still speaking.
That is why my photo is not vanishing. It is resistance.

text:
SOUTH CAROLINA — BLACK VOTERS TAKE TWICE THE HIT FROM POLLING-PLACE CLOSURES. THE STATE WON'T INTERVENE.

In Clarendon County, South Carolina, Black residents make up roughly 42% of the population. But they're bearing a disproportionate share of the disruption after local election officials closed or consolidated six polling sites ahead of the November 3 election.

According to the ACLU of South Carolina, more than 61% of the county's Black voting population is affected. Black voters are twice as likely as white voters to be caught up in the changes.

Eight precincts now share just four voting locations. Roughly one in ten voting-age residents must travel outside their precinct to cast a ballot.

The ACLU says the changes violate state law. County Democratic chair Patricia Pringle calls it deliberate voter suppression.

And the South Carolina Election Commission? It says it doesn't intend to take further action.

Who gave the board permission?

That's the question at the center of this fight.

During meetings in June and August, the Clarendon County Board of Voter Registration and Elections voted to eliminate the only polling locations serving five precincts, including Manning 1, Paxville, Panola, Sardinia-Gable and Summerton 2.

Board chairman Edward Gamble characterized the consolidations as changes in location, according to the ACLU. But the organization argues that concentrating multiple precincts into shared facilities goes beyond an ordinary relocation.

South Carolina law draws an important distinction. The General Assembly establishes precincts. Under a statute updated in 2025, Clarendon County's election board determines polling places with approval from a majority of the county's legislative delegation.

Whether that approval was obtained for these changes remains unanswered in the reporting reviewed.

That distinction matters. The board has administrative authority, but not unlimited authority. If the required approval wasn't obtained, the dispute goes beyond whether the changes were wise or fair.

It becomes a question of whether the board followed the law.

A disparity without an established motive

Pringle, who also serves as county auditor, believes the Republican-controlled board is intentionally targeting Black voters.

That accusation has not been proven.

State election official Conway Belangia has offered conventional explanations for polling-place changes: inaccessible buildings, insufficient space, staffing shortages and other logistical problems.

Those are legitimate reasons to reconsider a location. But listing possible reasons isn't the same as documenting why these particular sites were closed.

Meanwhile, the ACLU's analysis identifies a substantial racial disparity.

Consolidation can mean unfamiliar voting locations, additional travel and larger crowds sharing the same facilities. Whether those conditions ultimately reduce turnout remains unknown.

What is already measurable, according to the ACLU, is which voters are disproportionately affected.

The accountability gap

The ACLU asked the State Election Commission to intervene. The commission declined.

That leaves the disputed arrangements in place as Election Day approaches, with the ACLU considering further action.

There are still basic questions that deserve answers: Who approved the closures? What documented conditions justified them? Were voters properly notified? And why did the changes affect Black voters at twice the rate of white voters?

Clarendon County exposes something easily overlooked in voting-rights battles.

Political power isn't exercised only through legislation, district maps or disputes over who can vote. It also operates through administrative decisions about where people vote, how easily they can reach those locations and which officials are accountable for changing them.

In Clarendon County, the racial disparity is documented by the ACLU. The allegation of deliberate suppression remains unproven. And the legal basis for the closures still needs public scrutiny.

With November 3 approaching, the officials responsible for those decisions have far less time to answer for them than the voters have to adjust.

DID SAUDI ARABIA PAY $1 BILLION TO THE HOUTHIS TO STOP THE ATTACKS?

THE CLAIM. Riyadh offered the Houthis $1bn, routed through Tehran, for a ceasefire. One diplomatic source says Saudi Defence Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman (@kbsalsaud) brought the cash with him, aboard the Hercules C-130 he flew to Tehran in.

ORIGIN. Every version traces to one newspaper: Israel Hayom (@IsraelHayomEng), citing unnamed "diplomatic sources in the Gulf". A single ANI (@ANI) wire carried it to the Times of India (@timesofindia), NDTV (@ndtv), Siasat (@TheSiasatDaily), Asianet (@AsianetNewsEN), https://t.co/log8nk5rtZ and outlets in Nepal and Indonesia. Fars (@EnglishFars) carried it into Persian. Taiwan's Newtalk (@newtalk_tw) got it third hand, from an X account quoting Israel Hayom. Many headlines, one source.

WHAT IS INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED. The meeting. Saudi Arabia's foreign ministry confirms Khalid bin Salman went to Tehran with Mecca Joint Defence Alliance representatives, alongside Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin (@ikalin1) and Pakistan's Field Marshal Asim Munir, to meet President Masoud Pezeshkian (@drpezeshkian). AFP (@AFP) and Al-Monitor (@AlMonitor) report the same trip. The stated purpose was de-escalation and support for Qatari and Pakistani mediation. No money.

WHAT CUTS AGAINST IT, FROM THE SAME REPORT. A Saudi official would not confirm any transfer. And the same Israeli reporting states Riyadh's position: it will not accept a ceasefire under "military blackmail", and opposes sending funds before the Houthis return territory seized from Yemen's recognised government. An offer discussed is not a payment made, and the one article carrying the claim also records Riyadh refusing to pay.

WHY IT IS NOT ABSURD. A Saudi official said the dispute concerns understandings reached three years ago, under which Riyadh was to pay the Houthis directly for public sector salaries and reconstruction in return for quiet. The Houthis say Riyadh reneged. Saudi money going to Sanaa is an existing framework; what is new is the figure and the aircraft. Motive is not in doubt either: Houthi missiles have now reached Mecca and Medina.

THE ONE CHECKABLE DETAIL. The aeroplane. OSINT accounts have circulated a Saudi Air Force C-130H at Tehran's Mehrabad. But a separate feed attributed a 25 October Mehrabad C-130 landing to Iran's own air force, and one earlier arrival was logged with its transponder off. Military transports routinely fly dark and Iranian ADS-B coverage is thin. None of it is primary, and none of it can settle anything: tracking an aircraft proves a flight, not a cargo. There is no manifest and no unloading imagery.

WHY AN ISRAELI PAPER HAD IT FIRST. Israel is helping Saudi Arabia fight the Houthis. A defence official told the Jerusalem Post (@Jerusalem_Post) that an IDF intelligence unit passes targeting information to Saudi forces through US Central Command. Israeli reporters are therefore talking to people who know what passes between Riyadh and Sanaa, which is how Israel Hayom got this first. Being first is not the same as being right, and no second outlet has checked it.

WHERE THIS LEAVES IT. The meeting is real. The $1bn offer is possible, but it rests on one newspaper quoting sources it will not name. That any money actually changed hands is supported by nothing. Nobody in Riyadh, Tehran or Sanaa has denied the story, but it broke yesterday, so the silence proves nothing.

Jacob Allen Morley, 28, escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville late Sunday night. 

He is serving a life sentence for first-degree murder.

Surveillance video shows him breaching the perimeter fence while still in his prison uniform. Authorities say he then stole a white 2008 Ford F-350 pickup truck, Tennessee plate 138BBQV, around 1 a.m. Monday.

Morley was convicted of murdering his coworker, Cody Birchfield, whose body was found buried under Morley’s home in 2022. 

He is now on Tennessee’s Most Wanted list. 

Anyone with information is being offered $2,500 and asked to call 911 or 1-800-TBI-FIND.

text:
A 9-year-old boy was teased at school for wearing a homemade University of Tennessee shirt.
He didn’t have any official merchandise.
So for his school’s College Colors Day, he made his own.
He sketched a simple “U.T.” logo on a sheet of paper and pinned it to an orange shirt.
A few classmates laughed at him.
He came back from lunch in tears.
Then his teacher posted about it online.
The University of Tennessee noticed the post.
And rather than scroll past it, they turned his hand-drawn design into an official university T-shirt.
The response was huge.
More than 50,000 shirts were pre-ordered.
Then the university went a step further.
It offered him honorary admission to the Class of 2032, plus a four-year scholarship covering tuition and fees, if he later chooses to attend and meets the admission requirements.
He was mocked for making his own shirt.
Then thousands of people bought it.
And the university he was cheering for gave him a future to look forward to.

text:
In the summer of 1938, nearly everyone in the mountain community of Pine Ridge, Tennessee was struggling.
Jobs were scarce. Money was scarce. And for many families, food was becoming increasingly difficult to find. Yet every Saturday morning, people gathered outside the small farmhouse of Martha Collins. Martha was sixty-seven years old.

She wasn't wealthy. She didn't own much land. And she certainly didn't have extra money. What she did have was a wood-fired oven and a remarkable talent for baking bread. Each week she used flour from her own pantry, vegetables from her garden, and whatever ingredients neighbors could spare. Then she baked.
Loaf after loaf. Sometimes twenty in a day. Sometimes more.

Families who had no food often found fresh bread waiting on their porch before sunrise. Widows received deliveries. Children were never turned away hungry.
Travelers passing through town were invited to sit at her table. When people offered payment, Martha usually refused. If someone insisted, she accepted vegetables, eggs, or a promise to help another family someday.
Over time, her kitchen became a symbol of hope.
Neighbors began donating ingredients whenever they could.

Farmers brought cornmeal. Store owners contributed flour. Children helped deliver loaves across the community. One young boy later remembered asking Martha why she spent so much time baking for others.
According to his account, she smiled and replied:
"Bread rises better when it's shared."

Years later, long after the Depression had ended, residents still spoke about the woman whose oven never seemed to cool. Many forgot how much food she baked. Nobody forgot how many people she helped.
In the hardest years of the Great Depression, one elderly woman proved that kindness could feed far more than hunger.

At sixteen she was told her life was finished. At thirty-one she walked out of prison and began a different one.

Cyntoia Brown-Long was born in 1988 into circumstances that offered little protection. By her mid-teens she had been drawn into sex trafficking. 

In Nashville, at the age of sixteen, she shot and killed forty-three-year-old Johnny Allen. She maintained that she believed he was reaching for a weapon and that she acted in fear for her life. 

Prosecutors presented the killing as robbery. She was convicted of first-degree murder and sentenced to life in prison, with the possibility of parole set decades ahead.

Inside, the sentence did not remain static. She earned her GED, completed college coursework, and began mentoring younger women who faced similar histories. 

The work of rebuilding continued even while the walls stayed in place. Over time her case drew wider notice. Public figures, among them Rihanna and Kim Kardashian, joined calls for reconsideration of the sentence. 

In 2019 Tennessee Governor Bill Haslam granted her clemency. After nearly fifteen years, Brown-Long left prison at the age of thirty-one.

She did not step out of view. She has written, spoken, and advocated on the subjects of human trafficking and the treatment of juveniles in the justice system, treating her own experience as material for public argument rather than private closure. 

The girl who entered prison at sixteen had been given every institutional reason to believe the remaining years would be spent serving a single decision. 

The woman who left at thirty-one has spent the years since arguing that those earlier conditions—and the length of the punishment that followed—deserved sustained scrutiny. 

The distance between the two points is measured not only in time served but in the refusal to treat survival as the final act.

I trust that everyone knows the man is not qualified to "preach".  In fact, his use of scripture and it's application is against the very teachings of Jesus.  A receipt follows:

Evangelical and conservative Christian critics argue he's using the vocabulary and authority of the pulpit to push a political agenda they see as incompatible with Christianity — e.g., characterizing God as "nonbinary," calling Islam and Christianity "equal pathways to truth," and using Scripture to support abortion rights. 

They see the seminarian credential as a smokescreen for what they call "a press release for secular progressivism." One open letter from a longtime pastor noted that "many people understandably assume that your theological conclusions represent historic Biblical Christianity" because of his seminary status.

The entire open letter by Jeff Mullin appears below:

Dear Representative Talarico,

My name is Jeff Mullen. As a pastor who spent thirty years shepherding God's people, I have learned that what we believe about God shapes everything else. That is why I am writing this letter.

I do not write as a political opponent, but as a fellow citizen concerned about the growing confusion surrounding faith, truth, and Scripture. Because you frequently speak about Christianity, quote the Bible, and present your views as expressions of Christian conviction, I believe those claims deserve to be examined in light of God's Word.

One of my greatest concerns is that many people know you are currently pursuing a Master of Divinity degree at Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary while serving as a Texas State Representative and working toward ordination in the Presbyterian Church (USA).  As a result, many people understandably assume that your theological conclusions represent historic biblical Christianity. Your words, therefore, carry weight far beyond politics.

When theological claims are presented in the name of Christ, people naturally assume they are hearing biblical truth. My concern is that some of the positions you advocate may lead sincere people away from the clear teaching of Scripture and toward a version of Christianity that reflects the spirit of the age more than the Word of God.

Over thirty years of ministry, I have sat beside hospital beds, preached funerals, counseled struggling families, and watched countless people wrestle with questions of faith. One lesson stands above the rest: when we drift from Scripture, confusion always follows.

James warns that those who teach will be judged more strictly (James 3:1). That reality has humbled me throughout my ministry, and it should humble anyone who publicly speaks in the name of Christ.

For that reason, I offer these thoughts — not as an attack, but as a pastoral appeal for biblical clarity and faithfulness.

1. Concerning Your Statement That God Is Non-Binary

Throughout Scripture, God consistently reveals Himself as Father. Jesus taught His disciples to pray, "Our Father in heaven" (Matthew 6:9). Christ is the Son, and the Church is His Bride.

Every generation faces the temptation to reshape God according to its own values. Ancient cultures carved idols from stone. Modern cultures often carve them from ideology. Faithful Christianity begins by allowing God to define Himself rather than redefining Him according to cultural preferences. We do not improve upon divine revelation; we submit to it.

2. Concerning Your Statements About Islam and Christianity as Equal Pathways

Respect for people of different faiths is a Christian virtue. Surrendering truth is not. The suggestion that multiple religions ultimately lead to the same God stands in direct conflict with the words of Jesus Himself.

3. Concerning Your Position on Abortion

The consistent testimony of Scripture is that unborn children are known by God, created by God, and valued by God. The question is not whether the word abortion appears in the Bible. The question is whether the child in the womb is a human life bearing God's image. Scripture answers that question repeatedly and clearly. Christians have historically defended the unborn not because of politics, but because every human life belongs to God.

4. Concerning Your Call to "Decolonize" the Bible

5. Concerning Your Characterization of Jesus as a "Radical Feminist"

Yet calling Jesus a radical feminist places a modern political label on One who transcends every political movement. Jesus did not come to advance an ideology; He came to save sinners and establish the Kingdom of God. Every political movement must ultimately be measured against Christ — not Christ against a political movement.

6. Concerning Your Statements About Biological Sex

Scripture teaches that humanity was intentionally created as male and female. Genesis declares, "Male and female He created them" (Genesis 1:27), and Jesus reaffirmed that truth (Matthew 19:4). The Christian understanding of sex is rooted not in cultural tradition but in God's design. Our identity is not ultimately discovered through self-definition but through submission to the One who created us. God's design is not restrictive; it is wise and good.

7. Concerning Your Support for Same-Sex Marriage and the Reinterpretation of Biblical Sexual Ethics

These teachings are not expressions of fear or hostility. They are expressions of God's design for human flourishing. The call of discipleship is not the affirmation of every desire but the surrender of every area of life to the Lordship of Christ.

8. The Deeper Concern

The deeper concern behind these issues is the temptation to reshape Christianity so it aligns more comfortably with the values of the age. The Church has faced this pressure for two thousand years. The source changes; the temptation remains the same.

When culture becomes the lens through which we interpret Scripture, truth is eventually replaced by preference. The question for every generation is not whether the Bible aligns with the culture, but whether we are willing to align ourselves with the Bible.

Representative Talarico,

Politics is temporary. Elections are temporary. Legislative victories are temporary. Souls are not.

Scripture teaches that those who influence others bear a greater responsibility before God. James warns that teachers will be judged more strictly. Jesus warns against leading others astray. These truths should humble every pastor, teacher, author, influencer, and public servant who speaks in God's name.

For thirty years, I stood behind a pulpit knowing that one day I would answer to God for every sermon I preached and every truth I taught. The same is true for anyone who publicly speaks about faith and Scripture.

The older I get, the less interested I am in winning arguments and the more concerned I am about whether people know the truth.

My concern is not your political party.  My concern is whether the Jesus being presented to the public is the Jesus revealed in Scripture or a version reshaped by the spirit of the age.

America does not need progressive Christianity or conservative Christianity.  America needs biblical Christianity — faithful to God's Word, centered on Christ, and unafraid to proclaim truth in love.

My prayer for you is the same prayer I pray for myself: that every belief, every ambition, and every public statement would be brought under the authority of Scripture. Because one day neither of us will stand before voters, political parties, commentators, or public opinion.

We will stand before God and give an account.

Respectfully,

Jeff Mullen
Pastor Emeritus
Follower of Jesus Christ

According to the latest research from TrendForce, global data center power capacity demand is projected to reach 161 GW by 2026—an annual increase of approximately 31%—with AI servers accounting for 33.4% of this total. The firm further forecasts that the gap between power grid delivery capacity and data center demand will widen significantly after 2028, reaching a shortfall of 268 GW by 2030. Meanwhile, Gartner predicts that global data center electricity consumption will hit 565 TWh in 2026, a 26% year-over-year increase, with AI-optimized servers expected to account for 31% of that total.

This may represent a major, once-in-a-generation wealth-creation opportunity over the next decade.

Below are 8 stocks in the "AI power" sector with the potential for 10x growth or more:

1. $CEG (Constellation Energy) — The largest nuclear power plant operator in the U.S., leading in power supply contracts for data centers. With a debt-to-equity ratio of just 0.8x, it is well-suited for a conservative, stable portfolio.

2. $VST (Vistra) — An independent power producer (IPP) that sells electricity directly to AI data centers. It offers greater upside potential than traditional utilities, though it also carries a heavier debt burden.

3. $GEV (GE Vernova) — A "pick-and-shovel" play for AI-related power infrastructure, boasting a massive backlog of gas turbines and grid equipment, with an increasing share of orders coming from data center clients.

4. $OKLO (Oklo) — A developer of small modular reactors (SMRs); the market is closely monitoring the progress of its project in Groves, Texas, from groundbreaking to initial criticality.

5. $SMR (NuScale Power) — A representative player in the SMR space. Commercialization milestones have lagged behind expectations, making the finalization of power purchase agreements (PPAs) a key development to watch.

6. $ETR (Entergy) — A regulated utility serving the U.S. South, including regions with high concentrations of data centers (such as Louisiana). It offers lower volatility compared to independent power producers. 7. $VRT (Vertiv) — A core provider of power management and thermal infrastructure for data centers, benefiting from the power distribution requirements of high-density AI racks.

8. $PWR (Quanta Services) — A contractor specializing in power grid construction and maintenance; expanding transmission lines is a prerequisite for addressing the 268GW capacity gap.

Take note—completely free of charge.

**Risk Warning:** There is significant divergence within the "AI-driven power demand" narrative. Gartner projects that data center electricity consumption will exceed 1,200 TWh by 2030—a level that the power grid will be unable to meet. Furthermore, while the construction cycle for power infrastructure spans years, stock prices can sometimes price in years' worth of expectations within just a few months. Regulatory approval delays, grid interconnection queues, and bottlenecks in equipment delivery are all real-world variables that could impact the "10x potential" thesis.

text:
One of the most poignant stories about Sam Houston's final years concerns a quiet visit he made to the San Jacinto battlefield, accompanied by Jeff Hamilton, the formerly enslaved man who had served as his personal attendant for years. The story comes from Hamilton himself, and it offers a glimpse of Houston looking back on the greatest triumph of his life.

Hamilton was born enslaved in Kentucky in 1840 and brought to Texas as a child. In October 1853, when he was just thirteen, he was separated from his mother and sold at an auction in Huntsville. Sam Houston purchased him, and Hamilton subsequently became his personal attendant, traveling companion, and eventually a trusted member of the household. Hamilton remained with Houston after the latter announced the emancipation of the people he enslaved in 1862.

The battlefield visit is recounted in Hamilton's memoir, "My Master: The Inside Story of Sam Houston and His Time," originally published in 1940, which I highly recommend. Hamilton recalled that Houston instructed him to drive to San Jacinto before they returned home.

As Hamilton remembered it:
"The General didn't speak a word on the way – he was wrapped up in his own thoughts."

They eventually reached the large oak tree where Mexican general Antonio López de Santa Anna had been brought before Houston as a prisoner following the Battle of San Jacinto in April 1836.

"The General sat on the ground under the tree for a long time, never speaking to me or looking at me."

He described Houston as having a distant expression and noticed that his eyes were wet with tears.

It's a remarkable image. The man who had commanded the Texian army to victory, secured Texas independence, served as president of the Republic twice, represented Texas in the United States Senate, and governed the state was now sitting silently beneath a tree, contemplating the place where his life and the history of Texas had changed forever.

Houston died in Huntsville on July 26, 1863, with Hamilton at his bedside. Hamilton lived until April 3, 1941, dying in Belton just thirteen days before his 101st birthday.

I read Hamilton's account of this and thought that i really is an incredible scene to contemplate, isn't it? The old warrior returning to the scene of his greatest triumph, perhaps knowing that time was running out and thinking that this would be his last visit, recalling all his friends and ruminating on all that had happened to him over the course of his unparalleled life.

Shown here: Jeff Hamilton (left) and Samuel Walker Houston at the Texas Centennial Celebration in Dallas, 1936. Jeff was 96 years old when this was taken.  You can buy Jeff's book online at all the usual places.

Every robot has different capabilities, and training data needs to reflect those differences.

That’s an important part of what @PrismaXai is building.

Instead of relying only on general-purpose robotics datasets, PrismaX offers custom data collection based on the specific task, environment, and robotic hardware a team is working with.

The idea is simple: researchers define what their robot needs to learn, and PrismaX collects data designed for that use case.

This approach is particularly relevant as robotics moves beyond controlled demonstrations toward more specialized real-world applications.

PrismaX is also heading to CoRL 2026, taking place November 9–12 in Austin, Texas, where the team will be at Booth #1100.

For me, the interesting part isn’t just the conference appearance. It’s the focus on solving one of robotics’ practical bottlenecks: getting the right training data for the right hardware.

Better models matter, but the data behind them is equally important.

text:
What they did about it.

This is Humble's plan as The Oil Weekly boxed it on September 9, 1927, under the headline "Operators Accept Humble Proration Plan for Yates Field." Humble, the only crude buyer in the field, was building a trunk line to the coast and offered to take 30,000 barrels a day from October 1, no more. Its president, W. S. Farish, called the lease owners together in August.

Proration means holding every well back to its share of what can be moved or sold; here the limit was the pipelines. The box works it out. The "outlet" is 30,000 barrels plus whatever goes to storage. Item (d) names the fraction, "allowable production": the outlet divided by the field's potential. Item (e) lets each lease run its own potential times that fraction. Item 7, one producing well per 40 acres near producing wells, did not survive to the signed agreement.

Eighteen companies signed. Gulf did not. A committee under W. A. Moncrief of Marland ran it, with a field man, B. C. Clardy. The small photo is Clardy, in a fedora and a dark coat, one hand in his pocket, in front of a frame house. The caption says he "tells them how much they can run each day. He is umpire in charge of proration."

It was field-wide, it was voluntary, and it was voluntary because it had to be. Texas antitrust law was read as "not permitting limitation of production, storage or marketing by agreement." So they did not limit production, on paper. They shared the outlet, and pinched the wells in to match: each lease's wells choked back to the lease's share.

🧵12/18

Credit: The Oil Weekly, September 9, 1927, p. 27; Internet Archive; public domain. Second image: The Oil and Gas Journal, December 22, 1927, p. 23; Internet Archive; public domain. The Texas-law quotation is from National Petroleum News, September 14, 1927, p. 22.

text:
Anduril and Qualcomm are moving into a corner of the PC market where durability, component provenance, and government purchasing rules can matter more than weight or consumer-friendly pricing. Their planned BlueChip product line will begin with a hardened laptop designed for military personnel, government agencies, first responders, and law-enforcement users.

Orders are expected to open in 2027. Although Anduril has not released a complete specification sheet or final price, the initial model is being built to withstand rain, dust, and demanding field conditions. Rugged construction comes with familiar compromises. BlueChip is expected to be heavier and offer less battery life than mainstream business laptops such as Dell systems or Microsoft Surface devices.

The more consequential element is inside the chassis. According to TechCrunch, more than 90% of the prototype's component value reportedly comes from suppliers in the United States or allied countries. Anduril's longer-term objective is an option with a fully domestic supply chain, extending beyond final assembly to displays, metals, magnetic components, and other parts.

That is an ambitious target. Modern laptop manufacturing depends on a highly distributed supplier network developed over decades, particularly across Asia. Anduril's founder acknowledged that some components, including the display itself, are currently available only from China, even when related parts such as display glass can be sourced in the United States.

text:
I am Sophia, 32. I restore historic hotels for a living. I fix broken things, reinforce crumbling foundations, bring forgotten beauty back to life.

This was the seventh night in a row I had cooked a full dinner. Seven nights sitting alone in the dark waiting for a family that was never going to arrive.

My parents and my younger sister Hannah flew from Chicago to California. Not to see me. To spend my money.

Every night around 6 p.m., the same text.

"Traffic is crazy, sweetie. Maybe tomorrow!"

"Hannah wanted to see the sunset at the pier, we'll catch you later!"

I stared at the congealing fat on the roast.

For six years I had been the pillar holding up their entire life. When Dad's business struggled, I quietly paid their Chicago mortgage to stop foreclosure. When Mom needed out-of-network meds, I paid the pharmacy directly. Hannah, the golden child, 25, influencer, never held a job more than three months, constantly needed "childcare emergencies" for a dog she couldn't afford or "car trouble."

I tracked it all in an encrypted spreadsheet.

Total: $62,840.

I bled myself dry working 80-hour weeks on scaffolding, breathing plaster dust, to buy a fraction of their love. And they couldn't drive 30 miles to eat pie.

My phone lit up on the linen.

Two notifications.

First: Instagram. Hannah posted. My parents and Hannah clinking huge glasses of white wine on a sun-drenched oceanfront deck. Sunset orange and violet behind them.

Caption: "Best family week ever! #Blessed #OceanViews #LivingOurBestLife"

No mention of me. Thirty miles away. They weren't just ignoring me. They were celebrating my absence.

Second notification: High-priority fraud alert from my bank.

PENDING CHARGE FLAGGED FOR REVIEW: $4,500. Merchant: Oceanview Luxury Rentals.

My heart stopped. I tapped details. The charge was made using my stored credit card - the one I saved on my mom's laptop two years ago to pay a medical bill.

Dad had said weeks ago they "found a great deal" on a beach rental. He lied. They just stole my card, assuming I was too stupid to notice or too desperate to confront them.

I stared at the screen. $4,500 glaring back.

Something inside me snapped. Not loudly. Structurally.

The heartbroken daughter who kept trying to repair the cracks died in that dining room. The restorer took over.

I stopped seeing them as a broken foundation to save. I saw them as a condemned building to demolish.

My hand stopped shaking. I selected the charge and pressed 'Report as Stolen.'

Charge disputed. Card frozen pending fraud investigation.

I stood up, methodical. Walked to the kitchen, grabbed a heavy-duty trash bag, came back. I swept the entire untouched tenderloin straight off the platter into the garbage. Carrots, potatoes after it. Picked up the lemon meringue pie and dropped it onto the meat. The glass dome shattered in the sink.

I tied the bag shut as my phone started ringing. Loud. Frantic.

Hannah.

I let it ring three times, then answered on speaker.

"Hello?" I said, even.

"Sophia! What the hell is wrong with your card?!" she shrieked. "The rental agent is right here! They're threatening to call police because payment bounced! We're standing in the lobby with all our luggage! Fix it right now! Mom is having a panic attack!"

In the background, Dad's booming voice: "I told you she was incompetent, Hannah! Tell her to authorize the damn transaction!"

They stole from me and were mad at me for the inconvenience.

"You used my card without authorization, Hannah," I said flatly. "That's why the bank flagged it. Because it was stolen."

"Oh my god, Soph, get over yourself! We're family! Dad said you offered to help! It's not stealing if it's family! Just call fraud and give them the pin so we can get our keys! You're ruining our last day!"

text:
S&P Dow Jones Indices and Kalshi are joining forces to build the next generation of financial markets.

The Dow launched in 1896. The S&P 500 in 1957. The idea was simple: bring individual stocks together into a single benchmark, giving people a clearer view of the broader market.

Over time, products built around those benchmarks transformed investing. Index funds, ETFs, futures, and options gave investors ways to gain diversified market exposure and hedge broad market swings.

These indices became foundations of global finance. More than $20 trillion is indexed or benchmarked to the S&P 500 alone.

Today, this structure extends beyond stocks to bonds, commodities, currencies, and more.

The next step is to bring that structure to the events that shape everyone’s lives.

Through this partnership, S&P Dow Jones Indices and Kalshi will work together to create indices composed of Kalshi event contracts.

Think about what that opens up.

An index of political power. An index of supply chain risk. An index tracking AI’s impact on employment. An index of sports outcomes that affect broadcasters, advertisers, cities, and small businesses. An index of weather risks that shape harvests, energy demand, and business revenues.

Each would bundle event contracts into a single indicator, helping people understand how related risks are evolving.

Over time, products built around these indices could offer diversified exposure to those events and new ways to hedge their impact.

The events that shape our lives could become as easy to track and gain exposure to as the S&P 500.

text:
Microsoft just offered buyouts to 60,000 employees. Olympia's big idea for this moment? A brand-new income tax.

On Monday, Microsoft offered "voluntary exit" packages to about 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its 223,000-person global workforce. These are offers, not departures. Microsoft itself expects only 3-5% to take them, and it ties its cost-cutting to AI spending and restructuring, not to Washington's tax code.

But it isn't happening in a vacuum.

Microsoft filed two WARN layoff notices with the state this year: 605 Washington jobs in July, 277 more in September. That's 882.

Big Tech WARN notices filed in Washington in 2026:
• Amazon: 2,777
• Meta: 1,894
• Microsoft: 882
• Oracle: 834

6,387 Washington workers from four companies. In ten months.

Seattle-Bellevue-Kent information-sector jobs: 127,100 in Sept. 2025. 125,800 in Sept. 2026 (BLS).

And employers? In AWB's spring survey, 24% of Washington employers said they're considering moving their business out of state. 38% plan to expand in another state. Just 9% plan to expand here.

Totally normal. Nothing to see here.

So what's actually on your ballot?

I-645 does three things:
1. Repeals the 9.9% tax on individual income over $1 million that the Legislature passed this year, before it ever takes effect in 2028.
2. Bans state AND local taxes on individual income, or "measured by" it.
3. Defines "income" in law, so calling it an "excise tax" doesn't get around the ban.

"Relax, it's only millionaires."

Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen, the tax's chief sponsor, has said he personally favors a broader-based income tax and that down the road the Legislature could look at lowering the $1 million threshold. One Democratic state rep has said she could support extending it to households earning $250,000, at a lower rate.

Funny how "just the rich" never stays just the rich.

Who's paying to keep it? No on 645 has raised $12.8 million. About $11.4 million of that, roughly 89%, came from unions, per PDC filings compiled by FactHub. The Yes side: $2.21 million.

Yes, the state's fiscal note says I-645 means $11.4 billion less in projected revenue through 2031. Projected. From a tax that doesn't start until 2028 and hasn't collected a dime.

Washington's tech economy is not invincible. When the biggest employer in your backyard is offering exits to a quarter of its workforce, the answer is not a new tax its own sponsor is already talking about expanding.

Vote YES on I-645.

text:
Accessing a world-class education from one of the globe's most elite academic institutions no longer requires surviving a highly selective admissions process. 

Through its pioneering MIT OpenCourseWare (OCW) platform, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology has systematically digitized and published the instructional materials for more than 2,500 courses. This expansive digital archive spans virtually the entirety of the university's undergraduate and graduate curricula. This enables independent scholars, professional developers, and curious intellects anywhere on Earth to utilize these premium materials without incurring any financial burden, navigating an application process, or committing to formal student registration.

The depth of the available resources depends heavily on the specific subject matter, but the repository routinely provides comprehensive lecture notes, authentic homework assignments, past examinations, curated syllabus reading lists, open-textbook access, and high-definition video recordings of actual classroom lectures. By opening these digital vaults, MIT provides unrestricted access to foundational coursework across a broad array of disciplines, including advanced computer science, mechanical engineering, theoretical mathematics, quantitative business economics, and the humanities. This initiative transforms what was once exclusive institutional knowledge into a global public good.

However, users must understand the critical operational distinctions between independent open-learning and formal university enrollment. The OpenCourseWare platform functions strictly as a self-directed reference archive rather than an interactive, instructor-led classroom environment. Because participants study entirely at their own pace without faculty evaluation, the platform does not award traditional academic credits, official course grades, verified certificates of completion, or formal university degrees. Despite the lack of institutional credentials, the initiative offers an extraordinary, unprecedented opportunity to master complex academic subjects using the exact materials designed by leading professors at a premier global research institution.
