text:
Michelle Singletary: "this is dollars and cents with michelle singletary. and i'm michelle singletary. we're at a point in history where money, how we make it and how we spend it, is rapidly changing. some of the traditional ways of handling our finances are outdated, unsustainable, or just plain out of touch. but there is tried and true financial advice that still makes sense. that's why i'm here to help you make sense out of your dollars. some episodes i'll speak about money with everyday people, and other times, including today, we'll hear from an expert. today's guest is lauryn williams, a four-time olympian who medaled in relay racing and bobsledding. now she's the coach, but in a completely different field. lauryn is a financial planner who draws on her experience as a competitive athlete to help young professionals build a strong foundation for lasting success. she also offers actionable advice in her book, a four-time olympian's guide to professional track and field. i wanted to know more about how lauryn's unique career path shapes the advice she gives and what she's hearing from her young clients about the economic landscape. so lauryn, i am super excited that you're here. so if you don't mind, let's just go back in time. you won your first olympic medal in 2004. tell me about your athletic career from that point."

Lauryn Williams: "yeah, i've had a really nice life. so 2003, i was a sophomore in college and i made it to the national championships. and i was kind of middle of the pack. and i was like, gosh, i made it here, but i've beat a lot of these girls before. so my junior year in college, 2004, the only thing i wanted to do was win the ncaa title. i had no thoughts or possibilities in my mind of going to the olympic games when i thought of it. it was just win the ncaa title. well, when i set a goal, i just knocked it out of the park. i ran the second fastest time in the world at the national championships and won, and immediately became america's olympic hopeful for the 2004 games. and so that's where my career started."

Michelle Singletary: "i love it. i really just admire you, 'cause i am not an athlete. i tripped going across the floor. i was the person that they picked last when they were picking teams, and it hurt my little feelings. so just anybody who can do that, i just have such admiration for you. so now i'm going to get up in your business."

Lauryn Williams: "come on, bring it. i'm an open book."

Michelle Singletary: "oh, good, good, good. i love it when people say that. so people might think, you were an athlete, so you're an olympic medalist, a national championship, so you must be rich. you must be financially set. were you?"

Lauryn Williams: "girl, i am rolling in all the dough, all the dough. i make it rain. i wipe my behind with dollar bills in the morning. all of that, no, that is not true at all. so my very long story short, there were many financial hangups that i had during the course of my career. but the first was choosing a financial advisor. so at 20 years old, like i said, i became a professional athlete. i left my eligibility in college, which nowadays it's different. they have this nil thing. athletes can earn money in college, but at that time i had to give up eligibility to become a professional athlete. i knew enough to know, as a junior in college, as a finance major, that i didn't know enough to do anything on my own. and this is when personal finance wasn't a major. it was just general, broad finance. so i had a lot to learn. a family friend introduced me to a financial advisor. i didn't know that all advisors are not created equally. some don't have your best interest at heart. and i ended up in the hands of somebody who didn't teach me a whole lot about financial literacy, didn't really understand what was happening in my financial life at 20 years old or where i came from. so i am one of eight children. i have five sisters and two brothers. there was not a lot of income. my dad had leukemia growing up. he was on disability. so there wasn't a lot of earnings coming in. and so we did a lot of making it work, making a dollar out of 15 cents, if you will. and there just wasn't a way for me to know or understand what to do when i started earning $200,000 a year at 20 years old. and so mistakes were made. lots of mistakes were made, michelle."

Michelle Singletary: "what do you think was the biggest mistake? because people think you just hired a person and you set it and forget it. what didn't happen that should have happened?"

Lauryn Williams: "yeah, i'd say the first mistake is not understanding, like i said, what the advisor's job was to do, and not understanding what i needed. and so, like i said, i didn't know that i was financially illiterate. i knew i didn't know a lot about money, but i didn't know how dangerous it was to not have somebody who was gonna guide me, who was not focused on my literacy. so the guy that i hired was focused on investment management. he earned a commission for everything that he invested on my behalf. and so my budget didn't matter to him. whether or not i had debt, when i went to buy a home, he was like, sure, go ahead. i did always call and ask him, but i really needed somebody to look and analyze. and i think that's the difference in what a certified financial planner does, or how they're taught to do, is think about how much house can you afford? what does it look like to pay this mortgage for 30 years? because we all know that most professional athletes are not gonna have a career of 30 years. so i'm earning $200,000 at 20. it's a great living for a 20-year-old, but what kind of house can i afford? and will i be earning $200,000 a year 10 years from now? i probably should have bought less house. so i bought two homes."

Michelle Singletary: "two."

Lauryn Williams: "two. i'm telling you, girl, mistakes were made. mistakes were made."

Michelle Singletary: "so why did you buy two homes?"

Lauryn Williams: "i bought one in 2004, thinking, okay, this is a good place to start. and immediately felt like i was outgrowing that home. around the corner from my house, literally walking distance, there was a bigger, nicer home, and i wanted to move in that home. my mom moved shortly after to florida to follow behind and help me with some things. and i let my mom stay in the smaller house, and then i bought the bigger house. and this is, like you said, 2004, 2006 with the second purchase. you know what happened to the market, right?"

Michelle Singletary: "i do know. wow."

Lauryn Williams: "and so within a year or so of me buying these homes, one of them, i was completely upside down in it. there was no way that i could offload it for what i purchased it for. i had a $4,500 a month mortgage. like i said, 30 years, i was about to pay that mortgage."

Michelle Singletary: "can we just pause for just a second? 'cause my heart flooded. wow, $4,500 a month. wow. at 21, 22 years old, something like that."

Lauryn Williams: "exactly. and like i said, the advisor didn't help me understand that, hey, you probably won't be able to, before this long term, you don't need a second home. the smaller home that you're in is just fine. but like i said, you're looking at the money that's coming in. you see how well you're doing in the moment, and everyone tells you, of course real estate's the best thing. everything will be fine."

Michelle Singletary: "that's what they say."

Lauryn Williams: "that's what they say. they, i don't know who they is."

Michelle Singletary: "who is they? who is they? i wanna slap they."

Lauryn Williams: "i know, all the time i wanna slap they."

Michelle Singletary: "so you had two mortgages. the one was $4,500. what was the other mortgage? who was, your mom, taking care of that mortgage?"

Lauryn Williams: "it was about $2,000 a month, and my mom and then some other people moved in. i was covering some, but other people were paying rent, and it was kind of getting covered, if you will."

Michelle Singletary: "yeah."

Lauryn Williams: "yeah, but then my mom ended up moving out, and so then i was back on the hook for that mortgage. i had to put renters in that house. it was a mess. but the very long story short there, because like i said, i got so many stories, we could talk for three, four hours."

Michelle Singletary: "i would love it, but you don't have that much time."

Lauryn Williams: "you don't have that much time. in 2017 — i bought the house, like i said, in 2006 — in 2017 i was still upside down in that house. and i sold it right at the beginning of the pandemic and was still upside down in that house."

Michelle Singletary: "wow."

Lauryn Williams: "yeah, that's how bad that was as a purchase that i made. and so yeah, you learn from these different mistakes. you become better because of them. i think one of the biggest pieces of the puzzle, like you said, the original question was, oh, you're an olympian, you're rich, right? and it's like, i made a good living. i could have been in a better financial situation when i retired from sport than i was in. i feel like i basically started from scratch at the point that i realized i had all these different things that i couldn't afford. but i did rebuild. and i feel like i'm financially stable now. i make my decisions based on what long-term me wants to accomplish in life. and i don't know that i would be where i am today if i hadn't made those mistakes, but i do also wish that i had some proper guidance along the way so i didn't have to make such expensive mistakes."

Michelle Singletary: "so what was your biggest financial concern when you were a competitive athlete? and then if i could follow up with that, did your teammates and colleagues have similar concerns?"

Lauryn Williams: "i don't think my teammates or colleagues had the same concern. my concern was always kind of catastrophizing, if you will. like, what happens if i fall down and break my leg? i realized that this money could go away at any point. so my first contract with nike was five years. and then i did a second contract with a company called saucony for four years. and that kind of took me through my whole track and field career. but i knew there were reductions. if you didn't perform, you could be reduced. i knew that, like i said, if your season was ended, there was no prize money coming, because you couldn't compete in each race where you would earn the prize money. and so i was always wondering about that. and one of the things my parents told me was so important was education. and i honestly got to the university of miami on that track scholarship. and i was so grateful to my coach for the opportunity to get the education that i felt like i needed to repay her by working hard at track. track was not the goal or the mission or the vision for me. it wasn't to become an olympian initially. that was the thing that kind of fell into my lap as i worked hard to be able to repay her, because i was thinking, okay, i got to be smart. i got to get an education, because the education is the way that you make money."

Michelle Singletary: "yeah. so just for people who don't understand, 'cause i don't understand, when you have these contracts with these major retailers like nike, is it you get money for the five years no matter what, or there's some, along the way, is there a point, like you said, if you get injured, you can't wear the sneakers no more. i mean, how does that work?"

Lauryn Williams: "yes, you can be cut. so in olympic sports, you usually have a sponsor. so like i said, nfl, nba, you're paid by the nfl, nba. you're a w-2 employee of that company. and then you get the sponsorships on top of that. for olympic sports, the sponsorship is the income. the united states olympic committee, usa track and field, i was never an employee of either of those. those were just the umbrella under which i competed. and so nike was my main source of income, and then the olympic year would come and maybe a small company would come in here or there and i would get some extra dollars in because of that. and so nike gave me, like i said, a four-year deal. they paid me annually. if you were not in the top 10, you could be reduced. if you're not in the top five, you could be reduced a certain amount. if you did not compete in enough races, i think it was like a five-race minimum per year that you had to compete in. there were certain races that were completely, like a nike-specific race on this day or this time, you had to be at those or you could be docked for that as well. but there were also incentives, of course. so if you won an olympic medal, you got an extra $100,000 added to your base salary for the following year, in addition to a $100,000 bonus, as an example. so there were some good things in there as well, but there were definitely things to make sure that if you don't perform, that you're not just collecting a paycheck sitting around saying that you worked for said shoe company."

Michelle Singletary: "right, right. that's so interesting. was there ever any financial coaching available to athletes?"

Lauryn Williams: "in my day, no. i am that person now. i do a lot of talking. we do webinars at the united states olympic committee. we created some programs and things through usa track and field at one point in time. but most of that even is kind of something that's hit or miss. sometimes they want to hire you. they don't want to spend the extra money on pieces of the puzzle like that. no, there was no financial coaching for me at the time that i was competing. and there was no advice on, like i said, even how to choose a financial advisor, outside of them providing some coaching directly to me."

Michelle Singletary: "did you, i'm just curious, did the athletes ever talk to each other about what they were doing with their money, or giving you advice, or vice versa? how, in the locker rooms, as you're heading to the starting line, did you go, hey girl, did you invest in x?"

Lauryn Williams: "no, we were also not having those conversations. and i think that is a real mindset shift that has happened in this generation of athletes, is that those conversations are being had, even if they don't fully understand what they mean or what they need to be looking into. i think that people are a lot more open about their money and trying to figure out what they should be doing. we were not having those conversations at all. when those conversations started, i was toward the end of my career. i decided to look for, like i said, a different financial advisor, and then that didn't work out. so i had a second financial advisor, actually, to kind of round this story out. that advisor worked with professional athletes, but also didn't care for me well. i thought that that would go better because they had other, they had big-time nfl players and stuff as part of their book of business. they ended up investing a bunch of nfl players' money in a casino. the casino never opened, and they all lost 100% of their money."

Michelle Singletary: "wow."

Lauryn Williams: "and so that advisor kind of closed shop in the middle of the night and snuck out of town. it was just a big mess."

Michelle Singletary: "oh, that's terrible. my gosh. you know what i love about your story is, and i think when i'm doing this show, i always sort of like to pause and say, this is a teaching moment, y'all. so what lauryn is saying, she's not saying don't trust any financial planner, because she is one herself and finally found someone who was interested in her. but you've got to do your due diligence. you gotta listen and see what they tell you. and that's what i really love, the fact that you are a financial planner now, 'cause i had similar experiences. the first planner we ever hired, my husband and i, girl, all he did was take, we had investments here, he moved it here, same investments, and made money off the same, i mean, literally the same investments. i was like, i just paid you $1,800. you just moved something from one hand to the other. i was hot. i was hot, girl."

Lauryn Williams: "and the fees that you can't see. oh my goodness, right."

Michelle Singletary: "it almost turned me off from the business, i have to tell you. like you, i didn't come from a family that had any money. we didn't know what a financial planner was. nobody hired. it didn't even make no sense that you hire somebody to help you make money. you gotta pay them to help you make money. that doesn't sound any sense. but fortunately for me, we landed on another planner who did exactly what she said. she listened to us. she knew us. she looked at everything. and i still have her plan from like 20 years ago. it's about this thick. and we went and did everything she said. and my husband and i are doing quite well for ourselves, put our kids through college with no debt, because of that financial planner. so what i love is that you might get some duds. hopefully you don't get a dud, but if you do, don't get turned off from the industry, because there's some people out there who will care about you."

Lauryn Williams: "absolutely. and i think that's a key thing i always like to drive home, is how to not end up in the hands of a dud. obviously, nobody can make 100% guarantees, but that due diligence is important. and for me, i'm never recommending anyone that is not a certified financial planner, that is fee-only, and is a fiduciary. if you can get all three of those things, then you've limited the possibility that they are going to be a dud drastically, in my opinion."

Michelle Singletary: "now you use that word fiduciary. it is another one of my little teaching moments. so what does that mean? 'cause that's a big word. and i know somebody might be listening going, i don't know what that means. and it's okay that you don't know what it means, but what does that mean?"

Lauryn Williams: "exactly. it took me a while to figure it out. and so it means that the person that is working with you legally needs to do what is in your best interest. and it's crazy to me that in the financial industry, we have people who do not have to be a fiduciary. they do not have to do what's in your best interest. you're like, wait, what? the alternative to being a fiduciary is doing what is suitable for a client. so this million dollars of life insurance that i'm gonna earn the next 18 months of the premium on is suitable for you, michelle. but this million-dollar policy would cost you half as much, and it's not gonna earn me as much, but it's also suitable for you. i'm gonna sell you this because it's suitable. a fiduciary would say, hey, this one that is more cost-effective for you is the one that i'm gonna sell you. being legally obligated to do what is in the client's best interest is what a fiduciary is."

Michelle Singletary: "so the thing that you say is, hey, are you required to do what's in my best interest? just ask that line."

Lauryn Williams: "exactly, exactly. it's like, you can't remember the fancy fiduciary word. it's simple to remember. hey, i want you to be on my side. are you legally obligated to do what's in my best interest?"

Michelle Singletary: "what is something you wish you knew when starting your athletic career?"

Lauryn Williams: "something i wish i knew during my athletic career is, your days are numbered here on planet earth. your days are also numbered as an athlete. you want to be setting yourself up now so that your future self is thanking you and not wanting to slap you in the face. and i think if someone would have framed it like that for me, you're 20, but someday you will be 40. someday you will be 60. someday you will be fill in the blank. and you really need to start thinking about that person today, because that matters."

Michelle Singletary: "that's such great advice. so you were the first american woman to win a medal in both the summer and winter olympic games. clearly you had an incredibly successful career as an athlete. when did you pivot to finance?"

Lauryn Williams: "i pivoted to finance after the second bad financial advisor. so i had one bad experience, found another guy, had a second bad experience, and a good old-fashioned google search led me to trying to figure out, how do i handle my finances on my own? and i stumbled upon the certified financial planning coursework, not knowing that it was a different part of the industry, not really understanding what the certification meant. just having read the summary and said, this is more what i was hoping to get from the advisors, what they're saying they teach in this course. and so i blindly enrolled in it, trying to teach myself about finances, not trying to become a financial advisor."

Michelle Singletary: "you are a go-getter. i love you, girl. you just like, i'm gonna learn myself."

Lauryn Williams: "that's it. like you said, anything you could do, i could do better. and i was like, at that point i'd had these two advisors. i'm like, i could definitely do this better than y'all. and so i started to learn things about personal finance, like i said, through the certified financial planning coursework. but i also started to ask my friends. and that was one of the things you were alluding to earlier, were you guys talking about it? it was the first time that i felt comfortable talking to my friends about it, because i was like, oh, i just read about a 401(k). do you have a 401(k)? i have this thing called a sep ira, and so somebody had set that up for me, but i didn't know how it worked. i was reading about how it worked in the book, because two financial advisors, nobody took the time to explain that to me. and so i'm like, well, maybe you have a sep ira. and i started to ask my friends questions, and i realized that i was not the only person that was ignorant about my finances. some of them would tell me, girl, my people handle that. other people would be like, no, i don't have any of that. i don't have anything. and it would be a conversation, and i was like, oh, there's a real need for this in the athletic community. there's a real need for us to understand our finances as well, as opposed to just earning this money and going out and spending it."

Michelle Singletary: "yeah. and that line where people say, my people handle that, even with people handling that, you need to know, right?"

Lauryn Williams: "exactly. and what i always said to my clients, even in my prospective client meetings, i said, my goal for you is that by working with me, you're at brunch with your girlfriends and you're like, i have a financial planner and this is our plan. and you can sit there and you can articulate what it is that is happening in your finances without telling them how much money you make or how much money you got saved. because so many people get so kind of paralyzed thinking about the numbers. like, oh my goodness, what if they ask me how much money i make? it doesn't matter. you shouldn't be ashamed to say those numbers either, because nobody can take the money out of your pocket or directly out of your bank account. but you, at the bare minimum, without having to say any numbers, should be able to describe what your plan is for people."

Michelle Singletary: "yeah, i love that. know what's going on, know what you don't know, and know what you need to know, basically."

Lauryn Williams: "exactly."

Michelle Singletary: "was there a specific moment that you recall feeling like this was your next chapter?"

Lauryn Williams: "yes. i was in switzerland talking to a fellow athlete, and i had asked him. he had earned quite a bit more than me. he was the same event, but had done much better. and so i knew he was earning more, because males and females were not earning the same. and like i said, he had performed better. so i was like, he's probably earned at least double, if not triple, what i've earned during his career. and i hope that he set himself up well. and i asked him a series of questions which he knew none of the answers to. and i was just like, i need to be able to help. this is somebody that i care about. this is somebody i know. this is the chance for generational wealth to be starting to be built amongst the african-american community. and at that time is when i started to realize, i didn't know those terms. i didn't know generational wealth and things like that. but i was just like, he has such a great earning opportunity. and i don't think he was a big spender, but he had no clue what to do with his finances. and i'm like, this is the kind of person that i would want to be able to help, because he deserves to have money to be able to pass down from generation to generation."

text:
SIGNAL INTELLIGENCE BRIEF
Published: October 27, 2026 | 10:55 AM ET

Thesis:
The S&P 500 has turned positive over four weeks, yet wider credit spreads, bond volatility on the 100 line and a technology sector still falling say the growth worry has not gone away.

WHAT MATTERS
The S&P 500 is up 0.29% this morning and up 0.52% over four weeks, but the Nasdaq 100 is down 2.57% and the equal-weight version of the index is up 3.90%. The headline index tells you little about how the typical stock is doing. Two gauges say more. High-yield credit spreads, the extra yield that riskier companies pay over government bonds, were 338bps on October 23, 30bps wider (+30bps 4wk) and well above their 12-month average of 288bps. Wider spreads mean lenders want more pay for risk. The MOVE index, which measures how much traders expect Treasury yields to swing, is 100.34. It has eased 6.26 points over four weeks, but a reading at 100 still means the bond market is unsettled. The stock index is rising and these two gauges are not relaxed, and the gauges have usually been the earlier signal.

WHAT IS HIDDEN
A long-term bond yield has three parts: expected inflation, the real return investors want after inflation, and a term premium, the extra pay for locking money up for many years. The 10-year yield is 5.00%. Expected inflation, read from the gap between ordinary and inflation-protected Treasuries, is 2.34% and unchanged over four weeks. The real yield is 2.66%, down 17bps over four weeks (October 23 reading). So the long end is not rising on inflation fear. It stays high because the real cost of money is high, and it is easing because growth is being priced lower. 

Bond volatility explains the rest. The MOVE index runs 5.67 times the VIX, and that ratio has come down 0.97 over four weeks, so stock volatility is catching up with bond volatility. Liquidity offers some cushion. The Treasury's cash balance was $982.5bn on October 23, higher over four weeks (+37.2bn 4wk). A larger Treasury balance pulls cash out of the banking system, and the reverse repo facility, the usual buffer, holds only $0.2bn, so there is little spare cash to absorb it. Overnight funding is steady, with the secured overnight rate at 3.93%. Other plumbing data has not moved: no new 10-year or 30-year auction since October 8, no new dealer inventory or repo data since October 14, no new Treasury bill share reading since September 30, no new foreign-holdings share since August 2026, and no new reading on Treasuries held at the Fed for foreign central banks since October 21. In our cross-asset basket (stocks, bonds, gold and others), 0/6 assets are down more than 1% today.

WHAT IS MISPRICED
Leadership is the mispricing. Over four weeks the leader is Energy +11.25% and the laggard Communication Services -6.37%. Utilities are up 8.0% and consumer staples 7.3%, while technology is down 3.2%. Defensive sectors are up 6.9% against 3.5% for cyclicals. A market led by oil producers and defensive shelters does not look like one confident in growth, and the index is only holding up because the typical stock is rising. Gold is also not doing its job. At $4,061.80 it is down 2.90% over four weeks even though real yields fell 17bps (October 23 reading) and oil climbed. A fresh flight to safety would show gold rising as credit widens, and gold fell.

WHAT MARKETS DISAGREE ON
Oil and bonds tell different stories. Brent is up 13.33% over four weeks, which argues for inflation. Breakevens at 2.34% are flat, real yields are lower, credit is wider and the curve is positive, which argues for a growth scare. In our read the evidence favours the growth-scare side, although only half of the cross-checks line up, so this is a lean and not a verdict. Equities add a third voice. FactSet's update dated October 23 has 24% of companies reported, 83% of them beating profit estimates and earnings growth above 25%. That supports the index, while technology, small companies and stock-fund outflows say the gains are narrow. Households disagree with the market again. The University of Michigan October survey has them expecting 4.7% inflation over the coming year and 3.5% over five to ten years, against a market breakeven of 2.34%. If households are right, the Fed has little room to ease.

WHAT TO WATCH NEXT
The stress signal is high-yield spreads widening past 50bps over four weeks, from 30bps at the October 23 reading, with MOVE moving back above its current 100.34 and technology still falling. That would show pressure moving from stocks into credit. The relief signal is the Nasdaq 100 and the Russell 2000 catching up with the equal-weight index while spreads narrow. The live event risk is Iran. Reporting dated October 27 has US Central Command saying US forces remain in the strait, while Iran's president calls the blockade unilateral sanctions and warns that attacks on Iranian energy facilities would threaten global security. Brent would move first on any verified reopening.

text:
How much do you need to earn to afford the typical home for sale? Nationally, it’s about $44.86 an hour.

That’s from an affordability chart by R.J. Weiss at The Ways to Wealth. He took each state’s median listing price for August, assumed 20% down and a 30-year mortgage at 7.32%, which was Freddie Mac’s average last week, and kept the payment to 30% of gross pay for a full-time worker. The math checks out.

Here in Colorado, it takes $60.12 an hour. That’s about $125,000 a year to buy a median-priced home listed around $569,000. At the top are Hawaii at $77.78, California at $77.15 and Massachusetts at $76.62. At the low end are West Virginia at $27.47, Louisiana at $29.06 and Ohio at $30.54.

And that’s not even the whole payment. The chart only counts principal and interest. Property taxes, homeowners insurance and HOA dues can easily add a few hundred dollars a month or more. It also assumes 20% down, which is a big hill to climb on its own. On a $569,000 home, that’s almost $114,000.

There are a couple of things in buyers’ favor. A median listing isn’t a starter home, and most first-time buyers shop below it. And the 30% rule is a budgeting guideline, not what lenders actually use. Lenders look at your total debt compared with your income, and they’ll often approve more than you should comfortably spend.

As someone saving for a house myself, here’s how I’d use this. Figure out what the homes you actually want cost, not the statewide median. Get the full payment, including taxes and insurance. Then compare it with your take-home pay, not just your gross income. Look at the levers you can pull: a smaller house, a different neighborhood or county, a bigger down payment or first-time buyer assistance programs, which Colorado and many other states offer.

The numbers are tough right now. Knowing your real number is still better than guessing.

Sources: The Ways to Wealth, Realtor(dot)com, Freddie Mac, Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (FRED)

text:
The Condon Committee declared Snippy's 1967 death a mundane infection. Veterinarian Dr. Wallace Leary later found two bullet holes in the skeleton. The investigation had already closed before the physical evidence was fully recovered.

That sequencing is the finding worth examining.

Our research traced the documented record of the Lady case — the three-year-old Appaloosa near Alamosa, Colorado, found dead on September 9, 1967, and misnamed 'Snippy' by press — through primary sources including the original AP story, the Condon Report, Denver Public Library archives, and Colorado Life Magazine.

What field records show is this: the carcass was discovered approximately a quarter-mile from the Harry King Ranch. The head and neck were completely stripped of flesh and skin, with cuts the AP described as entirely smooth, no jagged edges. No blood at the scene. No hoofprints near the body, though Lady's own tracks reportedly ended 100 feet away. Fifteen circular exhaust-like marks covered a 100-by-50-yard area nearby. A three-foot bush was found flattened. A strong medicinal odor was reported. Internal organs — brain, heart, lungs, thyroid, abdominal organs — were documented as missing.

Alamosa County Sheriff Ben Phillips initially attributed death to a lightning strike without visiting the site.

The University of Colorado Boulder, operating under the Air Force's Condon Committee, then dispatched pathologist Dr. Robert Adams and investigator Wadsworth Ayer. Their conclusion, recorded in the official Condon Report: 'There was no evidence to support the assertion that the horse's death was associated in any way with abnormal causes.' Infection was cited. Scavenger access through a cut was offered as explanation for tissue removal.

The investigation closed on that finding.

Documented evidence then traces a forensic gap: Dr. Wallace Leary, examining the skeleton post-investigation, discovered two bullet holes — reported in Colorado Life Magazine. That detail does not appear in the Condon Report because the skeleton had not been fully examined before the committee concluded its work. Separately, two Alamosa State College students later claimed they had shot the horse weeks after the initial discovery.

The cross-domain connection our research surfaced is this: the Condon Committee's 'mundane infection' conclusion was not merely wrong or right — it functionally ended the physical evidence recovery phase before the skeleton had been fully examined. The investigative framework determined the scope of evidence collected, not the other way around. That is a forensic sequencing failure, and it is documented, not speculated.

The strange part is this: the bullet holes are the most conventionally verifiable physical finding in the entire case. Two entry wounds in a skeleton are not ambiguous. They were not found because the investigation was not looking by the time the skeleton was fully examined.

The high-strangeness elements — the circular exhaust marks, the missing organs, the absent blood, the smooth precision cuts — remain genuinely unresolved. SOMETHING in that sequence of findings does not reconcile cleanly with any single cause, mundane or otherwise. But the forensic record as it stands was shaped by a process that concluded before the evidence was complete.

If you have documentation, local accounts, or corroborating field observations from Alamosa County or the broader San Luis Valley, share what you know.

410 Stainless Steel QDT - 21.17" - Round Bar - 134.5" - Finkl Steel Sorel

Grade 410 is a general-purpose, martensitic stainless steel containing 11.5–13.5% chromium. A 21-inch forged round bar in this alloy delivers high strength, hardness, and wear resistance, making it ideal for heavy-duty industrial shafts, large valves, and high-stress structural machinery components.

Key Characteristics:
• Martensitic Alloy: Magnetic in both annealed and hardened conditions, featuring a nominal composition of 11.5%–13.5% chromium and up to 0.15% carbon.
• High Hardness & Strength: Heat-treatable via quenching and tempering to achieve high tensile and yield strengths, with typical hardness reaching 35–39 HRC or higher depending on thermal processing.
• Forged Integrity: A 21-inch diameter forged bar provides a refined grain structure and deep internal soundness compared to cast or rolled equivalents, optimizing load-bearing capacity under severe mechanical stress.
• Corrosion & Wear Resistance: Offers good resistance to fresh water, air, mild chemicals, and steam, though lower than austenitic grades like 304 or 316. Maximum corrosion resistance is achieved only after hardening and surface polishing.
• Fabrication Considerations: Machinable in the annealed state; welding requires pre-heating (150–260°C) and immediate post-weld annealing to prevent cracking due to its martensitic structure.

Primary Applications:
• Heavy Machinery & Shafts: Large-diameter pump shafts, compressor shafts, and heavy rotor components.
• Power Generation: Steam and gas turbine blades, valve stems, and fasteners operating at moderate temperatures.
• Oil, Gas & Petrochemical: Fractionation tower internals, high-pressure valve bodies, and well-head equipment components.
• Tooling & Wear Parts: High-strength studs, bolts, wear plates, and specialized cutting or impact tools.

text:
My sister hasn't spoken to me in eight months because I got pregnant by her husband, and somehow, I'm the only person in this family being treated like a monster.

I'm 27, my sister Vanessa is 32, and we grew up in Charlotte, North Carolina. She's always been the family favorite. Perfect grades, perfect wedding, perfect house, perfect husband.

Her husband, Ryan, is 35. They've been married for six years.

And before you decide I'm some jealous little sister who spent years plotting to steal her husband, let me explain how this actually happened.

Vanessa and I were never as close as people thought. She loved being the successful older sister who gave me advice, corrected my decisions, and reminded everyone that she was the responsible one.

Whenever I struggled financially, she'd offer help, then bring it up at family dinners like a reminder that I hadn't figured my life out yet.

When I lost my apartment two years ago, she and Ryan let me stay in their guest room.

I was grateful. I paid for groceries, helped clean the house, and watched their daughter whenever they needed me.

But Vanessa started acting like I was a permanent inconvenience.

She'd complain if I used too much hot water. She'd criticize my clothes. She once told me Ryan was getting tired of having another adult in the house.

So I asked Ryan whether that was true.

He said no.

He told me I was welcome to stay until I got back on my feet.

That conversation became the beginning of something I should have stopped immediately.

Ryan started confiding in me about his marriage. He said Vanessa was always criticizing him, that they barely spent time together, and that he felt like an employee in his own home.

I listened.

Then I started telling him things about myself that I probably shouldn't have shared with my sister's husband.

One night, Vanessa went away for a work conference. Ryan and I stayed up watching movies after his daughter went to bed.

He told me he sometimes wondered what his life would have been like if he'd met someone who understood him better.

I should have changed the subject.

Instead, I asked him whether he was happy with Vanessa.

He said he didn't know anymore.

Then he kissed me.

I kissed him back.

We slept together that night.

The next morning, I told him it could never happen again.

He agreed.

Three days later, we did it again.

And again.

For two months, I was sleeping with my sister's husband while living under her roof.

But here's what everyone conveniently ignores: Ryan was a grown man with a wife and child. He made his own decisions.

Why am I being treated like I somehow hypnotized him?

Then I missed my period.

I took three pregnancy tests.

All positive.

And when I told Ryan, he sat down on the edge of the bed and started crying.

His first question wasn't whether I was okay.

It was, "How are we going to tell Vanessa?"

I looked at him and said, "WE aren't telling her anything. YOU are."

Apparently, I was already the only person in this situation who understood that other people needed to take responsibility for their own choices.

Or at least, that's what I told myself.

text:
The reforms aim to simplify tax administration, reduce duplication and make the system more predictable. Their success will depend on how fairly they are implemented and whether the benefits outweigh the compliance burden on individuals and businesses.

6. ELECTRICITY-SECTOR REFORM

The Electricity Act 2023 opened the way for states to establish and regulate their own electricity markets rather than relying exclusively on the previous centralised structure.
By May 2026, the Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission reported that 15 states had transitioned to regulating their state electricity markets, including Edo State.  (NERC)

This is a significant legal and regulatory change that may encourage local investment and alternative power arrangements. It should not, however, be confused with a nationwide resolution of Nigeria's persistent electricity-supply problems.

7. ROAD AND TRANSPORT INFRASTRUCTURE

The administration has pursued large highway projects and other federal road interventions, including the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway and Sokoto–Badagry Superhighway.
In an October 2026 update, the Federal Ministry of Works reported completion of the first 47-kilometre section of the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway, with further sections under construction. The ministry also listed other completed or substantially advanced road and bridge projects.  (Ministry of Information)
These investments could improve transport links and facilitate the movement of goods and people. Because several flagship schemes remain under construction, their full economic impact is yet to be established.

8. HOUSING FINANCE

The administration introduced the Ministry of Finance Incorporated Real Estate Investment Fund to expand access to long-term mortgages.
By August 2026, the Presidency reported that the fund had disbursed ₦140 billion through 21 financial institutions, supporting 2,018 mortgages across 27 states. The programme offers qualifying borrowers fixed-rate financing over periods of up to 20 years. (The State House, Abuja)
This is a measurable initiative in housing finance, although the number of mortgages delivered remains small relative to Nigeria's overall housing needs.

9. INTERNATIONAL FINANCIAL STANDING

Nigeria's external financial position also showed several positive developments. The IMF reported that the country regained access to international financial markets, while Nigeria was removed from the Financial Action Task Force's increased-monitoring list in October 2025 and the European Union's corresponding list in January 2026. S&P also revised Nigeria's outlook from stable to positive in November 2025. (IMF eLibrary)
These developments can support international financial confidence, but they do not automatically translate into more jobs or higher living standards.

WHAT REMAINS A MAJOR CHALLENGE?

Any honest assessment must also consider the difficulties Nigerians continue to face.
The IMF estimated that poverty had reached 63% under Nigeria's national poverty measure and that 27 million people faced food insecurity in autumn 2025. It also identified insecurity as a continuing burden on investment, agriculture and oil production. 
High living costs, household financial pressure, electricity supply, unemployment and insecurity remain important measures against which the administration's results should be judged.

MY OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE TINUBU ADMINISTRATION’S RECORD SO FAR

The Tinubu administration has introduced major changes in Nigeria’s economy, foreign exchange policy, education funding, minimum wage, taxation, electricity regulation, infrastructure and housing finance. These are important developments and deserve to be examined on the basis of facts, not political loyalty or personal prejudice.

Some of these changes have produced measurable results, while others are still works in progress. At the same time, many Nigerians continue to struggle with the cost of living, food prices, poverty and insecurity.

text:
انتهى الاجتماع الرباعي في طهران بين تركيا وباكستان وإيران والسعودية.

لمن يتساءل عمّا حدث، فمن الواضح لي أن السعوديين ذهبوا إلى طهران حاملين عرضاً يتضمن تنازلات كبيرة للإيرانيين، مقابل التوسط لدى أنصار الله لوقف هجماتهم على السعودية، والحصول على ضمانات بإبقائها خارج نطاق الرد الإيراني في حال أقدمت الولايات المتحدة على قصف منشآت الطاقة الإيرانية.

ولكن إيران لن تقدم شيئاً ملموساً للسعودية إلا إذا تضمن العرض السعودي تنازلات استراتيجية حقيقية، تبدأ بسحب القواعد العسكرية الأمريكية من منطقة الخليج، وتنتهي ببناء تحالف أمني إقليمي تعترف فيه دول الخليج بسيادة إيران الكاملة على مضيق هرمز، وبحقها في نقض أي وجود عسكري أجنبي في الخليج.

باعتقادي، هذا الاجتماع عنوان لمرحلة جديدة في المنطقة، تتلخص باعتراف خليجي واضح بأن إيران أصبحت سيدتهم الجديدة، وأن عليهم التفاهم معها لضمان أمنهم واستمرار دولهم.

ولكن هنا تكمن المعضلة السعودية. فالسعوديون مطالبون بالتعقل والتفاهم مع إيران بما يضمن مصالحهم، بعيداً عن الأمريكيين، بينما هم في الحقيقة لا يمتلكون الاستقلال السياسي والعسكري الذي يسمح لهم باتخاذ مثل هذا القرار بحرية.

ولفهم هذه المعضلة، يكفي العودة إلى تاريخ الهند تحت الاستعمار البريطاني. فقد كانت هناك مئات الإمارات والممالك التي يحكمها الراجات والمهراجات والنواب، مثل حيدر آباد وكشمير. وكانت لهذه الممالك قصورها وحكامها وجيوشها وإداراتها الخاصة، وتبدو وكأنها دول مستقلة، بينما كانت بريطانيا تتحكم في علاقاتها الخارجية وتفرض عليها سيادتها العليا.

والأمر نفسه حدث في مصر بعد الاحتلال البريطاني عام 1882. فقد بقي الخديوي على عرشه، واستمرت الحكومة المصرية في ممارسة مهامها، ولكن القرار الحقيقي في القضايا الكبرى كان بيد البريطانيين.

وهكذا هي طبيعة العلاقة بين دول الخليج والولايات المتحدة. فالاستقلال الشكلي ووجود الحكومات والجيوش والأعلام لا يعني بالضرورة امتلاك السيادة الحقيقية، خصوصاً عندما تكون الدولة عاجزة عن اتخاذ قراراتها الأمنية والعسكرية الكبرى بمعزل عن إرادة القوة الأجنبية التي تعتمد عليها لحمايتها.

وهنا مأزق السعودية تحديداً. فهي تريد التفاهم مع إيران لإنقاذ نفسها من حرب قد تدمر منشآتها النفطية واقتصادها، ولكن هذا التفاهم سيصطدم بالضرورة بالمصالح الأمريكية، لأن ما تريده إيران يتعارض جذرياً مع استمرار الهيمنة العسكرية الأمريكية على الخليج.

السعودية عالقة بين نارين: نار إيرانية قد تحرق منشآتها النفطية إذا استمرت في الارتهان للأمريكيين، ونار أمريكية قد تواجهها إذا قررت الخروج عن إرادة واشنطن والتفاهم مع طهران.

والمشكلة أن السعودية أمضت عقوداً تبني أمنها على الحماية الأمريكية، لتجد نفسها اليوم أمام تحول هذه الحماية إلى السبب الذي يعرض وجودها للخطر.

text:
Rev War Tales
An Impressive Navy
27–28 October 1776, River Thames, London. Press gangs from Deptford and Woolwich swept the river, taking more than a thousand seamen from civilian vessels. The men were forced into the Royal Navy. On October 25, the king issued a proclamation offering bounties for voluntary enlistment and pardons for deserters who returned. Two days later, before the offer could take full effect, the press began. About twenty boats, manned and officered, came up the river on the flood tide. They boarded ships and took every man except the master and mate. One lieutenant was shot while boarding. Eight seamen drowned trying to swim ashore. That night and the next day, the gangs worked from Gravesend to Rotherhithe. West India ships lost crews who had already been paid advance wages. The Lord Mayor ordered the arrest of press officers operating within his jurisdiction. The navy needed men for the American war. The press on the Thames supplied them by force.

🚨 A 3-YEAR-OLD BOY, A FOOTBALL MATCH, AND THE POLICE. THIS STORY IS CRAZY. 😳⚽

Meet Nevada Pierre, a three-year-old boy from Florida whose football skills have taken social media by storm.

But what happened during his youth football match on October 24 has sparked a massive debate about how we treat young talents.

Nevada was playing in an i9 Sports youth soccer league against children older than him. Videos show the little boy dribbling past opponents and scoring goals with remarkable confidence for his age.

But instead of the match being remembered for his talent, it ended in controversy.

According to his mother, Martasia Griffin, adults began complaining about Nevada's dominance on the pitch. She alleged that the league was trying to stop her son from playing because he was too good and kept the ball for too long.

Then came the moment that shocked the internet: POLICE ARRIVED AT THE FOOTBALL FIELD.

His father was furious, questioning why authorities had been called over a three-year-old playing football.

The league director offered a different explanation. He told officers that Nevada was exceptionally talented but alleged that the boy had pushed other players. He also claimed that disagreements with Nevada's parents over substitutions and the rules had contributed to the confrontation.

His mother disputed that account, insisting that her son was being excluded because of his ability.

The Winter Park Police Department later clarified that officers had responded to a reported dispute between league officials and the parents. No arrests were made, nobody was formally trespassed, and officers did not force the family to leave.

The league, i9 Sports, has since contacted the family and begun reviewing the incident.

But the most heartbreaking part is what Nevada's mother says happened afterward: the experience left him upset and reluctant to return to that particular field, even though he still wants to play football.

Think about that for a moment. He's only THREE YEARS OLD.

At that age, a child should be learning, enjoying the game, making friends and falling in love with football.

If he is genuinely ahead of his peers, shouldn't the adults be looking for a suitable environment where he can develop while ensuring the other children also get their chance to play?

Of course, talent doesn't excuse pushing or poor behaviour. Every child deserves safety, fairness and guidance. But disagreements between adults should never become a burden that a young child has to carry.

What do you think? 👇⚽

text:
TRIPTYCH: FEAR, VANITY, AND MONEY

Donald Trump's presidency increasingly resembles a triptych: three paintings united by a single disturbing theme.The first depicts fear,the second an obsession with personal greatness, and the third the extraordinary financial opportunities created by political power. Together,they reveal a struggle that reaches far beyond one man's ambitions.

The first panel is fear.Trump knows that leaving the White House means losing some of the extraordinary protections associated with presidential office. His long history of lawsuits, investigations, and legal controversies makes the prospect of returning to private life particularly uncomfortable. Presidential immunity has limits, and even the power of pardon cannot erase offenses prosecuted under state law.

His repeated suggestions about serving a third term are therefore difficult to dismiss as harmless jokes. The Constitution permits only two elected presidential terms. Yet Trump continues testing political boundaries, while his movement increasingly revolves around personal loyalty rather than traditional Republican principles. Even the possibility of a family successor raises questions about whether he sees the presidency as public service or a dynasty to be inherited.

The second panel is vanity. Trump seems incapable of receiving enough praise. Awards, portraits, ceremonial honors, and declarations of historic greatness have become essential features of his political identity. His fixation on the Nobel Peace Prize is particularly revealing. The president of the world's most powerful country publicly complains about recognition from an independent Norwegian committee, as though international diplomacy were a competition for personal trophies.

FIFA's peace award only added to the spectacle. Perhaps Putin should establish a special Z-Peace Prize for his American counterpart. The ceremony could feature golden statues, enormous portraits, and an orchestra performing the national anthem of Trump's ego. Emperor Nero would probably appreciate the performance.

But behind the comedy lies a serious problem. Democratic institutions are supposed to serve citizens, not glorify their temporary leaders. When loyalty to a president becomes more important than loyalty to the Constitution, the distinction between a republic and a personal regime begins to disappear.

The third panel is money. Trump's business empire has experienced six corporate bankruptcies and numerous legal disputes. Yet presidential authority offers opportunities unavailable to ordinary businessmen. A single announcement about tariffs, sanctions, or oil can move financial markets dramatically. Anyone exploiting privileged knowledge of such decisions could potentially earn enormous profits.

His legal battles with media corporations raise additional questions. ABC and Paramount reached substantial settlements in disputes with Trump. Such agreements are not automatically improper, but when a sitting president sues companies whose interests may be affected by government decisions, the potential conflicts deserve scrutiny.

The same applies to wealthy political donors, government contracts, and compensation claims involving public funds. Political influence must never become a private financial instrument. Taxpayers' money belongs to citizens, not to presidents, their relatives, or their supporters.

Now consider all three paintings together.Fear creates the incentive to preserve power.Vanity demands unconditional admiration. Money makes political authority extraordinarily valuable.Combined, these forces can threaten the independence of courts, journalism, government institutions, and ultimately democracy itself.

For Ukraine,this American struggle is not an abstract political drama.We are fighting for survival against Russian aggression.Decisions made in Washington determine whether our soldiers receive weapons,whether sanctions constrain Moscow,and whether the democratic world remains united.

Washington State 

PAID FAMILY MEDICAL LEAVE PAYROLL TAX INCREASE  

Oct. 27, 2026

Washington paid leave tax hits 1.2% cap for 2027, lawmakers eyeing lift

Oct. 27, 2026

Washington workers will see a higher deduction on their paychecks come January 1, 2027 as the state collects more taxpayer money for its paid leave program.

The Washington State Employment Security Department recently announced that the total Paid Family and Medical Leave premium rate will increase to 1.2% of gross wages, up from 1.13% in 2026.

Paid Leave is funded by premiums collected from employees and employers in Washington State. By law, the Employment Security Department recalculates the premium rate annually in October based on program usage and premiums collected the previous year.

“More than 221,000 individuals have claimed Paid Leave benefits in the first 9 months of 2026, totaling more than $1.8 billion," the department's release said.

The rate has been steadily increasing since its inception.

“The 1.2% rate is triple the program’s starting rate of 0.40% in 2019 and a 6.2% increase from last year," wrote Washington Policy Center’s Elizabeth New who heads up WPC’s Center for Worker Rights and Health Care Policy.

"This new rate of 1.2% is also PFML’s current statutory cap — a cap that some lawmakers say they want to bust,” she added. 

Washington's average annual covered wage is $99,810, using the 2025 wage figure reported by the Employment Security Department.

A worker making that wage, along with their employer would have paid more than $1,100 dollars into PFML last year.

Employees pay 70.7% of the total premium. Employers pay the remaining 29.3%.

Groups such as Washington Work and Family Coalition advocate for the program.

"At some point, almost everyone needs to take time away from work, whether to care for a new child, help a family member who is sick, or recover from their own illness," the group said on its website.

"Care is the foundation of our economy — we wouldn’t have a workforce with no one to care for employees — and it’s a key component of leading a fulfilling life.

In her recent article, New noted that PFML is not the safety net many people were sold.

“Lower-wage workers use the program less, while middle- and higher-wage workers account for a larger share of claims," she wrote.

"In fiscal year 2026, workers making $61 or more an hour accounted for 19% of PFML claims, compared with 8% for workers in the lowest wage group — more than twice the share.”

In a Monday interview with The Center Square, New explained that lower income workers often can’t afford to take a cut in pay offered by PFML, which for lower income workers, pays 90% of a weekly wage, maxing out at $1,647 per week. 

“I think people really need to realize that they could be making more money if it weren't for programs like this. And the money that they earn could be used on needs that they have,” said New.

“So, for the past few years in the legislature, they've been saying, this program's so popular, we might need to increase the cap," New added.

"So, there's talk about raising the cap to 2%. So, this is concerning. We're constantly taking money from some workers who need it and giving it to others who don't.”

SB 5292 was introduced in the 2025 session and originally sought to require the Employment Security Department Commissioner to set the paid family and medical leave program premium rate based on the Office of Actuarial Services annual report.

As passed, the bill did not lift the cap entirely, but New said she expects some version of that part of the legislation to resurface.

Efforts to change PFML

“Legislators should be discussing repeal of this misguided program or at least benefit-side changes to it, instead. Sen. Curtis King, R-Yakima, has suggested several of them, including my favorites — ending repeat use of PFML and limiting the duration of benefits,” wrote New.

🌎 The Donroe Doctrine, in real time

Haiti's gang problem just got a franchise solution.

President Bukele offered to fix Haiti, with conditions: "We can fix it. But we'll need a UNSC resolution, the consent of the host country, and all the mission expenses to be covered."

Now check the list:
✅ UN Security Council resolution: done, co-written by the United States in September 2025.
✅ Host country consent: Haiti's sole remaining leader is a prime minister Washington backed when his council's mandate ran out.
✅ Expenses covered: the State Department lined up about $100 million in other people's money.

Bukele bid two years ago, and the US found the cash. Coincidence? Maybe. But it's the kind of coincidence that comes with a C-130 and warships parked off Port-au-Prince.

Translation: America draws the plans, chairs the meetings, flies the planes, and passes the hat. Somebody else's soldiers kick in the doors.

It's the hemisphere's first franchise model of foreign policy. Washington owns the brand; local operators supply the muscle.

The old Monroe Doctrine told Europe to keep out of the neighborhood. The new one organizes the neighborhood watch, and the neighbors walk the beat.

Speaking of neighbors: the Dominican Republic already had about 11,000 troops on its Haitian border. On Sunday, President Luis Abinader sent two more battalions, plus heavy equipment and artillery, and says he's in "permanent session" with Bukele and the Gang Suppression Force.

Venezuela got the hard version. Haiti is getting the outsourced version, run by the president who emptied El Salvador's streets of MS-13 and now warns Haiti's gangs, in Creole: "We already finished the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish you too."

The bigger picture: a world-realigning doctrine that started with an unremarkable State Department terrorist designation in May 2025 now has a coalition, a task force, a target list, a UN force, a paymaster, and, as of this week, boots on the ground that aren't American.

No new wars.

🇻🇪|A profound shift is underway in Venezuela, where the illusion of democratic transition has collided with the reality of a foreign-backed carve-up of the nation's wealth. The protests erupting across the country are not merely a demand for elections; they are a rejection of a new form of colonial administration that has turned the state into a subsidiary of the U.S. Treasury. The "democracy" being offered by Washington is a carefully managed enterprise designed to legitimize the theft of the world's largest oil reserves.

💥 The Architecture of a Managed State

The foundation of this new arrangement was laid on January 3, 2026, when U.S. forces captured President Nicolás Maduro and transferred him to New York. In his place, the U.S. installed former Vice President Delcy Rodríguez as interim leader, making it clear her hold on power depended on staying in Trump's good graces. This was not a transition to democracy; it was a transfer of operational control.

The financial mechanism of this control was established almost immediately. Washington brokered the greater part of Venezuela’s oil exports, channeling the proceeds into an account controlled by the U.S. Treasury, which now decides how and when the revenue is spent. The Venezuelan state, in effect, lost its fiscal sovereignty.

🎯 The Oil Deal: 65 Billion Barrels and a 100-Year Concession

The material prize was formalized on August 28, 2026, when President Trump announced an agreement purportedly giving Washington control of 65 billion barrels of Venezuela's proven oil reserves, calling it "the biggest oil deal in world history". The terms were staggering: a 100-year concession, to be run by a private company under de facto U.S. government control. Trump promised the deal would come at "no cost to the U.S. taxpayer" while allowing the U.S. to "replenish its strategic stockpiles". The Venezuelan government confirmed the arrangement, offering conflicting details on its duration and terms, a clear sign of a diminished sovereignty and informal U.S. dominion.

📜 "You’re Not Going to Street-Protest Your Way Into a Democracy"

The U.S. response to the genuine democratic aspirations of the Venezuelan people was swift and revealing. When opposition leader María Corina Machado returned to Caracas and demanded elections be held in 2027, while criticizing the massive oil deal, Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a veiled but unmistakable warning: "You're not going to street-protest your way into a democracy".

The U.S. was not interested in a free vote that might jeopardize the oil arrangement. Instead, Washington backed a different dialogue process negotiations between the interim government and a faction of the opposition led by Dinorah Figuera, a process that excluded Machado and the apparent 2024 election winner, Edmundo González Urrutia. The message was clear: democracy is acceptable only if it is the right kind of democracy, one that does not interfere with the extraction of resources.

⚔️ The Mirror: A People Demanding What Was Taken

The protests of October 2026 are the physical manifestation of this contradiction. Thousands took to the streets in Caracas, Valencia, Maracay, and Maracaibo, demanding free elections and an end to the foreign exploitation of their oil. For the demonstrators, the connection is direct: they are demanding a government that answers to them, not to a foreign treasury.

A young student in Maracay explained her participation: "I've been through so many hardships, so many problems because of the dollar, and difficulties studying. I have high hopes for my country and for our next leader and president". The hardship is not abstract. It is the lived experience of an economy managed for external extraction, where the nation's wealth flows into an account in Washington while its people struggle.

The U.S. narrative of "promoting democracy" collapses under the weight of its own actions. It captured a president, installed a compliant successor, seized control of the national treasury, signed a century-long oil concession, and then warned the opposition that protest is not the path to democracy. The Venezuelan people are being told that their voice does not matter, that their resources belong to the empire, and that the "transition" will be managed by those who delivered their country into foreign hands.

Long live the people of Venezuela. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.
